artigo.texto: NESTA EDIÇÃO. A disputa do Redata sobre o uso do gás natural abre espaço para tecnologias capazes de reduzir suas emissões. Células a combustível, integração com biometano e captura e armazenamento de carbono estão entre as alternativas. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: A possibilidade de incluir o gás natural entre as fontes de baixa emissão que os data centers terão que contratar para receber incentivos no Brasil segue indefinida, enquanto o mercado aguarda a regulamentação da política sancionada no dia 15 de setembro. A expectativa era que o decreto fosse assinado nesta segunda (28/9). Com o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), o governo espera atrair investimentos da ordem de R$ 500 bilhões, a partir de benefícios fiscais de até R$ 7,2 bilhões entre 2026 e 2028. Para as isenções de tributos federais, as instalações precisarão comprovar a contratação de energia elétrica 100% renovável ou de baixa emissão. E é este termo que está em disputa no governo. A Fazenda, responsável pelo desenho do programa, tem pressionado para que o presidente Lula (PT) sancione o decreto regulamentador sem incluir o gás natural como fonte energética incentivada, mantendo assim a ênfase em fontes renováveis. A disputa coloca em lados opostos o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), publicamente favorável ao uso do gás natural no programa, e a Fazenda, contrária à inclusão. Na sexta-feira (25/9) à tarde, representantes do setor privado de gás natural se reuniram com interlocutores do Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) para tentar destravar as conversas, que permanecem bloqueadas na Fazenda. Entre as possibilidades discutidas estão excluir o gás, aceitá-lo integralmente ou permitir seu uso condicionado a mecanismos de compensação, como créditos de carbono, uso de biometano e tecnologias de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS). Ou, ainda, de que forma será aceita a utilização do gás, a exemplo de backup em situações de queda de energia. Fontes que participaram da reunião afirmaram à agência eixos que, sem o gás natural no decreto, o Redata cria uma espécie de reserva de mercado para as energias renováveis, o que pode trazer desafios para projetos de data centers no Sul e Sudeste do país. Leia na matéria de Gustavo Gaudarde e Gabriel Chiappini Alta demanda, diferentes possibilidades A atração de infraestrutura digital para o Brasil significa uma alavanca da demanda energética e abriu uma frente de disputa sobre quem irá abastecer os centros de dados. O MME contabiliza 38 GW em pedidos de conexão de data centers à rede — o equivalente a quase um terço da capacidade instalada do país. No mundo todo, o consumo de energia por servidores de inteligência artificial deve dobrar até 2030. Estimativas da Kearney apontam que em 2025, os servidores de IA representaram entre 23% e 27% da eletricidade consumida pelos centros de dados. Enquanto o IDTechEx projeta que a capacidade instalada de energia em data centers em todo o mundo ultrapassará 300 GW até 2036, cerca do triplo do valor atual, com a aceleração do crescimento da IA exigindo cada vez mais mais eletricidade. E mesmo com as big techs fechando contratos de longo prazo com parques eólicos e solares, investindo em startups de baterias e apostando nos pequenos reatores nucleares, o gás natural também segue no radar como opção de energia firme — e é aí que diferentes possibilidades começam a se desenhar. Como o gás pode ser baixo carbono A grande crítica de quem é contra o gás natural como “fonte de baixa emissão” no Redata vem do fato de o combustível ser de origem fóssil e liberar emissões de gases de efeito estufa que contribuem com as mudanças climáticas. Mas há caminhos para reduzir esse impacto climático e eles vão desde os mais acessíveis, como substituição de geradores a diesel e a integração com o biometano, até aqueles que ainda precisam ganhar escala e viabilidade econômica, como as células a combustível e o CCS. Ainda de acordo com a recente análise do IDTechEx, o uso de células a combustível abastecidas por gás natural liberam menos CO2 do que os processos de combustão tradicionais e podem, posteriormente, passar a funcionar com 100% de hidrogênio renovável, quando este ganhar escala. Um exemplo dessa aplicação vem da American Electric Power (AEP) que, em janeiro de 2026, fechou um acordo de US$ 2,65 bilhões para implantar até 1 GW de células a combustível de óxido sólido da Bloom Energy em data centers de AI. A captura de carbono é outra solução, com potencial para reduzir as emissões de CO2 de usinas termelétricas convencionais a combustíveis fósseis em mais de 95%, aponta o IDTechEx. Em outubro de 2025, o Google anunciou seu primeiro projeto de captura e armazenamento de carbono, em parceria com a Broadwing Energy, em Decatur, Illinois. A intenção é capturar e armazenar permanentemente aproximadamente 90% de suas emissões de CO2 de geradores a gás. Projetos como esses, no entanto, precisam de precificação do carbono e financiamento para serem competitivos. Além de dependerem de infraestrutura de transporte e armazenamento de CO2, o que pode fazer com que novos projetos de CCS em larga escala levem mais de cinco anos para serem desenvolvidos Segundo a consultoria, na União Europeia e América do Norte, onde há precificação de carbono e políticas de financiamento, esses projetos tendem a se tornar mais atrativos primeiro. Cobrimos por aqui Curtas Onda de calor. O Inmet alerta para uma onda de calor que atinge os estados de Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Minas Gerais, Goiás, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná e Santa Catarina. As temperaturas devem ficar 5°C acima da média nessas localidades nesta segunda-feira (28). (Agência Brasil) Acima de 40ºC. Cidades do interior do Centro-Oeste, Sudeste e Sul do Brasil podem registrar temperaturas superiores a 40°C neste início de semana, em decorrência da onda de calor que atinge boa parte do país desde sábado. artigo.texto: Listen to this article in summarized format The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has entered its definitive phase in January 2026. CBAM, essentially, puts a carbon cost on imports into the European Union. It requires EU importers to pay for emissions embedded in select carbon-intensive goods (based on carbon emissions during production) they import. The CBAM obligation is linked to the EU carbon price, while any carbon price already effectively paid on those emissions in the country of production can be deducted. Also Read | On Edge: The Great Nicobar project faces a great engineering question The EU importer pays the border carbon charge, but the economic burden can ultimately be passed back to the Indian exporter through lower margins, higher prices, or reduced competitiveness. The United Kingdom is also preparing to introduce its own mechanism in January 2027. For India, this policy creates a new trade calculation. A factory may meet every conventional requirement for exporting a product, but its emissions could still determine how much more that product costs when it reaches a foreign market. New Delhi is, therefore, trying a new route of its own: putting a price on emissions at home and building a domestic carbon market. Also Read | Beating the Heat: India’s data centre dream and the 50°C reality in its path The question is whether India can make carbon pricing work as an industrial policy—so that money associated with carbon emissions is invested in cleaner electricity, steel, technology and infrastructure inside the country instead of being collected at the borders of its trading partners. The border tax mismatch The stakes are high for India. Carbon-intensive industries such as steel, aluminium, cement and fertiliser are an important part of the country’s export economy. India’s merchandise exports touched $441.78 billion in FY26, with metals remaining a major export category. The exposure to the EU’s CBAM, moreover, is concentrated heavily in metals. The EU’s CBAM currently covers six sectors: iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. According to NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly report released this month, annual metals exports stood at about $34.8 billion in 2025, with iron, steel and aluminium accounting for roughly 78% of that trade. Steel, in particular, is seeing strong export growth. India exported 6.94 lakh tonnes of finished steel worth ₹5,541.2 crore in August 2026, up 31.3% in volume and 41.5% in value from August 2025. During April-August, finished-steel exports reached 29.86 lakh tonnes worth ₹23,646.6 crore, rising 34.1% in volume and 32% in value. The challenge is compounded by the carbon intensity of India's metals production. Indian metals have notably higher carbon intensity than the global average, mostly because primary steel production relies heavily on coal-based Blast Furnace–Basic Oxygen Furnace routes and coal-fired Direct Reduced Iron processes, rather than cleaner gas-based or Electric Arc Furnace routes, according to NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly (April–June [Q1] FY27). The scale of India's exposure to European markets adds another layer. NITI Aayog estimates that the EU accounts for approximately 22% of India's combined steel and aluminium exports. In the iron and steel sector, India’s trade exposure to the EU stands at 39.3%, meaning nearly two-fifths of its steel exports are destined for the European market. A June 2026 working paper by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER), titled Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM): Impact on India’s Steel Exports to the EU and Carbon Tax Incidence, estimates that India’s steel exports to the EU could fall by 24% under the CBAM, based on simulations using the ICRIER Samriddhi Model, a GTAP-E-based general-equilibrium model. For India, therefore, the task at hand would be to ensure that the growth of its manufacturing exports is not undermined by a new cost imposed on the carbon content of those goods. The country has stepped up preparations for the EU's CBAM, including the creation of a Committee on Export Preparedness for EU CBAM. Indian verifiers—independent, accredited third-party verifying bodies empanelled under the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)—have begun aligning plant auditing protocols with the EU's carbon registry, ahead of the first annual CBAM declarations due by September 2027 for emissions embedded in 2026 exports. At the same time, Britain has agreed to recognise India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), meaning qualifying carbon payments made in India can be taken into account under the UK's CBAM. The recognition reduces the risk of exporters paying twice, but it does not eliminate the problem: the amount of relief depends on the carbon price actually paid in India. That distinction gets to the heart of India's challenge. Ajay Srivastava, founder of Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), warned that India's carbon price is likely to remain much lower than the price faced by exporters in Europe. “The EU carbon price is currently about €75 per tonne of CO₂, compared with roughly $10 in China (which operates a similar domestic compliance Emissions Trading Scheme), and India’s emissions-trading system will take time to become fully operational,” Srivastava said. Even if India's system is recognised overseas, he added that it “will not remove the border charge...Even after implementation, a large price gap is likely to remain, leaving Indian exporters liable for substantial CBAM payments in the EU and UK.” This creates the central tension for India: a domestic carbon price can keep some carbon-related revenue inside the country, but only rapid decarbonisation can ultimately reduce the carbon bill itself. artigo.texto: I recently attended the ribbon-cutting for a factory expansion. For the event, the workers were gathered outside — hundreds of them. For a company west of the Blue Ridge, where the population is overwhelmingly white (this particular county is 92% white), I was struck by the diversity that I saw gathered in the parking lot and an adjacent hillside — lots of Black and Latino workers. Later, while touring the inside of the plant, I saw several Latino women who were installing some sort of electrical gear on the factory’s product. I asked the company for demographics and was told that 53.3% of the workers were non-white, the biggest group of those being Latino — 41.3%. In short, this seemed the kind of workforce that Democrats usually claim to represent. There’s just one catch, though: These workers at the Munters plant in Botetourt County make heating, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment for data centers. Both parties have been racing to express their concern about data centers, although Democrats have gotten there first and tend to be the most vocal. Beth Macy, the Democratic candidate in the 6th District, has been among the first to call for a moratorium on data center construction. There may well be good reasons for this: Data centers are driving up demand for energy and drinking lots of water. However, for better or for worse, they are also driving the economy. ING Global Market Research, a Dutch financial multinational, issued a report this summer that concluded that AI now represents one-third of the U.S. economic growth in 2026. Likewise, an economic forecast issued recently by the University of Virginia’s Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service also highlighted AI’s role in the economy. “The national economy enters the middle of 2026 with growth and slightly stronger momentum than earlier in the year,” the report said. “The stronger outlook reflects increased artificial intelligence-related investment, particularly in information technology, software, and data centers.” “Economic growth” is often a vague phrase and one that doesn’t always translate into benefiting everyone. The beneficiaries of data center growth are popularly (and not incorrectly) assumed to be tech billionaires. However, there are also lots of working-class tradespeople who are seeing unprecedented growth in their fields due to data centers. In political terms, this is called “cross-pressure,” where political coalitions find themselves pulled in opposite directions. We’ve seen this before: When Virginia was roiled by proposed natural gas pipelines (such as the Mountain Valley Pipeline), environmental groups — a key part of the Democratic coalition — opposed the pipelines. However, many labor unions — another key part of the Democratic coalition — backed them. As politicians, especially Democrats, rush to slow down data center growth, I have to wonder whether they will encounter some of the same cross-pressures — and what the economic implications of slowing down data centers will be. More broadly, I wonder how much of the controversy over data centers is, or will be, a class conflict where Democrats find themselves aligned against the blue-collar workers who are benefiting directly from the data center boom. We may not be at that point yet, and we may never get there. However, it’s demonstrably true that the data center boom is driving employment — and wages — in certain fields and in certain places. That employment is not necessarily with data centers themselves (which average about 50 workers per site, according to a state study) but in the data center supply chain, where the jobs show up in the hundreds and hundreds, such as Munters. Tom Perriello, the Democratic candidate in the 5th District, recently criticized Republican incumbent John McGuire for voting for a particular tax deduction that tech companies have been making use of. Perriello’s campaign cited a Politico story that reported: “ The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure. And that’s eligible for generous tax breaks on investments Republicans included in their 2025 tax cuts.” The Democratic criticism of that vote is that tech companies didn’t need this tax break, that they’d be making these investments anyway, so all the Republicans did was vote for a tax break that has reduced revenue and driven up the deficit. That seems a worthy debate to have, but let’s go back to the first sentence: “The tech world is pouring oceans of money into chips, data centers, power supplies and other components of the artificial intelligence infrastructure …” That’s where the job growth is happening. Data centers themselves generally don’t create a lot of jobs — a 2024 study by the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission put the average employment at about 50 jobs for each 250,000-square-foot facility. By contrast, employment at Munters in Botetourt has tripled over the past four years and now stands at 827. Business is so strong that the company just added a new production building. This is part of a larger ripple effect of job growth emanating from data centers. A study by the consulting firm PwC found that data supply chain jobs in the country add up to about 4.5 million, about 4.5 times as many as employed in data centers themselves. That’s almost the same size as the nation’s hospital workforce and more than the number of truck drivers in the country, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the American Trucking Association. In short, that seems like a lot of people. A report this year by the Randstad human resources company found that an “analysis of over 50 million job postings found that, since late 2022 — marking the mainstream introduction of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) — vacancies for HVAC engineers — critical for installing and maintaining data center cooling systems — have increased by 67%. artigo.texto: BYD's Next-Gen Seagull and Seal 07 Take Shape as Solid-State Battery Timeline Slips to 2030 Published on 09/28/2026 at 18:01 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is pressing ahead on two fronts at once: refreshing the volume models that carry its home-market sales, and laying out a long-range battery roadmap that won't bear fruit for years. The company unveiled design sketches and specifications for the second-generation Seagull on 22 September, while confirming that commercial mass production of solid-state batteries is targeted for around 2030. A bigger, punchier entry-level hatchback Sketch images of the redesigned Seagull — sold in export markets as the Atto 1 and known in Chinese as Da Haiou, or "Great Seagull" — were released by the head of sales for BYD's Ocean series. The compact EV moves to a rear-wheel-drive platform with a multi-link rear suspension and seating for five, according to media reports. Output from the electric motor climbs to 95 kW (127 PS), a substantial step up from the 55 kW (75 PS) unit in the current car. A market launch in China is slated for before the end of 2026. The Seagull's overhaul follows a string of other additions to the line-up. Earlier in September, BYD launched the Sealion 08, a flagship SUV in the Ocean range offered in both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid form. That rapid cadence of new and updated nameplates is central to the manufacturer's effort to defend its position against cutthroat competition at home. Seal 07 grows, gains LiDAR option Alongside the Seagull, BYD published the first official images and specifications for the second generation of its Seal 07 sedan. The car gains noticeable length and wheelbase, and will be available as a plug-in hybrid or as a pure electric version with a motor producing up to 300 kW. Buyers can also specify a roof-mounted LiDAR system for advanced driver-assistance functions. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? Solid-state cells: 2030, and not a Blade replacement On the technology side, BYD is aiming for large-scale commercial output of solid-state batteries around the end of the decade, leaning heavily on sulfide-based solid electrolytes in its development work. Chief scientist Lian Yubo said the new cells are not intended to immediately displace the established Blade battery, which uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. The two are expected to be deployed in parallel, with solid-state technology reserved for premium models for the time being. That timeline puts BYD alongside rivals such as Toyota, which is also targeting its first vehicles with solid-state packs in 2027 and 2028. Charging build-out and an Australian fleet push Management is simultaneously pushing harder outside China. The company plans to erect 90,000 fast-charging stations by 2028, with 20,000 in place before the end of 2026, another 30,000 during 2027 and a further 40,000 in 2028. In Australia, BYD is deepening its push into commercial sales. Stephen Collins, chief operating officer of BYD Australia, said the fleet share of the country's sales mix has climbed from roughly 8% to 20% within a year, with a medium-term target of the mid-30% range. First-half profit drop weighs on the shares Heavy spending on products and expansion is colliding with a slowdown in earnings momentum. In the first half of 2026, net profit attributable to shareholders fell 20.54% year on year to RMB 12.33 billion. Revenue for the six months to June slipped 7.13% to RMB 344.82 billion. Second-quarter net profit did rise 30% to RMB 8.2 billion, but that fell short of analyst expectations for growth of around 48%. The stock reflects that caution. BYD shares changed hands at EUR 8.70 on Tuesday, down 1.6%, and at EUR 8.76 in a separate reading, a daily decline of 0.9%. Either way, the equity sits 30% below its 52-week high of EUR 12.49. Whether the coming model launches and higher overseas ambitions can durably support growth momentum should become clearer in the next set of quarterly figures. artigo.texto: 247 – Conversas extraídas pela Polícia Federal do celular de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-controlador do Banco Master, registram o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), mencionando um “formato de sociedade” durante as tratativas para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) que estava em nome da cunhada do parlamentar. O conteúdo das mensagens foi divulgado nesta segunda-feira (28) pelo site Fatos Online e confirmado pela Folha de São Paulo. Os diálogos começam em março de 2024 e também registram contatos sobre um projeto de lei relacionado ao mercado de carbono, o Fundo Garantidor de Créditos (FGC) e a disponibilização de uma aeronave. Motta afirma que não há ilícito nas conversas e rejeita qualquer relação de favorecimento. Motta menciona “formato de sociedade” Uma das conversas ocorreu em 9 de março de 2024, em meio às negociações para a aquisição de uma área onde funcionava uma fábrica de cimento em João Pessoa. Na mensagem enviada a Vorcaro, Motta tratou diretamente da negociação e mencionou um modelo societário que, segundo ele, já havia sido combinado. “Boa noite amigo! Td bem? Desculpa incomodar no sábado, estou aqui reunido com o pessoal para finalizar a negociação de compra da área aqui de JP. Conforme falamos, já temos os documentos assinados passando a empresa para minha cunhada ela iniciou a negociação com a Adriana mas acredito que ela não tá sabendo do formato de sociedade que ficou combinado”, escreveu Motta. Na sequência, o parlamentar pediu orientação ao então banqueiro: “Quando puder me orienta como devemos proceder pq o prazo é curto para saldar com Intercement [empresa que atua na produção de cimento]”. Segundo a Folha, a cunhada de Motta havia contratado naquele período um empréstimo de pelo menos R$ 22 milhões com o Banco Master. O jornal informou anteriormente que o valor teria sido solicitado diretamente pelo parlamentar. Os recursos foram utilizados na operação de compra do terreno da antiga fábrica de cimento. “Confiança e parceria” Quatro dias depois da primeira mensagem, outro diálogo registra Motta tratando do andamento da operação. Após Vorcaro informar que estava em uma reunião com “nosso amigo”, o deputado respondeu: “Certo, meu sogro está até aqui, queria levar ele pq acabamos agora de desenrolar as assinaturas que faltavam para poder prosseguir o pagamento. Se vc achar conveniente, analisa e me avisa”. Em 15 de março, Motta voltou a procurar Vorcaro. O parlamentar disse que estava “passando para agradecer a confiança e a parceria”. “Deu tudo certo a tempo de cumprir o contrato. Depois vamos marcar uma conversa para traçar os próximos passos, acredito que vamos ter êxito no projeto! Forte abraço!”, afirmou. Vorcaro respondeu: “muito feliz de estarmos juntos! Te admiro muito e esse é o início de uma parceria de vida”. Motta então escreveu: “com certeza meu amigo, a admiração é recíproca!”. Empréstimo de pelo menos R$ 22 milhões O crédito concedido pelo Banco Master serviu para financiar a aquisição, em abril de 2024, de um terreno com mais de 400 hectares pertencente a uma fábrica de cimento desativada em João Pessoa. A área deverá ser loteada para receber um novo bairro da capital paraibana. Segundo a reportagem, Bianca Medeiros, irmã da esposa de Motta, adquiriu em março de 2024 todas as cotas da ETC Participações. Uma semana depois, assinou o contrato de empréstimo com o Master, oferecendo as cotas da empresa como garantia. Bianca afirmou ao jornal que o crédito foi usado na compra do terreno. A área tem dimensão próxima de três vezes a do Parque Ibirapuera, em São Paulo. O preço pago pelo terreno foi de R$ 45 milhões, enquanto o valor fiscal registrado nas matrículas era de R$ 101 milhões. O valor fiscal é calculado pelo poder público municipal e serve, entre outras finalidades, como referência para tributação. Projeto de carbono aparece nas conversas Os diálogos também mostram que a interlocução entre Motta e Vorcaro alcançou um assunto em discussão no Congresso Nacional. Em novembro de 2024, os dois conversaram sobre um projeto de lei relacionado ao mercado de carbono. De acordo com a Folha, Motta encaminhou a Vorcaro mensagens que havia recebido com informações sobre o texto aprovado pelo Senado. No dia 19 daquele mês, Vorcaro perguntou: “consegue encontrar mais tarde hoje”. Motta respondeu: “sim. Pegando o texto aqui para te mandar”. Os trechos publicados registram a interlocução sobre a proposta, mas não demonstram, isoladamente, a ocorrência de favorecimento legislativo. Motta menciona estudo sobre o FGC O Fundo Garantidor de Créditos também aparece nas mensagens recuperadas do celular de Vorcaro. Em 23 de março de 2024, Motta pediu ao então controlador do Master que lembrasse sua equipe de preparar um estudo sobre o fundo. “Quando puder lembra de pedir a seu pessoal o estudo daquele assunto do FGC, se vc for a Brasília essa semana podemos voltar a falar para ver onde podemos tentar encaixar esse assunto”, escreveu o parlamentar. O trecho divulgado não detalha qual era especificamente o assunto relacionado ao FGC nem o que Motta quis dizer com a possibilidade de “encaixar” o tema. Aeronave foi colocada à disposição Outro diálogo, de 27 de abril de 2024, indica que Vorcaro colocou uma aeronave à disposição do deputado. Motta perguntou ao banqueiro de onde partiria o avião que faria seu deslocamento de Guarulhos, em São Paulo, para Brasília. “Já vai estar te esperando”, respondeu Vorcaro. Motta nega ilícito e favorecimento Procurado, o presidente da Câmara afirmou, por meio de sua assessoria, que sempre manteve interlocução com diferentes setores durante sua atuação parlamentar. “Enfatizo que não há nenhum ilícito retratado nos diálogos publicados e repudio a tentativa de atribuir conversas descontextualizadas a qualquer relação de interesse espúrio ou de favorecimento por minha parte. Tenho uma vida limpa, assim como é limpa a minha atuação política nesses 15 anos de vida pública”, declarou. Motta também afirmou que o emprésti

artigo.texto: Decade Energy has signed a Supply Framework Agreement with Sungrow for the supply of up to 200 MWh of battery energy storage equipment for projects across France. The agreement is intended to support Decade Energy’s plans to scale the deployment of battery storage across its growing portfolio of projects in the country. It also establishes a framework for the company to move from developing individual battery storage projects toward a more standardized, repeatable delivery model. Under the agreement, core supply terms will be established in advance, allowing Decade Energy to streamline procurement and reduce project-level complexity. The company said this will enable its teams to focus on site-specific engineering, grid connection and construction requirements across individual projects. Baptiste Perlin, VP of Infrastructure at Decade Energy, said the company’s framework with Sungrow is aimed at building the partnerships and systems required to deploy battery storage at greater speed and scale as France’s electrification progresses. Battery energy storage is gaining importance as power systems integrate increasing levels of renewable generation while electricity demand rises across the transport, buildings and industrial sectors. The agreement is expected to strengthen Decade Energy’s supply chain and delivery capabilities as it expands its project pipeline. Weiyi (Eric) Da, ESS Manager at Sungrow Europe, said the agreement combines Decade Energy’s project pipeline with Sungrow’s energy storage technology and local service capabilities to support the delivery of scalable battery storage projects in France. Sungrow has installed more than 1,000 GW of power electronic converters globally and operates more than 520 service outlets worldwide. The framework agreement forms part of Decade Energy’s broader strategy to establish technology partnerships, infrastructure and delivery capabilities for the faster deployment of battery storage projects in France. artigo.texto: New data centers in neighboring Maryland to get additional scrutiny under governor’s order Trending Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore is commissioning a state task force to examine new data center proposals and advise local jurisdictions considering the projects. The final decision on data center projects still rests with local governments, Moore said during a news conference Wednesday morning in Annapolis. "Our administration will always stand with the people, and the state will not go around a local community's 'no,'" Moore said. Moore said he also plans to advocate for the repeal of a state tax exemption for data centers, established in 2020, during the next legislative session, which begins in January. Moore's new task force, which will be staffed by seven state agencies, will evaluate proposals based on whether they align with the state's principles, which include protecting electricity ratepayers from cost burdens, providing sufficient environmental protections and having the support of the community, among other factors. "They need to pay their own way, or they need to go away," Moore said. The task force will decide whether projects are "aligned, conditionally aligned or not aligned" with the state's principles. It will have purview over projects that expect to consume at least 25 megawatts of electricity at their peak demand. The governor also established a public online dashboard, which will be updated monthly and list data center proposals and certain specifications about them, including the name of their developer, expected peak energy demand and anticipated water use. "Any company seeking the state's help will have to make commitments that are specific, that are measurable, and importantly, that are public," Moore said. The task force's determination about a data center project does not have the power to unilaterally sink it, but it could have weighty implications for a data center developer. Moore's executive order calls on his agencies to delay their consideration of permits for data center projects that are considered "not aligned" with the state's principles. "Agencies shall defer substantive review until the developer documents all required local land use approvals," reads the executive order. And in order for a data center developer to receive an incentive, grant, loan or financing from the state, it must be considered aligned or conditionally aligned with the state's principles, per Moore's order. Projects that get a favorable decision from the task force also could get other perks, including letters of support, or advocacy from state officials before other bodies such as regional electric grid operator PJM or the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. Going forward, Moore also commanded his agencies not to enter into any non-disclosure agreements with data center developers, operators, or site-selection agents. The order states that any such agreements already signed will be honored, but not renewed or extended. Moore's executive order stops well short of a ban or pause on data centers. But Moore indicated in a recent interview with Punchbowl News, a Washington, D.C.-based political news site, that if a statewide moratorium bill landed on his desk next year, he would sign it. During Wednesday's news conference at the State House, Moore called moratorium decisions a "local jurisdictional issue." "We don't have that authority, but what we do want to do is making sure that we are clear and transparent with our local jurisdictions about what type of elements need to be in place in order to receive state support," Moore said. Moore's order attracted criticism from groups that have called for him to embrace a ban, including Andy Ellis, the Green Party candidate for governor. "We're demanding a ban," Ellis said in a statement Wednesday. "A moratorium is a half-measure, but a task force is nothing. It's lip service, it's cowardly, and it does nothing to stop extractive corporations." Environmental group Food & Water Watch said in a statement it was "glad the governor is pledging to roll back the tax exemptions and wants to regulate this wild industry," but argued that further steps are needed, including a statewide pause. For instance, Moore should also push to repeal a bill he supported in 2024, which exempted diesel back-up generators at data centers from an approval process at the Maryland Public Service Commission, said Jorge Aguilar, southern regional director with Food & Water Watch, in a statement. "Moore's announcement is a step in the right direction," Aguilar wrote. "It's not the full leap to action Maryland needs." The Chesapeake Climate Action Network is also calling for a statewide pause, and for the legislature to "finish the task" with additional conditions on any future data centers. "Given the deepening climate crisis, Gov. Moore and the General Assembly must explicitly require all new data centers run on 100% clean energy. Period. Full stop," said Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, in a statement. Maryland Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) argued Moore's plan contradicts his previous statements calling for Maryland to lead on technology, AI and data centers. "You cannot recruit an industry with one hand while taxing it and taking away its incentives with the other," Hershey said. "That kind of inconsistent economic policy makes Maryland less competitive and gives businesses another reason to invest somewhere else." Moore argued on Wednesday that the new state guidelines for data center projects will provide clarity for developers hoping to locate projects in Maryland. Moore's data center task force will be spurred to action when a data center developer makes any new request of the state, such as when a developer applies for a state permit. artigo.texto: Seoul, South Korea – A recent analysis by the Korean Ministry of Intellectual Property shows that South Korea ranked first globally in the number of patent applications for energy storage systems (ESS) for power grids over the past 20 years, totaling 6,030 applications. The analysis was based on data submitted to the five leading global intellectual property organizations (IP5) between 2004 and 2023. This period saw a staggering 125-fold increase in the number of innovations, jumping from just 32 applications in 2004 to 4,010 by the end of the study period. A biotechnology that stores generated electricity Energy storage systems are a vital technology that stores generated electricity for use when needed in homes, industrial facilities, and various power grids. By nationality, South Korea topped the list with 41.3% (6,030 cases). China came in second with 5,176 cases (35.4%), followed by the United States with 1,283 cases (8.8%). Japan had 1,220 cases (8.4%), and Germany 250 cases (1.7%). Extensive Korean dominance among the world’s top companies The analysis confirmed the significant superiority of Korean companies in technological innovation. Four Korean companies secured positions among the top 10 global companies in this sector. LG Energy Solutions topped the list with the most applications, registering 4,605 cases. China’s CATL came in second with 2,653 cases, and Samsung SDI ranked third with 242 cases. LS Electric and Samsung Electronics also stood out, securing seventh and eighth place respectively, with 114 and 78 cases. Safety technologies and long-term storage management In terms of precise technical classification, storage device safety and management technology—which focuses on monitoring device condition and preventing heat and fire hazards—accounted for the largest share with 7,705 cases (52.8%). This was followed by long-term storage technology, designed for storing and supplying energy for extended periods, with 5,338 cases (36.5%). Energy conversion and interconnection technology came in third with 10.7%, representing 1,562 cases. The Korean industry is making progress in the areas of safety assurance Commenting on these results, Park Jae-hoon, director of the Communications Inspection Bureau, affirmed that this significant development reflects the progress of the Korean industry in areas such as safety assurance, long-term storage, and efficient network connectivity. He also emphasized the ministry’s commitment to actively supporting Korean companies in rigorously and promptly protecting their intellectual property rights. This aims to enhance their competitiveness in capturing overseas power grid markets.

artigo.texto: India’s shift towards renewable power is expected to create a major requirement for energy storage, with over Rs 4 lakh crore of storage-related investment estimated to be needed by FY32, according to CareEdge Ratings. The report said India’s power sector is moving from a challenge of adding generation capacity to a new challenge of integrating increasing renewable capacity into the electricity system. While non-fossil sources account for around 50 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity, they contribute around 29 per cent of actual electricity generation. This gap makes energy storage, transmission infrastructure and flexible generation increasingly important as the share of renewable power rises. The report highlighted that India’s energy storage requirement is expected to reach around 411 GWh by FY32, compared with operational storage capacity of around 54 GWh as of June 2026. It stated, “CareEdge Ratings estimates storage-related capex of over Rs 4 lakh crore to meet FY32 requirements”. It also added that the rise in storage requirements reflects the need to integrate renewable generation into the power system and ensure that electricity produced from variable renewable sources can be managed effectively. Battery and pumped storage gain importance The report also pointed to a sharp increase in standalone storage-based tenders. Such tenders rose to around 21 GW in FY26 from 7 GW in FY25, indicating growing activity in the energy storage segment. The agency highlighted the complementary roles of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Plants (PSPs) in supporting India’s power transition. Both technologies are expected to have an important role as the country adds more renewable generation capacity. Coal power retains a role in the transition At the same time, CareEdge Ratings said coal-based thermal power is entering a multi-year phase of improved credit stability and renewed investment relevance. Well-contracted coal-based thermal power assets are likely to remain important for meeting growing electricity demand while also providing the flexibility required to integrate increasing renewable capacity, the report said. This indicates that the expansion of renewable energy is likely to be accompanied by investments in other parts of the power system rather than replacing conventional generation immediately. Storage and flexible generation would help manage renewable power, while transmission infrastructure would be required to move electricity across the grid. Transmission investment to rise The transmission sector is also expected to see significant investment. The report estimates a capex outlay of around Rs 5.19 lakh crore during FY27-FY31. However, the agency identified several execution-related challenges for the transmission sector, including right-of-way issues, forest clearances and coordination requirements. Despite these challenges, it said the stable cash flow profile and long concession tenures of operational transmission assets continue to support the sector’s credit profile. Published on September 28, 2026

artigo.texto: A Weg (WEGE3) anunciou dois projetos estratégicos de expansão de capacidade que, segundo o Citi, aumentam a exposição da empresa a temas relevantes de infraestrutura de energia, como data centers (centro de dados) e modernização da rede. Na América do Norte, a companhia vai investir US$ 165 milhões para ampliar a produção de geradores. Com a conclusão prevista para 2030, o banco afirma que a capacidade global de geradores da companhia deve subir de 10 para 50 unidades por dia, com operações no México, nos Estados Unidos, no Brasil e na China. No Brasil, a empresa informou que está ampliando o projeto de baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês para Battery Energy Storage System), elevando o investimento planejado para R$ 330 milhões e a capacidade anual para 4GWh. Os analistas Andre Mazini, Kiepher Kennedy e Piero Trotta observam que o movimento ocorre antes do primeiro leilão de BESS no País, esperado para dezembro de 2026, e avaliam que a Weg se posiciona para capturar a necessidade crescente de integrar geração renovável intermitente. O relatório destaca ainda que o anúncio do projeto de BESS ocorreu apenas sete meses após a primeira divulgação da fábrica em Itajaí (SC). O plano original previa capacidade anual de 2 GWh, mas a revisão dobra o volume para 4 GWh e aumenta o investimento total de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões. Na leitura do Citi, a aceleração do plano indica confiança no mercado emergente de armazenamento de energia no Brasil e reforça o posicionamento da empresa em um segmento da cadeia de transição energética. A expectativa é que as operações comecem no segundo semestre de 2027. Para o banco, os dois anúncios reforçam a estratégia da companhia de se aproximar de data centers e armazenamento de energia, apontados como vetores estruturais de crescimento para a próxima década. O Citi também diz ver a WEG negociada a 29 vezes lucro. O Citi tem recomendação neutra para a Weg, com preço-alvo de R$ 49, o que representa um potencial de alta de 4,22% ante o fechamento da ação da empresa na última sexta-feira, 25.

artigo.texto: India to add up to 50 GWh battery storage capacity over next 2 yrs: Crisil Battery storage deployment is set to rise sharply from 1 GWh in FY26 as renewable energy expands and storage-linked projects gain a larger share of government auctions Listen to This Article India’s renewable energy sector is set for a significant surge in battery energy storage system (BESS) deployment, with 45-50 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of capacity expected to be commissioned over the current and next financial year, compared with just 1 GWh as of last fiscal, according to Crisil. The ratings agency said the growth is attributed to a strong pipeline of projects under implementation and continued policy support. Capacity additions could have been even higher, but 8-9 GWh of awarded capacity faces a higher risk of delay, moderating the overall deployment outlook. The analysis covers bids awarded between FY24 and FY26 across 100 renewable energy developers. Crisil said the growing need for storage is a consequence of the rising share of renewable energy (RE) to 39 per cent of India’s installed power generation capacity and 15 per cent of energy generated last fiscal. As RE generation is intermittent, it has increased the need for firm and peak-hour power supply. This has elevated the importance of energy storage solutions, particularly BESS. The requirement is especially acute for solar projects because electricity demand peaks in the evening, when solar generation is negligible and BESS can address this mismatch. In line with its objective of integrating a larger share of RE into the national power grid in a sustainable manner, the government has accelerated storage-linked auctions. Projects incorporating BESS accounted for nearly 40 per cent of total auctioned capacity in FY26, up sharply from about 5 per cent in FY24 and FY25. Also Read “As a result, 50-55 GWh of BESS capacity is scheduled for commissioning across FY27 and FY28. Of this, around 40 GWh has been awarded through government-led auctions, where distribution utilities are the offtakers, while the remaining 10-15 GWh is expected to serve commercial and industrial consumers directly or be deployed in the merchant market,” Crisil said. However, 21 per cent of the under-construction BESS capacity, equivalent to about 12 GWh, faces weak return potential, which may lead to some delays in commissioning. The risk has emerged because battery prices have hardened in 2026, while tariffs bid out for these projects were relatively low. “Developers typically procure batteries about a year after securing project bids. Consequently, most projects awarded in 2025 are now exposed to higher battery prices, which have rebounded from the lows witnessed in 2025. As battery prices were consistently coming down till 2025, developers appeared to have bid aggressively on the assumption that prices would continue their downward trajectory,” said Manish Gupta, senior director and deputy chief ratings officer at Crisil. However, in reality, battery prices have increased and, at these prevailing levels, project returns may be insufficient to achieve a typical target internal rate of return of 12-14 per cent, according to Crisil. Consequently, developers may defer implementation in anticipation of more favourable battery pricing. Further, around 8-9 GWh out of this 12 GWh of planned capacity is exposed to an additional challenge: limited implementation experience among project sponsors. While BESS projects typically face relatively lower land acquisition and connectivity-related challenges compared to conventional renewable energy projects, equipment procurement remains a key risk given the sector’s continued dependence on overseas suppliers for batteries and other critical components. artigo.texto: O mercado offshore vive um superaquecimento na cadeia de fornecedores e que pressiona as decisões finais de investimentos (FIDs, na sigla em inglês) de novos sistemas de produção de óleo e gás. Em entrevista ao estúdio eixos, durante a ROG.e 2026, o consultor Carlos Mastrangelo destacou que o momento pede mais criatividade da indústria na busca por alternativas. Confira na íntegra. Segundo ele, hoje as novas plataformas de óleo e gás competem por equipamentos (como turbogeradores) com o boom de desenvolvimento de projetos de data centers e terminais de gás natural liquefeito (GNL). “As empresas que estão entrando para colocar um projeto novo de desenvolvimento, que são projetos de bilhões, estão tendo que enfrentar preços aquecidos, tendo que enfrentar uma competição que é uma competição quase injusta com vários outros ramos da sociedade, principalmente os grandes data centers”. Nesse contexto, uma tendência, aponta Mastrangelo, é a simplificação e a diversificação na forma de executar projetos. “E até mesmo na forma de você encarar um projeto novo. Não fazer exatamente da mesma forma que foi feito no passado, porque a indústria tem que ter mais robustez de buscar uma forma mais simples de executar”, complementou. A agência eixos entrevista as principais lideranças do setor em um estúdio próprio dentro do evento, que é o maior encontro global da indústria de energia. O estúdio eixos na ROG.e 2026 tem patrocínio de OceanPact, Prio, United Airlines e Vibra. Principais assuntos tratados: - Mercado offshore vive superaquecimento, com preços altos e dificuldade de prever o petróleo, pressionando decisões de FID. - Indústria compete por equipamentos com data centers e terminais de GNL, disputando turbogeradores e chips. - Superaquecimento eleva preços e gera falta de equipamentos e pede mais criatividade da indústria na busca por alternativas. - Tendência é de simplificação e padronização, com unidades menores e reaproveitamento de equipamentos. - Caminho crítico migrou do casco para o topside, e indústria estuda reduzir topside para voltar a conversões. - Inteligência artificial pode aumentar atividades a bordo no curto prazo ao criar backlog de tarefas humanas. - Brasil mantém liderança em FPSOs, e conteúdo local depende de perenização e visão de longo prazo. artigo.texto: -- Kuehne+Nagel and CATL, a global leader in new energy technologies, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to establish a strategic collaboration in battery logistics, transport electrification and emissions reduction initiatives. The partnership will initially focus on practical initiatives including the electrification of CATL transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks provided by Qiji, which is set to launch in China this year. Additional areas of collaboration include battery recycling and aftersales support, as well as energy storage and charging solutions for logistics sites. Together, these activities support both companies' Scope 3 emissions reduction ambitions across their logistics and transportation value chains. "As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share a commitment to accelerating the energy transition and achieving a net-zero emissions future," said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. "Our elevated partnership will not only contribute to both parties' sustainability targets, but also help advance a greener future." "Battery-electric vehicles are essential to decarbonising road freight," said Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel. "Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both high-performing and operationally viable. By combining CATL's battery expertise with our logistics knowhow, we can advance initiatives that help reduce our own emissions and those of our customers." The partnership comes at a time of rapidly growing demand for electric vehicles and energy storage solutions. In 2024, demand for EV batteries increased by more than 75%, while battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand through a growing network of gigafactories worldwide. artigo.texto: Geral Rússia destrói data centers ucranianos e mina potencial militar do país, diz analista Ataques visam prejudicar operações cibernéticas e controle de drones na Ucrânia, aponta especialista. Os ataques diários da Rússia às telecomunicações e aos data centers ucranianos visam minar a capacidade da Ucrânia de travar a guerra, controlar drones e montar operações cibernéticas e fraudulentas dentro da Rússia, afirmou à Sputnik Aleksei Leonkov, analista militar russo. Leonkov apontou que a presença de empresas proeminentes ligadas ao Pentágono, como Blackbird e Palantir, nesses locais não é coincidência, porque elas fornecem o poder de computação para coordenar operações de combate, incluindo o processamento de alvos de drones. "Todos esses centros, especialmente os de Kiev, desempenharam um papel duplo. Oficialmente, forneciam telecomunicações, acesso à internet, conectividade. Extraoficialmente, estavam integrados ao circuito de comando e controle de combate", ressaltou. Na avaliação do especialista, essencialmente, todas as informações sobre o comando das forças ucranianas, dados de inteligência e similares fluíam por esses centros. O analista avalia que a Rússia está interrompendo o componente militar em primeiro lugar, e isso começará a impactar o comando e o controle de combate. Isso afetará também os ataques terroristas da Ucrânia realizados com drones. O especialista não acredita que derrubar os centros levará a um colapso completo das capacidades digitais dos militares ucranianos e dos atores cibernéticos, dado o potencial de explorar data centers em lugares como a Estônia e o sul do Cáucaso, que estão fora do alcance da operação militar especial. No entanto, se os centros fossem fechados, ter que importar esse equipamento incrivelmente caro novamente e ligar tudo de volta seria extremamente caro para a Ucrânia, concluiu. Anteriormente, o analista militar britânico Aleksander Mercouris analisou em seu canal no YouTube que o dinheiro ocidental pode ajudar Kiev e o atual líder ucraniano, Vladimir Zelensky, a se manterem por algum tempo, mas não muito. artigo.texto: Oregon’s second largest investor-owned electric utility could soon directly assign the costs of new energy projects and infrastructure needed for data centers to data center operators. Pacific Power last week agreed to the deal following months of negotiations with staff of the Oregon Public Utility Commission, the watchdog Citizens’ Utility Board and a handful of environmental and community advocacy groups. The Citizens’ Utility Board in a news release Tuesday called the agreement “the strongest from a for-profit electric utility yet” under Oregon’s new POWER Act, which mandates the state’s monopoly electric utilities create a separate rate class for data centers to ensure other customers aren’t subsidizing the massive energy demand from the server farms. Both Pacific Power and the state’s largest electric utility, Portland General Electric, have raised customer rates 50% since 2020, while most customer classes became more energy efficient, and data centers grew to make up nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sales statewide. The three-member Public Utility Commission is expected to approve Pacific Power’s deal on Nov. 13, according to Charlotte Shuff, a spokesperson for the Citizens’ Utility Board. Shuff expects the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing the tech companies, will attempt to appeal. The coalition also appealed a recent PGE proposal to assign costs based not on how much each rate class is driving “peak demand” on the system, which is moments when usage is at its highest point. The state utility commission rejected the appeal, but the citizens’ board expects the coalition will bring the case to the Oregon Court of Appeals. While Pacific Power’s plan assigns costs based on who is driving overall demand, PGE’s plan assigns costs based on how much each customer class is growing and adding to the system’s highest demand periods. After the state’s Public Utility Commission approved PGE’s proposal in July, the company announced rates for data centers would increase by nearly 30% while residential payers would see their bills decline slightly. Pacific Power’s proposal goes further than PGE’s by requiring new data centers that receive electricity from Pacific Power to cover the costs for all new energy generation and storage projects needed to power them, including new power plants and batteries, even if those additions also benefit other customers. Data centers would also pay for any upgrades that are needed to serve them, even if those same upgrades benefit other customer classes. Data centers would be responsible for the cost of all wires and poles built for them to receive distributed power, and all costs related to energy purchased on the market from other companies to power them. If a 100 megawatt transmission line is needed to serve a 50 megawatt data center as well as other residential and industrial customers, the data center would pay for 50% of the transmission line, directly corresponding with its overall demand, according to the citizens’ board. New transmission lines can cost several million dollars per mile to build, and the West is in need of more than 12,000 miles of new transmission according to one recent estimate. Shuff said Pacific Power’s proposal came a long way in recent months and “to their credit they (Pacific Power) worked really hard to get to this. We’re really pleased with where we landed,” she said. The utility serves more than 650,000 Oregon customers, and has seen energy demand grow by 8% between 2013 and 2023 due to data centers, according to a Sightline Institute analysis of U.S. Energy Information Administration data. PGE is the state’s largest electric utility, serving 930,000 customers, and has absorbed the most data center load growth of any private utility in the state during the last decade, according to that analysis. PGE’s system of charging customers based not on overall demand growth but “peak demand growth” is driven in part by the fact that they serve a higher number of small data centers in densely populated counties, according to Bob Jenks, executive director of the Citizens’ Utilities Board. Pacific Power’s data center customers are mostly large facilities in more rural parts of the state. It’s easier to make the case that building a new transmission line in Washington County could benefit all customer classes, who are all using more air conditioning in the summer, he explained, “whereas if you build a data center in Madras, it’s pretty clear whether or not new energy investments and infrastructure costs associated with that are for the data center or not,” Jenks said. Drew Hanson, a PGE spokesperson, reiterated in an email the different challenges the two utilities face. “(Pacific Power’s) service area is larger and more spread out, so a single data center may require infrastructure built specifically for that customer, such as a new transmission line, substation, or power resource. In those cases, costs can be tied more directly to the customer creating the need,” he said. Pacific Power’s plan applies to future data centers, while PGE’s applies to future and existing data centers. Pacific Power will need to address costs associated with its current data center customers and their demands next spring. The company has just a handful of data center customers at present “but dozens want to get onto their system, and some of them are massive,” Jenks said. artigo.texto: INDIANTOWN – The Village Council here voted unanimously Sept. 10 to direct its legal counsel to began drafting a data center moratorium and transparency ordinance, a week and a half after the recently-elected Board majority fired the village manager and replaced its long-term attorney in a quest to fulfill campaign promises of pausing such applications. In addition to replacing Village Manager Taryn Kryzda with former Stuart City Manager Michael Giardino on Sept. 1, the Council replaced Village Attorney Wade Vose with one of his colleagues because he’d acknowledged his reluctance to recommend Indiantown’s participation in a data center moratorium. Two days afterwards, Community Development Director Deana Freeman tendered her 30-day notice, realizing her work on at least three data center applications had put her in the cross-hairs of an angry group of area residents. Giardino told the Hometown News that he tried to persuade Freeman to stay on, but when she declined, he told her to make her resignation immediate. The interim village manager has now assumed Freeman’s responsibilities as well. Interim Village Attorney Janet Smith launched the moratorium discussion during the latest meeting. “What we would like to proffer to the Council is two ordinances,” she said. “They will both have to go through planning and zoning and come before you on two separate readings. You will have public comment at each of those meetings. The first one is the moratorium that we feel will be legally defensible. The second one is the transparency ordinance.” The last ordinance was in response to public outcry that Freeman had allegedly signed a non-disclosure agreement with a potential data-center developer, which caused much of the opposition to believe it was a common practice in Village Hall in order to keep residents in the dark. Smith admitted that she had not personally seen the NDA in question but had since submitted a public records request for a copy. Around the Sept. 3 date of Freeman’s resignation letter, a purported copy of that NDA began circulating on Indiantown Facebook pages. The Hometown News could not authenticate that document, however. “I’ve only been told that there was one NDA,” she continued. “I’m still waiting to see about getting it, so that’s in the process. I did hear that NDAs were frowned upon by the Council and the community.” Smith acknowledged there were other methods utilized by municipalities to protect industry trade secrets that could still be implemented in the future. “I have statutory exceptions that the Council can use for trade secrets,” she explained. “If someone is bringing forward a proposal considered a trade secret and they’re willing to indemnify the Village while they speak to us so we can protect their records, then we have that opportunity. So, an NDA should not be needed.” The interim attorney hopes to begin the ordinance process with the Planning, Zoning & appeals Board on Oct. 1, followed by the Council’s first reading Oct. 8. “On Oct. 22, we would have it back before you for second reading and adoption,” she concluded as she read her draft language to the Board. “This would become an ordinance for the Village.” Mayor Phyllis Waters Brown was the first to comment afterward, repeating her concerns of potentially clashing with developers over Senate Bill 180 and other Florida statutes. “This is not a surprise to anyone – I do not want wish to go to court,”she said. “What is wrong with having an open house for all of them, [so] we learn what we need to learn. Let them show us and teach us what we’re asking for and do a moratorium on the ones that may come after.” “Nothing in what I’m proposing would stop you from doing that,” Smith responded. “There’s nothing against having a workshop or a town hall. I’m not giving you any solution that can’t be stopped. If you want to do anything in-between working with the interim manager, you still have that opportunity.” After Councilman Anthony Dowling made a motion to follow Smith’s recommendations -- which was seconded by Councilwoman Janet Hernandez -- a handful of public speakers addressed the Board. Clemenstville resident Linda Byczko started them off. Like several others who’ve actively pushed for the moratorium, Byczko does not live within the Indiantown Village limits and could not vote in the last election. Instead, those county residents lobbied Village residents to vote to make a change. “I think you need time to write regulations to protect the Village,” she said. “The land development regulations right now are very weak: They do not address what you have going on here.” Rory Greenberg has submitted a data-center application for the former Florida Steel Corp. site and stressed his desire to collaborate with the community. “This industry’s moving very fast,” he said. “I think working together and being self-regulating is the best approach. We’re not looking to move fast; we’re just looking to move in earnest. You guys pick the expert, I’ll hire them.” The face of the local opposition, Eric Miller, followed Greenberg to the podium. Like Byczko, he couldn’t vote, but it was of his own doing. During the incorporation movement, he successfully lobbied to keep his Little Ranch area outside of the Village limits. “Mr. Greenberg is right,” he said. “What you’re proposing and you’re going to vote on here is what could have started last February had there been open dialogue and everything not kept in dark rooms. We wanted a seat at the table to make sure what was coming in here was going to be safe. This gives us a framework to work in. You’ve been given another opportunity to work with us, the people that live in this area.” The attorney for the Silver Fox 606 data center applicant, Ethan Loeb subsequently advised the Council of potential litigation. “Certain organizations from our perspective have private property rights that are vested,” he said. “My client’s one of them. artigo.texto: NIMBY digital e a conta de energia da inteligÃªncia artificial e datacenters A inteligência artificial não mora na nuvem. Ela ocupa terrenos, usa equipamentos, consome eletricidade, rejeita calor e exige redes de transmissão e fibra ótica. É legítimo perguntar quem pagará por essa infraestrutura e o que receberão as comunidades que a abrigarem. Uma pesquisa divulgada em 22 de setembro pelo Fórum Econômico Mundial registra a expectativa de seus economistas-chefes de que os data centers contribuam para o crescimento, mas também tragam pressão sobre serviços públicos, poucos empregos diretos e resistência local. É um alerta importante. Não é, porém, uma lei da física nem uma sentença para todos os países e projetos. A demanda por energia já cresce por razões muito mais amplas. Queremos casas mais confortáveis, ar-condicionado, mobilidade elétrica, serviços digitais, equipamentos de saúde e processos produtivos mais sofisticados. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers responderão por cerca de um décimo do crescimento mundial do consumo elétrico até 2030: uma parcela relevante, mas inferior à de motores industriais, climatização de edifícios e veículos elétricos. Culpar exclusivamente a IA por toda alta da conta de luz seria tão impreciso quanto afirmar que ela não terá impacto algum. Também precisamos distinguir duas coisas que frequentemente aparecem misturadas. Uma família pode pagar mais porque passou a consumir mais eletricidade e, portanto, a usufruir mais serviços e conforto. Pode pagar mais, também, porque subiu o preço de cada quilowatt-hora. Nesse segundo caso, importam os custos da geração, das redes, dos encargos e dos tributos, assim como as decisões sobre quem financia novos investimentos. Chamar tudo isso de “efeito dos data centers” encobre escolhas de política energética e distribuição de custos que devem ser transparentes. Uma grande instalação mal localizada pode, sim, disputar capacidade elétrica e água com a população. Se a rede precisar ser ampliada para atendê-la, não é aceitável simplesmente espalhar a conta entre consumidores residenciais sem demonstrar os benefícios correspondentes. Mas o resultado pode ser diferente quando o empreendedor paga pelas instalações que provoca, contrata geração renovável adicional, ajuda a viabilizar armazenamento e flexibilidade e se instala onde há capacidade ou geração hoje restringida. No Nordeste, essa possibilidade merece estudo projeto a projeto: energia renovável sujeita a curtailment não equivale automaticamente a suprimento firme, disponível 24 horas por dia. O mesmo rigor vale para a água. Um circuito fechado dentro do data center não assegura consumo hídrico próximo de zero: é preciso saber como o calor será finalmente rejeitado. Em regiões de escassez, a localização e a tecnologia de refrigeração devem ser escolhidas antes da licença, com divulgação de captação, consumo efetivo, origem da água e desempenho verificado. Reúso, refrigeração seca e sistemas híbridos são alternativas a comparar, não promessas genéricas. Quanto aos empregos, não devemos vender um data center como uma fábrica que manterá milhares de trabalhadores em seu interior. Seu valor potencial está também na construção, nos serviços especializados e, sobretudo, no que uma região consegue desenvolver ao redor da infraestrutura: pesquisa, formação, computação, aplicações de IA e empresas locais. Esse efeito não nasce sozinho. Requer contratos, investimento em pessoas e instituições capazes de ligar a capacidade computacional à economia regional. A resistência das comunidades tampouco pode ser descartada como medo do futuro. Uma pesquisa da Universidade da Pensilvânia encontrou oposição à instalação de data centers próximos entre 61% dos adultos consultados nos Estados Unidos. Esse dado não descreve automaticamente o Brasil, mas ensina algo: as pessoas percebem quando os custos são locais e os benefícios, distantes. Reprimir ou execrar data centers não resolve a demanda por processamento. Afastá-los sem critério pode apenas transferir consumo de energia, impactos e oportunidades para outros lugares. A resposta é estabelecer condições para recebê-los: conexão planejada; custos de expansão atribuídos com justiça; energia progressivamente menos emissora; metas auditáveis de eficiência elétrica e hídrica; participação das comunidades desde o início; e contrapartidas proporcionais, verificáveis e duradouras. Feito assim, um data center pode deixar de parecer um grande consumidor que chegou para disputar recursos e tornar-se parceiro na expansão da infraestrutura local. As comunidades não têm obrigação de acolher qualquer projeto. Têm o direito de exigir que ele melhore, em vez de encarecer, suas condições de vida. Portanto, a questão é menos sobre quem pagará essa conta, e mais sobre quem colherá os benefícios e quem fará regras impedirão que o futuro dos datacenters seja construído às custas dos seus vizinhos. Jean Paul Prates é advogado e economista com mais de 40 anos de experiência internacional, reconhecido como um dos principais especialistas no setor energético e de recursos naturais. Foi Presidente da Petrobras, Senador da República, Secretário de Estado de Energia e fundador do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia – CERNE. Atualmente é sócio da Altiva Inteligência Estratégica, Head do LIDE Energia e conselheiro de empresas e associações setoriais.

artigo.texto: Pune: COEP Technological University and JSW Projects have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to set up what they describe as Indiaâs first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre at the universityâs Chikhali Research Park, with an investment of over Rs 800 crore across two phases. The centre will focus on developing and testing lithium-ion battery cells, along with sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. The initiative is expected to create over 1,000 jobs linked to the battery ecosystem and provide a platform for students and faculty to work with industry engineers on commercially relevant technologies. In the first phase, the centre will undertake battery-cell design, simulation and prototyping. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility with the capability to manufacture cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 Ah. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud said the partnership could help develop indigenous alternatives to imported batteries while giving students hands-on exposure to advanced battery technology. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said the partnership would help develop cells suited to Indian climatic conditions and applications. âCells are the new fuel of this century,â he said, and added that India needed to build domestic capabilities to manufacture them. The project aims to bridge the gap between academic research and industry by enabling joint research, technology development, publications and intellectual property creation. The centre is also expected to support applications in electric vehicles , grid storage and clean energy.

artigo.texto: Zeon Corporation Key supplier for automotive and industrial seals According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Hydrogenated Nitrile Rubber (HNBR) Compounds market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global market for hydrogenated nitrile rubber (HNBR) compounds is entering a period of accelerated transformation, with demand projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate of 9–13% through 2035. This growth is not merely a continuation of historical trends but a structural shift driven by the rapid build-out of battery manufacturing capacity and grid-scale energy storage infrastructure. HNBR compounds, known for their superior chemical resistance, high-temperature stability, and mechanical durability, are increasingly specified for sealing and gasketing applications in equipment that handles aggressive electrolytes, thermal management fluids, and high-voltage insulation environments. While traditional industrial sealing segments continue to provide a stable demand base, the energy sector is emerging as the primary growth engine, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe. However, the market faces supply-side constraints: 5–8 major producers control an estimated 65–75% of nameplate capacity, leading to extended lead times of 6–10 weeks for specialty grades. Qualification cycles for energy-grade compounds have lengthened to 12–18 months as OEMs demand rigorous aging and chemical-exposure validation. Despite these challenges, the outlook to 2035 remains robust, with capacity additions targeting clean-room compounding and twin-screw extrusion lines purpose-built for energy-sector specifications. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market size, growth trajectory, demand structure, supply capability, trade flows, pricing, and competitive landscape, offering a data-driven view for manufacturers, distributors, investors, and procurement teams navigating this dynamic market. The baseline scenario for the global HNBR compounds market anticipates a compound annual growth rate of 9–13% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 240–280 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the accelerating deployment of battery gigafactories and grid-scale energy storage systems, which require high-performance sealing solutions capable of withstanding aggressive electrolytes and thermal cycling. In the baseline, Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing region, accounting for an estimated 45–55% of global HNBR consumption in the energy domain, driven by gigafactory construction in China, South Korea, and Southeast Asia. Europe and North America follow, supported by renewable integration projects and data-center backup power investments. Supply-side dynamics are expected to remain tight through the early forecast period, as capacity expansions are concentrated among a few major producers and qualification timelines for new entrants stretch to 12–24 months. Price premiums for HNBR over standard NBR are projected to persist in the 60–100% range, with energy-grade compounds commanding an additional 15–25% premium. Feedstock cost volatility for acrylonitrile and butadiene poses a risk to margin stability, though quarterly contract resets provide some flexibility. Overall, the baseline scenario assumes no major demand-disrupting technological substitutions, but acknowledges that alternative elastomers or sealing technologies could capture niche applications if qualification bottlenecks persist. The market is expected to remain structurally concentrated, with strategic partnerships and capacity investments shaping competitive dynamics through 2035. The battery manufacturing and energy storage sector is the primary growth engine for HNBR compounds, driven by the global build-out of gigafactories and grid-scale storage projects. HNBR seals are critical in electrode coating and electrolyte filling equipment, where resistance to aggressive electrolytes and thermal cycling is essential.
