artigo.texto: Data center developers, investors, and communities across California face a changing development landscape as new requirements impact some of the industry’s most consequential land use and infrastructure issues. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a package of seven bills (AB 1577 – Bauer-Kahan; AB 2383 – Zbur; AB 2469 – Papan; AB 2619 – Papan; SB 886 – Padilla and McNerney; SB 887 – Padilla; SB 1168 – McNerney) on September 21 addressing the electricity, water, and environmental impacts of data centers. The new laws impose additional reporting requirements, address responsibility for electric grid and water infrastructure costs, and establish conditions data center projects must meet to qualify for streamlined judicial review under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). But the significance for developers extends beyond the individual requirements contained in the legislation. At the state level, California is establishing a framework seeking to address questions about power capacity, water supply, infrastructure, environmental review, and community impacts. At the same time, various cities and counties are taking their own approaches to data center development, creating a patchwork of local regulatory landscapes that can vary considerably from one jurisdiction to another. The result is an increasingly complicated development environment. While a site may appear suitable from a real estate or engineering perspective, depending on the local rules, the entitlement process can vary from straightforward to incredibly complex. Two near-identical sites in different locations may face entirely dissimilar entitlement paths depending on the jurisdiction’s rules, available infrastructure, and local response to data center development. Early diligence is thus key to a successful data center project. According to the state, the legislative package is intended to provide communities with more information about proposed projects while protecting utility customers from costs associated with data center growth. Specifically, the seven bills address data centers through three closely related areas: electricity, water, and environmental impacts. On electricity, the legislation addresses grid upgrade costs, energy procurement, and rate structures. The state says the new laws are intended to prevent costs associated with serving data centers from being shifted to other ratepayers, and the laws require projects to pay for necessary grid upgrades and comply with California energy procurement requirements. For water, proposed data centers must provide information to local governments and water suppliers about water use, supply, efficiency, and drought planning, and the projects will be responsible for upgrades needed to provide water service. Regarding environmental review, the legislation clarifies that data centers are not categorically exempt from CEQA. At the same time, the legislation also allows for expedited judicial review for qualifying data centers that meet certain environmental requirements. Projects must demonstrate that they meet state standards involving energy, water, and fuel consumption and will not shift costs to ratepayers before qualifying for that treatment. For developers, the new legislation means that infrastructure planning must become part of site selection and entitlement strategy early in the process. For example, data centers are energy-intensive, with the largest data centers typically including onsite power generation. However, proper energy planning also requires understanding available natural gas supplies, grid connectivity requirements with the local power provider, if desired, and a host of related regulatory requirements. California’s new framework is intended to prevent data center costs from being shifted to other ratepayers, meaning that when deciding whether a project is feasible, developers must consider all aspects of energy costs and availability early in the planning process. Water presents a similar issue. The new disclosure requirements mean that developers should be prepared to address anticipated water use and its relationship to local supply, efficiency, and drought planning. For developers evaluating competing sites, the relevant questions extend beyond whether water service exists. The availability and reliability of that supply, anticipated demand, and cost of necessary improvements may all affect project feasibility. CEQA adds another layer. The new legislation makes clear that developers should be prepared to engage in robust environmental review for virtually all data center projects, and that the potential for streamlined judicial review is deeply intertwined with questions about energy, water, fuel consumption, and infrastructure costs. Taken together, the laws reinforce a broader trend in data center development: data centers are no longer primarily a technology issue. They involve significant land use and infrastructure issues, with decisions about where and how facilities are developed increasingly tied to the capacity and priorities of the communities around them. Thus, California’s new laws make it clear that infrastructure and land use analysis should not be treated as separate tracks. They increasingly need to inform one another early in the strategy process. The new state laws establish a broader framework, but they do not create a uniform entitlement process across California. Developers must still navigate the land use requirements of the city or county in which a project is proposed. That local landscape is evolving rapidly. Some jurisdictions are reconsidering how, where, and even if data centers should be permitted, while others are continuing to process projects under existing rules. artigo.texto: O Atlético-MG fechou uma parceria na área de data center com a Huawei. A empresa chinesa será fornecedora de servidores, soluções de armazenamento de dados e sistemas de backup para a Arena MRV, estádio do clube mineiro, em Belo Horizonte. O contrato é de cinco anos e a instalação da infraestrutura de dados está prevista para começar em novembro. A implantação e o acompanhamento da operação serão feitos pela SYX-AI, integradora parceira tecnológica da Huawei no Brasil. O clube informou que, a partir desse contrato, a Arena MRV passará a operar integralmente com tecnologia da Huawei na área de infraestrutura de dados. Como parte do acordo, o vice-presidente de Negócios do Atlético-MG, Márcio Freire, e o diretor de Tecnologia, Leandro Evangelista, visitaram instalações da fornecedora na China. Com base na experiência, os executivos indicam que, nos próximos anos, soluções de Inteligência Artificial (IA) podem ser incorporadas à operação do estádio, como para monitoramento do público que frequenta os jogos de futebol. Segundo o Atlético-MG, além da infraestrutura tecnológica, a parceria poderá ser estendida para atividades relacionadas ao futebol, como análise de desempenho, dados e scouting. "Estamos sempre nos atualizando, e a Huawei está muito à frente no que se refere à tecnologia. Ficamos muito satisfeitos com essa oportunidade. Foi um momento de conhecer as estruturas da Huawei, as cidades, entender o que eles estão realizando e avaliar como podemos agregar essas tecnologias ao futebol e à Arena MRV", afirma Evangelista, em nota.

artigo.texto: WEG investe R$ 330 mi em fábrica de baterias A WEG, multinacional catarinense do setor eletroeletrônico, anunciou nesta sexta-feira (25) a ampliação do projeto de sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, denominado BESS, em construção em Itajaí, no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina. O investimento total foi elevado para R$ 330 milhões, consolidando a aposta da companhia no mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. A decisão ocorre em um momento estratégico, às vésperas do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, previsto para dezembro de 2026. A empresa destacou que a ampliação do projeto da planta em Itajaí faz parte da estratégia da companhia de apoiar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. O movimento reflete a confiança da WEG na expansão da demanda por soluções que integrem fontes renováveis à matriz elétrica, um desafio crescente para o setor energético nacional. Investimento reforça aposta em armazenamento O novo aporte eleva o compromisso financeiro da WEG com a unidade fabril, que já estava em construção. A atualização do projeto incorpora maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, o que permitirá ampliar a capacidade produtiva da planta. Com isso, a companhia busca se posicionar de forma competitiva para atender à demanda projetada pelo leilão de reserva de capacidade e por outros segmentos do mercado. O BESS (Battery Energy Storage System, ou Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias) é uma tecnologia essencial para os sistemas elétricos modernos. Ele permite armazenar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade — como em dias ensolarados ou com ventos fortes — e disponibilizá-la quando a geração é insuficiente ou a demanda é alta. Essa flexibilidade contribui para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico, maior eficiência operacional e melhor aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos. A decisão da WEG de ampliar o projeto também sinaliza uma leitura positiva do ambiente regulatório brasileiro. O Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento, marcado para dezembro de 2026, é apontado como um marco para o setor, pois deve criar um mercado formal para sistemas de armazenamento em larga escala. A empresa, no entanto, não detalhou projeções de receita ou participação esperada nesse certame. Impacto para a indústria e comércio Para empresários e comerciantes do interior paulista, o movimento da WEG pode ter reflexos indiretos relevantes. A expansão da capacidade produtiva de baterias tende a impulsionar a cadeia de fornecedores de componentes eletrônicos, serviços de engenharia e logística, gerando oportunidades de negócios para pequenas e médias empresas. Além disso, a consolidação do armazenamento de energia pode reduzir custos operacionais para indústrias e comércios que buscam maior previsibilidade no fornecimento elétrico. Especialistas do setor apontam que o armazenamento em baterias é peça-chave para a integração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, que são intermitentes por natureza. Com sistemas BESS, empresas podem armazenar energia excedente gerada em horários de pico de produção e utilizá-la em momentos de tarifas mais altas, otimizando a conta de luz. Esse benefício é especialmente atrativo para o agronegócio e a indústria de transformação, segmentos fortes na região noroeste paulista. A WEG não divulgou cronograma atualizado para a conclusão das obras da fábrica em Itajaí, tampouco a capacidade produtiva final após a ampliação. A fonte não detalhou se haverá geração de empregos diretos adicionais em decorrência do novo investimento. No entanto, a elevação do aporte sugere um compromisso de longo prazo com a produção local de sistemas de armazenamento, o que pode fortalecer a competitividade da indústria nacional no setor. Contexto do leilão de reserva O primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento Nacional, previsto para dezembro de 2026, é aguardado como um divisor de águas para o mercado de baterias no Brasil. O certame deverá contratar potência e energia de sistemas de armazenamento, criando um fluxo de receita previsível para os investidores. A WEG, ao ampliar sua fábrica antes do leilão, demonstra intenção de participar ativamente desse novo mercado. Para as empresas do interior paulista, o leilão pode abrir espaço para projetos de armazenamento associados a usinas solares e eólicas, muitos deles localizados no estado de São Paulo. A redução de custos de baterias, impulsionada pela produção local, pode viabilizar sistemas de menor porte para comércios e indústrias, ampliando o acesso a essa tecnologia. A fonte não detalhou, porém, se a WEG pretende comercializar soluções BESS diretamente para o varejo ou apenas para grandes geradores e utilities. Em resumo, o aumento do investimento da WEG em sua fábrica de baterias em Itajaí reforça a tendência de crescimento do armazenamento de energia no Brasil. A iniciativa deve gerar efeitos positivos na cadeia produtiva e abrir novas oportunidades para negócios que dependem de energia confiável e de custo competitivo. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é o valor do investimento da WEG na megafábrica de baterias em Santa Catarina? A WEG elevou o investimento para R$ 330 milhões na megafábrica de baterias em Itajaí, Santa Catarina. Onde a WEG está construindo sua nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias? A nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, chamada BESS, está em construção em Itajaí, no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina. Qual é o papel do BESS nos sistemas elétricos modernos, segundo a WEG? O BESS permite armazenar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade e disponibilizá-la quando necessário, contribuindo para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico, maior eficiência operacional e aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos, especialmente na integração de fontes renováveis como solar e eólica.

artigo.texto: NH Investment & Securities Signs Carbon Credit Cooperation Agreement with Trinity Aviation for Domestic and International Markets Cooperation in Supplying CORSIA Credits and Consignment Trading of Domestic Emission Permits Collaborating to Support Airlines Responding to Carbon Regulations NH Investment & Securities and Trinity Aviation signed a carbon market business agreement on the 21st at Trinity Aviation headquarters located in Gangseo-gu, Seoul. After the signing ceremony, Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities (right), and Dongbin Seo, Executive Director of Management Support at Trinity Aviation (left), took a commemorative photo. Photo by NH Investment & Securities View original image NH Investment & Securities announced on September 28 that it had signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Trinity Aviation on September 21 for "mutual cooperation concerning the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and the Emissions Trading Scheme for greenhouse gases." This agreement marks the first case in which a domestic securities firm and an airline company have established a strategic partnership encompassing the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic greenhouse gas emission permits. Trinity Aviation plans to align with the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s aviation sector carbon reduction policy and the implementation direction of CORSIA, by linking NH Investment & Securities’ expertise in the carbon market and financial capacity to its own needs for procurement of emission permits. The company emphasized that the significance of this MOU lies in connecting airlines’ acquisition of emission credits and cost management for procurement to the specialized services of a financial institution. Purchasing emission credits requires not only consideration of the necessary quantity and timing, but also a careful review of market prices and trading conditions. Both companies will collaborate to establish stable and efficient procurement plans based on demand information and market analysis. As part of the collaboration, Trinity Aviation will first secure 20,000 tons of CORSIA credits through NH Investment & Securities, and plans to obtain at least 10% of the emissions that need to be offset, in stages, before the Phase 1 settlement deadline in January 2028. The two companies will use this transaction as a starting point for cooperating on CORSIA credit supply, sharing information such as projected mandatory quantity and procurement timing to strengthen the foundation for mid- to long-term procurement. The companies will also cooperate on establishing and operating a consignment trading framework for the domestic Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS). NH Investment & Securities will support Trinity Aviation’s smooth trading of carbon credits through its proprietary consignment trading system for emission permits, and provide specialized information on market analysis and policy trends. As a result, Trinity Aviation will be able to establish a systematic support system that covers both domestic emissions trading and procurement of CORSIA credits. Gunhoo Park, Head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, stated, "This agreement is meaningful as a strategic collaboration model that connects a securities company’s expertise in carbon finance with the real emission credit needs of airlines. We will support airlines’ stable acquisition of emission credits based on the supply of CORSIA credits and consignment trading of domestic credits, and expand customized carbon finance services that help respond to procurement costs and market fluctuations." artigo.texto: BYD unveils its first heavy-duty electric semi and it packs 1,000HP, charges in 20 minutes and carries a huge battery warranty Published on Sep 27, 2026 at 6:04 PM (UTC+4) by Ben Thompson Last updated on Sep 27, 2026 at 6:04 PM (UTC+4) Edited by Mason Jones BYD has unveiled its first heavy-duty electric semi, and it can be charged in 20 minutes. And that’s not the only impressive stat attached to the ET44. Capable of hauling 44-ton combinations and packing 1,000HP, there’s no questioning the power of this new offering from BYD. It’s enough to make us ask – should Tesla be worried? How BYD is on the rise If you’ve spent any length of time reading automotive news these past few years, the rip-roaring success of BYD won’t have passed you by. The Chinese carmaker has been flexing on its competitors for a long while now, whether it’s charging EVs in freezing cold temperatures or getting its SUVs to drive on three wheels. And that’s not forgetting their sales figures, which have been soaring around the world, from South America to Australia. With their back-to-back successes, it’d only make sense that the company would be looking to expand. And what better way to take on its primary rival – Tesla – than by putting out a semi truck? As you will undoubtedly know, the Tesla Semi has been making headlines all over the place, whether it’s being driven by Jay Leno or generating buzz for the weight of its battery. But after all that, is it about to get upstaged by the ET44? Let’s take a closer look. The ET44 is a heavy-duty semi to be reckoned with BYD has said the ET44 is capable of hauling a full 44-ton combination. It can’t be a coincidence that this is the maximum payload allowed on European roads. It also surely can’t be a coincidence that this is four tons more than what the Tesla Semi is capable of. Powered by an LFP Blade Battery, the ET44 can reach a peak power of 735kW (just under 1,000HP). It’s not just in physical capabilities that this semi poses a threat to Tesla – it’s also expected to be cheaper. It’s anticipated to arrive in Europe by 2027, with expansion in Canada, Australia, and the UK likely to follow. But it’s not such a clear-cut clean sweep for the ET44, as noted by YouTuber The Electric Viking. “[The Tesla Semi] charges at up to 1.2 megawatt with 548 or 822 kWh packs. So [BYD] has the charging edge and Tesla clearly has the bigger battery and will get significantly more range,” he explained. “The headline here is BYD’s own megawatt chargers. This truck pulls more than 1.5 megawatt and goes from 20 to 80% in about 20 minutes. So, it’s the fastest charging truck. “The real story here though, is BYD turning up with the truck, the battery, the megawatt charger, and the financing all under the same roof. Every other truck maker is waiting on someone else to build the chargers.” When asked whether he thought the ET44 posed a threat to the Tesla Semi, he gave a nuanced answer. “The short answer is that the ETT44 is the first serious competitor the Tesla Semi has faced in Europe and no threat at all in America — and even in Europe I expect the Semi to sell better. Tariffs decide the American half of that before the trucks do,” Sam Evans, The Electric Viking, told Supercar Blondie. “The ETT44 is a brand-new truck with no track record anywhere, no European factory named, and no customer deliveries until the second quarter of 2027. “Add the fact that the Semi enters Europe duty-free and BYD’s truck doesn’t, and I expect the Tesla Semi to outsell the ETT44 in Europe, not the other way round. “What BYD has really done is give Tesla its first proper competitor — a cheaper truck with a longer warranty and a one-stop package — and that will keep Tesla’s European pricing honest. “That’s good for every haulier in Europe, but it doesn’t make the ETT44 the better truck.” Timeline of BYD 1995: Founded by Wang Chuanfu with 20 employees, initially manufacturing nickel-cadmium batteries to compete with Japanese suppliers. 2000 – 2002: Becomes China’s first lithium-ion battery supplier to Motorola and Nokia. The company is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. 2003: Acquires Xi’an Tsinchuan Auto, to pair its battery technology with vehicle manufacturing. 2005: Releases its first mass-produced ICE vehicle, the F3 2008: First plug-in hybrid, the F3DM, is launched. 2013 – 2015: Introduces the ‘Dynasty’ line of plug-in hybrid and electric vehicles. 2022: The company stops producing ICE vehicles to focus on BEVs and PHEVs, while launching global expansion across Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America. 2023 – 2024: Surpasses 3 million NEV sales and overtakes Tesla in quarterly global pure-EV sales. 2025 – 2026: Expands further, opening manufacturing hubs across Brazil, Thailand, and Europe. Ben joined Supercar Blondie in February 2025 after being published by international organizations including LADbible, The Sun, the New York Post, and the Daily Mail. He covers supercars, rare and collectible vehicles, aviation, luxury assets, and the fascinating people behind them. His reporting has explored everything from seven-figure supercars and historic Ferrari collections to unusual aircraft adventures and extraordinary automotive discoveries from around the world. Ben has also gained first-hand insight into vehicle craftsmanship and customization, including visiting specialist workshops to see bespoke vehicles up close.

artigo.texto: Arevon Energy marks construction milestone at 250 MW Cormorant battery storage project in Daly City, California Arevon Energy hit a construction milestone at its Cormorant Energy Storage Project in Daly City, California, on September 16, 2026. The celebration brought state and local officials, project partners, labor and business leaders, and community members to the site of what will become a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage facility — big enough to power 321,000 homes for up to four hours at peak demand. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2027. Arevon marks construction progress at Daly City battery storage site The September 16 milestone wasn’t just a photo op. It pulled together a genuinely broad group — state and local officials, California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) representatives, labor and business leaders, community members — all there to recognize how far the project has come since construction kicked off in March 2026. Arevon CEO Justin Johnson put the project’s purpose plainly: “Cormorant represents the kind of critical energy infrastructure California needs to meet growing electricity demand while strengthening grid reliability.” Store power when there’s plenty of it, deliver it when the grid needs it most. That’s the whole idea. Cormorant is a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage project in Daly City, California, developed and operated by Arevon in partnership with Primoris Services Corporation. Daly City Mayor Glenn Sylvester echoed that framing, noting the project positions the city as an active contributor to statewide infrastructure goals — not merely a host community. Commercial operations remain on track for 2027. Project expanded and backed by long-term power agreement with MCE Cormorant didn’t start out at its current scale. Originally designed at 188 MW/752 MWh, it was later bumped up to 250 MW/1,000 MWh. That expansion came with a key partner: MCE, a community electricity provider serving more than 1.8 million residents and businesses across Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, and Solano counties, which contracted for the additional capacity under a long-term offtake agreement. The partnership goes beyond buying power. MCE’s Acting CEO Vicken Kasarjian noted that more than $500,000 from the contract will flow directly to local community programs. “This project has a direct community benefit,” he said — pointing to built-in funding for initiatives supporting Bay Area residents. On the construction side, Arevon is working with Primoris Services Corporation’s Renewables group, and at peak the project employs around 175 workers. Grid reliability and environmental benefits expected over project lifetime Battery storage projects like Cormorant absorb electricity during off-peak hours — when solar generation is high and demand is lower — then release it when the grid is under stress. That charge-and-dispatch cycle is what makes storage a reliability tool, not just a clean energy one. Cormorant uses lithium iron phosphate battery technology, which carries a strong safety record and a long operating life. Both matter for a project expected to run for decades. Over its lifetime, the facility is projected to avoid 191,800 U.S. tons of CO₂ annually and save more than 4.2 billion gallons of water — figures that reflect displaced emissions and the water savings compared to conventional thermal generation. The CPUC sees projects like this as essential. Energy Division Director Molly Sterkel said the agency expects more than 20 GW of new clean resources to come online by 2032, with battery storage described as “a critical part of that effort” — particularly for filling the reliability gap when solar drops off in the evening and demand stays high. Economic impact and community investment in Daly City Beyond the grid, Cormorant is expected to generate more than $73 million in property tax revenue over its lifetime, flowing to local schools, infrastructure, and public services. That’s a long-term fiscal benefit that outlasts the construction phase by a wide margin. Arevon has built relationships with more than a dozen local organizations throughout the project’s development. Partners include Bayshore Elementary School District, Jefferson Union High School District, Daly City Partnership, Pilipino Bayanihan Resource Center, Bayshore Community Center, Pacific Islands Together, and John’s Closet, among others. The company’s involvement has spanned donations, sponsorships, scholarships, memberships, and volunteer work — a range that signals sustained engagement rather than a one-time check. Mike Stancil, Executive Director of the Daly City Partnership, described Arevon as “a caring and compassionate corporate partner.” Arevon itself operates more than 6.3 GW of solar and energy storage projects across 18 states and holds the No. 1 developer ranking in Solar Power World’s 2026 Top Solar Contractors List for California. Cormorant is one of several recent California storage projects the company has brought through development and into construction. A long-term agreement with MCE Cormorant is a 250 MW/1,000 MWh battery storage project in Daly City, California, developed and operated by Arevon in partnership with Primoris Services Corporation. It operates under a long-term agreement with MCE, which serves the broader Bay Area, and is expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. The project can power 321,000 homes for up to four hours during peak demand. Projected outcomes include avoiding 191,800 U.S. tons of CO₂ annually, saving more than 4.2 billion gallons of water over its lifetime, and generating more than $73 million in local property tax revenue. More than $500,000 from the MCE contract is earmarked for community programs in the region. artigo.texto: BYD Says Its New Solid-State EV Battery Tech Is Nearly Ready For The Open Road Switching from lithium-ion to solid-state batteries promises to extend the range and charging speeds of electric vehicles, and Chinese car maker BYD believes it's in a "leading position" to commercialize the technology. BYD's Executive Vice President Stella Li shared the claim in a recent interview with Carwow's Spanish outlet, alongside the news that BYD would release its first car with a solid-state battery in 2027. "Talking about solid-state batteries, BYD is in the leading position," Li said. "We're in the leading position for commercialization and technology. So to prove that, next year, we have one model that will be the first one with that technology." Li's comments further confirm plans shared by Sun Huajun, the Chief Technology Officer of BYD's battery subsidiary FinDreams, at a battery conference in February 2025. At the time, Sun said BYD would offer its first demonstration and installation of solid-state batteries in 2027 before the technology enters mass production around 2030, CarNewsChina reports. While that means people will be able to buy cars with the company's sulfide solid-state batteries, that doesn't mean its traditional lithium batteries will be phased out, BYD Chief Scientist Lian Yubo shared at the same conference. "Solid-state batteries will be mainly used in high-end models, empowering each other with lithium iron phosphate batteries, and used in vehicles of different levels," Lian said. In comparison to lithium-ion batteries, which move ions between positive and negative terminals through a liquid solution of dissolved lithium salts, solid-state batteries replace the liquid with solid electrolytes made from oxides, polymers or sulfides (the kind BYD is developing). Solid electrolytes give solid-state batteries higher energy density, which opens up the possibility of smaller, lighter batteries and a longer range on a single charge. Solid-state batteries are also theoretically safer because they're far less prone to catching fire and they're able to operate at extreme temperatures, an issue current lithium-ion batteries struggle with. Advertisement The problem with using the battery technology as it exists now is cost, which is why BYD suggests you'll see its solid-state batteries on more expensive models first, like possibly a future version of its Denza Z. The company is one of several car makers planning to ship a vehicle with solid-state batteries in the next few years. For example, Toyota committed to offering cars with solid-state batteries by 2027 or 2028; Mercedes-Benz began testing a solid-state EQS model and shared that it would ship the technology before the end of the decade; and Stellantis began road testing a solid-state Dodge Charger in 2026. Earlier this year, Honda struck up a new partnership with QuantumScape to develop solid-state batteries it hopes will help it reach carbon neutrality by 2050. The potential for solid-state battery technology is exciting, but most car makers are only in the first leg of the race. artigo.texto: - China has prioritized breakthroughs in all-solid-state technologies to accelerate the roll-out of next-generation batteries. - The plan also calls for improving sodium battery performance and supporting corporate mergers and restructuring. China aims to achieve initial large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, accelerating the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Monday released its new battery industry development plan for the fifteenth five-year period, setting a roadmap for 2026 through 2030. The document, dated September 14, was jointly issued by 7 government agencies, including MIIT, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Transport. The plan calls for steady growth in China's new battery industry through 2030, alongside breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. Beyond the all-solid-state battery deployment target, it sets goals for long-life lithium batteries to reach 15,000 charge-discharge cycles and for leading manufacturers to achieve product defect rates at the parts-per-billion (PPB) level. All-solid-state batteries are a key technological priority. The document calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, focusing on improving ionic conductivity and cycling stability while optimizing costs. Specific measures include improving interfacial contact, extending cycle life, advancing pressure-system engineering and scaling up production of high-performance solid electrolytes. The plan also calls for combining high-voltage, high-capacity cathode materials with new lithium-metal-based anodes and anode-free designs, while developing manufacturing equipment such as isostatic presses for solid-state batteries. China plans to build a supply system centered on lithium batteries, complemented by sodium and flow batteries, while strengthening its ability to commercialize all-solid-state and ultrafast-charging batteries. For sodium batteries, the document emphasizes cost, safety and resource availability advantages, calling for the development of cold-resistant, high-energy-density power batteries and energy storage batteries with long cycle lives. Industry consolidation and supply chain security are another focus. The document supports corporate mergers and restructuring and calls for faster exploration and development of domestic lithium, cobalt and other mineral resources. On recycling, the plan requires companies to establish used-battery collection systems aligned with their sales volumes. It also encourages them to build recycling capacity in major export markets where conditions permit. The document proposes a digital identity management system for products including new energy vehicle (NEV) power batteries, exploring internationally accepted battery passport arrangements and promoting mutual recognition of carbon footprint data. The battery plan follows China's September 11 release of its fifteenth five-year development plan for the intelligent connected NEV industry, which targets a 70% share for NEVs in domestic new passenger vehicle sales by 2030. The earlier automotive plan also called for tighter management of power battery production capacity. The latest battery plan further defines priorities for technology development, manufacturing upgrades and broader applications.

artigo.texto: Li Auto's Li Xiang Responds to "De-CATL" Debate: In-House Development Isn't About Opposing Suppliers, But Deep Collaboration Li Auto (02015.HK) Chairman and CEO Li Xiang published a public statement on September 28 responding to the recently heated industry debate over "de-CATL-ization." He stated clearly that interpreting in-house development as "de-XX-ization" and positioning oneself against suppliers reflects zero-sum thinking, and that Li Auto has never used such an approach to define its self-development strategy. Li Xiang emphasized in his post that outstanding Chinese smart EV companies would never define their strategies with such a narrow mindset. He cited examples: Apple's A-series chips, Nvidia's and Qualcomm's flagship chips are mostly designed in-house and manufactured by TSMC; Tesla's self-developed batteries are produced in collaboration with CATL (300750.SZ), LG, and Sunwoda (300207.SZ). This model has not weakened TSMC, CATL, or Sunwoda—it has made them stronger. "Automakers define product experience, system architecture, and quality standards more deeply, while partners leverage their professional capabilities in engineering, manufacturing processes, and scaled delivery," Li Xiang wrote. "A good OEM-supplier relationship is not about who replaces whom, but about making products better through deeper collaboration." The Threefold Logic of Self-Development Li Xiang further elaborated on three core reasons Li Auto insists on deep battery self-development. First, to deliver user experiences that lead industry standards and build solutions for unmet needs first. He noted that users don't care about underlying electrochemical terminology—they care about whether range holds up, how long long-distance charging takes, whether performance stays stable in extreme heat or cold, and how safety baselines are guaranteed. From the industry's first extended-range large battery to the physics-defying 5C ultra-fast charging, to improvements in LFP battery low-temperature performance, state-of-charge accuracy, and longevity, these hardcore battery metric breakthroughs often have no ready-made solutions on the market. Second, to make the battery an integrated part of the intelligent vehicle, achieving a "1+1>2" whole-vehicle experience. Li Xiang believes the battery is by no means an isolated component—it and the vehicle must form a complete living organism with full end-to-end connectivity. Deep integration of cells, PACK, BMS, thermal management, electric drive, and vehicle control not only improves system-wide safety and quality, but also enables continuous OTA evolution years after delivery—charging strategies can be optimized, energy management can be refined, and low-temperature performance can keep improving. Third, full-lifecycle data connectivity so users don't have to pay for supply-chain division of labor. Li Xiang stated that the physical battery must ultimately become a data battery; connecting battery and vehicle data represents a higher level of battery specialization. The value of this data connectivity lies in: any微小 anomaly during production can trigger early warnings and be resolved before installation and delivery; problems can be solved before users even sense potential risks. This also ensures absolute consistency in after-sales service and repair standards. Thanking "Comrade-in-Arms" CATL In his post, Li Xiang specifically mentioned the partnership with CATL. He revealed that Li Auto established its battery R&D team back in 2015, and when certain product definitions were doubted by everyone, it was CATL that collaborated on joint development and turned the impossible into reality. "Here, I want to especially thank our comrade-in-arms CATL. It was Li Auto's deep product definition, our joint development, and CATL's strong support that helped Li Auto create products that continue to lead the industry," Li Xiang wrote. The context for this statement is that as more automakers begin in-house development and manufacturing of core components like batteries, views such as "de-CATL-ization" have emerged in the market, sparking considerable controversy. Li Xiang's response aims to clarify: self-development does not mean cutting ties with suppliers, nor does it mean replacing them. "Li Auto never wants to 'de-XX-ize' anything. On the contrary, we welcome every outstanding partner to achieve deep integration with Li Auto and together push user experience to the extreme," Li Xiang stated. "Times are changing, and the only standard by which we evaluate change is whether it can create greater value for users: delivering better products, providing better services, and bringing better experiences. Changing for users is the ultimate starting point of all of Li Auto's choices." The Pace of Self-Developed Battery Rollout Li Auto plans to equip all models with self-developed batteries once production capacity successfully ramps up. Li Xiang previously stated that in the long term, batteries and chips will be the company's most important technological barriers and moats. "Self-development represents our hope to hold future-facing core technology barriers in our own hands, like Apple and Huawei." From an industry perspective, Li Xiang's statement reflects the deep restructuring currently underway in China's new energy vehicle supply chain. The trend of automakers extending upstream and self-developing core components is increasingly evident, and how to balance self-development with external supply chain relationships is becoming a strategic question every automaker must answer. Li Xiang's answer: self-development is not about becoming an island, but about pulling the best partners closer and together making the user experience better. This stance is consistent with Li Auto's long-standing product-first philosophy. artigo.texto: Gotion High-tech Teams Up with Volkswagen on €3.2 Billion Lithium Battery Bases in Europe and Africa Gotion High-tech (002074.SZ) has taken a decisive step in its overseas power battery strategy. After the market close on September 28, the Chinese battery maker announced plans to jointly invest approximately €3.222 billion (approximately $3.7 billion) with PowerCo, the battery subsidiary of Volkswagen Group, to form joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco for lithium battery and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode material production. The same day, a wholly owned subsidiary of Gotion also signed engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts with PowerCo Spain worth a combined €1.094 billion (approximately $1.2 billion). According to the announcement, Gotion High-tech and its wholly owned subsidiaries Gotion High-Tech (HK) Limited, Gotion GmbH and Gotion Power Africa S.A.S. plan to sign an investment agreement with Volkswagen AG and its wholly owned subsidiaries PowerCo SE and Power Holdco Lux S.A. to establish three joint ventures in Valencia, Spain; Šurany, Slovakia; and Kenitra, Morocco. Total project investment is estimated at approximately €3.222 billion (approximately $3.7 billion), of which the Gotion side will contribute approximately €1.598 billion (approximately $1.8 billion) and the PowerCo side approximately €1.624 billion (approximately $1.8 billion). Gotion's contribution will be funded by its own capital and self-raised funds. The three projects differ in capacity planning and equity structure. The Valencia JV hosts the largest lithium battery project, with planned annual capacity of 29.1 GWh and total investment of approximately €2.262 billion (approximately $2.6 billion); upon completion, Gotion will hold 49% and PowerCo 51%, with PowerCo as the controlling party. The Šurany JV will run an 8.4 GWh lithium battery project with total investment of approximately €480 million (approximately $546.3 million); Gotion will hold 51% and PowerCo 49%, with Gotion as the controlling party. The Morocco JV focuses on the upstream materials segment, with planned annual capacity of 100,000 tonnes of LFP cathode material and total investment of approximately €480 million (approximately $546.3 million); Gotion will likewise hold 51% and control the venture. The capacity and investment structure of the three projects is summarized below: The two European battery plants have combined planned annual capacity of 37.5 GWh, and cathode material produced by the Morocco project will be prioritized for supply to these two plants. The equity arrangements form a clear complementary structure: the Valencia base is controlled by PowerCo, deeply integrating Gotion into Volkswagen Group's core European cell supply system; the Slovakia and Morocco projects are controlled by Gotion, helping the company establish self-directed manufacturing footholds in the European and African markets. Beyond equity stakes, the announcement disclosed several arrangements material to the transaction: the Valencia project does not involve a newly established company — instead, the Gotion side will acquire a 49% stake in the existing PowerCo Spain through a capital increase, with PowerCo retaining control after the transaction. The construction scope of all three projects excludes land and factory buildings, and each project is expected to take no more than five years to build. The announcement also clarified that cells produced by the two European battery plants will prioritize meeting Volkswagen Group's demand in Europe, with specific purchase volumes and supply guarantee arrangements to be determined in subsequent formal agreements. In addition, the investment agreement has not yet been signed; the plan was approved by Gotion's board of directors on September 28 but still requires shareholder approval and government clearances in China and abroad. Beyond the equity investment, the EPC contracts add another business dimension to the partnership. Gotion Spain, a wholly owned subsidiary of Gotion High-tech, plans to sign with PowerCo Spain a Phase 1 drying room turnkey contract and a Phase 2 EPC contract for the 29.1 GWh Valencia lithium battery project, with a combined contract value of €1.094 billion (approximately $1.2 billion). The Phase 1 contract is valued at €295 million (approximately $335.7 million) and the Phase 2 contract at €799 million (approximately $909.3 million), both on a fixed lump-sum basis. This means Gotion will participate not only as a shareholder but also as the EPC contractor, directly generating construction-phase revenue. Because Volkswagen (China) Investment Co., Ltd. holds 24.28% of Gotion High-tech and is its largest shareholder, Volkswagen Group and its subsidiaries constitute related legal persons of the company, making both matters related-party transactions. The announcement shows that connected directors abstained from voting, and the relevant proposals still require shareholder approval and government clearances in China and abroad. artigo.texto: CATL's Choco-Swap Network Tops 2,500 Stations in China Ahead of National Day Free Trial CATL (03750.HK) subsidiary Choco-Swap hit a critical juncture on the eve of China's National Day holiday. With the official completion of the Lanzhou Chengguan North Binhe East Road station, Choco-Swap's cumulative nationwide station count surpassed 2,520 as of September 29, covering 200 cities across 31 provinces, with nearly 20,000 brand-new CATL batteries deployed into inventory. From September 30 to October 7, Choco-Swap will launch a "99-Second Swap Across China" free battery-swap trial program, giving new energy vehicle (NEV) owners a chance to experience the efficiency advantage of the swapping model during peak travel season. Network Expansion: From Core Cities to County-Level Penetration Since the start of this year, Choco-Swap has maintained an industry-leading expansion pace. First- and second-tier cities in China now have full coverage, small and medium-sized cities account for more than 80% of stations, and over a quarter of the cities where stations are located rank first in the industry for station density. The network layout is spreading outward from core hub cities in contiguous clusters, penetrating deeply into the "capillary" markets of small and medium-sized cities and county-level areas. The highway swap network is breaking new ground simultaneously. According to plan, 1,000 highway swap stations will be deployed between 2026 and 2027, creating an "11 vertical, 9 horizontal" highway swap backbone grid, aiming for an average of one pair of swap stations every 100 kilometers, with support for multi-brand and multi-model sharing. Battery Management and Technical Safeguards On the battery side, a full-lifecycle digital management and digital-twin monitoring system tracks and evaluates the health status of every battery in inventory in real time, ensuring the safety and stability of swap services. The dual-track network buildout—urban and highway—is accelerating in tandem. The breadth and density of urban station coverage, combined with the planned highway backbone grid, constitute the two core growth curves for Choco-Swap in the charging infrastructure space. Industry Impact and Competitive Landscape Battery swapping, as one of the key pathways for NEV energy replenishment, is transitioning from early pilot exploration to large-scale deployment. Leveraging its cost and technology advantages on the battery manufacturing side, CATL is deeply binding its swap network with battery asset operations, creating differentiated competitiveness distinct from third-party swap operators. The launch of the free swap program during the National Day holiday serves both as a concentrated showcase of network capability and as a market strategy to drive user awareness and cultivate swapping habits. artigo.texto: Seven Chinese ministries issue 15th Five-Year Plan for next-gen batteries: accelerating all-solid-state battery industrialization, improving recycling systems Seven Chinese government agencies led by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology jointly issued the "15th Five-Year Plan for the New-Type Battery Industry" on September 28, laying out arrangements across two main fronts—technology breakthroughs and recycling utilization: on one hand accelerating breakthroughs in all-solid-state battery industrialization technology and making forward-looking arrangements for next-generation battery systems; on the other hand improving the spent battery recycling and utilization system to promote efficient use of recycled resources. The plan calls for deepening research on fundamental and forward-looking scientific questions in new-type batteries, and strengthening original innovation and disruptive technology breakthroughs. It promotes collaborative process innovation across battery materials, structural design, manufacturing technology, and system integration, aiming to improve intrinsic safety, energy and power density, structural strength, and lightweighting. For all-solid-state batteries, the plan explicitly focuses on improving ionic conductivity and cycling stability, optimizing costs, and other key directions to accelerate breakthroughs in industrialization technology. It also makes forward-looking arrangements for next-generation battery systems including new alkali metal-ion batteries, multivalent-ion batteries, metal-air/sulfur batteries, multifunctional composite structural batteries, and nuclear batteries. In the recycling segment, the plan requires implementation of the extended producer responsibility system, pushing companies to establish spent battery recycling systems—whether self-built or commissioned—that match their product sales volumes, and accelerating the construction and operation of recycling service outlets. Specific measures include: supporting R&D and industrial application of technologies and equipment for refined dismantling of new-type batteries, low-cost utilization, and efficient extraction of valuable elements; improving the refinement and automation levels of spent battery dismantling, crushing, sorting, and smelting processes; guiding localities to rationally allocate processing capacity commensurate with regional spent battery generation volumes, and promoting resource concentration toward competitive enterprises. Additionally, the plan proposes guiding companies to deploy spent battery comprehensive utilization capacity in major export markets for new-type batteries where conditions permit, in order to enhance resource security capabilities. artigo.texto: POSTECH Researchers Uncover Mechanism Behind Manganese-Based Cathode That Gains Capacity With Repeated Charging South Korean researchers at POSTECH have for the first time uncovered the operating principle behind a next-generation battery material that gains usable capacity as it undergoes repeated charge and discharge cycles. The team demonstrated experimentally that internal structural changes—long viewed solely as a culprit in battery degradation—can be precisely controlled to simultaneously boost both performance and lifespan. POSTECH announced on the 28th that a research team led by Professor Hong Ji-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Professor Park Kyu-young of the Department of Battery Engineering and Department of Materials Science and Engineering has identified the structural transformation mechanism of manganese-based cathode materials, which are drawing attention as a next-generation EV battery material. Dr. Lim Guk-hyun of the Department of Battery Engineering and Lee Ho-jun, an integrated program student in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering, also participated in the research. The material at the center of the study is lithium-rich layered oxide (LMRO). This substance has been considered a leading next-generation battery candidate because it can store roughly 20% more energy than conventional nickel-based cathodes while reducing the use of expensive nickel and cobalt. However, it has suffered from a critical weakness: capacity and operating voltage both decline with repeated charge-discharge cycles. Moreover, studies on the underlying cause had produced conflicting findings about the battery's final internal structure, leaving the precise mechanism shrouded in uncertainty. The research team focused on the phenomenon of oxygen escaping from within the cathode during charge-discharge cycles. LMRO originally has a structure in which lithium and metal atoms are arranged in orderly layers, like a brick wall. But with repeated charging, the oxygen that holds this arrangement firmly in place gradually escapes, and the lithium and metal atoms intermix, eventually transforming the material into a disordered rock-salt structure with almost no regularity. The key discovery is that the amount of oxygen released determines the degree of structural change. The higher the voltage to which the battery was charged, the greater the oxygen loss—and correspondingly, the more the internal structure became disordered. The team confirmed that oxygen release can be precisely controlled by adjusting the depth of charge. This is where an unexpected result emerged. While oxygen loss might at first glance appear to damage the battery, when the structure becomes appropriately disordered, the pathways available for lithium transport actually increase, boosting usable capacity. A material with finely tuned oxygen loss demonstrated durability, retaining 98.4% of its initial performance after more than 200 charge-discharge cycles. "By controlling the battery's operating temperature or surface environment, we can regulate oxygen loss and structural change," said Professor Hong. "This can be applied to designing next-generation EV batteries tailored to specific applications." The significance of this research lies in reframing structural change—previously dismissed as an aging phenomenon to be avoided at all costs—as a design tool. By controlling the degree of disorder through either promoting or suppressing oxygen loss, the findings open a path to designing application-specific optimized materials: high-capacity batteries for long-range driving, or long-lifespan batteries for commercial vehicles where durability is paramount. The research was published in Energy & Environmental Science, an international journal in the energy field. The paper was included in the journal's "Hot Articles"—the top 10% of papers selected by the editorial board—and was also selected as a front inside-cover paper. The study was conducted with support from the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology and the Korea Institute for the Advancement of Technology under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy; the National Research Foundation of Korea under the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute. The EV battery market is currently being rapidly encroached upon by Chinese-made lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which compete on price. LFP batteries offer low cost, but their lower energy density translates to shorter driving range, and repeated charge-discharge cycles cause permanent loss of available lithium and increased internal resistance, gradually reducing capacity. LMRO is viewed as an alternative that targets both LFP's price competitiveness and nickel-based batteries' performance, as it can achieve higher energy density while reducing nickel and cobalt usage. That said, since this study establishes the principle at the laboratory level, additional validation is needed before commercialization. Long-term reliability at the actual battery cell level, reproducibility in mass-production processes, and integration with thermal management systems remain as follow-up tasks. Nevertheless, as the first study to quantitatively explain the fundamental mechanism of battery degradation and convert it into a design strategy, it is regarded as research that charts the direction for next-generation high-energy-density cathode development. artigo.texto: Raton, New Mexico is among the latest in a line of jurisdictions to consider a moratorium on data centers. In a standing room only meeting last week city commissioners voted down the idea. Resident and business owner Kimberle Burke presented city commissioners with an informal petition signed by hundreds of residents recommending that the city oppose data centers and approve a moratorium. Concerns included environmental impacts and unintentionally influencing the city's efforts to rebrand. “We're hoping that the Raton city commissioners are not simply shining us on at these meetings, that you're truly listening to us and we're not screaming in the dark,” Burke told the commission. Commissioner Daniel Campbell voted against the moratorium and said the city owned utility wouldn't be able to meet the needs of a data center due to its limited energy and water capacities. “I don't believe that it's a necessary step that we need to step out there and be the first municipality in the state (NM) that does it,” he said during the meeting. Other commissioners raised concerns over the legality of the moratorium or how it could affect existing data centers in the city, including one that has been there for 25 years. Currently multiple counties in New Mexico have passed moratoriums on data centers, including Raton's Colfax County. Colfax County passed the moratorium last month, but it doesn't apply to incorporated areas like Raton, a town of 6,000 residents. Across the state line and to the north, the city of Colorado Springs also owns its utilities. A controversial data center was approved by the city planning department. That decision was appealed by residents and is now in the hands of the city council. Earlier this year Raton's city commission signed a preliminary agreement with a company that was considering building a data center in an old K-Mart building in the center of town. “It feels like they tried to slip it in under our nose and didn't say anything about it,” Burke told KRCC. She said shortly after residents found out about the proposal, they started the petition to let local leaders know how the community felt. However, she said the board's decision bucks the will of the people and has shaken her trust in her local government. “The way it feels to all of us here is ‘We don't really care what y'all want. This is going to happen whether you like it or not’.”

artigo.texto: Data centers may provide a major economic development opportunity for local communities in Wisconsin, but concerns around water and energy use and potential costs to residents have made them increasingly controversial. A new report from the Wisconsin Policy Forum aims to put those issues — and Wisconsin’s data center debate — into context. Researchers examined tax incentives supporting those projects as well as their energy and water use. Three major data center projects are in varying stages of development in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Others have been proposed but canceled in DeForest, Greenleaf and Janesville as polling has shown the issue to be toxically unpopular with the public. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Communities have ‘significant protections’ under data center incentive deals State law allows qualified developers to avoid paying sales and use tax on most purchases supporting the construction and operation of a data center. The Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimates Wisconsin will lose out on $1.5 billion in sales tax revenues related to data center construction between 2024 and 2028, as well as forgo $369 million annually in sales tax revenue related to data center operations. Wisconsin is one of 38 states that offer tax incentives to data centers. Jason Stein, one of the report’s authors, said without its sales tax exemption, Wisconsin might not have attracted the prominent developments. “I think it’s reasonable to think that a lot of this investment — maybe most of this investment — would not have occurred without the incentive,” he said. The report says the state could “recoup a significant portion of the forgone sales tax revenues” if the sales tax exemption helped attract a significant share of data center investment to Wisconsin. That’s through income and sales taxes paid by construction workers and corporate income taxes paid by construction companies, as well as additional taxes paid by utilities serving data centers. Data centers are also expected to generate increased property tax revenues in the communities hosting them. Researchers reviewed local development agreements in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam, as well as proposed deals in communities where developments fell through. They found that, in general, local communities were striking “reasonable deals” that included financial safeguards. Those safeguards often included limits on municipal borrowing, guaranteed property values and incentives tied to project performance, the report said. “If the developer and the community follow through on their agreement and it moves forward as laid out, then those agreements offer substantial protections for the communities,” Stein said. “There are significant protections in each of these deals.” Data centers use water, but Wisconsin water use has declined While much of the public debate around data centers in Wisconsin has centered around water use, policy forum researchers found the bigger challenge is meeting the large electricity demands of those projects while protecting existing ratepayers. That’s because water use in Wisconsin has declined over the past generation as some heavy industry left the state, industrial and residential users became more efficient and electric utilities shifted some energy generation from “water-intensive” coal plants to natural gas and renewable energy, the report said. From 2011 to 2024, water withdrawals in the state fell by more than 500 billion gallons, or almost 24 percent, according to the report. The three main data center projects in Wisconsin are projected to use less water than the decline in water withdrawals over that period, the report states. “We were on this track to use less and less water because of changes in our society, and maybe this will slow that down somewhat,” Stein said. “But that is a different thing than saying, ‘Oh my gosh, we’re using more water than ever before.’” For example, Racine Water Works, the utility providing water for Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant, saw its annual water sales decline by 2.3 billion gallons from 2000 to 2025, according to the report. That’s “more than 250 times” as much water as the 8.4 million gallons annually Microsoft’s data center will use when fully operational, the report states. Electricity demand expected to rise significantly While long-term declines in water use are expected to help offset demand from data centers, Wisconsin’s electricity demand is expected to grow, in large part driven by demand from data centers. Peak demand from all customers on the grid is expected to rise from 14.6 gigawatts in 2024 to 19.9 gigawatts by 2030, the report states. A recent report from state utility regulators found data centers were driving that projected peak demand growth. The report found that the state Public Service Commission modified proposals from We Energies and Alliant Energy establishing rates for data center-scale customers to shield existing residential customers from costs associated with data centers. But it remains to be seen how data centers will affect transmission rates, which are set at the federal level, said Tyler Byrnes, one of the report’s authors. “It’s a little bit easier to do the math on one power plant for one data center, whereas you’re starting to divide up electrons moving across power lines (and) across state lines, so it’s more complicated,” he said. He also said there is not currently an approved data center rate framework for developments of that scale outside the service territories of Alliant Energy and We Energies. He said policymakers may want to consider adopting a statewide framework for electric rates tied to data centers. artigo.texto: A ABINEE (Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica) decidiu integrar a área de armazenamento de energia à sua estrutura de atuação. A iniciativa, segundo a entidade, amplia as frentes já existentes e busca acompanhar a convergência entre diferentes segmentos tecnológicos ligados à eletrônica, à energia e às novas aplicações de baterias. A primeira reunião do novo grupo responsável pelo tema incluiu discussões sobre os desafios e as oportunidades relacionados às novas tecnologias de armazenamento e às suas aplicações. Nova abordagem A decisão, de acordo com a associação, está relacionada à rápida evolução tecnológica do setor, à diversificação das aplicações e à necessidade de desenvolvimento de um arcabouço técnico e regulatório adequado. A proposta é criar um espaço coordenado para o diálogo técnico e institucional e para a formulação de posicionamentos sobre temas que afetam o mercado. Entre os objetivos estão contribuir para segurança jurídica, competitividade da indústria, inovação e desenvolvimento sustentável do mercado brasileiro. A ideia é reunir diferentes dimensões envolvidas no armazenamento, em vez de tratar a tecnologia de maneira isolada. Da bateria ao BESS A ABINEE relaciona a nova área à própria trajetória de atuação no segmento de baterias. A entidade destaca que sua experiência vai das pilhas e células eletroquímicas aos acumuladores tradicionais e, mais recentemente, aos BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) e aos sistemas integrados de armazenamento em larga escala. A abordagem proposta também tem o objetivo de ser transversal. A entidade pretende acompanhar questões industriais, tecnológicas, regulatórias, ambientais, tributárias, de segurança e conformidade, considerando todo o ciclo de vida das baterias — da pesquisa e fabricação à logística reversa. Com a incorporação do armazenamento, a ABINEE destaca ainda que pretende colocar sua experiência em representação institucional e conhecimento técnico a serviço dos associados e do fortalecimento desse mercado. artigo.texto: Fabricantes chineses enxergam na corrida por data centers de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos uma janela de oportunidade, segundo reportagem da CNBC. A avaliação ocorre mesmo com a disputa entre as duas maiores economias do mundo pelo domínio da tecnologia. Aposta no mercado americano A Brightray, empresa de infraestrutura de IA registrada em Singapura, vê “um potencial muito grande no mercado americano”, afirmou à CNBC S.K. Lee, vice-presidente global da companhia. Sua única fabricante é a chinesa PrefabDC, que produz data centers pré-fabricados, enquanto a Brightray gerencia as obras. Segundo a empresa, o modelo reduz em ao menos metade o tempo de construção, que hoje leva de dois a três anos nos EUA, de acordo com analistas do setor ouvidos pela CNBC. Os EUA concentravam 5.427 data centers de IA em 2025, ante 449 na China, segundo dados do Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence citados pela CNBC. Gigantes como Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon e Meta devem gastar cerca de US$ 765 bilhões combinados neste ano em infraestrutura de IA. O CEO do JPMorgan, Jamie Dimon, disse recentemente que o valor pode chegar a US$ 1 trilhão no próximo ano. Já o governo chinês planeja investir US$ 295 bilhões em data centers nos próximos cinco anos. Para Jeffrey Ding, especialista em IA e professor da George Washington University, as empresas chinesas geram menos receita com serviços de IA, o que limita investimentos e reflete uma demanda menor por esses serviços. Tensão geopolítica A relação entre os países, porém, segue complicada. A visita do presidente chinês Xi Jinping a Washington trouxe novo foco à dinâmica comercial, e a IA foi tema destacado nas conversas com o presidente Donald Trump. Autoridades americanas temem riscos de cibersegurança e dependência da China em infraestrutura crítica, e o governo Trump avalia proibir modelos chineses de IA de pesos abertos e novos tipos de componentes chineses para data centers. Benjamin Boucher, analista de cadeias de suprimentos da Wood Mackenzie, disse à CNBC que o ambiente é desafiador por causa das tarifas e das restrições recentes. Ele lembra que os EUA enfrentam escassez de componentes essenciais, como equipamentos elétricos, e prazos longos de entrega, enquanto a China oferece prazos mais favoráveis. Maior fabricante do mundo, o país já fornece transformadores, baterias e cabos de fibra óptica ao mercado americano. Na fábrica da Brightray em Yangzhou, Lee explicou que os materiais e equipamentos vêm de várias partes do mundo, com uma fatia grande da China por causa da integração de sua cadeia produtiva.

artigo.texto: A Rússia ataca o centro de dados da Vodafone em Kyiv. TPO - O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que suas forças atacaram uma série de alvos de infraestrutura logística, de comunicações e militar na Ucrânia, incluindo um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que, durante a noite, suas forças realizaram ataques com drones contra múltiplos alvos na Ucrânia , incluindo centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, e centros de comunicação. "Na noite passada, as Forças Armadas Russas continuaram a realizar ataques com drones visando centros de logística, infraestrutura portuária e de transporte, centros de comunicação e navios operados pelas forças armadas ucranianas", diz o comunicado. De acordo com a versão russa, um dos alvos do ataque foi um centro de dados da Vodafone em Kiev. Moscou acusa a empresa de ser uma das principais fornecedoras de serviços de telecomunicações móveis e internet para as forças armadas ucranianas, incluindo a transmissão de dados de inteligência. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que as tropas russas também atacaram um centro logístico da Zammler na vila de Krasilovka, na região de Kyiv, que armazena e distribui ajuda militar ocidental para a Ucrânia. Na região de Odessa, a Rússia afirma ter atacado o centro logístico de drones Kalinsh em Ilyichovka, que se acredita armazenar drones interceptores FPV. O lado russo também afirmou ter atingido vários alvos no porto de Kiliya, incluindo o quartel-general da base naval de Vostok da Marinha ucraniana, um posto avançado da Guarda de Fronteira ucraniana, quatro depósitos de equipamentos militares e parte da infraestrutura portuária. artigo.texto: Industry steps up with lithium-ion battery storage guidance Lewis Tyler Share this content UKWA and UKMHA publish guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage The UK Warehousing Association (UKWA) and the UK Material Handling Association (UKMHA) have published new guidance to help warehouse operators manage the risks associated with the growing use and storage of lithium-ion batteries. The two trade bodies have worked in parallel to provide practical advice covering both smaller batteries and larger traction batteries used to power warehouse equipment. The guidance was launched at a UKWA Member Connect event in Felixstowe, where Clare Bottle from UKWA and David Goss from UKMHA discussed key highlights for warehouse operators. Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly used across the economy, from laptops, e-bikes and scooters to industrial machinery such as forklifts. While batteries are an important part of the transition away from fossil fuels, the organisations note that unmonitored batteries can, in rare circumstances, enter thermal runaway and cause fire. The new guidance includes recommendations on storing batteries in cool, dry conditions, limiting long-term storage and separating battery types. It also provides advice on monitoring stock, preparing emergency plans and training staff. Clare Bottle, Chief Executive of UKWA, said: “Developments in battery technology are having a huge positive impact, making our lives more convenient, changing the way we move around, and helping the transition away from fossil fuels. All of these batteries move through the supply chain before ending up in businesses or people’s homes, so it is vital we get the storage and handling of them right. “There’s no reason, with proper precautions, that batteries can’t be stored safely. Many warehouses are doing so already. This guidance will help others get to grips with the issue and understand how they can manage the risks. It is a market that will only grow, so it’s important the UK has a wide range of warehouse operators equipped with this knowledge.” David Goss, Technical Director of UKMHA, said: “Lithium-ion batteries have been transformative, not only for consumers but also for powering the equipment essential to today’s fast and efficient logistics sector. “As with any technology, sensible precautions are necessary to minimise the risk of an incident. Whilst lithium-ion batteries have proven safe and reliable, effective risk management requires an understanding of the potential for hazards due to the release of stored energy or chemicals. “Through this collaboration, UKWA and UKMHA have developed complementary guidance addressing the storage of both industrial truck traction batteries and the smaller batteries in warehouse environments.” Both guidance documents are available from UKWA.

artigo.texto: Liftoff: Google is realizing Elon Musk's dream of AI data centers in space Next week, Google will be living out Elon Musk's dream of putting AI data centers in space — and they'll be doing it with help from Musk's space exploration company. On Thursday, October 1, 2026, Google will load an experimental satellite on SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket and launch it in space. The satellite is part of Google's Project Suncatcher initiative, which seeks to set up AI data centers in space. The experimental satellite will be able answer simple A.I. prompts from space, according to the New York Times. In a blog post about Project Suncatcher, Google explained the potential benefits of sending data centers into orbit: You May Also Like Cooling orbital data centers is a crucial research challenge. TPUs generate a large amount of heat in a small area, which needs to be diffused safely or the chips are at risk of overheating. But in space, there’s no airflow. In a vacuum, you can only diffuse heat via radiators, which requires a totally different approach to cooling electronics. As the New York Times reported, Google isn't sending a full-on orbital data center this time; it's sending the potential precursor to one. The satellite, named MVP, contains four “tensor processing units,” which are specialized chips with the computing power of one server in a data center here on Earth. The computer chips will be powered by the satellite's solar panels, which will provide one kilowatt of power to the chips. Google says that this is all it needs for this particular experiment, which will test how the hardware fares in outer space. The satellite is expected to operate in space for a period of one year. While in orbit, the computer chips will be able to process short queries for up to 15 minutes while Google's Gemini AI responds. After a 15-minute period, the chips will need to shut down to cool with a special cooling system, as fans typically used in computer systems don't work in space. After that one-year period, the satellite will stop operating but will continue to orbit the Earth for a total of six years before the planet's gravitational pull brings the satellite down, burning it as it falls through the atmosphere. When Musk's SpaceX acquired Musk's AI company xAI earlier this year, Musk explained that one of the main reasons for the companies to combine was so that they could work on putting AI data centers in space. "Current advances in AI are dependent on large terrestrial data centers, which require immense amounts of power and cooling," Musk said in a statement at the time of the acquisition. "Global electricity demand for AI simply cannot be met with terrestrial solutions, even in the near term, without imposing hardship on communities and the environment." In the long term, space-based AI is obviously the only way to scale," Musk continued. Google seems to agree with Musk. Shortly after Musk shared his orbital AI data center goals, Google announced Project Suncatcher, which the company greenlit in May 2025. It's important to note, however, that these are very early days for the orbital data center ambition. If these experiments prove that the project is at all feasible, it would likely be years, if not decades, before Google and Musk's vision comes to fruition. But Thursday's launch is certainly a first step in potentially building out AI data centers in space. Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox?
