artigo.texto: BYD says it is close to bringing solid-state battery technology to production vehicles, with the Chinese car maker planning to introduce its first model using the technology in 2027. The company believes it holds a strong position in both the development and commercialisation of solid-state batteries, which could eventually offer electric vehicles longer driving ranges, faster charging and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion technology. BYD targets 2027 for its first solid-state model BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li confirmed the company’s plans in a recent interview with Carwow’s Spanish outlet. She said BYD was in a “leading position” in solid-state battery development and commercialisation, adding that the company would use a production model to demonstrate the technology. “Talking about solid-state batteries, BYD is in the leading position,” Li said. “We’re in the leading position for commercialisation and technology. So to prove that, next year, we have one model that will be the first one with that technology.” The comments build on plans previously outlined by Sun Huajun, chief technology officer of BYD’s battery subsidiary FinDreams. Speaking at a battery conference in February 2025, Sun said BYD expected to demonstrate and install solid-state batteries in vehicles in 2027, with mass production expected to follow around 2030, according to CarNewsChina. The planned launch does not mean BYD intends to abandon its existing lithium-based batteries. Lian Yubo, BYD’s chief scientist, said at the same conference that solid-state batteries would initially target higher-end vehicles. In contrast, lithium iron phosphate batteries would continue to serve other parts of the market. “Solid-state batteries will be mainly used in high-end models, complementing lithium iron phosphate batteries, and used in vehicles of different levels,” Lian said. This approach would allow BYD to introduce the newer technology without immediately replacing the battery systems already used across its electric vehicle range. Solid-state batteries could improve range and safety Solid-state batteries differ from conventional lithium-ion batteries mainly in the electrolyte that moves ions between the battery’s positive and negative electrodes. Traditional lithium-ion cells use a liquid electrolyte containing dissolved lithium salts, while solid-state designs replace the liquid with a solid material. The solid electrolyte can be made using materials such as oxides, polymers or sulphides. BYD is developing sulphide-based solid-state technology, which could provide higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion cells. Higher energy density could allow manufacturers to build smaller, lighter batteries while maintaining the same amount of stored energy. Alternatively, manufacturers could use a battery of similar size to today’s packs while increasing available energy, potentially extending an electric vehicle’s driving range. Solid-state technology could also offer safety benefits. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use flammable liquid electrolytes and can experience thermal runaway if cells are severely damaged or develop certain faults. Solid electrolytes are less prone to this type of behaviour, although solid-state batteries are not automatically risk-free. Another potential advantage is performance across a wider temperature range. Extreme heat and cold can affect battery performance, and solid-state technology is being developed partly to address these limitations. However, several technical and manufacturing challenges remain before solid-state batteries can be produced at the scale and cost required for mass-market electric vehicles. Manufacturing complexity and material costs remain major barriers, helping explain why early applications are expected to appear in more expensive models. BYD joins growing solid-state battery race BYD is not the only car maker working towards production solid-state batteries. Several major manufacturers have announced plans to introduce the technology in vehicles during the second half of the decade, although development schedules and commercial availability vary between companies. Toyota has previously targeted 2027 or 2028 for vehicles equipped with solid-state batteries. Mercedes-Benz has also been testing solid-state battery technology in an EQS-based vehicle and expects to introduce the technology before the end of the decade. Stellantis has taken another step towards commercialisation by beginning road testing of a solid-state battery-powered Dodge Charger in 2026. The testing is intended to evaluate the technology under real-world driving conditions rather than solely in laboratory environments. Honda has also been developing the technology and announced a partnership with QuantumScape earlier this year. The companies are working on solid-state battery technology as part of Honda’s longer-term efforts towards carbon neutrality by 2050. For BYD, the 2027 vehicle will provide an important step towards determining how its sulphide-based solid-state cells perform in a production car. The company has indicated that wider adoption is likely to follow later, with mass production targeted around 2030. The development could eventually give electric vehicle manufacturers another option to improve range, charging performance, and battery packaging. For now, however, solid-state batteries remain an emerging technology, and manufacturers are still working to overcome the cost and production challenges of bringing them to large-scale vehicle production.

artigo.texto: LG lança chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar para data centers de IA Equipamento tem capacidade de 480 a 600 toneladas de refrigeração por unidade; segundo a empresa, o sistema pode recuperar a capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o retorno da energia. A LG Electronics lançou um chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar voltado a data centers de inteligência artificial. O equipamento utiliza um compressor com mancal magnético sem óleo e um sistema de free-cooling que aproveita o ar externo frio para reduzir a carga de trabalho do compressor. Segundo uma simulação interna da LG, o free-cooling por refrigerante consumiu aproximadamente 30% menos energia ao longo de um ano que o sistema hidrônico comparado. O cálculo considerou uma unidade de 1.750 kW operando a 100% da capacidade sob as condições climáticas da região metropolitana de Seul. O consumo real pode variar conforme a instalação e a operação. Em caso de queda de energia, uma fonte ininterrupta integrada permite a parada segura do eixo do compressor. Após o restabelecimento da eletricidade, o chiller pode recuperar a capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos, conforme as condições de teste informadas pela empresa. A LG também apresentará uma solução modular de resfriamento hidrônico na Data Centre World Asia 2026, marcada para 29 e 30 de setembro, no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. O módulo reúne bombas de água gelada e um tanque de armazenamento térmico e pode ser montado em fábrica para simplificar a instalação no local. James Lee, presidente da LG ES Company, afirmou que a empresa continuará a ampliar seu portfólio de resfriamento diante do aumento da densidade e da geração de calor nos data centers de IA. – Resumen (español) LG Electronics lanzó un chiller centrífugo enfriado por aire para centros de datos de inteligencia artificial. El equipo tiene una capacidad de 480 a 600 toneladas de refrigeración por unidad y utiliza un compresor con cojinete magnético sin aceite. La empresa también presentará una solución modular de enfriamiento hidrónico en la Data Centre World Asia 2026, en Singapur. Summary (English) LG Electronics has launched an air-cooled centrifugal chiller for AI data centers. Each unit has a cooling capacity of 480 to 600 refrigeration tons and uses an oil-free magnetic bearing compressor. The company will also present a modular hydronic cooling solution at Data Centre World Asia 2026 in Singapore.

artigo.texto: Last week, I walked my fields at Trails End Farm in Bradford as the sun came up over the hills. It’s the kind of quiet that reminds you why people move to New Hampshire — and why those of us lucky enough to live here fight so hard to protect it. That’s why I strongly support Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s proposed moratorium on new data centers in New Hampshire. Across the country from Colorado to Virginia, from Texas to right here in New Hampshire, massive new data center facilities are popping up. Recently proposals for new data center projects in Nottingham and Bow have received a lot of attention and public scrutiny — rightfully so. Here’s what the data shows. Data centers are among the most power-intensive facilities ever built. A single large-scale facility can consume as much electricity as a small city. When those facilities plug into New Hampshire’s grid, they drive up demand. When demand outpaces supply, ratepayers pay more. Every family heating their home. Every small business running its equipment. Every farmer keeping the lights on in the barn. They all pay more so that a data center — excuse me, an “innovation hub” — can run its servers around the clock. New Hampshire has a brand. We call it the New Hampshire Advantage. Low taxes. Common sense regulation. A quality of life worth protecting. That advantage doesn’t survive if we allow our energy infrastructure to be overwhelmed by facilities that offer almost nothing to our communities in return — no meaningful jobs, no tax base that justifies the strain, no benefit to the Granite Staters who actually live here. Gov. Ayotte is right to pump the brakes. A moratorium isn’t anti-business. It’s pro-New Hampshire. It says: we will think carefully before we commit our grid, our ratepayers and our communities to something we cannot easily undo. That is conservative governance. That is good stewardship. Any farmer will tell you — you don’t exhaust the land for a single season’s profit. Because apparently, “data center” has become a dirty word — and when a dirty word starts costing you a permit, the instinct in some corners is simple: find a cleaner word. So now, Granite Staters, you may start hearing about proposed “server farms” or “innovation hubs” coming to a town near you. Don’t be fooled. An innovation hub that requires hundreds of megawatts of power, consumes millions of gallons of water for cooling, generates little local employment and plugs directly into our electrical grid is not an innovation hub. It’s a data center. Calling it something else doesn’t change what it draws from our communities — or what it leaves behind. I’ve spent my career in business and academia studying how markets work. I’ve run hotels. I’ve taught marketing. And I know a rebranding campaign when I see one. This is one of the most transparent examples I’ve encountered in public life. The product hasn’t changed. Only the label has. And the label is designed to get past the very guardrails that Gov. Ayotte and this legislature are trying to put in place to protect New Hampshire’s ratepayers and energy grid. My message to those who want to sneak a data center past a moratorium by slapping a new name on it is simple: we see you. The people of New Hampshire see you. And we are not going to let a branding exercise substitute for honest policy. If you have a facility that draws industrial-scale power from our grid, it will be evaluated as what it is — not what you’ve chosen to call it this week. New Hampshire’s energy future is too important to leave to clever marketing. Our ratepayers deserve honesty. Our grid deserves protection. And our communities deserve leaders who won’t be talked out of common sense by people with a thesaurus and a permit application. I’m one of those leaders. And I’m not going anywhere. Sen. Dan Innis, from Bradford, represents District 7 in the New Hampshire Senate.

artigo.texto: Wisconsin Rapids Alder Michael Timm will have to campaign to keep his job after residents forced a recall election over an email he sent a local business. It’s all tied to yard signs showing opposition to a local data center proposal. While data centers have been a contentious issue across Wisconsin, they’re especially so in Wisconsin Rapids where developer wanted to turn the site of a historic paper mill into a data center facility. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The issue has brought out vocal opposition, large audiences at local meetings and complete changes of data center policies in the small community. Amid the local debate in July, a local hotel bar made available “No Data Center” signs for those who wanted them. In an email, Timm contacted the business and expressed his belief that the signs were unpopular and had led another local business to close down. But in the months that followed, local sentiment swung hard against the proposal. An August forum held by the data center developer and led by former New York City Mayor Eric Adams devolved into heckling and jeering. And this month, the city’s planning commission unanimously recommended denying developers a conditional use permit for the paper mill proposal. When Timm’s email became public, data center opponents called on him to resign and started an effort to recall him. Kaitlyn Federwitz was one of the residents who gathered votes for the recall and is a co-founder of the South Wood County Neighbors for Responsible Development organization. The group has been leading the charge against data center proposals in Wisconsin Rapids. They’re also behind the “No Data Center” signs, which locals can buy to show their opposition. She specifically pointed to Timm’s email to the Hotel Mead as a reason her group started the recall effort. In a statement, Timm said he hasn’t done anything wrong. “There was no threat, no demand, no ultimatum, and no suggestion of any consequence if (Hotel Mead) declined” to stop distributing the signs,” Timm said. “It was simply my opinion. They considered it and voluntarily agreed.” Timm sent the message from his personal email, but in the first two lines identified himself as a city alder and gave his connections to the Chamber of Commerce. The recall effort has two phases: a recall primary on Oct. 27, followed by a recall election on Nov. 24, according to the city. If a primary is not required, local voters in District 7 will decide on Oct. 27 whether Timm will remain in office. Timm responds to claims he ‘pressured’ business In his statement, Timm said he wanted to address claims he had “improperly pressured or threatened the Hotel Mead” over the No Data Center signs. He also released the July email chain at issue. Using a personal email, Timm shared his opinion with Hotel Mead staff that selling the anti-data center signs at the bar could hurt the businesses. “Not sure if you are aware but they tried doing that at 1716 and the bar went out of business,” the email states. Federwitz said that bar closed for personal reasons. “We were working with a local bar, who was holding events for us where we had days where we could sell our signs,” she said. After the closure, the Neighbors group talked with the Hotel Mead bar, who allowed the signs in. “And it came to light that Michael Timm had found out that that was happening, and he sent an email to all the managers at the Hotel Mead,” Federwitz said. “By allowing this, you’re alienating A LOT of people from your establishment,” Timm wrote in the email. “While I remain neutral on the issue, I know several people that won’t be going in there knowing this is going on.” Federwitz said this is not the first time Timm has communicated with locals on data center issues. “He had a very strong stance, not entirely pro-data center, but also definitely speaking in their interest,” Federwitz said. Timm did not respond to a request for comment. The Neighbors group noticed Timm was regularly replying to Facebook comments about local data center topics — according to Federwitz, “in ways that were not necessarily super professional, and really, taking a fighting-back stance against people who were asking questions.” Timm also shared a response email, dated the same day, from Tucker Christensen, the Hotel Mead’s general manager. “Honestly I was opposed to selling the signs here,” Christensen said, adding he did not want the hotel to be part of the data center discussion. Christensen said the decision to sell the signs was made by the hotel’s owners, who thought it would be “harmless.” Timm’s words found support from the general manager, according to the alderman’s Facebook post. “I have spoken to (the owners) regarding your concerns, and I hope they reconsider,” Christensen said, thanking Timm for his opinion. The Hotel Mead went on to host one of the data center developer’s open houses on Sept. 13. “Businesses have every right to decide what they sell on their own property,” Timm wrote later in his statement. “I respected their response then, and I respect it now.” Once locals had the required 252 signatures, the recall was approved by the local council on a vote of 6-0, with one abstention. Timm is a first-time alder, who was elected, running unopposed, in 2025. His term expires in 2027. In his statement, he said he would not resign and said the recall would put “unnecessary costs onto the taxpayers, and I continue to face threats and harassment by people outside my district, I will not abandon my community.”

The debate is being amplified by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's call for stronger AI safeguards following revelations that an OpenAI model hacked a government website. Co-director of the Centre for AI and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne, Jeannie Paterson joins "Bloomberg: The Asia Trade" to discuss the future of Australia's AI ambitions. the AI investment roll out data center at roll out is real. There isn't a terms of trade boom associated, a national income boom, and just the level of investment relative to GDP isn't big. And while economists continue to debate the benefits and the risks of Australia's Data Center boom, developers are facing growing opposition. Goodman Group has just shelved plans for an $840 million facility in suburban Sydney after facing significant community resistance. The state of Victoria has also recently banned data centers in residential areas and the Federal Senate has begun an inquiry. That debate, of course, also being amplified by AI security concerns. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called for stronger AI safeguards after an open AI model hacked a government website. Joining us now is Genie Patterson who's a co-director at the Center for AI and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne. Genie, really great to have you with us and even as we speak, we're learning from Anthropic planning to warn its potential IPO investors that advanced AI could pose, quote, catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Extraordinarily strong language from, you know, one of the biggest players within AI. What do you make of these risks and are policy makers really well and truly behind the curve in terms of being able to regulate or even come up with appropriate guard rails here? Um, well, the claims are extraordinary for a company that's about to, um, have an IPO, um, release shares to the shock stock market. Um, and it may face greater scrutiny in terms of corporate governance, quite frankly. Um, but in the short term, before that happens, um, it's interesting to think about the regulation. There are actually existing laws against hacking and accessing, um, data sets or websites in an unauthorized way, um, both in the US and here. And what we really haven't seen is an effort yet to enforce those laws or equivalent civil law penalties. And I think there'll be a lot of discussion about that to the extent that Anthropic isn't operating in Australia at the moment or at least isn't training models in Australia. It's hard for Australian law to reach that company. That will change if we get the predicted investment by Anthropic in Australia to use data centers to train models. You mentioned a really interesting point and and I wanted to get a bit more on that because jurisdiction issues are just one of the complexities of this emerging area, right? Do you think that would be helped by having more consensus or perhaps stronger frameworks that are multilateral between different governments? Absolutely. I mean this we've seen over the weekend calls for countries to ban together to agree on some baseline standards or what are sometimes called red lines for AI development. and that's clearly going to be helpful. but I'd also make the point that much of the conduct we're seeing is already very close to unlawful, if not unlawful. Um, and really, I suspect that it's geopolitics about who's building the models and concerns about China's models that are stopping sort of a clear-eyed view on how we actually enforce what increasingly are looking like either reckless conduct or intentionally criminal conduct. It's interesting in the prospectus from Anthropic, we're also hearing more details. It's highlighting the risks associated with their own AI models and they include, Genie, self-preserving behaviors, attempts to resist shutdown or to conceal and manipulate information and behavior that quote resembles blackmail. Does this sort of bring to the forefront how different AI regulation needs to be compared with existing regulation that we have for other technology? Um, well, it does in the sense that um, AI works with more autonomy and works faster and therefore the effects of unregulated AI can be catastrophic more quickly than we've perhaps experienced with other technologies. But that said, we do know how to do safety regulation. Um, we know how to put in place rules, we know how to have reporting and moreover in the case of very dangerous industries, we send in um inspectors to to actually inspect on how safety rails have been imposed by say the um atomic industry. and you know, um, Sam Otman has even raised, I think the possibility of external um inspectors. artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution is accelerating technology development to preempt the future battery market despite multiple headwinds, including an electric vehicle chasm (temporary demand slowdown). According to the battery industry on the 28th, LG Energy Solution invested 725.9 billion won in research and development (R&D) expense in the first half of this year. This is the largest amount ever for a half-year period. The number of patents is also increasing significantly. LG Energy Solution holds the most patents among battery makers worldwide, with 62,140 registrations and 105,350 applications. A representative next-generation battery technology held by LG Energy Solution is the solid-state battery. A solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte, reducing risks that occur when the cathode and anode come into contact and maintaining shape even under external shock, a technology that maximizes safety. "Graphite-based solid-state" is a technology in which LG Energy Solution has strength, and for electric vehicles in 2029 it can maximize energy density per volume by using only the current collector without an anode material. It also announced a battery development roadmap to commercialize "anode-free solid-state" for Humanoid Robot and urban air mobility (UAM) in 2030, pursuing a strategy of differentiating technical approaches to suit market characteristics. To address high manufacturing expense and process complexity, LG Energy Solution has put "dry electrode" technology at the forefront. The dry process that omits the organic solvent drying step is evaluated as a next-generation method that can not only dramatically reduce equipment investment and process expense, but also drive innovation across battery production in terms of manufacturing time and space efficiency. LG Energy Solution is widening the technology gap by filing more than 450 dry electrode–related patents worldwide. It holds key patents such as the "dry electrode fibrillation and tensile strength improvement technology," essential for mass-production-grade dry electrode manufacturing, and has also secured technology applicable to both cathodes and anodes regardless of active material particle size. Sodium batteries are also a technology LG Energy Solution is focusing on. These batteries store and release electricity using sodium instead of lithium ions. They offer price competitiveness due to advantages in materials and supplies procurement and expense, and are known for excellent low-temperature output. LG Energy Solution said in a roadmap released last year that it plans to apply sodium batteries to 12V and 24V automotive lead-acid replacements, energy storage systems (ESS), and small electric vehicles. Prismatic LMR (lithium manganese rich) batteries are another technology drawing attention recently. These batteries significantly reduce cobalt content to boost cost competitiveness while also raising energy density. LG Energy Solution recognized early the potential of combining LMR cathodes with silicon anodes and proactively built a patent foundation. It is also securing competitiveness across materials and processes. In November last year, LG Energy Solution signed a "strategic partnership for aerospace battery cell research and development" with U.S. startup South 8 Technologies (hereafter South 8), which developed the world's first liquefied gas electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries, and agreed to jointly develop next-generation space batteries operable in extreme ultra-low temperatures down to minus 60 degrees. In September last year, the FRL research team, in which LG Energy Solution and KAIST are jointly conducting research, published in the leading journal "Nature Energy" research results on a lithium metal cell that can travel more than 800 km on a single charge, has a lifespan exceeding a cumulative 300,000 km, and can reduce charging time to 12 minutes. In October, through joint research with Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH and Sungkyunkwan University, it also developed a core electrolyte technology that can simultaneously improve the low-temperature performance and thermal safety of lithium-ion batteries. An LG Energy Solution official said, "We are continuously expanding R&D investment to secure differentiated technology leadership," adding, "We will not stop at simply developing new technologies, but will introduce technologies with high mass producibility and completeness that can broaden the base of the battery industry."

artigo.texto: Trinity Airways(091810) said on the 28th that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on mutual cooperation regarding the carbon offset and reduction scheme for international aviation (CORSIA) and the emissions trading system with NH Investment & Securities. It is the first business agreement signed in Korea between an airline and a financial company in the fields of CORSIA and the emissions transaction system, and the two companies said they plan to expand cooperation across the entire carbon credit market. The agreement was prepared to proactively strengthen CORSIA response capabilities and establish a cooperation framework for the carbon credit market in line with the carbon reduction policy for the aviation institutional sector promoted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport and the overall direction of CORSIA implementation. The MOU centers on multifaceted cooperation, including the exchange of information and the establishment of a joint response system for CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas carbon credit market and policies; the joint promotion of projects related to carbon credits; and various activities for the development of the carbon market. CORSIA offsetting is carried out by securing eligible carbon credits corresponding to the required offset amount within the set implementation period and then retiring them in the registry. Retiring credits means permanently deleting the secured carbon credits from the registry so the credits cannot be used again. Trinity Airways purchased 20,000 tons (t) of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and signed a contract to retire those credits to proactively prepare for the obligation. It also plans to gradually secure more than 10% of the Phase 1 volume that must be offset by Jan. 2028 by additionally purchasing eligible credits by the end of this year to ensure stability in complying with greenhouse gas regulations and to ease uncertainties in the supply and demand of carbon credits. The signing ceremony was held on the 21st at Sono Trinity Commons in Gangseo-gu, Seoul, and was attended by Seo Dong-bin, executive in charge of corporate management support at Trinity Airways, Park Geon-hu, head of the Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, and other key officials from both companies. Seo said, "Through cooperation with NH Investment & Securities, we will strengthen our capabilities in sourcing and managing credits and build an efficient response system from a mid- to long-term perspective."

artigo.texto: The Pune battery technology centre planned by COEP Technological University and JSW Projects will receive an investment of more than Rs 800 crore and is expected to create over 1,000 jobs across the battery ecosystem, according to the memorandum of understanding signed by the two institutions. The centre will be established at COEP’s Chikhali Research Park in two phases. The partners describe it as India’s first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre, with work focused initially on lithium-ion battery cells and later expanding to sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. The first phase will cover battery-cell design, simulation and prototyping. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of manufacturing cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 Ah. The facility is intended to take technologies beyond laboratory research and towards testing and development at pilot scale. The partnership will bring COEP students and faculty into projects with industry engineers. It will support joint research, technology development, academic publications and intellectual property creation, while providing hands-on exposure to commercially relevant battery technologies. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud said the collaboration could help develop indigenous alternatives to imported batteries. The university said the centre would also create an institutional platform for training and research linked to the wider battery ecosystem. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said the partnership would focus on developing cells suited to Indian climatic conditions and applications. “Cells are the new fuel of this century,” he said, adding that India needed to build domestic capabilities to manufacture them. The proposed centre is expected to support applications in electric vehicles, grid storage and clean energy. Its planned research scope places Pune’s academic and industrial capabilities within a sector that requires cell design, validation and manufacturing expertise, rather than only battery assembly. The MoU does not specify an operational opening date in the information available. The project’s immediate milestones are the rollout of the first phase for design, simulation and prototyping, followed by the planned cell validation and pilot-scale manufacturing facility in the second phase.

artigo.texto: Segundo o New York Times, o Google está se preparando para lançar um satélite de teste em órbita no dia 1º de outubro, marcando o início de sua ambição de construir centros de dados de IA operando no espaço, usando energia solar para processar tarefas de inteligência artificial. O satélite, chamado MVP, será lançado pelo foguete Falcon 9 da SpaceX a partir da Base da Força Aérea de Vandenberg, na Califórnia. Este ainda não é um centro de dados completo, mas sim o primeiro teste do projeto Suncatcher. Em testes realizados em solo, o satélite, com tamanho aproximado de uma geladeira, foi submetido a testes de vibração e teve seus processadores de IA acionados. O Google marcou cada parafuso do dispositivo para monitorar alterações sutis após o processo de teste. De acordo com o The Guardian , o MVP está equipado com quatro Unidades de Processamento Tensorial (TPUs), equivalentes à capacidade computacional de um servidor em um centro de dados. Painéis solares fornecem cerca de 1 kW de energia, o suficiente para o satélite realizar consultas simples de IA. O Google prevê que o satélite poderá processar consultas em cerca de um ano e permanecer em órbita por até seis anos antes de retornar à atmosfera. O problema da energia e do custo A ideia de instalar centros de dados no espaço surge da crescente demanda energética da inteligência artificial. Enquanto os centros de dados terrestres exigem quantidades enormes de eletricidade, os satélites podem acessar uma fonte de energia solar mais abundante e consistente. O Google não é a única empresa interessada nessa ideia. Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos e Sam Altman também manifestaram apoio à construção de centros de dados fora da Terra. No entanto, o projeto ainda enfrenta obstáculos significativos. Os satélites ficam expostos à radiação no espaço, e o custo de seu lançamento permanece elevado. Embora os custos possam diminuir com o desenvolvimento da indústria espacial, a construção de uma rede de centros de dados em órbita continua sendo um problema a ser resolvido. O Google estima que o custo de operação de um centro de dados orbital poderá se aproximar do custo de um centro de dados terrestre em meados da década de 2030, à medida que os custos de lançamento diminuírem. O professor Brandon Lucia, da Universidade Carnegie Mellon, acredita que a expansão de um satélite de teste para uma rede massiva exigiria muitos anos e um capital enorme. Segundo ele, esta ainda é uma área com poucos precedentes. James Manyika, um executivo sênior do Google, também se mostrou cauteloso quanto ao cronograma. Ele citou o processo de desenvolvimento da tecnologia de carros autônomos do Google, que levou cerca de 15 anos desde a pesquisa inicial até a implementação prática. O maior desafio é a dissipação de calor. Um dos maiores desafios enfrentados pelo Google foi o resfriamento dos chips. Na Terra, os data centers utilizam ventiladores e sistemas de refrigeração para dissipar o calor dos processadores. No espaço, os ventiladores não funcionam da mesma maneira. Portanto, o Google precisou desenvolver um sistema de condução térmica multicamadas para transferir o calor dos chips para um dissipador de calor externo no satélite. No projeto experimental, as TPUs foram colocadas na placa de circuito impresso, conectando-se ao material de transferência térmica e, em seguida, às camadas de alumínio e cobre, antes que o calor fosse transferido para o dissipador de calor. Atualmente, esse sistema permite que o chip opere por cerca de 15 minutos antes de precisar esfriar. Esse tempo é suficiente para lidar com consultas Gemini relativamente curtas. O Google planeja lançar mais dois satélites no próximo ano. A longo prazo, a empresa quer construir grupos de satélites que operem em formação, com mais de 80 satélites em uma rede. Se o projeto avançar, o Google poderá até mesmo projetar satélites dedicados maiores, aproximadamente do tamanho de um campo de futebol . Uma aposta a longo prazo O projeto Suncatcher teve origem numa ideia de Blaise Agüera y Arcas, que acreditava que as necessidades energéticas da IA poderiam impulsionar uma abordagem completamente nova para a infraestrutura computacional. Em fevereiro de 2025, o Google realizou testes de resistência à radiação em seus chips em um laboratório nuclear. Os processadores foram expostos a radiação equivalente a aproximadamente cinco anos de operação no espaço. Pequenos erros de dados causados pela radiação geralmente podem ser corrigidos reiniciando o chip. Em maio de 2025, a equipe do projeto apresentou sua ideia ao CEO Sundar Pichai, com a presença do cofundador Sergey Brin. O projeto recebeu então sinal verde. Inicialmente, o Google planejava lançar dois satélites em 2027. No entanto, a empresa decidiu antecipar o lançamento para este ano e assumir um risco maior. A Planet Labs foi contratada para construir os satélites, enquanto os chips foram instalados em uma plataforma de satélite pré-existente. Com o MVP, o objetivo do Google não é provar que data centers em órbita estão prontos para substituir instalações terrestres. A empresa está testando se os componentes mais críticos do conceito podem funcionar em um ambiente espacial. Travis Beals, líder do projeto, acredita que, mesmo que tudo corra bem nos próximos cinco anos, os resultados iniciais podem não ser significativos o suficiente para gerar mudanças imediatas. Mas, a longo prazo, ele vislumbra um futuro em que o processamento de consultas Gemini a partir do espaço possa se tornar uma prática comum. artigo.texto: Bruce Lear lives in Sioux City and has been connected to Iowa’s public schools for 38 years. He taught for eleven years and represented educators as an Iowa State Education Association regional director for 27 years until retiring. He can be reached at BruceLear2419@gmail.com Growing up, organized sports consisted of little league, or high school baseball in the spring and summer. Fall and winter meant basketball, since our school was too tiny for football. No adult had yet figured out NBA, and MLB dreams were a sure money maker—so there were no sports academies or traveling leagues. But we did have the town basketball court. It was a kid sanctuary where kid law prevailed. No adult supervision, no minimum or maximum age, and both genders were welcome. The rules were simple and strictly enforced. If you cried, you left. We called our own fouls loosely. If you overshot, and the ball went into the crick, you retrieved it. There were arguments, and fights, but there was urgency to end conflict, because finishing the game was more important than the fight. We needed rules or our game would be swallowed by conflict. Now, like the basketball court, data centers need clear and enforceable rules, or Iowa small towns and rural life will be swallowed just like our basketball games. Currently, Congress seems to lack urgency and understanding on how to catch up to the data center invasion. That sounds like a bad movie, but it’s a serious threat. Even the creators of AI are warning there needs to be a slowdown. That means the urgency to govern is in the hands of local and state lawmakers. It’s time to play catch up. History tells us this happened before during the industrial revolution. As industry grew and became more powerful, there were no laws regulating child labor, worker safety, wages, and other general working conditions. Working class people suffered, while robber barons lived in gilded mansions. I fear the new crop of robber barons are tech billionaires who are quickly trying to build data centers before the laws catch up. They promise high paying jobs but offer no guarantees. They don’t acknowledge their huge consumption of electricity and water, and they ignore the impact these large structures will have on the community. The adage “History may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes” is on target—even if Mark Twain probably never said it. I can hear that haunting rhyme echoing across Iowa corn fields while politicians dither. President Donald Trump said, “Towns that reject data centers risk becoming backwards and poor.” But in a recent Emerson College poll, 60 percent of Iowans believe data centers will negatively impact the environment. Both candidates for governor have proposed new restrictions on data centers. The Iowa legislature needs to act quickly and decisively. Here are my suggestions for regulating data centers in Iowa. In 1991, Iowa lawmakers allowed gambling but also passed strict guidelines. For example, the Iowa Gaming Commission had to approve the location, communities had to vote to see if the majority supported the idea, and each casino was required to provide a percentage of revenue to a separate nonprofit organization for distribution to benefit the community and surrounding area. I’m on one of those boards now. I believe this model would work for data centers, along with five other requirements. 1. Billion-dollar tech companies don’t need tax breaks to locate in Iowa. 2. The tech company must strengthen the electrical grid and pay for its use. 3. The tech company must in writing assure the community there is sufficient water supply and pay for upgrades to the system and water used. 4. The tech company must reduce the noise pollution. 5. The tech company must guarantee the number of permanent jobs. Data centers may be an innovation revolution impossible to prevent, but it should be regulated. No one should ever threaten violence, but we should vote for politicians willing to seriously regulate data centers. Top photo is by Chad Davis, available via Wikimedia Commons.

artigo.texto: A Kyivstar, que lidera o mercado de telefonia celular ucraniano, foi atingida por um bombardeio russo no domingo (27), segundo o TecMundo. A companhia informou à agência Interfax que ninguém se feriu. Na mesma ofensiva, um data center da Vodafone teria sido atingido, de acordo com o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. A Vodafone, dona da segunda maior rede celular da região, não quis se pronunciar. Outro data center na capital ucraniana também foi alvo da ofensiva de domingo, que feriu um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky. Conforme a Reuters, estruturas do tipo usadas por operadoras locais estão entre os alvos prioritários. Em um dos episódios, explosões cortaram a conexão de aproximadamente 100 mil residências ao longo da semana, principalmente em Kiev e cidades vizinhas, segundo o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. Autoridades ucranianas afirmam que os bombardeios comprometeram sistemas críticos de segurança, elevando o risco de mortes durante ataques. O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Andrii Sybha, declarou no X que a Rússia mira centros de dados para interromper o fluxo de informações. Ele também mencionou drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, variante capaz de voar acima de 600 km/h e em altitudes maiores, o que dificulta a defesa aérea. No mês passado, um drone guiado por IA matou três civis no país. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: NineDot Adds 20 MW Battery Energy Storage Site NineDot Energy has opened its largest battery energy storage site to date in Hunts Point, New York. The new system adds nearly 20 MW of capacity to the local electricity network. NineDot expects it to become fully operational before next summer. The project shows how community scale battery energy storage can help grids handle peak demand. It can also improve grid resilience during heat waves and other periods of high electricity use. Battery Energy Storage Supports Peak Demand The Hunts Point system can deliver nearly 20 MW of power when electricity demand rises. According to NineDot, this is enough to supply nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours. The system can also reduce the need for nearby gas fired peaker plants. Utilities typically rely on these plants when electricity demand reaches high levels. Batteries offer another option by storing electricity and returning it to the grid when demand increases. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said Adam Cohen, NineDot’s Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” NineDot built the project on the former site of a fuel oil trucking company. The company expects the battery to support further electrification in Hunts Point. Future demand could include electrified markets and truck fleets. NineDot Targets 400 MW in 2026 NineDot has already used its battery fleet to support the grid during periods of high demand. During New York’s July 1 to 4, 2026 heat wave, nine NineDot projects exported nearly 34 MW at peak times. The batteries supported Con Edison’s local distribution network as well as the wider state transmission system. Currently, NineDot operates 11 projects across six locations in Staten Island and the Bronx. Together, they provide 39 MW of battery capacity. Meanwhile, the company continues to expand its battery energy storage portfolio. More than 60 additional projects are now in development. Its total project pipeline exceeds 1 GW. By the end of 2026, NineDot aims to have 400 MW of battery storage in operation, under construction or in development. Electricity networks face growing demand from electrification and renewable energy deployment. Distributed battery storage can help networks respond to those changes. In particular, batteries can supply power during peak periods and reduce pressure on existing grid infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Stakeholders call for carbon trading framework reforms DAR ES SALAAM: CARBON trading stakeholders have called for reforms to carbon trading framework after Carbon Tanzania temporarily halted its YaedaEyasi Landscape Project due to shifting global market demands and rising compliance costs. The suspension comes as international buyers increasingly favour carbon credits certified under the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market’s (ICVCM) Core Carbon Principles (CCP), while existing domestic regulations make it costly for local projects to meet the new standards. Speaking to the Daily News recently, Carbon Tanzania Chief Executive Officer, Ms Sally Capper said the project had suffered a sharp decline in funding as buyers shifted away from traditional REDD+ forest protection credits. “The decision comes as the project faces a sharp decline in funding as a result of global demand that is prioritising Core Carbon Principles (CCPs)-labelled carbon credits, which entail high costs to upgrade projects to new methodologies and a prohibitive domestic regulatory framework,” Ms Capper said. She said the temporary suspension would allow stakeholders to address the challenges and identify solutions that would enable the project to transition to CCPlabelled standards and secure long-term funding. The Yaeda-Eyasi Landscape Project protects about 108,000 hectares of dryland forest in northern Tanzania, the ancestral homeland of the Hadza hunter-gatherers who have lived in the area for thousands of years. Implemented since 2013 through a partnership between Carbon Tanzania and Hadza and Datooga communities, the project works with 11 villages involving about 63,000 people across Manyara and Arusha regions. Ms Capper said the changing voluntary carbon market had significantly reduced demand for conventional REDD+ credits, with many buyers now preferring carbon removal projects over emission reduction initiatives. She said Tanzania also lacks some of the national datasets required under the new CCP methodologies, making it difficult for local project developers to transition their credits quickly to meet emerging global standards. According to her, the combination of changing market expectations and regulatory costs has disrupted revenues earned by communities participating in carbon projects. “Funds are actively being sought to bridge the gap until the project can upgrade,” she said. While reaffirming Carbon Tanzania’s commitment to its community partners, Ms Capper said the current framework places an unsustainable financial burden on project developers. “Our primary duty is to ensure they continue to receive the financial benefits of their stewardship. To do that, we need to bridge this funding gap and work alongside other stakeholders to build a regulatory framework in Tanzania that actually enables high-quality carbon projects to succeed,” she said. She said similar regulatory challenges had also forced Carbon Tanzania to pause development of another project covering the Tongwe and Masito forests in western Tanzania. The company is evaluating how that initiative can achieve long-term success for local district councils, surrounding communities and the company within the existing regulatory framework. Ms Capper said the experience highlighted the importance of transparent and supportive policies in unlocking both the economic and ecological value of Tanzania’s forest resources. “To make nature-based carbon projects viable in Tanzania over the long term, the national carbon trading regulatory framework needs to be reformed,” she said. She warned that without regulatory changes, high investment and compliance costs could threaten the viability of community-based carbon projects across the country. According to 2024 Uongozi Institute report, Carbon Trading in Tanzania, also calls for stronger regulatory and institutional frameworks, improved coordination across the sector and benchmarking Tanzania’s carbon trading system against more developed regional and international markets.

artigo.texto: The Baltimore Banner’s annual innovation conference returns for a second year with a program focused on the infrastructure supporting digital businesses and the research institutions helping develop new products and companies. BannerX will be Sept. 30, in Columbia, Maryland. The event launched last year to explore how organizations could navigate the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. This year, the conversation shifts to what it takes to build and sustain the foundation in this space through four main discussions: - Data center development - The risks of adopting AI - Collaboration in the life sciences - How tech intersects with economic policy The program also includes a conversation on Maryland’s innovation future, bringing technology, public policy, workforce development and economic strategy into one discussion. It will explore how those areas intersect and the role of partnerships across government, industry and the broader business community. Speakers leading the conversations represent a range of perspectives from academia, government and industry. They include W. Mason Emnet, senior vice president of public policy at Constellation; Jason Michael Perry, founder and chief AI officer at PerryLabs; and Monica Lopez, privacy officer at VHC Health and cofounder and CEO of Cognitive Insights for AI. Also slated to participate is Bezawit Sumner, chief information security officer and senior director of security and compliance at CRISP Shared Services; Mary Morris, director of innovation initiatives at the University of Maryland, Baltimore; and Bret Schreiber, senior vice president of life sciences and technology at Fulton Financial Corp. Together, the sessions aim to help answer questions like: “Who is prepared to use a new technology?” “What infrastructure does it require?” “Which organizations need to work together to put it into practice?” With the central discussions plus space for networking, the event creates a venue for conversation between the people and institutions involved in turning technological capability into everyday use. BannerX takes place Sept. 30, 2026, on the first floor of 10285 Lakefront at 10285 Little Patuxent Parkway in Columbia, MD. Doors open at 8:30 a.m., and the program runs from 9 to 11:30 a.m. Tickets are $45 and include the discussions, networking and breakfast. The full agenda and registration are available online.

artigo.texto: A U.K. lab test detected only trace lithium in battery material provided by Finnish startup Donut Lab, and the company has cited the result as support for its argument that the much-discussed cell is not lithium-ion. Even so, the test left major questions unanswered — Donut Lab disassembled the sample before analysis, and, as Electrek reported on Sept. 23, no production vehicle used the battery. Here's what to know Intertek's lab in Wilton, U.K., reported 3.4 ppm lithium by weight and 632 ppm sodium in a small amount of material identified as the anode, cathode, and current collector, per Electrek. "We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery," Donut Lab CEO Marko Lehtimäki explained. Lithium-ion cells typically contain lithium at much higher levels. If the tested material truly came from a functioning Donut Lab cell, the result would seem to rule out the battery chemistry most commonly used in the market. Intertek did not attempt to determine the battery's complete chemistry and was asked only to measure lithium and sodium. The material also reached the lab in "tear down condition" from Donut Lab, so Intertek was not the party that opened a sealed cell. Electrek noted that the published report labeled the material only as "Pouchcell – Cell 1." It said nothing in the document clearly connected that sample to the Donut "V1.5" unit VTT used in energy-density testing. More background Better batteries can help cut EV charging time, extend driving range, strengthen backup power during blackouts and storms, and eventually lower costs for drivers, fleets, and cities transitioning away from fuel-burning vehicles. That promise helped Donut Lab attract significant attention at CES in January, when it said it had the "world's first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing." But the company's timeline has since come under greater scrutiny as independent testing has slowly emerged. Questions about Donut Lab's claims intensified in June, when Electrek reported that battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts reviewed the voltage curve and swelling data from a Donut Lab cell sent to VTT. They said it behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion battery with a graphite anode. VTT also measured 185.7 watt-hours per pound (409.3 watt-hours per kilogram) on a Donut cell cycled between 2.3 and 4.25 volts — numbers that fit familiar lithium-ion territory. What's being done? Companies including Toyota, Samsung SDI, Factorial, and QuantumScape have solid-state cells working in lab settings and prototype vehicles, even if large-scale production remains a difficult step. Lehtimäki admitted that the battery was "already in production," but also acknowledged that the 185.5 watt-hours per pound (409 Wh/kg) cell "is not even the cell that's going to be shipped to customers." Where can I learn more? Questions about Donut Lab's battery underscore a broader push to improve chemistry, safety, and real-world EV performance. These stories explore battery advances aimed at extending range and reducing reliance on conventional materials. • Researchers found lithium titanium phosphate could ease range limits that still worry EV buyers. • Engineers are testing long-range lithium-ion batteries with potential for EVs and airplanes. • At the University of Hong Kong, a high-temperature design could open new battery paths. artigo.texto: A carbon credit may be traded as a single unit, but its value is shaped long before it reaches a buyer. Decisions about project ownership, finance, data, verification and benefit-sharing determine who participates, who carries the risk and who ultimately benefits. As new regulations and international partnerships expand market access, these questions are becoming increasingly important across Africa. They will be central to the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026, taking place from 13 to 15 October at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda. The summit will convene African governments, project developers, investors, buyers and technical experts involved in decisions across the carbon-market value chain. Countries are approaching these decisions from different regulatory, economic and environmental positions. While recent developments in East Africa demonstrate growing market activity, questions concerning international requirements, technical capacity, investment and benefit-sharing are relevant across Africa. Ousmane Fall SARR, Coordinator of the West African Alliance on Carbon Markets and Climate Finance, says: “African countries are developing carbon markets from different starting points. Stronger African expertise and regional cooperation will be important if the continent is to contribute to the standards and market practices that determine how its projects compete, attract investment and create value.” Against this continental backdrop, East Africa provides a timely example of how the market is developing. In January 2026, Rwanda and Singapore invited applications for carbon-credit projects under their bilateral Implementation Agreement, aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Credits from authorised projects may be used by eligible Singapore-based carbon tax-liable companies to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions, subject to both governments’ requirements. Across the continent, carbon market frameworks are rapidly taking shape. Kenya and Uganda are strengthening regulatory oversight, regional partnerships are helping governments build market capacity and infrastructure, and South Africa is advancing reforms to modernise its carbon-credit ecosystem and attract investment. Together, these developments are bringing greater focus to questions of authorisation, project ownership, verification, pricing and access to international buyers, while also raising expectations that carbon finance should deliver sustainable economic and development value beyond the credit itself. Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director for CMAS, says: “A carbon credit may be the final product, but behind it are decisions about ownership, data, risk, pricing and who ultimately benefits. The conversations in Kigali will examine what credible participation looks like across the full carbon-market value chain.” These decisions have consequences beyond individual transactions. Carbon finance is increasingly connected to conservation, agriculture, soil restoration, food security, clean energy and waste management. Its success will therefore also be judged by whether projects produce credible environmental outcomes and lasting benefits for African economies and communities. A practical example comes from the Chinko Conservation Area in the Central African Republic, where revenue from the Chinko Carbon Project is channelled through a community fund that supports locally selected initiatives, including the expansion of a medical centre in Agoumar. At CMAS 2026, African Parks and Welthungerhilfe, both Bronze Sponsors, will share perspectives on how carbon finance can support conservation, climate resilience, food systems and community development, while highlighting broader questions around project governance, impact and the distribution of value. From project-level impact to market-wide structures, these questions will underpin discussions at CMAS 2026. The programme will address government authorisation, buyer requirements, pricing and offtake, investment risk, early-stage finance, registries and African measurement, reporting and verification capacity. It will connect the question of who sets the terms with the practical requirements for building credible, investment-ready projects and transactions. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with UNDP and the African Development Bank as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. Taking place ahead of COP31, CMAS will focus attention on the decisions behind every carbon credit and what they mean for African governments, projects, investors and communities.

artigo.texto: This Albertan trades in a murky carbon market crucial to Carney's pipeline deal When Ana Avramovic was young, art school was her plan. She landed a job trading power instead, and 20 years later runs her own Calgary firm, dealing in something you can’t see or touch. And the stakes are enormous Article content Everything Ana Avramovic sells sits as numbered entries in a government registry, and none of them are hers. She trades carbon credits, a job so unusual even her mother doesn’t fully understand what she does for a living. She came to carbon from power trading, having cut her teeth at Calgary-based TransAlta Corp. Ask her whether leaving a traditional paycheque to build a firm of her own was brave or reckless. The answer depends on the day. “Overall, excited,” she says. “And then sometimes like, oh my God, what am I doing? What have I done?” When she traded power, explaining her job took one gesture toward a window. “You see that hotel?” she says. “Somebody has to sell them electricity.” Carbon is trickier. You can’t see electricity either, but everyone knows what it’s for. She founded Carbon Merchant in July 2026 to trade industrial carbon and clean fuel credits. Every big emitter in Alberta, from oilsands operators to power producers and miners, has a limit on what it can release into the atmosphere. Beat the limit and you earn credits for cutting emissions. Miss the benchmark and you buy them from somebody who did. Avramovic is the broker in the middle, helping buyers and sellers find each other. The 42-year-old works in a market so opaque that outsiders can’t make sense of it. And, yet the stakes are enormous. The market is one of Canada’s biggest levers against climate change. Its design is a signature priority in Ottawa and lies at the centre of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s deal with Alberta on a possible West Coast pipeline for oil. But there are flaws, too. Critics worry the market is falling short and flooded with cheap credits, which means that meeting the rules is far less expensive for industry. For Avramovic, it is personal. She has two young children, and they will inherit whatever this market does or fails to do. She chose the work because it was the one place her own effort might count. “I’m just one person. It’s not like I can fix it all,” she says, “but I can at least do a little part.” Location, location, emissions Avramovic rents an office at Pavilion, a coworking space in downtown Calgary. She starts around 7 a.m., and her day is nonstop: ICE chat, where energy traders connect on the Intercontinental Exchange, plus texts, calls, Teams meetings, in-person meetings and coffee, lots of it. “A lot of my day is just communicating with different people and figuring out what are they doing, what are they looking to do,” she says. Most of her deals are spot work: one buyer, one seller, done in days. The deal she is building now is slower — a multi-year clean fuel arrangement. She is not matching a buyer to a seller on something that already exists; she is building the deal itself, putting sides together for years rather than for a week. Those are the harder matches. “It’s the challenge, the hunt. That’s what makes it fun,” she says. Avramovic’s work is similar to what a real estate agent does, minus the house. A company calls knowing what it needs but not who has it. Avramovic knows who does, and who needs to sell before its deadline. The property just happens to be carbon, so there is nothing to walk through and no keys to hand over, just a line in a registry that moves out of one account and into another. She takes a fee when the deal closes, or a monthly retainer from clients who want to know where prices are heading. Alberta’s industrial carbon market is the biggest in Canada, and it exists because the province requires it, and has since 2007, when Ed Stelmach’s government put a price on industrial carbon. No one in North America had priced industrial carbon before Alberta did. The European Union got there first. The regulation is meant to be the stick. “But then, within that regulation,” Avramovic says, “there’s also a carrot that if you do those actions, you can then create credits and monetize them.” The actions are emissions cuts. One credit is not the same as another. Each one carries a vintage, like wine, the year it was created. One made in 2024 is good until 2029, then it expires. On the open market, these credits trade for less than $30 a tonne. The alternative is paying $95 a tonne into a government fund. In recent years, big emitters have used as many credits as the rules allow, Avramovic says. Those prices are about to go up. Sarajevo to power trading Avramovic was born in Sarajevo. The family escaped in the early 1990s, when a war started, and moved to the coast of Croatia, where her mother is from, and lived with her maternal grandparents. Her father escaped in the summer of 1994. Her parents applied to immigrate to Canada, and they arrived in June 1995, two weeks after her 11th birthday. She wanted art school. Her parents had crossed an ocean to start over in a new country, and they wanted their daughter to have a profession. She went to the Haskayne School of Business at the University of Calgary, and after graduation took a creative job at Critical Mass, a Calgary agency that was doing some of the first advertising on the internet. On a whim she answered an ad for a real-time power trader at TransAlta. The desk was hiring four new traders for Alberta, she says, two women and two men. “I just put my hand up,” she says. She got one of the four. Power is a 24-hour commodity, so the desk ran 12-hour shifts, two days, two nights, then days off, moving power between regions to capture the gap between what it cost to send and what it fetched at the other end. “I was lucky at TransAlta because they were trying to prioritize hiring more women onto a trade floor,” she says. “And so, I got my chance that way.” Trading is still a man’s business, she says, and whi

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. artigo.texto: Segundo o InvestNews, análise da The Economist divulgada neste domingo (27) mostra que a indústria europeia vive crise concentrada, não generalizada. Montadoras e químicas perdem terreno, enquanto fabricantes de equipamentos para data centers e empresas de defesa ampliam atividades. A produção de veículos da União Europeia está 17% menor que antes da pandemia. A China, que já rendia lucros às montadoras europeias, agora lança carros mais rápido e com custos menores. Em 2025, a UE importou € 559,4 bilhões em mercadorias chinesas e exportou € 199,6 bilhões, com déficit de quase € 360 bilhões, segundo o Eurostat. Antes de subsídios, a eletricidade industrial na França e na Alemanha custa cerca do dobro da registrada nos EUA ou na China, conforme a Economist. Desde o começo de 2023, o emprego na manufatura da UE caiu cerca de 2%, para 28 milhões, e quatro quintos dessa perda vieram da Alemanha. No mesmo período, vagas para engenheiros e técnicos cresceram 7%. Empresas buscam novas receitas: Vestas e MTU Aero Engines vendem manutenção; Siemens comprou empresas de software; Solvay e K+S buscaram reduzir exposição à oscilação dos preços de energia. Componentes chineses podem baratear a produção europeia, e estudo do Banco Central Europeu associou essas importações ao avanço da produção. artigo.texto: The blue-collar AI job market is booming. Will data center backlash make it go bust? - AI is stimulating job creation in traditionally blue-collar professions. - Welders, plumbers, HVAC technicians, and electricians are all finding their skills in high demand for data center buildouts, though many of the construction jobs are temporary in nature. - Recent moves by states including New York and Texas to slow development, as well as local freezes across the U.S. in response to intense public backlash, could impact the labor market trend. When most people think of AI and jobs, the conversation often pivots to which occupations are most likely to be obliterated by its arrival. But, at least for some professions, the AI boom has been an employment one too. AI is creating jobs in a variety of trades that prop up the sprawling ecosystem that powers giants like Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and others. The construction and maintaining of data centers and the entire AI ecosystem is requiring a new generation of HVAC technicians, construction workers, line workers, and pipefitters. "These are occupations that are becoming increasingly important to the AI economy," said Maria Flynn, president and CEO of national nonprofit Jobs for the Future. While data centers are the part that gets the publicity, they are only one piece of a much larger puzzle, requiring upgrades in transportation and modernization of the energy grid. "We are seeing major sources of demand that are converging at the same time," Flynn said. The skilled jobs often come with attractive pay. Flynn said an apprentice level technician can take home $40,000 to $60,000, with experienced electricians commanding north of $100,000. Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at online employment marketplace ZipRecruiter, is seeing salaries even higher for more specialized, high skill roles. Bachaud said that the mean minimum salary for data center jobs spiked by 125.1% year-over-year to nearly $208,000. "This is suggesting that highly specialized, top-tier engineering roles are pulling the overall average up drastically," Bachaud said. While many traditional blue-collar workers are seeing a boost, including truckers, the biggest blue collar beneficiaries, according to Bachaud's data, are welders and pipefitters. Postings for those jobs are up 164% year over year. While that could be partly the result of a small sample size as more data centers are built, even if each one only needs a few pipefitters, the demand for these roles will increase, she said. The construction demand is also uneven with some places getting in on it more than others. Houston and Birmingham have seen particularly robust growth. "Places with more land to expand and build, which are often places where building regulations make development easier, cheaper, and faster, will likely be where expansion continues, versus coastal hubs that have higher costs and more regulatory burdens," Bachaud said. That means an electrician or pipefitter in Birmingham will probably have more of a buyer's market than one in Boston. None of this surprises Justin Sinkovich, associate professor and associate director of the School of Business and Entrepreneurship at Columbia College Chicago. In his view, the usual AI jobs narrative of displacement is incomplete, with the data center counter-story as one example. While AI may automate some work, its deployment depends on the buildout of infrastructure, including not only data centers but also substations, cooling systems, water, and piping infrastructure, which AI cannot build. "Positive effects on the labor market are already visible, with an increased demand for cooling and HVAC engineers, industrial automation technicians, and traditional trade workers like construction workers and electricians. HVAC-engineering wages have risen, and many technical professionals entering data-center roles are seeing a pay premium," Sinkovich said. He pointed to Louisiana as a specific example, where both Amazon and Meta have massive projects. "Amazon committed $12 billion to a new data center with 540 new on-site jobs, including 1,700 electricians, technicians, and security personnel. Meta's Hyperion project in Louisiana is $27 billion," Sinkovich said. "These projects create demand for on-site workers and therefore cannot be offshored or conducted remotely, unlike manufacturing and software," he added. He also said there is a longer-term story of AI enabling more decentralized and dynamic energy systems. This not only improves energy efficiency but also creates additional work to build smart controls, battery systems, microgrids, and distributed energy infrastructure. Economic optimism vs. public skepticism Recent research from global real estate services firm Cushman & Wakefield indicates that every 100MW of new data center development creates nearly 1,300 jobs in the local economy, generating approximately $110 million in annual wages, $344 million in gross output, and $187 million in gross regional product. And many of these jobs aren't ones requiring a diploma. In fact, many of them are better suited to a path through trade school. But the optimistic shovels on the ground analysis don't match the national mood. Seventy percent of Americans oppose a data center being built in their local area, according to Gallup, and a New York Times/Siena poll conducted this month found roughly two-thirds opposed regardless of party — Democrats, independents and Republicans alike. Even where data centers are proceeding at a robust clip and creating the most jobs public opinion has turned against them. Fifty-seven percent of voters oppose one in their own community, according to a Texas Politics Project poll, enough that some experts see Democrats gaining ground in the Lone Star State.
