artigo.texto: A blaze at the Moss Landing Power Plant in California has been linked to remediation work following the major battery energy storage system (BESS) fire at the site in January 2025. Firefighters from North Monterey County Fire District were dispatched to the facility on 18 September 2026, where they found smoke and flames coming from the north side of the site. As reported by the Santa Cruz Local, the site was evacuated of personnel with no injuries reported and a shelter-in-place warning was issued for surrounding areas as a precaution because of potential health risks associated with smoke and debris. The incident also affected traffic on the nearby Highway 1. Officials subsequently described the incident as a “flare-up” connected with clean-up operations following the January 2025 fire. The latest fire occurred in the Moss 300 building, which was extensively damaged during the original incident and experienced another fire in February 2025. Moss Landing’s Vistra battery storage facility comprises three buildings known as Moss 100, Moss 300, and Moss 350. Following the January 2025 incident, approximately 45,000 batteries reportedly remained intact and charged. Work has since been taking place to remove and de-energise them. At the time of this most recent incident, US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) officials said approximately 3,600 batteries remained to be removed from Moss 300, with some caught up in the latest incident. The incident was stabilised by 19 September, responsibility for continued monitoring was subsequently returned to facility personnel, and the shelter-in-place order was lifted. EPA on-scene coordinator Kazami Brockman said the remediation presented continuing challenges, saying, “this situation is complex”. Work crews have had to pause the clean up when encountering areas where removing batteries could create a risk of further flare-ups and officials have warned that additional incidents remain possible as work progresses. Katherine Hull, Federal On-Scene Coordinator for the EPA, said: “We’ve been doing everything that we absolutely can to prevent this from happening. Unfortunately, this did happen. So we just continue to monitor the batteries, and it’s a priority for us to get these batteries moved out of the building as quickly and as safely as we can.” Air monitoring during the incident did not record concerning concentrations of fine particles, while officials reported no detections of hydrogen fluoride as a result of the blaze. As reported by the Mercury News, Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church said the latest incident again highlighted concerns surrounding the safety of battery energy storage installations. “It’s frustrating that this has continued to happen,” he said. “This fire is alarming for the community, bringing to the forefront once again that safety is paramount in every way we deal with battery energy storage systems.” He added: “While we need reliable and efficient battery energy storage systems, the key is that they really must be safe at all times whether while in operation or in a clean up.” Officials said the flare-up was not expected to alter the existing clean-up schedule, although unstable batteries remaining inside the damaged building mean further fires cannot be ruled out.

artigo.texto: Advait Energy’s arm signed a supply deal with HiTHIUM for up to 1 GWh of battery cells to feed its upcoming storage plant in Gujarat. Advait Battery Ecosystem, a step-down subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions Ltd, signed a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM on 18 September, the company said in an exchange filing. HiTHIUM is a global energy storage manufacturer, listed as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 supplier. Battery energy storage systems, called BESS, hold power so it can be used later, on power grids and in factories. Advait plans to assemble them in Gujarat, and it needs battery cells to do that. This deal covers the need. The plant needs cells first. HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic cells, with up to 1 GWh of purchases over the next 12 months. GWh is a measure of stored energy capacity. LFP cells are widely used in stationary storage because of their long life and stability. The contract price is $49.5 per kWh for up to 350 MWh of cells. Pricing beyond that will depend on future project orders. The cells will go to a planned assembly plant at Gangad in Gujarat, with a capacity of 2.5 GWh a year. It will put together modules and packs, fit them into containers and commission the systems for utility, commercial and industrial customers. The company says commercial production should begin soon. Bhushan Shahane, chief operating officer of Advait Battery Ecosystem, said a dependable, world-class cell supply is central to delivering cost-efficient storage systems as the plant scales up. The 1 GWh covers about 40% of the plant’s yearly capacity. It is a supply framework, not a firm order for the whole amount, and actual use will depend on production schedules and customer demand. For HiTHIUM, the deal opens a supply link with an Indian storage manufacturer. The listed parent is also widening its business. artigo.texto: A LG anunciou nesta segunda-feira (28) que passou a integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network (NPN) como Parceira Preferencial em Soluções de Energia e Resfriamento. A colaboração amplia a atuação da companhia no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura para data centers voltados a cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial. Segundo a LG, o aumento da densidade computacional dos data centers de IA exige sistemas capazes de lidar com cargas térmicas maiores. Nesse cenário, a empresa está ampliando seu portfólio de soluções de resfriamento líquido, voltadas principalmente para infraestruturas de alta densidade. A companhia também destaca a integração das soluções de resfriamento desde os estágios iniciais do planejamento dos data centers, permitindo considerar as necessidades térmicas e de energia na própria concepção da infraestrutura. LG tem CDU de 2,6 MW qualificada pela NVIDIA Entre os principais produtos apresentados pela LG está uma Unidade de Distribuição de Fluido de Resfriamento (CDU) de 2,6 MW. Segundo a empresa, o equipamento foi qualificado como NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU e atualmente possui a maior capacidade de resfriamento entre as soluções que receberam essa qualificação. A LG também concluiu a qualificação de infraestrutura de IA para modelos de 600 kW e 1 MW. De acordo com a companhia, o processo de avaliação considerou critérios técnicos relacionados ao desempenho de resfriamento, recursos de failover e confiabilidade. As qualificações fazem parte da estratégia da LG para atuar em diferentes etapas da infraestrutura térmica necessária para data centers de IA de alta densidade. Resfriamento líquido direto ao chip As CDUs desenvolvidas pela LG utilizam uma arquitetura de resfriamento líquido direto ao chip (DTC, Direct-to-Chip). Nesse sistema, o fluido de resfriamento é direcionado diretamente para componentes que geram grande quantidade de calor, incluindo CPUs e GPUs. A solução pode trabalhar em conjunto com sistemas tradicionais de resfriamento a ar já instalados no data center. A combinação permite criar uma arquitetura híbrida, utilizando o resfriamento líquido nos componentes de maior demanda térmica enquanto mantém parte da infraestrutura convencional para outras áreas do ambiente. O avanço desse tipo de tecnologia está relacionado ao aumento das cargas de processamento utilizadas por sistemas de inteligência artificial. A LG afirma que suas CDUs foram desenvolvidas para lidar com essas demandas térmicas em infraestruturas de alta densidade. LG prepara CDU de 4 MW para qualificação A empresa também revelou planos de ampliar sua linha de soluções. Até o final de 2026, a LG pretende buscar a qualificação da NVIDIA para uma CDU com capacidade de 4,0 MW. A iniciativa deve ampliar a capacidade do portfólio voltado a data centers de IA e complementar os modelos de 600 kW, 1 MW e 2,6 MW já mencionados pela companhia. A LG não divulgou, no anúncio, uma previsão de conclusão do processo de qualificação do modelo de 4 MW além da indicação de que pretende buscá-la até o fim deste ano. Soluções serão apresentadas em evento em Singapura As CDUs da LG que concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura de IA da NVIDIA serão apresentadas na Data Centre World Asia 2026 (DCWA 2026). O evento está programado para acontecer entre 29 e 30 de setembro, no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. A participação permitirá à LG apresentar suas soluções de resfriamento líquido para data centers e os modelos que já passaram pelos processos de qualificação relacionados à infraestrutura de IA da NVIDIA. Parceria mira expansão da infraestrutura de IA A entrada da LG na NVIDIA Partner Network como Parceira Preferencial em Soluções de Energia e Resfriamento coloca as soluções de gerenciamento térmico da companhia dentro do ecossistema de parceiros da NVIDIA voltado à infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. “Integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network como Parceira Preferencial em Energia e Resfriamento é um passo importante em nossa estratégia para apoiar a expansão do ecossistema global de IA”, afirmou James Lee, presidente da LG ES Company. Segundo o executivo, a LG pretende trabalhar com a NVIDIA no desenvolvimento de soluções de resfriamento destinadas aos desafios térmicos dos data centers de IA. Com as CDUs de 600 kW, 1 MW e 2,6 MW já qualificadas e o plano de buscar a qualificação de um modelo de 4 MW, a empresa pretende ampliar sua presença no segmento de infraestrutura térmica para data centers de alta densidade. - Categorias Participe do grupo de ofertas do Mundo Conectado Confira as principais ofertas de Smartphones, TVs e outros eletrônicos que encontramos pela internet. artigo.texto: A WEG (WEGE3) anunciou nesta segunda-feira (28) um investimento de US$ 165 milhões (R$ 840 milhões) para ampliar sua capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte. O plano busca atender à crescente demanda por geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos Estados Unidos, impulsionada especialmente pela expansão dos data centers. Segundo comunicado ao mercado, o projeto será executado em duas fases. Ao fim da expansão, prevista para 2030, a capacidade global da companhia chegará a cerca de 50 geradores por dia. Atualmente, a empresa pode produzir 10 unidades diárias. WEG terá nova operação de geradores no México A primeira etapa prevê investimento de US$ 24 milhões na compra e adequação de um prédio industrial no México, destinado à montagem de geradores. O início das operações está previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, a WEG investirá US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais. A localização ainda será definida, mas ambas ficarão na América do Norte. Com a conclusão do projeto, a capacidade global de produção será cinco vezes a atual, considerando as fábricas da companhia no México, nos Estados Unidos, no Brasil e na China.

artigo.texto: Larsen fights for guardrails on data centers Published 1:30 am Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Submitted by the Office of Rep. Rick Larsen. U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen (WA-02) joined 110 House Democrats in a letter to tech industry leaders last Friday, demanding that all data center construction follow strict guardrails to protect consumers from electricity and water price hikes. “Data center projects and the energy systems and infrastructure that support them must be built and operated responsibly with a commitment to high-quality construction, good jobs, strong environmental stewardship, and strong partnerships with the communities they serve,” wrote the Members. The lawmakers stated that they would oppose new data center construction projects that failed to incorporate strong labor standards, negotiate community benefits agreements with local leaders and mitigate impacts on local air quality, drinking water and utilities costs for residents. “At a time when the nation’s power grid, roads, bridges, schools, and other public infrastructure require significant investment, data center development must strengthen rather than strain, these systems,” the Members continued. “Developers must also invest responsibly in grid infrastructure, including new generation and grid upgrades, to protect ratepayers from bearing the costs of data center projects’ energy needs.” The full text of the letter to tech industry leaders can be read at https://larsen.house.gov/uploadedfiles/final_open_letter_to_tech_industry_leaders_9.18.26.pdf. Larsen holds data centers accountable Last week, Larsen voted for legislation to protect families from higher electricity bills because of data centers in their communities (Ratepayers Protection Act). Larsen also cosponsors the Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act to roll back tax breaks for large artificial intelligence data centers in Republicans’ Big Ugly Law. Larsen supports tough, upfront restrictions on data centers: • No high electric bills for local families and small businesses. • No federal tax breaks. • No construction without community approval and union labor. • Data centers must pay their fair share to connect to and use the grid. • Data centers must use closed-loop water systems. A one-pager on Rep. Larsen’s work to hold data centers accountable can be found at https://larsen.house.gov/uploadedfiles/data_centers_one_pager_1.pdf.

artigo.texto: Bangor City Council votes to extend data center moratorium Published: Sep. 28, 2026 at 11:27 PM EDT|Updated: 7 hours ago BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor City Council has unanimously voted to extend a freeze on new data centers. Councilors voted 8-0 Monday night to add another 180 days to the city’s data center moratorium. Officials say Bangor faces growing interest from developers looking to build data centers, which take up large tracts of land and require massive amounts of power and water for cooling. Because city ordinances weren’t designed for facilities of this scale, councilors say the extra six months will give them time to draft zoning rules that protect local infrastructure, the environment, and neighboring property owners. artigo.texto: Portugal-headquartered Greenvolt Group has started construction of its 600 MW/2.4 GWh Siedlce battery energy storage system (BESS) in Poland through its utility-scale renewable energy business, Greenvolt Power. The project, expected to begin commercial operation by the end of 2027, will be Poland’s largest battery storage facility and one of Europe’s largest, it claims. BYD Energy Storage will supply the battery technology, with the project comprising 210 battery containers and 105 transformer containers equipped with power conversion systems. Siedlce is part of Greenvolt’s approximately 4.6 GW probability-weighted BESS pipeline, including around 2.4 GW in Poland. South Korean battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution has entered a strategic partnership with B2U Storage Solutions which is a US-based battery energy storage systems (BESS) manufacturer that works with repurposed EV batteries. Under the agreement, B2U will receive priority access to LG Energy Solution battery capacity and use its patented technologies to repurpose the batteries for grid-scale storage before recycling. The companies say their aim is to extend battery lifetimes and develop cost-competitive storage solutions for utilities, developers and large commercial users, including data centers. InoBat, a Slovakia-based BESS manufacturer and integrator is moving forward on its plans to list on the Nasdaq. The company along with Cartesian Growth Corporation II, a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), recently filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Their business combination agreement (BCA) values InoBat at $1.265 billion on a pre-money, pre-merger basis. Following completion, the combined company is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol INBT. InoBat counts Volkswagen Group-backed Gotion High-Tech, mining giant Rio Tinto, and Indian battery maker Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Limited among its strategic shareholders and partners. Alongside the transaction, InoBat is expanding its European manufacturing footprint in Slovakia. At its Voderady site, the company is developing a BESS module, pack and container assembly facility with a targeted annual capacity of 5 GWh. Meanwhile, GIB EnergyX Slovakia, its gigafactory investment with Gotion in Šurany, is developing a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell facility with an initial planned capacity of 20 GWh and targeted production start in 2027. The company is also advancing a sodium-ion battery roadmap in collaboration with Clarios and Altris. Decade Energy, a European developer of energy infrastructure for truck electrification, has signed a two-year supply framework agreement with Sungrow. The China-headquartered energy storage technology company will provide Decade Energy with up to 200 MWh of battery storage equipment in France. Decade Energy says this agreement is intended to support its growing French project pipeline. It will also enable the company to reduce complexity between projects and create a ‘repeatable’ delivery model across multiple sites. US-based SMT Energy has entered into an equity partnership with Climate Adaptive Infrastructure (CAI) for up to $268 million at the parent-company level. The investment, in addition to $32 million previously deployed by CAI into SMT assets, will support the development, construction and operation of battery storage projects across the US. SMT says the funding will enable it to develop and build energy infrastructure with an aggregate value significantly exceeding the equity investment. Its portfolio includes distributed-generation and utility-scale battery storage projects. Singapore-based renewable energy developer Vena Energy has secured a contract for its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project in Japan. The 46.8 MW grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS), under development near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture, was selected in Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). Vena Energy says the LTDA provides long-term revenue certainty to support investment in decarbonized power infrastructure. Nordic Solar, a Danish renewable energy company, has started commercial operation of a 20 MW/40 MWh BESS at its Moletai site in Lithuania. The battery is now integrated with the company’s existing 100 MW solar park, with hybrid trading now underway. The integration of solar generation and battery storage is expected to improve operational flexibility and enable the company to better utilize renewable power generation and market opportunities, stated Nordic Solar. The company switched on the 100 MW Moletai Solar Park in 2024 calling it the country’s largest back then (see Lithuania’s ‘Largest’ Solar Power Station Commissioned).

artigo.texto: During a recent trip to Sichuan Province in China, we got a chance to see BYD’s Flash Chargers up close. For those unfamiliar with the brand’s Flash Charging technology, these T-shaped structures provide EV charging at a rapid pace—around 9.7% charge per minute. According to BYD Philippines’ Adam Hu, these chargers are expected to arrive on our shores by 2027. The BYD Flash Chargers were first launched in China this year, with global rollouts expected for next year. The brand states that it can achieve charging times from 10% to 70% in only five minutes, and 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. During a live demonstration, the charging connector was plugged into a Denza Z9 GT, and while charging, a cup of pour-over coffee was being made on the side. The coffee was served in a cup just before the Z9’s battery topped off, achieving 97% from 33% in just seven minutes. What cars can use these chargers, you ask? Technically, anything with a CCS2 DC charging port can top up at these stations, but the Flash Charging feature is specific to cars with second-generation BYD Blade Batteries. In the Philippines, there are currently no cars equipped with the Blade Battery 2.0. However, the Denza Z9 GT and BYD Ti 7, which are both expected to come to the Philippines, are equipped with these batteries. The rest of the CCS2-equipped vehicles can charge at these stations but are limited to their maximum charging speed. OTHER STORIES YOU MIGHT HAVE MISSED: Fare hikes for jeepneys, buses, taxis, and TNVS take effect today Geely’s AI-powered EV charger will do sub-5min top-ups from 10% to 70% Even though most cars can’t take advantage of Flash Charging right now, it’s still a good thing that the infrastructure will be available. BYD and Denza’s future models will certainly feature Blade Battery 2.0 and later versions, so it shouldn’t be long before more consumers can use these ultra-fast chargers for their EVs.

artigo.texto: WTO to Review EU's Carbon Border Mechanism Challenged by Russia The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body has decided to establish a panel to examine the European Union's carbon border mechanism, which Russia has been challenging since May 2025. The World Trade Organization's (WTO) Dispute Settlement Body decided on Friday, September 25, to establish a panel to examine the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) as well as the European Union's Emissions Trading System for CO2. The decision follows a renewed request from Russia as part of the trade dispute it opened against the EU. The case had already faced an initial block from Brussels before the panel was ultimately established. A Mechanism in Force Since January 2026 The proceedings concern the European scheme applied since January 1, 2026, to imports of certain carbon-intensive products. According to the WTO, Russia had formally requested, on July 10, 2026, the establishment of a panel, after having sought consultations with the European Union and its member states as early as May 12, 2025. CBAM, known as MACF in French, aims to align the carbon cost borne by certain importers with that paid by European producers covered by the EU's carbon market. Its initial scope covers steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. The European Commission publishes a CBAM certificate price based on auctions under the European Emissions Trading System. This price stood at â¬75.36/tCO2e for the first quarter of 2026, then at â¬75.28/tCO2e for the second quarter of 2026, according to data released by the Commission. Russia Invokes International Trade Rules Moscow contests the European mechanism, arguing it violates the principles of international trade. In the proceedings registered with the WTO, Russia targets both the CBAM regulatory package and what it describes as an export subsidy linked to the European Emissions Trading System. Russia's complaint cites several provisions of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1994, as well as the Agreement on Import Licensing Procedures and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures. Russia also challenges the treatment of free allowances granted to certain European industries under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), which has been in force since 2005. Brussels Limits Dialogue with Moscow The European Union had rejected, on May 22, 2025, Russia's request for consultations. Brussels had then argued that such talks "could not be fruitful and could not lead to a mutually satisfactory resolution of the matter," citing the "extraordinary circumstances" created by the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Following Russia's request on July 10, 2026, the EU had blocked an initial establishment of the panel, an option available upon the first presentation before the Dispute Settlement Body. In practice, WTO rules subsequently lead to acceptance of a second panel request. In a communication to the WTO, the European Union states it will engage with the panel but not directly with Russia. Brussels stated: "As long as the Russian Federation continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, it cannot expect to be able to invoke WTO rules to improve access for its exports to the European Union market."

artigo.texto: Why the rush to build data centers? Let’s ignore all the technology chatter for now. Forget the debates about the infrastructure demands of these massive computing sites. And we’ll also sidestep the big question marks about artificial intelligence – the key driver of data center demand. If you follow the money, however, you see a major force behind developers’ thirst to construct data centers: They’ve been one of the nation’s hottest real estate investments. That’s what my trusty spreadsheet found when looking at Nareit indexes tracking values of real estate investment trusts owning properties across 15 key categories. These benchmarks calculate price swings and dividends paid. The value of trusts that own data centers rose 33% so far in 2026, the second-best performance in the REIT industry, and more than double a 15% gain for all trust assets. What’s performing better in 2026? Trusts that own lodging and resort properties are up 37% on a strong year for tourism. No. 3 is healthcare properties, up 23% as an aging population needs more medical services. Remember, real estate sectors like data centers often heat up when there’s a shortage of specific assets. Big gains in value, plus perceptions of high demand, often get developers in a construction mood. Not just this year Note that the investment buzz for data centers isn’t just a 2026 story. Data center values are up 43% from the start of 2024 through August 2026, the industry’s third-best result, and nearly double the 23% gain for all assets. The gains were only topped by healthcare properties, up 96%, and regional malls, up 69%. Shopping hubs are enjoying a go-out-to-shop renaissance. Trailing the pack So, what properties will developers avoid? Well, look at which property trusts trail the pack. In 2026, the worst places to be are casinos, down 5% as in-person gambling wanes; telecommunications properties, down 2% as cell phone growth ebbs; and timberland, down 1% amid weak construction demand for lumber. Looking longer-term, back to 2024, the trust laggards have been timberland, down 25%; telecommunications, down 16%; and owning single-family rentals, down 4%, as the housing market weakens and regulatory concerns grow. artigo.texto: Policy Considerations for Orbital Data Centers Orbital data centers could complement terrestrial infrastructure by processing selected workloads in space, particularly where data is generated in orbit. Their value will depend on technical performance, life cycle economics, market demand, and a regulatory environment that does not hinder testing and deployment. KEY TAKEAWAYS Key Takeaways Contents Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance 3 Advantages of Orbital Computing. 3 Technical and Economic Challenges for Orbital Data Centers 4 Policy Challenges and Recommendations for Orbital Data Centers 6 Introduction Orbital data centers are specialized satellites that support computing functions by processing data in space.[1] This emerging technology is attracting growing attention amid both rising demand for computing capacity and advances in commercial space capabilities.[2] As the global space economy continues to grow and more digital services rely on space-based infrastructure, orbital computing may become useful for selected space-based workloads. Government assessments, technical research, and industry feasibility studies are currently examining whether selected computing functions could be performed in orbit for specialized applications, although significant engineering and economic questions remain.[3] Today’s orbital data center concepts should not be understood as near-term substitutes for terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[4] Data centers on Earth benefit from mature supply chains, easier repair and upgrade cycles, and lower operating complexity. Orbital systems, by contrast, must operate in a harsher environment that includes radiation exposure, thermal management challenges, communications constraints, and high deployment and replacement costs.[5] If orbital compute clears current technical and economic hurdles, then the central policy consideration is whether orbital systems can perform specialized computing functions well enough to justify their operational complexity rather than whether they can replace terrestrial hyperscale data centers. Orbital computing can reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground. The strongest near-term opportunity for orbital computing lies in workloads that benefit from processing data where it is generated in space. These include Earth observation, remote sensing, and onboard spacecraft autonomy.[6] Over a longer time horizon, onboard or distributed computing could also become useful for certain lunar and cislunar missions, particularly where communications architecture or operational requirements favor local processing. In such settings, orbital computing may reduce bandwidth demands and improve operational responsiveness, particularly where decisions must be made in orbit rather than on the ground.[7] For that reason, orbital data centers are best treated as a complementary layer of digital infrastructure rather than a wholesale replacement for terrestrial systems.[8] Public policy should focus on ensuring that existing regulatory frameworks allow markets to identify and develop those applications for which orbital computing offers genuine comparative advantages, which could lead to orbital systems becoming a meaningful complement to the broader digital infrastructure ecosystem. Why Orbital Data Centers Are Gaining Relevance The simultaneous increase in demand for compute-intensive services alongside the improvement of commercial space capabilities is generating interest in orbital data centers. The Government Accountability Office’s (GAO’s) April 2026 “Science & Tech Spotlight” describes space-based data centers as “satellites that would house data processing and storage systems for AI and other computing needs,” potentially reducing the land, electricity, and water required by terrestrial facilities.[9] This framing, in the context of resistance to expanding terrestrial data center infrastructure, helps explain why the concept is now receiving policy attention, even though the underlying technology remains in an early stage.[10] Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases. Private-sector research has reinforced that interest. Google's Project Suncatcher is an exploratory initiative that examines the feasibility of scaling machine-learning compute in space using solar-powered satellite constellations, special processors, and free-space optical communications links.[11] Thales Alenia Space’s ASCEND project likewise presents space-based data centers as a feasibility question, indicating that orbital computing has become the subject of structured technical and commercial investigation.[12] The broader relevance is that orbital computing may become a useful layer of digital infrastructure for specific workloads before it becomes competitive with terrestrial cloud infrastructure.[13] A space-based architecture that is appropriate for one mission class may still be uneconomical for general-purpose computing, particularly where latency, maintenance, replacement, and scale economies continue to favor Earth-based facilities. Therefore, the current evidence supports measured attention rather than exaggerated expectations. Orbital data centers may eventually complement terrestrial infrastructure in specialized use cases, but their near-term significance will depend on whether the technical and economic constraints can be managed at acceptable costs. The role for policymakers is to create a regulatory environment that minimizes unnecessary barriers to testing and deploying this new technology. The true value of orbital data centers will be easier to assess once these regulatory barriers are reduced. artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Submer Group lança Corenix, empresa de data center modular para IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Submer Group anunciou em 28 de setembro de 2026 o lançamento da Corenix, uma empresa de infraestrutura de data center modular que atende neoclouds, hyperscalers e operadores de IA, e nomeou o ex‑executivo da Johnson Controls, Martin Renkis, como seu diretor executivo. A Corenix oferece plataformas de data center modular projetadas sob medida, baseadas em designs de referência da NVIDIA, que o Submer Group descreve como industrializados para IA em escala e entregues desde a construção e teste em fábrica até o comissionamento no local. A nova empresa tem sede em Houston, Texas, e foca na camada de implantação da infraestrutura de IA, reunindo energia de rack, refrigeração, rede e TI em um único sistema integrado, testado em fábrica, destinado a colocar capacidade de IA em operação em uma data fixa. Modelo de entrega fábrica‑para‑site De acordo com o modelo de entrega descrito pela empresa, a Corenix projeta, constrói, integra e testa em fábrica módulos completos e funcionais de data center — abrangendo TI, energia, refrigeração e rede — nas instalações de produção antes de entregá‑los aos locais dos projetos. A instalação, conexão à infraestrutura do site, teste de aceitação no local, comissionamento e preparação operacional ocorrem então no site do cliente. A Corenix gerencia o escopo do projeto acordado em ambas as etapas, combinando engenharia, manufatura, coordenação da cadeia de suprimentos e implantação no local em um único modelo de entrega. O Submer Group afirmou que as construções tradicionais de data center não conseguem acompanhar as demandas de energia, rede, refrigeração e capacidade de serviço da computação acelerada, nem a necessidade de suportar gerações sucessivas de computação de alta densidade, e que a Corenix foi criada para fechar essa lacuna. O grupo descreve a abordagem modular como oferecendo aos clientes um caminho repetível de uma arquitetura técnica aprovada até a capacidade operacional no local necessário, com cada plataforma baseada em um design de referência da NVIDIA e projetada sob medida para os requisitos específicos do cliente. Renkis afirmou que os clientes precisam de clareza antes de se comprometerem sobre o que deve ser construído, como será testado, quem é responsável e quando entrará em operação. “A Corenix coloca um programa datado e uma data de início em produção na mesa antes mesmo de existir um contrato”, disse ele. Ele acrescentou que uma equipe permanece responsável desde a integração e teste na fábrica até o comissionamento no local e a preparação operacional, com flexibilidade para suportar sistemas de computação acelerada atuais e futuros. Liderança Renkis chega à Corenix vindo da Johnson Controls, onde atuou como diretor executivo de Serviços de Infraestrutura de Data Center e desenvolveu ofertas de infraestrutura de IA que abrangem energia, refrigeração, recuperação de calor, operações e financiamento. Anteriormente, foi fundador e CEO da Smartvue, uma empresa de plataforma de hardware e software IoT adquirida pela Johnson Controls, e da Trainersoft, uma empresa de software corporativo de e‑learning adquirida pela OutStart, agora IBM. Patrick Smets, CEO do Submer Group, afirmou que as fábricas de IA estão gerando uma demanda sem precedentes por nova capacidade de data center e que o mercado precisa de uma forma mais rápida e previsível de construí‑la. “Estamos trazendo essa experiência para um negócio dedicado, criado para fornecer infraestrutura de IA em escala”, disse Smets, referindo‑se ao histórico do grupo na entrega modular de data centers e à expertise em engenharia, térmica e de infraestrutura que desenvolveu ao resolver desafios de computação de alta densidade. Estrutura e escala do Submer Group A Corenix baseia‑-se na experiência do Submer Group em engenharia térmica de alta densidade, implantação global de infraestrutura e operações. O grupo afirma que essa experiência foi comprovada em escala por um campus com centenas de megawatts de capacidade entregue como uma construção totalmente modular de computação em nove meses, desde o pedido até a entrega, juntamente com mais de uma década de engenharia de refrigeração líquida. A Corenix trabalha ao lado de duas empresas irmãs cujas capacidades apoiam os requisitos de implantação de infraestrutura de IA de ponta a ponta de um cliente: Rubix Data Centers, que desenvolve e opera campuses de data center de IA, e Radian Arc, que oferece GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service. O Submer Group, que se descreve como uma empresa de infraestrutura de IA de pilha completa, reúne empresas operacionais especializadas ao longo da pilha de infraestrutura de IA, abrangendo terra e energia até nuvem e edge. O grupo afirma ter implantado mais de 500 MW de infraestrutura refrigerada a líquido e possuir mais de 8 GW de terreno energizado nas Américas, EMEA e APAC. Fundado em Barcelona em 2015, o grupo opera globalmente com centros em Houston e Taipei. O site do grupo apresenta quatro camadas de capacidade: GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service, alimentados pela Radian Arc; desenvolvimento e operações de data center, alimentados pela Rubix; soluções de data center modular; e arquitetura térmica. O site também cita três laboratórios globais de P&D e mais de 90 redes de parceiros de telecomunicações em todo o mundo.

artigo.texto: Advait Battery Ecosystem, a subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions, signed a Master Supply Agreement with energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM for the supply of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells. Under the agreement, HiTHIUM will supply its 314 Ah LFP battery cells to support Advait’s upcoming battery energy storage system (BESS) assembly plant in India. 1 GWh Cell Supply to Support BESS Production Advait plans to procure up to 1 GWh of battery cells from HiTHIUM over the next 12 months. The supply arrangement will support the company as it moves towards commercial production and scales its domestic BESS assembly capabilities. Advait is developing a BESS assembly facility with an annual capacity of 2.5 GWh. The company plans to build capabilities across battery module and pack assembly as it expands its presence in India’s energy storage market. Securing a reliable battery cell supply is therefore an important part of Advait’s manufacturing strategy and will help establish a sourcing base for its initial production phase. 314 Ah LFP Cells for Energy Storage Systems The 314 Ah prismatic LFP cells will serve as the core energy storage component for BESS units assembled at Advait’s facility. LFP chemistry is widely used in stationary energy storage applications because of its combination of cycle life and thermal stability. Consequently, the cells are suited to applications requiring reliable and durable energy storage. Supporting India’s Battery Storage Supply Chain Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh facility forms part of its broader expansion into battery energy storage systems. The company is developing domestic assembly capabilities as demand for energy storage infrastructure increases alongside renewable power generation and grid modernisation. The company’s manufacturing strategy will integrate imported battery cells into locally assembled battery modules and packs. Over time, this approach could help strengthen domestic capabilities across the BESS value chain. HiTHIUM Expands Presence in India’s BESS Market For HiTHIUM, the agreement establishes a supply relationship with an Indian BESS manufacturer and expands the deployment of its 314 Ah LFP cell technology in India. Meanwhile, Advait will gain a defined cell supply base as it moves towards higher-volume commercial production. The planned offtake of up to 1 GWh over 12 months represents a significant portion of the facility’s 2.5 GWh annual assembly capacity, although actual utilisation will depend on production schedules and customer demand. Building Domestic BESS Manufacturing Capabilities The partnership will support Advait’s efforts to develop an integrated battery assembly ecosystem in India. By securing battery cells and combining them with domestic module and pack assembly capabilities, the company aims to establish a foundation for commercial BESS production. As India continues to expand renewable energy and modernise its power grid, battery energy storage systems are expected to play an increasingly important role in balancing electricity supply and demand. As reported by manufacturingtodayindia.com, Advait’s planned facility and its agreement with HiTHIUM position the company to participate in this growing energy storage market.

artigo.texto: ‘Cannot Give Up’: Hyundai’s R&D Boss On The Solid-State Battery Bet Hyundai's head of R&D expects that small-volume cars with solid-state batteries will hit the market within five years. Startups and big-time automakers alike continue to dump resources into solid-state batteries in the hope that this so-called "holy grail" technology will deliver blazing-fast EV charging and longer range. At the same time, conventional lithium-ion batteries now perform better than ever and continue to make strides. Just consider that Geely's latest technology allows for a 10-97% charge in under nine minutes. So is solid-state still worth chasing? According to Hyundai Motor Group research and development chief Manfred Harrer, the answer is a firm yes. "You cannot give up right now on that. That's clear," he told reporters last week. "You must be in the game." The batteries in today's EVs use a liquid electrolyte to transport lithium ions between a cell's anode and cathode. Solid-state batteries substitute that solution for a solid, often a ceramic or polymer, potentially bringing both safety and performance benefits. But nobody has cracked producing solid-state cells at automotive scale yet. Read Up On Solid-State Harrer said the potential advantages—a smaller battery, better fast-charging capability, and longer range—are hard to ignore. Within the next five years, he believes, there will be small-volume halo cars on the market with solid-state packs. That tracks with the timelines laid out by some other industry players; QuantumScape, for instance, expects its batteries to hit high-performance vehicles by the end of the decade. But the raw material costs will remain extraordinarily high for many years as the technology scales up, Harrer said, keeping the batteries out of the mass market. "You can solve, in the end, everything, but it comes with cost, tremendous cost," he said. Hyundai is developing solid-state batteries internally and alongside partners, like Solid Power. It's far from the only automaker investing in the technology, which Harrer calls "the big bet in the industry right now." Toyota has been working on solid-state for at least two decades and aims to put it in production in the next few years. Volkswagen is a big backer of QuantumScape. BMW is working with Solid Power. General Motors, Ford, Honda, and Nissan, among others, are working on it too. While some have trotted out demonstration prototypes—like a Ducati packed with QuantumScape cells or a Mercedes with Factorial's tech—none have put solid-state batteries into a car you can actually buy. Once the technology is mature, Harrer wants Hyundai to be there with its own supply chain and know-how. "We want to be the owner of this core technology, and that's the reason why we're also investing in our own battery manufacturing," he said. Harrer said the company sees a lot of value in deeply understanding what it takes to make batteries and the costs associated with that—because batteries are the most expensive part of an EV and because they also go into other electrified vehicles. Hyundai plans to put in-house nickel manganese cobalt cells in the Santa Fe extended-range EV that hits the market early next year. But it will be a considerably longer wait before solid-state makes its way into the mainstream, Harrer told reporters: "I am not believing you can solve the raw material cost problem in five years from now." artigo.texto: COEP Technological University (COEP Tech), Pune, and JSW Projects, a JSW Group company, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to establish an Advanced Battery Research & Development Centre at COEP Tech’s Chikhali Research Park. The Centre marks India’s first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale R&D platform, bringing lithium-ion cell technology development onto an academic campus in Pune for the first time. The collaboration positions COEP and Maharashtra as India’s battery-technology hub, with the potential to catalyse over 1,000 battery ecosystem-related jobs. It is a step towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s Net Zero 2070 ambition, anchoring the electric vehicle, grid storage and clean-energy future in Indian innovation. The partnership addresses one of the most persistent gaps in India’s innovation ecosystem: the distance between university research and industrial application. Under the MoU, COEP Tech’s faculty and students will work alongside JSW’s engineers on live, commercially critical technology, in an industry-academia collaboration model at the scale India needs. Prof. Sunil Bhirud, Hon’ble Vice Chancellor, COEP Technological University said, “This collaboration has the potential to create a strong indigenous alternative to imported batteries and make a significant contribution to India’s journey towards self-reliance. For students, it will provide a unique opportunity to learn and work on cutting-edge battery technologies. The scale and scope of the Phase I and Phase II collaboration between COEP Technological University and JSW make it a landmark industry-academia initiative. At a time when next-generation battery technologies are receiving significant research attention across the country, the partnership places research, innovation and technology development on a much larger platform. The collaboration has the potential to develop technologies that can reduce dependence on imported batteries and contribute to the vision of a self-reliant and developed India. The scale of this initiative makes it a significant step forward in strengthening India’s battery technology ecosystem. We are grateful for the valuable support extended by the Government of Maharashtra and the Board of Governors of COEP Technological University in enabling this important initiative.” Mr. Sajjan Jindal, Chairman, JSW Group, said, “Cell is the new oil. Just as oil powered the last century, battery cells will power this one, from electric vehicles to the grid. For decades, India has spent precious forex importing oil. This time, we must build the cutting-edge skills and capabilities to make these cells right here, for a new India. Our partnership with COEP Tech, with its 170-year legacy of engineering excellence, will bring industry and academia together to design, test and validate cells built for Indian conditions, and help shape India’s clean energy future.” A Shared Ambition Across the JSW Group The initiative draws on ambitions across the JSW Group, one of India’s most diversified industrial conglomerates. JSW Energy is aggressively building out grid-scale battery energy storage (BESS) alongside its renewable power business, while JSW Motors is expanding rapidly into electric mobility across every vehicle segment. Batteries sit at the heart of both ambitions, and JSW Group has committed to lead the indigenous value chain in this domain. Talent development, R&D capability, and a battery ecosystem at home are foundational to both the Group’s and India’s future. About the Engagement The project will be built in two phases, with a combined investment of more than ₹800 crore. Phase 1 will establish a Cell Research & Development Centre to design, simulate and prototype indigenous Li-ion and other advanced chemistry cells, including Sodium-ion. Phase 2 will scale this into a Cell Validation Centre capable of producing cells from 100-600 Ah. The batteries developed at the Centre are targeted to perform at par with the best in the world, while being built for India-centric climatic conditions and applications. The facility will serve as a foundation for joint research, publications, projects and IP development, taking India’s battery technology from lab to industry, on campus. Why This Matters - Pilot lines are what separate success from failure at giga-scale. The Centre allows JSW to de-risk the foundation before committing to giga-scale manufacturing. - It fulfils the Government of Maharashtra’s vision for COEP’s Chikhali Research Park as a hub for automotive and allied technology development. - It addresses India’s biggest structural gap in clean energy—with over 90% of the global Li-ion supply chain controlled by China—by building indigenous capability. - It positions COEP and Maharashtra as India’s battery-technology hub, with the potential to catalyse over 1,000 battery ecosystem-related jobs. - It is a step towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s Net Zero 2070 ambition, anchoring the EV, grid storage and clean-energy future in Indian innovation. This partnership between one of India’s most dynamic industrial groups and one of India’s most historic technical institutions marks the beginning of a journey that will shape the nation’s energy independence for decades to come.

artigo.texto: Perto de R$ 3,5 milhões em crédito de carbono já foram liberados a pecuaristas brasileiros em uma área de 950 hectares, antes mesmo de os créditos serem gerados e vendidos. A conta está na reportagem que deu ao jornalista Ariosto Mesquita o segundo lugar na categoria Sustentabilidade do IFAJ Star Prize 2026, prêmio da Federação Internacional de Jornalistas Agrícolas entregue no sábado (19), em Osijek, na Croácia. O trabalho premiado é “De utopia à realidade: dinheiro do crédito de carbono já remunera pecuaristas brasileiros”, publicado pela Revista Feed & Food, de Sorocaba (SP). Mesquita assina o texto e as fotos. É a segunda premiação internacional seguida do jornalista com uma reportagem sobre sustentabilidade na bovinocultura de corte, a criação de gado para carne. Os R$ 3,5 milhões e os 950 hectares estão na página de abertura da reportagem. Dividido pela área, o valor dá cerca de R$ 3,7 mil por hectare. A mesma página projeta novos projetos em mais 35 mil hectares nos biomas Cerrado e Amazônia até o fim de 2027, o que equivale a 37 vezes a área já contratada. O dinheiro chega antes de o crédito existir A apuração levou o jornalista a Porangatu, em Goiás, onde o produtor Rodrigo Barros de Azevedo recebeu US$ 62 mil poucas semanas depois de assinar um contrato de crédito de carbono. Pela cotação usada na reportagem, o valor equivale a aproximadamente R$ 360 mil. Em São Valério do Tocantins, nas fazendas Rio Verde, Bacabal e Spinelli, Mesquita encontrou o produtor Erivan Spinelli, que já havia recebido US$ 150 mil, cerca de R$ 870 mil, como antecipação de um projeto cujo crédito de carbono total foi estimado em US$ 451 mil. O adiantamento corresponde a um terço do que o projeto deve render ao produtor. As duas conversões citadas na reportagem indicam dólar em torno de R$ 5,80. Quem for comparar os valores hoje precisa refazer a conta pela cotação do dia. Quem antecipou o dinheiro é uma startup do Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, que decidiu pagar antes por arranjos silvipastoris, sistemas em que árvores dividem a mesma área com o pasto e o gado. A reportagem também ouviu técnicos, representantes do setor e integrantes da empresa. O elo com Mato Grosso do Sul está na premiação anterior A reportagem vencedora deste ano não passa por Mato Grosso do Sul. O estado aparece no trabalho anterior do jornalista, “Crédito de carbono chega à pecuária”, publicado pela Revista DBO e premiado em 2025 em Nairóbi, no Quênia, também com o segundo lugar. Naquele texto, um dos primeiros contratos de crédito de carbono da pecuária brasileira era o da Fazenda Saltinho, em Camapuã. Segundo a reportagem, a propriedade assinou contrato com previsão de receber cerca de US$ 270 mil, perto de R$ 1,45 milhão na cotação citada, com pagamento projetado para 2029. A diferença entre os dois trabalhos está no prazo. Em Camapuã, o produtor espera quatro anos pelo dinheiro. Em Goiás e no Tocantins, ele entrou em semanas. Um brasileiro levou o título de jornalista do ano Julio Cezar Huber, do Espírito Santo, ficou em primeiro lugar na categoria Cultura Rural com a reportagem “Caparaó: um território que transforma quem vive e quem visita”, publicada pela Revista Negócio Rural. O trabalho contribuiu para que ele recebesse também o título de Journalist of the Year, jornalista do ano, dividido com a australiana Pip Courtney. Huber ficou ainda em segundo lugar na categoria Digital Media com “Regenerar é semear o amanhã”. Os brasileiros participaram do prêmio por meio da Rede Brasil de Jornalistas Agro, a Rede Agrojor. O que o IFAJ Star Prize premia O prêmio reúne trabalhos jornalísticos produzidos em diferentes países sobre agricultura, pecuária, desenvolvimento rural e temas ligados ao setor. A categoria Sustentabilidade desta edição foi coordenada pelo jornalista australiano Kerry Staight. O certificado enviado à redação traz as assinaturas de Steve Werblow, presidente da federação, e de Adrian Bell, secretário-geral.

artigo.texto: China’s EV industry is pushing charging technology into territory that remains largely out of reach for passenger cars in the US. Geely’s latest battery technology is the newest example, promising charging speeds that could dramatically reduce one of the biggest frustrations associated with electric vehicles: waiting to recharge. Credits: Ars Technica Geely Unveils 2.2 MW EV Charging Technology Geely has introduced a new battery system capable of charging at up to 2.2 megawatts, with the company claiming it can recharge from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes. A more substantial 10% to 98% charge takes 8 minutes and 40 seconds, according to Geely. If the technology performs as claimed in real-world conditions, charging an EV could begin to resemble the experience of refuelling a conventional petrol or diesel vehicle. The battery uses AI-powered predictive thermal management to control temperatures during high-speed charging. Geely says the pack maintains an average temperature of around 55°C, while its peak temperature during charging reaches approximately 65°C. The company has also addressed concerns over battery degradation caused by repeated ultra-fast charging. AI Could Help Extend Battery Life According to Geely, its charging system uses AI-controlled micro pulses of current to reactivate lithium ions that accumulate at the negative electrodes during repeated fast charging. The automaker claims this approach can extend battery life by 20%. The battery pack has reportedly been tested in vehicles including the Zeekr 001 and Lynk & Co 10, suggesting that the technology is moving beyond the laboratory stage. The development reflects a broader trend among Chinese EV manufacturers, which are competing aggressively to reduce charging times while adding software and connected features to their vehicles. Instead of treating charging speed as a secondary specification, companies are increasingly making it a central part of the EV ownership experience. Geely Takes on BYD and CATL Geely’s figures are impressive, but the company is not alone in the race for faster charging. BYD introduced a battery system earlier this year capable of charging from 10% to 70% in around five minutes, while a 10% to 97% charge takes approximately nine minutes. CATL has reported even faster figures. Its latest LFP battery can reportedly charge from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, while reaching 98% from 10% takes 6 minutes and 27 seconds. That puts China’s leading battery manufacturers in an increasingly intense competition over charging speeds, with incremental improvements potentially becoming a major differentiator between EV models. For consumers, the significance is straightforward: if charging times continue falling toward single-digit minutes, range anxiety could increasingly be replaced by concerns about charger availability rather than the time required to use one. US Charging Infrastructure Still Trails Megawatt Levels The difference becomes particularly noticeable when comparing the charging infrastructure available in China and the US. Most Tesla Superchargers in the US currently top out at 250 kW, while newer high-power systems from other networks have pushed that figure higher. Electrify America offers chargers rated at up to 350 kW, IONNA has introduced machines capable of 400 kW, and ChargePoint has a 600 kW charger. Those figures remain well below Geely’s claimed 2.2 MW charging capability. The gap is not only about charging stations. Passenger EVs sold in the US also generally cannot accept power at the levels being targeted by China’s latest battery technology. American EVs Are Also Limited by Battery Hardware Hyundai and Kia’s popular 800-volt EVs, including the Ioniq 5 and EV6, can accept roughly 240 kW of DC fast-charging power. Porsche’s Taycan supports charging of up to around 320 kW. The newest generation of 800-volt German EVs is beginning to close that gap, with models such as the BMW iX3 and Porsche Cayenne arriving with 400 kW charging capabilities. However, even those systems remain significantly below the megawatt-level charging being developed in China. There is an important distinction, though: the highest charging speeds depend on more than the battery. Vehicles need compatible charging hardware, connectors, thermal systems and electrical infrastructure capable of safely delivering enormous amounts of power. Credits: The Economic Times Megawatt Charging Is Still Mostly for Heavy-Duty EVs In the US, megawatt charging remains primarily associated with heavy-duty electric vehicles such as buses and electric trucks. ChargePoint has indicated that two of its 600 kW charging units could potentially be combined through a common DC bus to deliver 1.2 MW through a single port. The company has also pointed to the Megawatt Charging System, or MCS, as a solution designed to handle the much larger power requirements of heavy-duty vehicles. For passenger cars, however, the technology remains considerably less mature. Geely’s announcement therefore highlights a widening technology race around one of the EV industry’s most important challenges. Chinese manufacturers are not simply increasing battery capacity; they are attempting to make the charging process dramatically faster. If these systems can achieve their claimed performance without compromising safety, cost or long-term battery durability, the traditional advantage of petrol vehicles—quick refuelling—could become considerably less significant.

artigo.texto: Vivo V80 launches with 7200mAh battery and 144Hz display Vivo is set to expand its mid-range smartphone portfolio with the launch of the V80 on October 6, 2026, introducing significant upgrades in battery capacity and display performance. Next-Generation Battery and Display Technology Vivo is set to expand its mid-range smartphone portfolio with the launch of the V80 on October 6, 2026, introducing significant upgrades in battery capacity and display performance. The most notable enhancement is the inclusion of a massive 7,200mAh battery, a substantial increase from the 6,500mAh cell found in its predecessor, the V70. This 11 percent boost in capacity is engineered to deliver extended usage times, addressing one of the primary demands of modern smartphone users who require reliable all-day performance without frequent recharging. Complementing the large battery is a 90W fast-charging capability, which Vivo claims can replenish 50 percent of the battery in just 30 minutes under laboratory conditions. This rapid charging technology mitigates the inconvenience of a large battery, ensuring that users can quickly top up their devices during short breaks. The physical dimensions of the phone have been carefully managed despite the larger battery; the V80 measures 7.69mm in thickness and weighs 203g, representing only a marginal increase over the V70. The visual experience is driven by a 6.59-inch AMOLED display with a 1.5K resolution of 2750 x 1260 pixels. The most significant display upgrade is the increase in the maximum refresh rate from 120Hz to 144Hz, providing smoother scrolling and more responsive interactions in supported applications. This high refresh rate is particularly beneficial for mobile gaming and navigating complex user interfaces, positioning the V80 as a compelling option for multimedia consumption and interactive entertainment. Advanced Camera System and Imaging Capabilities Vivo continues its partnership with ZEISS to deliver a sophisticated rear camera system on the V80. The primary setup features a 50MP main sensor with optical image stabilization, ensuring sharp and stable footage even in challenging lighting conditions. This is paired with a dedicated 50MP telephoto lens that offers 3x optical zoom and its own stabilization system, allowing users to capture detailed portraits and distant subjects without the quality degradation typically associated with digital cropping. The camera array is completed by an 8MP ultrawide lens, providing versatility for landscape and group photography. While Vivo advertises digital zoom capabilities up to 100x, the practical utility of the system lies in its high-resolution optical lenses. The front-facing camera is equally robust, featuring a 50MP autofocus sensor that ensures high-quality selfies and clear video calls, a critical feature for social media engagement and remote communication. Video recording capabilities include 4K resolution at 60 frames per second, alongside a Cinematic Video mode that applies movie-style color grading and depth-of-field effects. The integration of AI-powered lighting effects and tools for converting live photo elements into stickers adds a layer of creative flexibility, appealing to content creators and casual users alike. These software enhancements leverage the powerful hardware to provide a comprehensive imaging suite that competes favorably with higher-tier devices. Processing Power and Market Positioning Under the hood, the Vivo V80 retains the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 processor, the same chipset that powered the V70. While this means there is no generational leap in raw processing power, the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 remains a highly capable mid-range chipset, offering excellent thermal efficiency and sufficient performance for everyday tasks and demanding mobile games. The decision to retain the processor allows Vivo to optimize the software experience and maintain a competitive price point. The V80 is positioned to compete in a highly contested segment of the Kenyan smartphone market, where consumers are increasingly demanding premium features at accessible prices. The combination of a massive battery, high-refresh-rate display, and versatile camera system addresses the core needs of the target demographic. Competitors in this space, including offerings from Tecno and Infinix, will need to match these specifications to remain relevant. As the October 6 launch approaches, industry observers will be watching the pricing strategy and local availability of the V80. The success of the device will depend not only on its hardware specifications but also on Vivo's ability to provide robust after-sales support and software updates. For consumers seeking a balanced device that prioritizes battery life and imaging without compromising on display quality, the Vivo V80 presents a formidable option in the evolving mid-range landscape. artigo.texto: Processing and storing data is now pushing the frontier of economic development around the world, and huge amounts of capital are flowing into building out the infrastructure to support this big bet on cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence. The race to establish an advantageous position on the digital frontier is driving a major capex boom in the United States and elsewhere, and this wave has now fully arrived in Southeast Asia. Data centers require substantial land and resources, like electricity and water, and they need reliable connectivity such as access to subsea cable networks. Countries that have land, reasonably well-developed energy and telecommunications infrastructure and friendly regulatory environments are attracting investors and developers looking to ride the data center wave. Affordable inputs, like electricity, can sweeten the deal. It just so happens that many countries in Southeast Asia fit this bill. Malaysia is leading the pack. Clear policy guidance, well-developed infrastructure and close proximity to land-constrained Singapore are helping fuel a boom in data centers. The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone has seen a flurry of activity, but it is part of a broader phenomenon. In the first quarter of 2023, the Department of Statistics recorded a cumulative $11 billion of foreign investment in the information and communication sector, accounting for 5 percent of total foreign investment. By first quarter of 2026, this figure had risen to $32.5 billion, equal to 12 percent of total inbound investment. And there is no sign of slowing. According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the body that reviews and approves investment projects, between 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, $96 billion worth of data center and cloud computing projects were approved, including $24 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. These are project approvals rather than realized investment, but it gives a sense of the speed and scale at which the data center boom is unfolding across Malaysia. Indonesia is also seeing an uptick in data center investment. Like Malaysia, some of this is driven by demand from Singapore, particularly in and around the island of Batam. Nongsa Digital Park is a Special Economic Zone that offers eligible projects tax and other fiscal incentives. Combined with Batam’s strong subsea cable connectivity, this has fueled a wave of new data center construction in the area. There is also a lot of investment activity in and around Jakarta where a number of large industrial scale data centers are being developed by state-backed players such as Telkom, as well as private sector firms and investors. As reported by Antara News, Indonesia’s current data center capacity sits around 580 MW and the plan is to grow it to 1.3 GW in the near-term. Government data shows that investment in information services jumped from $967 million in 2023 to $3.4 billion in 2025 and it looks set to keep climbing. Thailand is also now rushing to add more data centers, with several large industrial-scale projects in the pipeline. According to the Board of Investment, in 2025 they received $24 billion worth of applications across 151 projects in the digital industry, mainly data centers. Not all of these projects will be approved and become operational, but it again gives a sense of the speed and scale with which this industry is moving. Vietnam is following suit, with local media reporting that the government plans to reach 870 MW of data center capacity by 2030. The trend is clear: data centers are beginning to pop up all around Southeast Asia, attracting billions of dollars in investment and uncorking a major construction boom. But a bigger, perhaps more fundamental, question is whether demand for digital services can justify these enormous outlays and the resources they will absorb. Investment is pouring into Southeast Asian digital infrastructure, with the expectation that businesses and consumers will spend billions of dollars on cloud computing, AI and other digital services in the years ahead. This is not unique to Southeast Asia, of course. The same assumption about future demand has been driving eye-popping capex investment in data centers and cloud computing all around the world, raising similar questions. What we can say for sure is that the data center boom has reached the major economies of Southeast Asia. Whether these massive bets on future demand for digital services pays off is anybody’s guess. But considering the amounts of money involved, how this plays out is something we should all be watching very, very closely in the months and years ahead.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Dados da empresa norte-americana Cushman & Wakefield apontam crescimento de 91% na capacidade operacional de data centers em São Paulo em um ano. No primeiro semestre deste ano, a capacidade chegou a 661 MW (megawatts), ante 346 MW no mesmo período de 2025. Com o avanço, São Paulo se tornou o terceiro maior mercado primário das Américas, atrás apenas de Atlanta e Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos. A empresa lembra que o desempenho do setor ocorre em meio à criação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), sancionado em 15 de setembro, que prevê a suspensão de tributos federais, como Imposto de Importação, PIS/Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação e IPI (Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados), sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização de empreendimentos de data centers. No eixo São Paulo-Campinas, a capacidade dos empreendimentos em construção cresceu de 148 MW para 250 MW. Além disso, há 2.066 MW em projetos planejados para a região. Esse volume equivale a mais de três vezes a capacidade atualmente em operação, mas não significa que toda essa capacidade será efetivamente construída. A concretização dos projetos depende de fatores como disponibilidade de energia e acesso à rede de transmissão, equipamentos, conectividade, licenciamento e existência de clientes interessados em contratar a capacidade. Apesar da expansão da oferta, a vacância permaneceu baixa, em 4,1%, o que significa que cerca de 96% da capacidade de colocation estava ocupada. Nesse contexto, segundo a Cushman & Wakefield, o Redata pode contribuir para a viabilização dos projetos planejados ao reduzir os custos de aquisição de equipamentos destinados aos empreendimentos elegíveis. A empresa projeta que esse crescimento deve se estender para além de São Paulo. Regiões do país com oferta de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, conexão de alta capacidade e terrenos preparados poderão disputar os próximos investimentos em data centers.

artigo.texto: By Brian Kennedy Pew Research Center Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year. And a majority say they’d be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area, according to a new Pew Research Center survey. The survey comes as protests against new data center construction have spread and as some state and local politicians have spoken out against data centers. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers. More than half of Americans (54%) now say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half say they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38%. And 49% say they are mostly bad for people’s quality of life nearby, up from 30%. The new survey was conducted from July 20 to Aug. 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Just 4% of Americans think data centers have a mostly good impact in each of these areas. Similar shares (between 21% and 24%) say data centers are mostly good and mostly bad for these things. Since January, there have been increases of 9 percentage points in the shares of Americans who say data centers are mostly bad for local jobs (from 15% to 24%) and local tax revenue (from 12% to 21%). Many Americans are still unsure or unfamiliar with data centers altogether. Shares ranging from 18% to 32% say they are not sure how data centers impact the five things the survey asked about. And overall, 12% say they haven’t heard of data centers. Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers. Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things the survey asked about. For example, rural Americans have become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for the environment (from 32% in January to 50% in August), home energy costs (32% to 46%) and the quality of people living nearby (28% to 45%). Most data centers currently being planned or under development will be in rural areas. Americans in urban and suburban areas have also become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for these things. As was the case earlier this year, Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents are more likely than Republicans and Republican leaners to view the impacts of data centers negatively. Still, Republicans’ views have also turned more negative: In the new survey, for example, 42% say the facilities are mostly bad for the quality of life of people nearby, up from 24% in January. Republican elected officials have staked out varying positions on data centers. While Trump has consistently supported their construction in his second term, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott previously supported expansion but issued a statewide moratorium on new data centers in August. Some Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, have also recently shifted their positions to support additional rules and oversight on data center construction and operation. Among Democrats and Republicans alike, views on the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are somewhat more negative than they were at the start of the year. But many people in both partisan groups either say that they’re not sure or that the effects are neither good nor bad. More Democrats now say the effects of data centers in these two areas are mostly bad than mostly good. Liberal Democrats have primarily driven this shift: For example, 34% of liberals now say data centers are mostly bad for local tax revenue, up from 19% in January. More Republicans continue to say the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are mostly good than mostly bad. Still, Republicans are now 7 percentage points more likely than in January to say the effects in both areas are mostly bad. The new survey also finds that 60% of Americans say they would be not too or at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Much smaller shares say they would be somewhat comfortable (19%) or extremely or very comfortable (7%) with this. Just over half of Republicans (54%) and about two-thirds of Democrats (68%) say they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new local data center. Liberal Democrats stand out, with 81% saying they’d be uncomfortable. Majorities of urban, suburban and rural Americans say they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area. Americans are more aware of data centers than they were earlier in the year. The share of Americans who say they have heard or read a lot about them has increased from 25% in January to 35% today. About 9 in 10 adults (88%) have now heard at least a little about data centers.

We are committed to meeting that responsibility at every stage of the project.” Lambda’s Commitments - Ratepayer Protection: Lambda will protect local ratepayers by paying for all electricity the facility uses and ensuring the project meets Oklahoma’s requirements under the state’s ratepayer protection laws. The company has also signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and is working to design the project to be a more flexible grid customer with the ability to shift or reduce certain computing loads during periods of peak demand. - Water Stewardship: The facility will implement closed-loop cooling technology that dramatically reduces water use compared with traditional data center cooling. - Siting Away from Residents: The project is being built at the existing MidAmerica Industrial Park with infrastructure designed to minimize impacts on surrounding residential areas. “Oklahoma is leading the nation in building the modern economy, bringing major investments to our state and creating opportunities that will benefit our people for generations to come,” said Governor Kevin Stitt. “Lambda has committed to taking responsibility for the energy costs associated with its facility, ensuring those costs are not passed along to residential customers while generating hundreds of millions in tax revenue and economic growth right here in Oklahoma. These are commitments that reflect the kind of responsible investment we want to see in Oklahoma.” “Major investments like this demonstrate the opportunity we have to continue growing Oklahoma’s economy and attracting innovative companies to our state,” said Oklahoma Department of Commerce CEO John Budd. “Lambda’s decision to build here is a vote of confidence in Oklahoma’s workforce, infrastructure and business-friendly environment. We look forward to supporting this project and the new opportunities it will create for Oklahomans, while continuing to build an economy that can compete for investment and high-quality jobs for years to come.” “Lambda’s decision to build in Mayes County represents a transformative commitment to economic development in our community,” said Chouteau Mayor Brenda Cunningham. “This project will bring an estimated $500 million in tax revenue to our county over the next decade, which will go toward supporting our schools, public services and local priorities.
