artigo.texto: Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD has confirmed plans to introduce its first electric vehicle equipped with a solid-state battery in 2027. The company says it is in a leading position in the development and commercialisation of the technology. Solid-state batteries could offer higher energy density, lower weight, longer driving ranges and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Key Overview - Company: BYD - Technology: Solid-state batteries - First model: Planned for 2027 - Initial application: Higher-end electric vehicles - Battery development: BYD’s FinDreams battery division - Expected mass production: Around 2030 - Existing batteries: Lithium iron phosphate batteries will continue across other vehicle segments BYD Confirms 2027 Solid-State Battery Plans BYD has confirmed that it plans to introduce its first electric vehicle using solid-state battery technology in 2027. BYD Executive Vice-President Stella Li said the company is in a leading position in both the technology and its commercialisation. The announcement follows plans previously outlined by BYD’s battery division, FinDreams, which indicated in 2025 that the company intended to demonstrate and install solid-state batteries in vehicles from 2027. Solid-State Batteries Could Improve EV Performance Solid-state batteries differ from conventional lithium-ion batteries primarily through the use of a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. The technology has the potential to provide higher energy density, which could allow electric vehicles to use smaller and lighter battery packs while maintaining or increasing driving range. Solid-state batteries are also expected to offer safety advantages because solid electrolytes are less prone to the thermal runaway associated with some conventional lithium-ion battery systems. The technology could also provide improved performance under certain temperature conditions. BYD Previously Targeted 2027 for Demonstration The 2027 timeline is consistent with plans announced by BYD in February 2025. At the time, Sun Huajun, technical director of BYD’s FinDreams battery division, said the company planned to begin demonstrating and installing solid-state batteries in vehicles in 2027. Mass production was expected to follow around 2030. BYD’s latest comments therefore reinforce the company’s previously stated development timeline rather than introducing a completely new target. Higher-End Models Expected to Use the Technology First The high cost of producing solid-state batteries remains one of the challenges facing wider adoption. Because of this, BYD is expected to initially use the technology in higher-end models. BYD Chief Scientist Lian Yubo previously said solid-state batteries would mainly be used in high-end models while lithium iron phosphate batteries continue to serve vehicles across different segments. This means the introduction of solid-state technology is not expected to replace BYD’s existing battery technologies across its entire vehicle range. Context is everything. The company’s approach is to use different battery technologies according to the requirements and positioning of individual vehicles. Solid-state batteries could therefore initially serve vehicles where their higher energy density and potential range benefits can justify higher production costs. As production technology develops, costs could become an important factor in determining how widely solid-state batteries are adopted. Other Automakers Are Developing Solid-State Batteries BYD is among several major automotive companies working on solid-state battery technology. Toyota has previously targeted 2027–2028 for vehicles using solid-state batteries. Mercedes-Benz has also been testing solid-state battery technology, while Stellantis has been conducting road testing involving a solid-state battery-powered electric vehicle. Honda has also been working with QuantumScape on solid-state battery development. The activity across several automakers reflects continued investment in battery technologies that could increase electric vehicle range and improve battery performance. Cost Remains a Major Challenge Despite the potential advantages, solid-state batteries remain more expensive to produce than established lithium-ion battery technologies. Manufacturers must also develop production processes capable of producing the batteries at automotive scale. For BYD, the initial use of solid-state batteries in higher-end vehicles could allow the company to introduce the technology while continuing to use established battery systems across its broader vehicle lineup. The company has not indicated that traditional lithium-based batteries will be phased out following the introduction of solid-state technology. artigo.texto: India’s carbon market is being built under pressure from a trade system in which emissions are becoming a direct cost of exporting. The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which entered its definitive phase in January 2026, requires importers to account for the carbon embedded in selected goods. For Indian steel, aluminium, cement and fertiliser producers, the issue is no longer only how much they manufacture or sell, but how much carbon is associated with every unit reaching a foreign market. That shift changes the meaning of industrial competitiveness. An Indian factory can comply with conventional export requirements and still face a commercial disadvantage if its production is more carbon-intensive than that of competitors. The EU importer pays the border charge, but the cost can travel back through lower margins, higher prices or reduced demand for Indian goods. The United Kingdom is preparing a similar mechanism for January 2027, widening the number of markets in which carbon intensity could influence export economics. India’s response is centred on the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, or CCTS, and on efforts to make domestic carbon pricing part of a broader industrial transition. The policy objective is twofold: retain some carbon-related economic value within India and reduce the emissions that generate charges abroad. The second objective is harder. A domestic market can allocate a price to emissions, but it cannot by itself provide the clean electricity, transmission, storage and production technologies required to lower emissions at scale. The size of the exposure makes this more than a climate-policy question. India’s merchandise exports reached $441.78 billion in FY26, according to the supplied report, while metals remained a major export category. The European mechanism currently covers iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. These sectors are closely tied to heavy industry, energy consumption and the infrastructure of industrial production. NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly, as cited in the report, puts India’s annual metals exports at about $34.8 billion in 2025. Iron, steel and aluminium accounted for roughly 78% of that trade. The EU represented approximately 22% of India’s combined steel and aluminium exports, while the EU exposure for iron and steel stood at 39.3%. That means the European market is not a marginal destination for Indian metal producers. For steel exporters in particular, changes in the cost of carbon can affect a substantial part of their external market. The export numbers also show why the timing matters. India exported 6.94 lakh tonnes of finished steel worth ₹5,541.2 crore in August 2026, according to the report, with volume up 31.3% and value up 41.5% from August 2025. Between April and August, finished-steel exports reached 29.86 lakh tonnes worth ₹23,646.6 crore, representing increases of 34.1% in volume and 32% in value. Strong export growth can increase exposure to carbon-related trade costs if production systems remain emissions-intensive. The structural difficulty lies in how Indian metals are produced. NITI Aayog’s Trade Watch Quarterly for April-June, or Q1 FY27, said Indian metals have notably higher carbon intensity than the global average. The report attributed this largely to the continued importance of coal-based Blast Furnace–Basic Oxygen Furnace routes in primary steelmaking and coal-fired Direct Reduced Iron processes, rather than cleaner gas-based or Electric Arc Furnace routes. This production profile means the carbon problem cannot be solved through documentation alone. Indian exporters need to measure and verify embedded emissions, but lower paperwork does not equal lower emissions. The trade system may reward accurate reporting in the short term, yet the lasting competitive advantage will come from changing the energy and technology used in factories. A June 2026 working paper by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations estimated that India’s steel exports to the EU could fall by 24% under CBAM. The estimate is based on simulations using the ICRIER Samriddhi Model, a GTAP-E-based general-equilibrium model. It is therefore a modelled scenario rather than an observed fall in exports, but it illustrates the scale of the risk facing a sector with significant European exposure. India has begun building the administrative architecture needed to respond. The Central government notified the CCTS in June 2023 under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act. The scheme is overseen by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency and uses emissions-intensity targets rather than an absolute production cap. Targets become stricter each year and operate in two-year compliance cycles beginning in FY 2025-26. According to a Press Information Bureau release cited in the report, the system covers more than 700 industrial units across seven emissions-intensive sectors, including steel, aluminium and refining. Companies that perform better than their assigned targets can earn tradeable Carbon Credit Certificates, with each certificate representing one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent reduction. Companies that fail to meet their targets can face penalties. The framework has also expanded to include sectors such as petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and secondary aluminium. The design reflects an attempt to connect industrial performance with market incentives. Yet the value of that incentive will depend on the strength of the market and the price attached to each reduction. Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, said the EU carbon price was about €75 per tonne of carbon dioxide, compared with roughly $10 in China, while India’s emissions-trading system would take time to become fully operational. His assessment was that recognition of India’s system overseas would not necessarily remove the border charge because a substantial price gap could remain.

artigo.texto: Os bombardeios russos deste domingo (27) atingiram em cheio a espinha dorsal das telecomunicações ucranianas: a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel do país, e data centers de concorrentes e provedores de internet foram alvos de ataques na região de Kiev. Segundo a Reuters, a Kyivstar informou à agência Interfax Ucrânia que sua sede na capital foi atingida, sem registro de vítimas. Horas antes, o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia havia declarado ter destruído um data center pertencente à Vodafone Ucrânia, segunda maior operadora celular do país. A companhia não respondeu aos pedidos de comentário. O presidente Volodymyr Zelenskiy afirmou que um data center em Kiev foi bombardeado duas vezes na manhã deste domingo, deixando dois menores e um adulto feridos. Na semana anterior, ataques a data centers de provedores de internet ucranianos já haviam interrompido o serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e na região vizinha, conforme o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Andrii Sybiha, escreveu no X que Moscou tem como alvo os principais data centers do país para interromper o fluxo de informações, e que alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais porque salvam vidas.

artigo.texto: A WEG anunciou a ampliação do projeto da nova fábrica de sistemas BESS, de armazenamento de energia em baterias, em construção em Itajaí. Anunciada em fevereiro deste ano, a unidade terá investimento estimado de R$ 330 milhões e capacidade anual de 4 GWh. A nova fábrica vai atender à demanda ligada à transição energética e tem início das operações previsto pro segundo semestre de 2027. O projeto reforça a estratégia da empresa de acompanhar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil, que está prestes a lançar o primeiro leilão de baterias, previsto ... O projeto reforça a estratégia da empresa de acompanhar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil, que está prestes a lançar o primeiro leilão de baterias, previsto pra dezembro. Na atualização do projeto, a WEG incorporou maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial que permitirão ampliar a capacidade produtiva. Continua depois da publicidade A fábrica contará com linhas automáticas e semiautomáticas de montagem, além de robôs móveis autônomos para movimentações internas. O complexo também terá um laboratório de testes, desenvolvimento e qualificação de produtos, responsável por aprimorar processos, garantir o controle de qualidade e acelerar a criação de novas soluções em baterias. Segundo o vice-presidente de automação e sistemas da WEG, Manfred Peter Johann, o investimento está alinhado à forte expansão do mercado de armazenamento de energia, impulsionado pelo crescimento das fontes renováveis e pela necessidade de maior flexibilidade e segurança pro sistema elétrico. “A ampliação deste projeto demonstra a capacidade da WEG de adaptar rapidamente seus investimentos para atender às necessidades do mercado e apoiar o desenvolvimento sustentável do setor energético brasileiro”, comenta. As baterias produzidas em Itajaí vão ajudar na estabilidade do sistema elétrico, na eficiência operacional e no aproveitamento dos recursos energéticos. O BESS, sigla em inglês para Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias, é uma tecnologia avançada que armazena energia elétrica em grandes baterias. A solução tem papel importante nos sistemas elétricos modernos, principalmente na integração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, permitindo guardar energia nos momentos de maior disponibilidade e ofertá-la quando necessário.

artigo.texto: Schneider Electric Unveils World's First Software-Defined Medium Voltage Switchgear to Expand AI-Ready Data Center Power Portfolio - World's first fully Software-Defined Medium Voltage architecture enables up to 3× faster ordering and manufacturing, up to 2× faster commissioning and zero-downtime upgrades - RM AirSeT™ 38 Software Defined extends Schneider Electric's SF₆-free medium-voltage technology to 38 kV for high-density, scalable data center architectures "The challenge facing data center operators today is not just keeping pace with AI growth, but building the resilient, efficient and scalable power infrastructure needed for an increasingly digital world," said Frédéric Godemel, Executive Vice President, Software-Defined Medium Voltage establishes a new category of power infrastructure Building on its broader Software-Defined Energy vision, Based on the comparison documented in Schneider Electric White Paper 303, the approach enables up to 3× faster ordering and manufacturing, up to 2× faster commissioning and onsite acceptance testing, compared with conventional engineered-to-order medium-voltage switchgear. It also reduces system complexity: in the 20-panel comparison, the software-defined configuration used 87% less control wiring, 91% fewer terminals and 85% less copper in that wiring, while providing digital connectivity and analytics for greater operational visibility. Key elements of the Software-Defined MV architecture include: - Standardized, configurable infrastructure: Replaces highly customized, engineered-to-order systems with modular hardware that can be standardized and deployed more quickly. - Software-enabled functionality: Shifts capabilities from hardware into software, allowing customers to add new features and performance improvements without physical modifications. - Digital-first deployment: Standardized modules, automated testing, and intuitive interfaces help streamline ordering, manufacturing, commissioning, and onsite acceptance. - Lifecycle flexibility: Over-the-air updates enable system upgrades without hardware replacement or operational downtime, while software-enabled capabilities support ongoing optimization and AI-powered predictive maintenance through EcoCare Services. The Software-Defined MV approach has been deployed in live operation through a pilot with Equinix in a colocation data center environment. Pilot programs continue through 2027, with broader availability to follow in 2028. To learn more, visit the Software-Defined MV switchgear page or read the Software-Defined MV white paper. To receive product and availability updates, register your interest. RM AirSeT 38 Software Defined extends SF₆-free MV gas-insulated switchgear to 38 kV As AI, high-performance computing and large-scale digital infrastructure drive rising power densities, many operators are planning 36/38 kV MV architectures to support higher power capacity, simplified MV backbone design, and scalable campus deployment. RM AirSeT 38 meets that need, giving hyperscalers and colocation providers greater flexibility as they modernize their electrical distribution strategies. RM AirSeT 38 is designed to support high-density, scalable deployments through: - SF ₆ -free technology: Uses pressurized pure air insulation and vacuum interruption technology instead of SF₆ (sulfur hexafluoride, a potent greenhouse gas), fluorinated gases, or proprietary gas mixtures. - Compact GIS design: Supports space-constrained, high-density installations while enabling standardized, repeatable MV architecture across data center deployments. - Software-defined capabilities: A standardized digital architecture designed to simplify configuration, accelerate commissioning and support lifecycle evolution. - Operational visibility: Digital monitoring and sensing options provide visibility into system performance, configurable to each customer's cybersecurity requirements. Order intake is planned to begin in 2027, with first deliveries expected in 2028. To receive updates on RM AirSeT 38, register your interest. Galaxy VXL brings high-density As AI deployments drive higher rack densities and more dynamic load profiles, data center operators need power infrastructure that responds quickly to fluctuating demand while maximizing white space. Galaxy VXL helps customers maintain reliable, high-quality power delivery for scalable growth and continuity in AI and high-performance computing environments. Key benefits include: - Industry-leading power density: Delivers up to 1.25 MW in a single frame while using up to 70% less space than predecessor systems, helping customers maximize IT capacity and floor space. - Optimized efficiency and sustainability: Galaxy VXL is designed to drive energy-efficient operations, lowering total cost of ownership, and support long-term sustainability initiatives – delivering a 31% reduction in lifecycle CO₂ emissions compared with its predecessor. - Validated for AI workloads: Designed for the dynamic power profiles associated with AI clusters and high-density compute environments, helping ensure power quality, resilience, and availability. - Scalable, service-friendly architecture: Schneider Electric's third-party verified Live Swap technology lets operators add, upgrade, or replace power modules without planned downtime, supporting future expansion while maintaining uptime. - Digital-first operations: Integrated EcoStruxure™ monitoring and digital services provide visibility, predictive maintenance, and lifecycle optimization across critical power infrastructure. Availability Galaxy VXL is available globally and supports both Lithium-ion and VRLA battery technologies, providing customers with flexible energy storage options to meet their resiliency, performance, and sustainability requirements. For more information, visit the Galaxy VXL product page. - Software-Defined Energy: The Next Era of Digital Infrastructure - Sept. 29 at10:10 a.m. :Melton Chang , Executive Vice President, P

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Lambda planeja novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park de Oklahoma Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Lambda anunciou planos em 27 de setembro de 2026 para construir um novo data center no MidAmerica Industrial Park, no condado de Mayes, Oklahoma, um projeto que a empresa disse que deve pagar cerca de $500 million em impostos nos próximos 10 anos, com base nas tarifas atuais. Receita Fiscal Projetada e Empregos Espera‑se que o projeto crie até 1.000 empregos de construção e até 100 cargos permanentes, de acordo com o anúncio da empresa. A instalação ficará localizada na seção sul do parque industrial e estará dentro da zona fiscal do Chouteau-Mazie Public School District. A prefeita de Chouteau, Brenda Cunningham, disse que o projeto traria uma receita fiscal estimada em $500 million para o condado ao longo da próxima década, financiamento que, segundo ela, seria destinado ao apoio de escolas, serviços públicos e prioridades locais. O comissário do condado de Mayes, Steve Grossman, afirmou que o investimento fortaleceria a base tributária local e criaria novos recursos para apoiar escolas, infraestrutura e outras prioridades da comunidade. O superintendente da Chouteau-Mazie Public School, Josh Gwartney, declarou que a receita permitiria ao distrito investir em instalações melhores, salários competitivos para professores, programas avançados e mais oportunidades de educação profissional e técnica. Proteção dos Consumidores de Energia e Compromissos de Recursos A Lambda afirmou que, em conformidade com a Oklahoma’s Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act, assumirá total responsabilidade pelos recursos e infraestrutura necessários para operar a instalação, incluindo o pagamento de 100 % dos custos de energia. A empresa disse que está projetando o projeto para ser um cliente de rede mais flexível, com a capacidade de deslocar ou reduzir determinadas cargas de computação durante períodos de pico de demanda. A instalação utilizará tecnologia de refrigeração de circuito fechado, que a Lambda afirmou reduzir drasticamente o consumo de água em comparação com a refrigeração tradicional de data centers, e a empresa disse que otimizará a eficiência energética. O projeto está sendo construído no parque industrial existente, com infraestrutura projetada para minimizar impactos nas áreas residenciais circundantes. O governador Kevin Stitt afirmou que os compromissos refletem o tipo de investimento responsável que ele deseja ver em Oklahoma. “A Lambda se comprometeu a assumir a responsabilidade pelos custos de energia associados à sua instalação, garantindo que esses custos não sejam repassados aos consumidores residenciais, ao mesmo tempo em que gera centenas de milhões em receita fiscal e crescimento econômico aqui em Oklahoma”, disse Stitt. O CEO do Departamento de Comércio de Oklahoma, John Budd, chamou a decisão da Lambda de construir no estado de um voto de confiança na força de trabalho, na infraestrutura e no ambiente favorável aos negócios de Oklahoma. O CEO da Grand River Dam Authority, Dan Sullivan, declarou que a Lambda financiará os custos iniciais de infraestrutura necessários para atender ao projeto, garantindo que essas despesas não sejam repassadas a outros clientes da GRDA. Sullivan afirmou que a concessionária criou um processo de planejamento focado e abrangente ao avaliar projetos potenciais dessa magnitude e fez os investimentos necessários na última década para estar preparada para projetos dessa escala. O projeto segue o anúncio de 14 de setembro de 2026 da Lambda, que havia assinado o White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Naquela declaração, a empresa afirmou que apoia políticas de proteção dos consumidores que exigem que os desenvolvedores de data centers paguem pela energia que suas instalações utilizam, e que apoia a expansão da capacidade de geração, o fortalecimento da rede elétrica, a manutenção de um serviço confiável e a proteção dos consumidores à medida que a demanda por infraestrutura de IA cresce. Processo de Seleção e Próximas Etapas A MidAmerica selecionou a Lambda dentre uma variedade de parceiros potenciais com base na abordagem da empresa ao desenvolvimento responsável e aos padrões de construção. David Stewart, CEO e membro do Board of Trustees do MidAmerica Industrial Park, afirmou que a MidAmerica e a GRDA adotaram uma abordagem deliberada para encontrar o parceiro certo. “Por meio do que chamamos de reverse RFP, começamos com os pontos fortes deste local e procuramos um desenvolvedor cujos planos entregariam valor duradouro à região”, disse Stewart. Ele afirmou que, à medida que a construção avançar, o projeto deverá criar aproximadamente 1.000 empregos e gerar oportunidades para fornecedores, empreiteiros e fornecedores locais. A Cloverleaf Infrastructure foi selecionada pela GRDA e pela MidAmerica para preparar o local no condado de Mayes para o desenvolvimento pela Lambda. Aaron Bilyeu, chief development officer da Cloverleaf, afirmou que o trabalho será orientado pelo Cloverleaf Standard, que ele descreveu como o compromisso da empresa de desenvolver infraestrutura crítica de forma responsável, transparente e em parceria com as comunidades que atende. O cofundador da Lambda e Chief Technology Officer, Stephen Balaban, disse que a empresa tem se reunido com líderes locais em Chouteau e no condado de Mayes para entender suas prioridades e ajudar a moldar seus investimentos de longo prazo na comunidade. O CEO da Lambda, Michel Combes, afirmou que a responsabilidade da empresa é garantir que o projeto entregue valor ao condado de Mayes, respeitando os recursos, a infraestrutura e as prioridades da comunidade. Lambda e MidAmerica disseram que, nas próximas semanas, continuarão se reunindo com líderes locais e residentes para ouvir e coletar sugestões que orientem o investimento na comunidade, e que mais informações sobre o cronograma do projeto e seu impacto econômico esperado serão compartilhada

artigo.texto: Parcerias Crusoe Revela Papel de Desenvolvedor no Campus de Data Center de IA da Google no Texas Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Crusoe anunciou em 28 de setembro de 2026 que é a desenvolvedora do campus de data center da Google em construção no Condado de Armstrong, nos arredores de Amarillo, Texas, um projeto que a empresa disse ser projetado para fornecer capacidade para alimentar IA avançada e onde mais de 5.500 trabalhadores qualificados estão no local diariamente. “Construir o futuro da IA requer um novo tipo de infraestrutura, começando pela energia. A estratégia da Crusoe é construir fábricas de IA diretamente na fonte de energia abundante e de baixo custo – tanto para melhorar a utilização dos ativos existentes quanto para catalisar a geração de nova energia”, disse Chase Lochmiller, CEO e cofundador da Crusoe, em o anúncio da empresa. Lochmiller descreveu o campus do Condado de Armstrong como um exemplo dessa estratégia centrada na energia e afirmou que a empresa está colocando energia limpa, nova e acessível em operação no local. A construção começou em junho de 2025 e continua em andamento, de acordo com o anúncio, que afirmou que o projeto está trazendo investimento significativo e empregos para a comunidade local. Lochmiller disse que a Crusoe está construindo no mesmo ritmo acelerado que estabeleceu em Abilene. Conexão Direta ao Vento e Projeto de Resfriamento O campus tem uma conexão direta com o parque eólico Goodnight 1 adjacente a Serena, uma instalação de 265,5 MW que está operacional, e o parque eólico Goodnight 2, também de 265,5 MW, que está em construção e foi catalisado pelo desenvolvimento da Crusoe no local. Quando a geração eólica excede a demanda do campus, o excedente de energia é devolvido à rede, um arranjo que Crusoe disse beneficiar os consumidores locais e reduzir a limitação da energia eólica do oeste do Texas. O projeto utilizará um sistema de resfriamento líquido de circuito fechado e não evaporativo que a Crusoe afirmou ser projetado para limitar significativamente a pegada hídrica da instalação, destinando-a principalmente a usos domésticos, como cozinhas. O Modelo de Energia Across the Meter Em uma postagem no blog publicada no mesmo dia, a Crusoe descreveu o modelo “across the meter” por trás do design do campus: co‑locar data centers de IA na fonte de geração para capturar energia que de outra forma seria limitada ou abandonada. A postagem afirmou que as áreas mais ventosas e as mais adequadas para produção solar costumam estar em locais remotos com demanda local limitada, o que pode levar os preços da energia a valores negativos quando a geração excede o consumo local, uma dinâmica agravada pela congestão de transmissão, já que muitas usinas enviam energia pelas mesmas linhas para mercados urbanos distantes. O post da Crusoe cita o Independent Market Monitor para o Relatório Estado do Mercado 2025 da ERCOT, que constatou que aproximadamente 4,7% da geração eólica foi reduzida em 2025, e uma estimativa da U.S. Energy Information Administration de que aproximadamente 5% da eletricidade é perdida durante a transmissão e distribuição. A empresa afirmou que seu modelo de negócios original levou data centers modulares a locais remotos de produção de petróleo para capturar gás que, de outra forma, seria queimado, e que a mesma lógica agora se aplica à energia renovável encalhada. Sob o design across-the-meter, um campus extrai energia incremental da rede quando a geração local é insuficiente e envia energia excedente para a rede quando a geração local supera a carga do campus. A Crusoe disse que a carga co‑locada também oferece aos desenvolvedores de renováveis um incentivo orientado pelo mercado para repotenciar e atualizar turbinas envelhecidas, porque os sites eólicos e solares existentes já possuem terras permitidas, acordos de interconexão e relacionamentos comunitários. Investimento na Comunidade e Portfólio do Oeste do Texas O anúncio informou que o investimento local na comunidade também inclui o Texas Energy Impact Fund da Google, que recentemente anunciou apoio a melhorias de eficiência em edifícios públicos e residências no Condado de Armstrong. A Google divulgou os primeiros beneficiários do fundo em 21 de maio de 2026, como parte de um compromisso de US$ 30 milhões com a resiliência e a acessibilidade energética no Texas. A postagem da Google informou que os beneficiários inaugurais incluem a Energy Management Alliance, financiada para expandir o treinamento de gestores de energia para comunidades rurais e financiar melhorias de eficiência em edifícios públicos nos Condados de Armstrong, Ellis, Haskell e Wilbarger, juntamente com reparos residenciais pré‑climatização nesses quatro condados por meio da Solar United Neighbors, do Texas Energy Poverty Research Institute e da aliança, e na região de Houston por meio do Houston Advanced Research Center. artigo.texto: German carmaker Volkswagen and Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion plan to invest some €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion) to expand their partnership, the companies said on Monday. Volkswagen and Gotion aim to set up three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco to "accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe." Under the plans, which are dependent on regulatory approval, a gigafactory currently being built by Volkswagen's battery division PowerCo in Valencia is to be transferred into a joint venture, alongside Gotion's plant in Surany, Slovakia. Volkswagen and Gotion also aim to set up a new production facility in Kenitra, Morocco, "to produce cathode material for LFP batteries." All three ventures are to be managed jointly, the companies said. Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo is to invest some €470 million by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake each in the Slovakian and Moroccan sites. In return, Gotion is to spend some €1.1 billion to acquire a 49% stake in the Valencia factory. Volkswagen's battery division PowerCo, which was established in 2022, is responsible for the development and production of battery cells. Its first factory in Germany's Salzgitter began production at the end of 2025, with another plant under construction in St. Thomas, Canada.

artigo.texto: Fox ESS has unveiled Power Beast, its new commercial and industrial energy storage system, at the company’s first large-scale APAC product launch. Held in Wenzhou, China, on 21 September 2026, the Fox ESS New Product Launch Event welcomed more than 200 customers from around the world. The open-air event marked a significant step in Fox ESS’s expansion into advanced commercial and industrial (C&I) battery energy storage. Power Beast combines the 125 kW H3 Plus hybrid inverter with Fox ESS’s high-voltage CQ series batteries. The CQ20 is described as the industry’s first modular C&I energy storage system with a fully integrated hybrid inverter. This integrated design allows businesses and installers to deploy a flexible, all-in-one commercial energy storage solution. Michael Zhu, CEO of Fox ESS, said: “Today, we are not only launching a product, we are demonstrating our capability as an integrated energy storage provider. Power Beast reflects our commitment to global clients by delivering higher efficiency, lighter weight, and smarter energy management.” Fox ESS puts Power Beast installation to the test The Power Beast launch went beyond a traditional product presentation. Lyren Liu, CCO of Fox ESS, shared insights into market growth and his perspective on battery storage. He then revealed a Cybertruck loaded with CQ batteries from behind a black curtain on stage. An installation team was invited to assemble a complete system live, with a timer displayed on the main screen. The team assembled battery packs comprising: - eight modules of CQ20; - 12 modules of CQ7; and - 12 modules of CQ6. Together, the system provided 316 kWh of energy storage capacity. The completed battery system was then connected to charging piles, a diesel generator, and a motor. Fox ESS completed the entire live demonstration in under 30 minutes. Power Beast offers scalable C&I battery storage Power Beast has been designed around modular expansion, allowing system capacity to grow alongside a business’s energy requirements. With one H3 Plus hybrid inverter, Power Beast can support capacities ranging from 28 kWh to nearly 1,000 kWh. The system supports several installation environments, including rooftop, outdoor, and indoor applications. For larger projects, multiple Power Beast systems can operate in parallel. In grid-connected mode, the system supports up to 100 units in parallel, providing total capacity of up to 96 MWh. In off-grid mode, Power Beast supports up to 30 units in parallel, reaching a total capacity of 28.8 MWh. Modular design simplifies commercial battery installation Fox ESS has also focused on reducing installation complexity. Power Beast’s modular architecture is designed to improve deployment efficiency and accommodate challenging or irregular installation environments. According to Fox ESS, the system’s design can reduce total installation time by 90 per cent. This modular approach gives installers greater flexibility when configuring commercial energy storage systems across different sites. Lighter C&I battery storage with integrated energy management Power Beast has been designed to integrate with multiple energy sources and loads. The CQ20 series batteries achieve a unit energy weight of 7 kg per kWh. This helps reduce the system’s physical footprint while maintaining energy output. Fox ESS has also incorporated a five-layer, end-to-end safety approach. This covers: - cell-level protection; - electrical design; - structural design; - active detection; and - emergency response. The system connects with FoxCloud 2.0, Fox ESS’s proprietary smart energy management platform. FoxCloud 2.0 provides real-time monitoring and visibility of energy flows, alongside detailed performance analysis. The platform also supports scheduling across up to 96 time slots, providing centralised smart energy management for Power Beast installations. Fox ESS introduces AI energy management agent Maimai Alongside Power Beast, Fox ESS introduced its AI agent, Maimai. Maimai provides product, installation, and usage information through natural dialogue. Using large-model conversational capabilities, the AI agent can interpret user requirements and provide relevant information at any time. Maimai can also generate optimised energy strategies using historical energy consumption patterns and real-time dynamic electricity prices. The technology adds another layer of intelligent energy management to Fox ESS’s growing commercial energy storage ecosystem. Michael Zhu said Fox ESS remains focused on creating products that deliver measurable value for customers. “We believe a great product speaks louder than marketing. That is why we aim to make our products the best kind of promotion, by delivering real value every single day,” Michael Zhu said. With scalable storage from 28 kWh through to multi-megawatt-hour deployments, Power Beast expands Fox ESS’s offering for businesses seeking flexible commercial battery storage. The combination of the H3 Plus hybrid inverter, CQ series batteries, FoxCloud 2.0, and Maimai also brings hardware, monitoring, and intelligent energy management into one C&I energy storage ecosystem.

artigo.texto: BYD, Batteries, and the Architecture of Dependence Dateline, Canberra, Austrlia I have just arrived in Canberra for the October 1 seminar hosted by the Sir Richard Williams Foundation. So no place better to start than by focusing on one of the themes in my latest book with Kenneth Maxwell on China’s informal empire. BYD is not simply a car company that got good. It is the clearest automotive expression yet of what I have called, with Kenneth Maxwell, the “Architecture of Dependency”: a strategy that pursues vertical integration of an entire value chain — from mineral extraction through midstream processing to the logistics that move finished goods to market — rather than conventional market access. In The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic, we traced this architecture through lithium refining, rare-earth processing, and port infrastructure such as Chancay. The global automobile is now a fourth front in the same campaign. BYD’s pricing is not merely competitive; it is engineered to convert every vehicle sold abroad into a node in a Chinese-controlled battery and software supply chain. A car buyer in São Paulo, Bangkok, or Budapest who chooses a BYD is not just choosing a product. They are choosing a dependency relationship whose terms were set upstream, in cell chemistry and mineral processing capacity that China already dominates. Toyota’s solid-state battery program in progress for launch projected within the next five years is the most credible industrial counter to this dynamic now on the table, not because it beats BYD on price, but because it proposes an entirely different chemistry, supply chain, and manufacturing geography. This article examines both halves of that contest: how BYD builds dependence, and Toyota’s bet to break it. BYD’s Global Expansion Strategy: Asymmetrical Market Penetration BYD’s rise has been startling in its speed. In April 2026 alone the company exported 135,098 vehicles worldwide, every one fully electric or plug-in hybrid, a figure that by some analyst estimates exceeded Tesla’s global monthly deliveries for the same month. SNE Research put BYD’s non-China deliveries at roughly 497,000 units in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year on year, placing it third worldwide behind Volkswagen and Tesla in overseas volume. BYD’s own target is 1.6 million overseas sales in 2026, backed by new or expanding plants in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey, with Spain under consideration. The strategy behind these numbers is not a frontal assault on the most fortified Western markets. It is what one industry analysis calls “asymmetrical market penetration”: BYD largely avoided the politically hardened U.S. market where tariffs and political resistance keep it effectively locked out and instead targeted the Global South and secondary Western markets where legacy automakers had grown complacent. Thailand became a regional hub and template for ASEAN expansion; Brazil, Hungary, and Turkey became manufacturing footholds that double as tariff workarounds and in June 2026 Canada cut its tariff on Chinese EVs from 100 percent to 6.1 percent as part of a broader energy and climate partnership with Beijing, opening a new North American corridor. What makes this expansion durable rather than opportunistic is BYD’s unparalleled vertical integration. Unlike Western automakers, which depend heavily on third-party suppliers for battery cells, semiconductors, and software, BYD manufactures nearly everything in-house, an inheritance from its origins as a battery maker before it built a single car. That integration is precisely why the company can build factories concurrently across continents while still undercutting incumbents on price: it is not buying components at a margin, it is capturing the margin at every stage of the chain. Chinese EV factories capable of producing more than 200,000 vehicles a year have sprung up in Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, Turkey, Hungary, and Brazil, offering vehicles that are, on average, around 20 percent cheaper than their Western counterparts even before subsidies are considered. Domestically, this expansion is not evidence of strength alone. BYD’s first-quarter 2026 net profit fell 55 percent, its worst showing in three years, as a brutal domestic price war and thinning subsidies compressed sector-wide margins to an average of 3.2 percent. Exports abroad, where BYD can command significantly higher average selling prices, have become less a growth option than a financial necessity which only sharpens the incentive to keep undercutting Western rivals in every market it can reach. The Battery Dependency Mechanism BYD began life as a battery manufacturer, and that lineage is the key to understanding its strategy. Its battery subsidiary, FinDreams, is one of the largest EV battery producers on earth, second only to CATL, and together the two Chinese firms anchor a domestic battery-cell industry that supplies the overwhelming majority of the world’s electric and plug-in-hybrid vehicles. This is where the automotive story connects directly to the argument Kenneth Maxwell and I made in The Australian, Brazilian, and Chinese Dynamic. China today controls 57 percent of global lithium refining and 85 percent of global rare-earth processing, even though Australia alone produces 45 percent of the world’s raw lithium. A nation can extract the resource from its own soil and remain, in our phrase, a “feeder economy” so long as it lacks the midstream processing capacity to break the refining monopoly. The battery pack under a BYD Seal or a Dolphin is that same architecture, miniaturized and rolling on four wheels: raw lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth inputs processed almost entirely within Chinese-controlled facilities, assembled into cells by Chinese battery makers, and sold into foreign markets as a finished vehicle whose entire value chain, mine to midstream to cell to car, never leaves Beijing’s sphere of control. artigo.texto: BSES holds industry workshop on BESS safety As battery energy storage becomes an increasingly important part of India’s clean-energy transition, BSES recently organised a three-day workshop on the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Safety Framework, bringing together power-sector leaders, global safety experts, utilities, fire and emergency services and industry professionals. The workshop focused on a priority: ensuring battery storage scales up safely, responsibly, and with the right level of preparedness. Discussions covered safety-by-design, early warning and detection, thermal runaway, recognised testing, emergency preparedness, evacuation protocols and first-responder readiness. The inaugural session was addressed by Ghanshyam Prasad (Chairperson, CEA); Amal Sinha (Director & Group CEO, BSES); Abhishek Ranjan (CEO, BRPL); Sunil Kumar Jha (Director General, FS, CD & HG); Santosh Kumar (COO, BYPL); Alok Kumar (Director General, AIDA); Asko Rajput (Chairman, Standards Committee, BIS); Tanya Singhal (Vice President & Country Head, GEAPP); and Dr Rashi Gupta (MD, Vision Mechatronics Pvt Ltd). The workshop moved beyond discussions to practical preparedness. A major highlight was a live thermal runaway demonstration in a battery module, followed by firefighting intervention by Delhi Fire Service personnel. The exercise helped participants understand how battery failures can develop and the challenges emergency responders may face. Global experts Richie Stephen (Senior Standards Project Manager, UL Standards & Engagement), Kurt Vollmacher (Director, Intotech & Fire Safety Trainer) and Dr Judy Jeevarajan (UL Standards & Engagement) shared insights on system testing, failure modes, manufacturing defects, battery ageing, fire safety and emergency response, drawing on experience. The workshop concluded with nine multidisciplinary teams working through emergency scenarios involving smoke at a BESS site, flooding at an installation, and post-fire dismantling and waste management. The exercise helped participants identify priorities, responsibilities and the safest course of action. The programme also drew on BSES’ experience with its pioneering 20 MW/40 MWh Kilokri BESS, reinforcing the need to keep safety at the heart of storage growth.

artigo.texto: Pennsylvania’s legislators return to the capitol Monday following a 10-week recess, with several unresolved issues awaiting action, including the future of skill games, regulation of data centers, rising utility costs and restrictions on cell phone use in schools. Skill Games Following a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling in June that determined skill games are slot machines, the legislature was given 120 days to establish a law to keep the industry alive. Advocates for skill games have encouraged Pennsylvanians to call their representatives to ask them to support bills that would regulate the machines. HB2213 and SB1079 are bipartisan measures. Rep. Danilo Burgos (D-197) is prime sponsor of the house bill. “This is about job security for community members across Pennsylvania,” he said. “And helping keep doors open at VA clubs, at VFWs, and a slew of other community groups that benefit.” Republican Sen. Gene Yaw (R-23) is prime sponsor of the Senate bill. “It’s going to be a tremendous hit to a significant number of Pennsylvanians if we don’t address it,” Yaw said. “I can’t remember anything that I have been involved in in the Senate that would affect so many people negatively in one instant happening.” The Senate only has six session days to address it before the deadline, but Yaw says lawmakers could reach an agreement. Last week, Rep. Brad Roae (R-6) proposed legislation to extend the deadline by six months. The House unanimously passed the bill in June, and Fiedler is hopeful for a Senate vote soon. Cell phone ban in schools There are two bills that would ban cell phone use in schools waiting to be voted on. HB1814 passed the house in June, while SB1014 was passed in the Senate in February. Polls show the majority of Pennsylvania voters support leaving cell phones out of the classroom. Shapiro called on the General Assembly to pass legislation during his February budget address, but a ban did not end up in the approved budget. “Students need to spend less time focused on their phones and more time focused on learning, on talking to their friends face to face, and on developing the critical skills they’ll need later in life,” he said. “I know there are bills in both chambers to do this — come together and send a bill to my desk.”

artigo.texto: Protests against data centers have exploded across the US, with communities revolting against a multitude of proven damaging effects on energy prices, clean air and water – and the devastation of tens of thousands of acres of agricultural land. Recent headlines in national publications report that farmers and rural communities are rejecting multimillion-dollar bids from institutional investors and tech companies to buy their farmland to build data centers. A farmer in Kentucky rejected $33 million for her farmland; another in Pennsylvania turned down a $15 million offer; and one farmer in Wisconsin even reportedly refused a whopping $70+ million bid. Land has become the next big asset class for investors, especially billionaires and private equity firms, to hide and protect their wealth. It is seen as a safe, low-risk way to park money to hedge against inflation – at the expense of farmers and local communities alike. These investors aren’t just seeking out farmland to build data centers. Just like they’re targeting housing, investment firms are buying up land and renting it back to farmers for a hefty profit. The 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL) Survey, released this March, shows that 87% of the more than 2 million landowners renting out farmland are non-operators – that is, they are not actively farming, and the majority of these landowners never have. While these landlords raked in more than $34 billion in rent combined, the total value of farmland held for rent is $1.7 trillion – up 47% since 2014. We are watching in real time the emergence of a long-term, non-farming rural landlord class. While the TOTAL survey provides a useful indicator of farmland ownership trends, it doesn’t give us the full picture. Farmland ownership has never been effectively tracked in the US with regularity, and what limited data exists is difficult to find. The data we do have shows that investment in farmland has risen dramatically over the past two decades. Companies like AcreTrader, Farmland Partners, and others that allow individuals to invest in farmland have become increasingly popular. The most alarming growth has come from institutional investors, like pension funds, private equity firms, and wealth management groups. The value of farmland held by institutional investors has more than doubled over the past three years up to $16.6 billion dollars by 2024, an eightfold rise since 2008. Based on publicly available data alone, the largest corporate owners of US farmland control more than 2 million acres. But why are farmers selling their land in the first place? The hard truth is that farming just isn’t working as a viable livelihood anymore, and hasn’t for years. In just five years from 2017-2022, we lost 159,000 US family farms. The Farm Crisis didn’t go away in the 1980s – it’s just become quieter and less visible to most. Chronic low and volatile prices across sectors, coupled with a handful of multinational corporations tightening their iron grip over global agriculture, have pushed farmers to the brink of existence. With farm debt at an all-time high, selling the farm for the best offer possible is often the only feasible way to escape dire financial straits. And when the farm is for sale, companies with billions in assets are primed to outbid new and beginning farmers seeking land to start their own businesses. The best opportunity we have to protect farmland comes from strong federal policies that safeguard land for multiple generations of working farms and ensure farmers make a living wage. Right now, the Farmland for Farmers Act is one of the boldest pieces of federal legislation to combat this worrying trend. Modeled after anti-corporate farming laws in Midwestern states, the bill would stop large corporate entities from being able to purchase farmland only to let it lie fallow in the hopes that its value will skyrocket over time, or to rent it back to farmers at a premium price. With policies like it, coupled with a Farm Bill that allows farmers to pay their bills and sustainably grow their businesses, farmers might stand a chance. It’s long overdue for policy solutions championed by federal representatives not afraid to stand up against deep pocketed special interests. We need Congress to enact policies like the Farmland for Farmers Act that fight back against the profiteering on the backs of farmers, communities, and our natural resources. The first step in protecting farmland means supporting the next generation of farmers to enter the business with confidence and without having to compete with billionaires. We need to ensure that farmers now and in the future actually have the land they need to feed us all. Tim Gibbons is the Executive Director of the National Family Farm Coalition, a national coalition representing 30 grassroots farm, ranch, and fishing organizations in Washington, DC. A life-long Missourian, Tim has spent decades organizing family farmers, ranchers, and rural residents in support of fair, healthy and thriving rural economies, fair markets, and clean water and air. Dena Hoff represents the Northern Plains Resource Council on the NFFC Board. Since 1979, she’s raised sheep, cattle, alfalfa, corn, and edible dry beans, among other crops, on her farm in Glendive, Montana. She is an active member of and advocate for her rural community.

artigo.texto: The CEO of T5 , a development company set to build what could eventually become the second largest data center in Illinois by square footage, spoke exclusively to NBC 5 Monday amid an outcry of opposition from local residents. "We haven't hidden behind anything," Peter Marin said. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. A group of residents called the Lake County Data Center Opposition Coalition has sued to block the project, claiming the village wasn't transparent about the project during public meetings. "it wasn't out in public. It wasn't open," said coalition leader Morgan Coghill. "It wasn't on the agenda of the Grayslake like town meeting. And because they knew it was going to be a problem." In a statement, Grayslake mayor Elizabeth Davies says there were 18 public meetings and “Every one of those meetings and hearings was open to the public, publicly noticed, and on the record.” The village has put out a fact sheet online assuring residents the project won’t increase power bills, and will bring in $1.4 billion in tax revenue over the next 20 years. Martin says the company has communicated directly with residents through public meetings, as well as pamphlets and billboards. Local "We did everything by the book," he says. The Grayslake facility will be large enough to house companies that build generative AI, but activists opposed to the project say there has been a lack of specifics. "Who's the tenant? Is it Anthropic? Is it OpenAI? Is it going to be a swarm of AI agents pouring out from this data center to attack our government websites?" Coghill asked NBC 5. Martin says the Grayslake data center will operate on a closed-loop system, which means it will rely more on power than water to cool the computer servers inside. The project is slated to consume up to 1.2 gigawatts of energy once all phases are complete, which is the equivalent to powering a city of about one million residents. Marin says T5 has a separate rate agreement with ComEd, and will be effectively paying for all the power it consumes, but coalition members say they aren't buying that argument. "All they do is tap into the same grid we're all using, and they're getting their electricity," said Coalition member Michael Smith. "And we're being told, 'hey, throttle down your electricity use during hot summers because we're taxing the grids.'" Martin says the Chicago region is attractive because Illinois is a high power-producing state and he believes the grid can easily handle the influx of data centers. And he says if communities here say no, data centers will just go somewhere else. "Data centers are in every part of your life from, you know, from 911 to the grocery store to shopping online, whatever you interact with, everybody touches a data center every day," he said. The two sides are set to meet in court in November, but preliminary site-evaluation has already begun on the land. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has urged Illinois lawmakers to pass the so-called "POWER Act" when they return for their fall veto session that month. The legislation would put strict new limits on a data center's water and power usage. The coalition members were unswayed by Marin's explanations, but told NBC 5 they had one remaining question for him: would he personally want a data center of this size in his community? "Yeah I'd be fine with it," he said. "You're not going to see the building. You're not going to hear anything that's going on."

artigo.texto: AI data centers erupt as major battleground in Florida governor’s race The three alarms of the AI boom Big picture view: TAMPA, Fla. - The nationwide boom in artificial intelligence is raising three distinct levels of concern among policymakers and the public: - Existential risk: Warnings from tech leaders that advanced AI could eventually escape human control. - Workforce disruption: The potential for rapid automation to eliminate millions of traditional jobs. - Physical infrastructure demands: The immediate environmental, energy and land-use impacts of industrial-scale data centers. While the first two alarms involve national and global debates, the third alarm has arrived directly in Florida, making the state's election a key factor in where these massive facilities go—or don't go. Loudoun County’s $1.2 billion trade-off The backstory: To examine what a data center boom looks like on the ground, Democratic candidate David Jolly traveled to Loudoun County, Virginia—commonly known as "Data Center Alley." While Loudoun County has been a tech hub since the late 1990s, rapid expansion over the past decade has steadily converted open land and wooded parcels near residential neighborhoods into industrial campuses. Today, Loudoun County hosts roughly 230 existing data center buildings, with another 100 facilities in the pipeline. The Virginia experience highlights the trade-offs facing local communities: - Community strain: Residents express concerns about noise and air pollution, industrial views replacing natural woods, and concerns over declining property values. - Massive tax revenue: Loudoun County Economic Development Director Buddy Rizer notes that data centers deliver approximately $1.2 billion in annual local tax revenue—an asset class unmatched by any other industry. That tax base funds local public schools, roads, and community projects, including a local recreation center featuring pools, weightlifting rooms and amenities built largely from data center revenue. Whether Florida should embrace Virginia's high-revenue, high-density model or block it at the state line, has become a core issue between the candidates. Jolly’s plan: A statewide pause, environmental review, and potential ban Democrat David Jolly argues that the state must step in to protect communities, public health, and natural resources before data centers proliferate across Florida. Jolly proposes a one-year statewide moratorium on new data center construction to study their impacts on Florida's air, water systems, energy grid, real estate values, and overall economy. Key pillars of Jolly's position include: - State jurisdiction & permanent ban potential: Jolly asserts that the state has a clear duty to intervene on environmental and health grounds. If research shows severe negative impacts, Jolly says he would extend the temporary moratorium into a permanent statewide ban. - Economic skepticism: While acknowledging short-term construction jobs, Jolly questions the long-term economic value of data centers relative to their resource consumption, raising concerns about the "functional obsolescence" of these massive structures 5 to 10 years down the road. - Quality of life and AI anxieties: Beyond noise pollution and real estate devaluation, Jolly notes that data centers have become a physical symbol of broader public anxieties regarding job loss, wage disruption, privacy, and security. - Clean energy contrast: Jolly strongly supports expanding solar, wind, and renewable technologies, stating that clean energy can lower utility bills, create jobs, and protect Florida's natural environment. Donalds’ plan: Local control, ratepayer safeguards Republican Byron Donalds strongly opposes a statewide pause, arguing that banning or stalling data center construction sends a dangerous signal to the business community that Florida is closed to capital investment. Donalds' strategy relies on local government authority and legislative ratepayer protections: - A departure on local preemption: In recent years, Florida's Republican-led state government has preempted local municipalities on a range of issues. However, on data centers, Donalds explicitly opposes state preemption, arguing that cities and counties should retain full authority to decide whether a facility belongs in their community. - Current ratepayer protection law & caveats: Donalds points to current state law—enacted through legislation sponsored by his running mate, Representative Bryan Avila—which requires large data centers to pay their full energy and water infrastructure costs, so traditional utility bills do not increase. However, that law applies specifically to Florida's four major investor-owned utilities (leaving municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops exempt) and relies on the Public Service Commission (PSC) for enforcement. - Transparency vs. past legislation: Donalds calls for full transparency for local data center proposals, stating there should be "no more NDAs" (non-disclosure agreements). Earlier legislative efforts sponsored by Avila sought to exempt data center plans from public records laws, but that transparency exemption failed to pass. Donalds emphasizes the consumer-protection provisions that did become law. - Replacing solar arrays with nuclear reactors: Skeptical of solar power—which he argues takes large tracts of land out of productive use for relatively low power output—Donalds states he is "dovish on solar and wind power." Instead, Donalds proposes placing four data centers on the footprint of a single solar array and powering them with an SMR (Small Modular Reactor)—a small nuclear fission reactor. Any excess electricity generated by the SMR would be fed back into the public power grid. - Protecting pristine land and tourism: Donalds argues Florida has available interior land to accommodate high-tech development without building next to residential homes or harming core tourism hubs like Disney, Universal, and state beaches. artigo.texto: The Chicago-based battery technology startup Pure Lithium is building its case around a simpler idea: remove some of the materials that make today’s batteries heavy, complex and deeply tied to overseas supply chains, then rethink how lithium reaches the cell in the first place. The race to build the next generation of batteries has produced no shortage of ambitious ideas. Solid-state cells, silicon anodes and new cathode chemistries have all been pitched as possible answers to the limitations of today’s lithium-ion technology. Pure Lithium is taking another route. The company describes itself as a vertically integrated lithium metal vanadium, or LVO, battery technology business. At the centre of its approach is its Brine to Battery™ electrodeposition technology, designed to turn unconventional sources of lithium into a battery-ready electrode without first going through the conventional compound-production route. The company says that process can create an electrode in a single day. That manufacturing philosophy is important to understanding Pure Lithium. Rather than treating lithium extraction, processing and battery manufacturing as disconnected stages, the company is trying to bring them much closer together. And at the battery level, its ambitions go beyond changing where lithium comes from. Pure Lithium is also working on lithium-metal cells that eliminate graphite from the anode. The technology highlighted in recent testing pairs a lithium-metal anode with lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry. Pure Lithium says this configuration removes the need for graphite as well as nickel, manganese and cobalt, materials that feature prominently in conventional battery supply chains. That matters because graphite remains one of the less visible dependencies in the battery industry. More than 90% of the world’s graphite processing takes place in China. In a conventional lithium-ion battery, graphite acts primarily as a host material for lithium ions during charging and discharging. Pure Lithium’s approach is to remove that host altogether and use lithium metal directly, opening additional room inside the cell for energy-storing material. For Chief Executive Emilie Bodoin, eliminating graphite is central to the company’s performance argument. “It’s half the weight and double the energy density of the battery that we’re all using today,” Bodoin said in an interview cited by InsideEVs. Those claims are still being tested against the realities of commercial production, but Pure Lithium has recently put forward a striking laboratory result. The company said one of its lithium-metal cells reached 9,315 charge-discharge cycles, with testing conducted at a 1C charge and discharge rate. That means the cell was repeatedly charged over one hour and discharged over another hour. Pure Lithium said the result was unprecedented for a lithium-metal battery tested under equivalent conditions. The test was not uninterrupted. Pure Lithium paused testing around the 6,000-cycle point while moving its headquarters from Boston to Chicago, leaving the cell at room temperature for roughly four months. When testing resumed, the company reported that the cell continued to show strong capacity retention. It also disclosed that some of the earlier fluctuations in the test were linked to a lack of temperature control and multiple power failures in its Boston laboratory. A previous test in January 2025 had shown that a Pure Lithium cell had maintained over 80% of its charge capacity after 2,200 cycles at the same 1C rate. It should be noted that the company has also claimed its Gen 1 battery to have 300 Wh/kg energy density, with its Gen 2 model projected to achieve 425 Wh/kg. However, the energy density of the particular cell used for testing 9,315 cycles was not provided. That distinction is important. Long cycle life in a laboratory cell is not the same thing as a commercially produced automotive battery, and Pure Lithium has not yet reached mass production. The company is currently building a pilot line in Chicago and is looking for partners to help commercialise the technology. Bodoin has said Pure Lithium is in discussions with more than 40 companies about scaling its approach. The way Pure Lithium manufactures its lithium-metal anode is another part of the story. Its battery is graphite-free, but not anode-free. Instead, lithium metal is deposited directly onto a copper current collector through electrodeposition until the required thickness is reached. In effect, the anode is formed as part of the manufacturing process rather than being produced through the conventional graphite-based route. Bodoin has described that electrodeposition step as a way of making the lithium anode in a single manufacturing stage. For Pure Lithium, that manufacturing method connects back to the bigger idea behind Brine to Battery™: shorten the distance between raw lithium and a usable battery component. It is an approach that could become increasingly relevant as battery companies rethink both chemistry and supply chains. Pure Lithium is not alone in pursuing lithium-metal technology. Factorial, Solid Power and QuantumScape are also developing graphite-free lithium-metal batteries, although their technical routes differ. Factorial and QuantumScape have focused on solid-state or semi-solid-state electrolytes, while Solid Power has been developing technologies around a sulfide solid electrolyte. Pure Lithium, by contrast, uses a liquid electrolyte and is placing particular emphasis on how its lithium-metal anode is produced. That difference may ultimately prove as important as the chemistry itself. The battery industry is not simply looking for a cell that stores more energy. Companies are also trying to reduce manufacturing complexity, lower material dependence and create supply chains that can operate closer to where batteries will eventually be produced. artigo.texto: Virginia rejoins carbon market as utilities seek $13 monthly charge after allowance prices surge - Virginia has rejoined the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, leading to a sharp increase in the price of carbon allowances that utilities must pay, potentially impacting electricity bills and state climate programs. Virginia's return to the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative has come with a sharp jump in the price utilities pay for carbon allowances, a change that could affect electricity bills and how the state funds climate and energy programs in the years ahead. Here's what to know Virginia has rejoined the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, or RGGI, an agreement among 11 states designed to cut carbon pollution from power plants. The state was part of RGGI from 2020 to 2023, before Gov. Glenn Youngkin withdrew it, citing high costs for little payoff, reported The Virginian-Pilot. In the first auction since Virginia's return, allowances sold for $37.65 each, more than double the $14.88 price from the last auction before the state left. That auction generated $259 million for Virginia, according to The Virginian-Pilot. "I think the people who designed this 15, 20 years ago knew the price was going to go up," said Steve Haner, senior fellow for energy and the environment at the Thomas Jefferson Institute for Public Policy, in an interview with the Pilot. More background Under RGGI, power producers must buy an allowance for every metric ton of carbon pollution they emit, and utilities like Dominion Energy can pass that cost on to customers. William Shobe, director emeritus of the University of Virginia's Center for Economic & Policy Studies, said prices have climbed roughly 14% a year since 2012 and are likely to keep rising as allowance caps shrink through 2033. Dominion is now asking state regulators to add a $13 monthly charge to a typical customer's bill to cover its allowance costs, up from about $4.40 a month before Virginia left RGGI. What's being done? Virginia has changed how it splits RGGI revenue. Before, half went to low-income energy efficiency programs and 45% to flood preparedness. Now, 45% is set aside for customer rebates, with the rest split between flood resiliency and low-income programs. Some environmental advocates worry the smaller flood-fund share could slow projects in Hampton Roads. Not every customer stands to benefit equally. Industrial and large retail users won't get rebates, which Haner said could push those companies to raise prices elsewhere to cover their higher utility costs. "Businesses just pass along their costs to the extent they can," Haner said. "Kroger's not going to get a rebate, Walmart's not going to get a rebate. Your small doctor's office might, but the hospital's not." Where can I learn more? Virginia's return to RGGI is part of a larger conversation about how state energy policy shapes power prices and cleaner electricity. • Virginia became the first state to take a solar-buying program statewide, cutting system costs. • Connecticut and Virginia moved to speed home solar as advocates pushed for cheaper power. • Across the U.S., energy storage installations kept rising as utilities prepared for demand. • In California, an unorthodox power market drove lower bills while clean generation expanded. artigo.texto: Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is facing growing scrutiny over the financing of its AI infrastructure after about $18 billion of loans tied to its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico were quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, according to the Financial Times, as reported by Reuters. The project is part of Oracle's AI infrastructure expansion with OpenAI, but local opposition over water and air-quality concerns and a regulatory setback involving a proposed natural-gas pipeline have raised questions about its development. Banks have also struggled to distribute the debt to other investors as concerns about Oracle's leverage have increased. Reuters noted that S&P downgraded Oracle in July to one notch above junk. Photo from Oracle website Oracle's AI Backlog Could Provide a Cushion for Rising Financing Needs The debt pressure is occurring alongside exceptionally strong demand for Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL)'s cloud infrastructure. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, cloud revenue rose 62% to $11.6 billion, while cloud infrastructure revenue increased 121% to $7.4 billion. Oracle's remaining performance obligations also reached $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year, providing substantial contracted demand to support continued infrastructure investment. The financing model is also becoming less dependent on Oracle funding every dollar itself. Oracle said $75 billion of its large AI contracts involved customers prepaying for GPUs or supplying the GPUs themselves, substantially reducing the capital it needs to raise for AI data centers. Oracle raised $43 billion of debt and $5 billion of equity in fiscal 2026, while expecting about $40 billion of additional debt and equity financing in fiscal 2027. If customer-backed contracts continue expanding, the revenue generated from infrastructure could increasingly offset the financing burden. Rising Infrastructure Costs Could Test Oracle's AI Investment Strategy The immediate concern is that Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) is committing capital faster than its infrastructure generates cash. Capital expenditures jumped to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026 from $21.2 billion a year earlier, producing negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027 alone, capital expenditures reached $28.5 billion, and Oracle expects fiscal 2027 spending to exceed the prior year. The balance sheet leaves less room for execution problems. As of August 31, Oracle had $125.3 billion of notes payable and other borrowings, compared with $37.1 billion of cash and marketable securities. It also had $34.6 billion of recognized operating lease liabilities and another $288 billion of additional data-center lease commitments expected to begin between fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2029.

artigo.texto: City of Hopkinsville to host public hearing over data center zoning What This Story Is About - Hopkinsville Community and Development Services is holding a public hearing to gather community feedback on proposed zoning amendments governing data centers. Why It Matters - The proposed changes will establish legal definitions, operational guidelines, and designated zoning districts for future data center developments, directly influencing local land use, infrastructure demand, and commercial growth. What Happens Next - Following the public hearing at Hopkinsville Community College, CDS will review public feedback and formulate recommendations before the proposed ordinance heads to the Hopkinsville City Council for final review and approval. For Context - Municipalities across Kentucky and the region are increasingly updating their zoning ordinances to manage the rapid rise of data center facilities, addressing potential impacts on electric grids, water systems, noise levels, and property boundaries. HOPKINSVILLE, Ky. (WBKO) - The City of Hopkinsville has announced Community and Development Services will hold a public hearing Monday evening to gather public input on proposed zoning regulations for commercial data centers. The hearing is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the Lecture Hall of the Hopkinsville Community College Auditorium Building, 720 North Drive. The proposed amendment to the Hopkinsville Zoning Ordinance outlines how data centers are defined locally, establishes siting and operational standards, and determines which zoning districts would permit such facilities. Residents and business owners are invited to attend and provide feedback before officials advance the amendment to local governing bodies for formal consideration. Copyright 2026 WBKO.
