artigo.texto: Buffalo, NY (WBEN) The Buffalo Common Council will vote Tuesday on whether to impose a two year moratorium on data centers in the city. Mayor Sean Ryan says the city previously looked at a moratorium. "We had been working on a one-year moratorium as an executive order, and then we kept in close contact with the state legislature and the governor, and so the state came in with a one-year moratorium. So we pulled back our executive order; it wasn't necessary anymore. Now the council has a two-year moratorium that differs significantly from the states, so we're going to take a look at that," says Ryan. But while the concern is companies coming in and buying land, he has a caveat. "We have to make sure that we don't inadvertently sweep up Roswell Park's computers, M&T Banks computers, Kaleida's computers, so we're going to be checking with all the University of Buffalo. So we're going to be checking with all these institutions that have rather large computer storage facilities to make sure that this somehow doesn't affect them," warns Ryan. Count Councilmember Mitch Nowakowski among those willing to vote for the moratorium. "I believe that a moratorium will allow the city of Buffalo to get in conjunction with the state of New York, with an ability to be able to better get ahead of data centers that are being proposed through you know the region, but also the country," says Nowakowski, who would like to take it from an urban planning standpoint. "I believe that a moratorium would allow the city of Buffalo planners to get ahead of if a data center was proposed in the city, where would it be most applicable or not? What environmental impacts would transpire if this happened? So we really have to take this from a planning perspective, but ultimately from an environment standpoint as well, to because of the the amount of water and electricity, and can the grid handle this? And ultimately, where would this, you know, where would a proposal go? I mean, we're we're a city of a quarter of a million people, and you know, we we hit with the vacant land that we do have. We would like it to be used for housing, and and and where in this city would this even be proposed? And even if it was appropriate, where where would this be? So taking this from a municipal planning perspective is not only the right thing to do, but it's it's the appropriate thing to also do for our city, our built environment, and for our residents." Leah Halton-Pope says she wants to make sure the city has the right infrastructure when it's ready. "A lot of people have an issue with environmental hazards and what it does to communities around it," she says. She notes underprivileged communities tend to be most affected. She says a moratorium allows to make sure the Green Code is up to date. The Council votes this afternoon at 2pm. Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium

artigo.texto: Capacidade de data centers em São Paulo cresce 91% em um ano Região do entorno da capital já é o principal parque de dados da América Latina, de acordo com levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield A capacidade operacional de data centers no eixo São Paulo–Campinas cresceu 91% em um ano, passando de 346 megawatts no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 661 megawatts no mesmo período de 2026, segundo levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield, empresa global especializada em serviços imobiliários corporativos. O resultado consolida a região como o principal mercado de data centers da América Latina. Além da capacidade já em operação, o eixo composto pelas duas cidades paulistas possui 250 megawatts em projetos em construção e outros 2.066 megawatts planejados. O volume planejado equivale a mais de três vezes a capacidade operacional atual e supera, somados, os projetos previstos em Querétaro, no México, Santiago, no Chile, e Bogotá, na Colômbia, que totalizam cerca de 1.47o megawatts. Apesar da expansão da oferta, a consultoria destaca que a vacância dos projetos que já estão em operação permaneceu baixa, ficando 4,1% no primeiro semestre no eixo de São Paulo, indicando a alta demanda por esse tipo de infraestrutura. A Cushman & Wakefield também destaca os novos impulsos que o Brasil deve receber com o Redata, novo regime de incentivos tributários aprovado em setembro. O Redata prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização desses empreendimentos. “O mercado brasileiro já vinha apresentando crescimento consistente antes da sanção do Redata”, disse Dennys Andrade, chefe de pesquisa e intligência de mercado da Cushman & Wakefield no Brasil. “A redução dos custos de implantação pode favorecer o avanço dos projetos, mas sua viabilidade continuará dependendo de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, terrenos adequados, licenciamento e segurança regulatória.” Com 661 megawatts em operação, o hub de São Paulo tem quase o dobro da capacidade de Querétaro, que registra 336 megawatts, e supera Santiago, com 272 megawatts, e Bogotá, com 58 megawatts. Consideradas todas as Américas, contudo, os Estados Unidos continuam sendo o principal centro deste mercado: o estado da Virgínia, por exemplo, seu maior parque, tem 12.338 megawatts em operação, enquanto a cidade de Atlanta possui 3.488 megawatts. Além disso, dos 38 gigawatts que já estão em construção em todo o continente (equivalente a 38.000 megawatts), 92% estão nos Estados Unidos.

artigo.texto: Amazon Taps Prysmian and Rio Tinto for Low-Carbon Data Center Cables. What Does it Mean for Investors? Prysmian is finding another way into the data-center buildout, and this time the story isn't about fiber. The Italian cable maker has partnered with Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) to supply electrical cables made with low-carbon aluminum for an Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) data center in Ohio. The cables will use aluminum produced with ELYSIS inert-anode technology, which Prysmian says eliminates direct greenhouse-gas emissions from the aluminum-smelting process and releases pure oxygen instead. For Prysmian investors, the project's significance lies in the fact that the technology Prysmian and Rio Tinto were developing earlier this year is now being put to use in a data-center project for Amazon. Bull Case The Amazon project gives Prysmian's work with ELYSIS something it didn't have when the company announced its expanded collaboration with Rio Tinto in March, which is a specific data-center application. Prysmian says this will be the first known use of aluminum produced through inert-anode smelting in a data center, and the cables will be manufactured at its Sedalia, Missouri facility. The project didn't emerge from a new supplier relationship either, as Prysmian and Rio Tinto (NYSE:RIO) signed a five-year supply agreement in 2023 for low-carbon aluminum produced using renewable hydropower from Rio Tinto's Canadian operations. They later strengthened the relationship through a joint development agreement before announcing their work with ELYSIS-produced aluminum in March 2026. Data centers were already part of the thinking at that point, as Prysmian said in March that its customers, particularly those in the data-center sector, shared similar sustainability commitments, while Rio Tinto specifically identified the rapidly expanding data-center sector as an area where lower-carbon aluminum could support decarbonization efforts. Amazon has now provided a concrete example, with AWS Vice President of Data Center Engineering Joern Tinnemeyer linking the Ohio initiative to Amazon's target of reaching net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040. The project also fits with targets Prysmian has set for its own business. The company is targeting Net Zero by 2035 and has said it wants sustainability-linked solutions to account for 55% of revenue by 2028. Bear Case There is an obvious reason not to get carried away with the announcement, as Prysmian has not provided a contract value or expected revenue contribution of the Amazon project. Without a contract value, volume figure, or expected revenue contribution, there is no basis for arguing that the Ohio data center will materially change Prysmian's financial performance.

artigo.texto: Data centers não podem virar mais um encargo na conta de luz Em artigo à CNN Infra, Lino Cançado argumenta que restringir o Redata às energias renováveis pode gerar encargos bilionários aos consumidores O Brasil encontra-se diante de uma oportunidade histórica com o avanço da demanda global por novos data centers, impulsionada sobretudo pelas soluções de inteligência artificial. A atração desses investimentos trará inovação, geração de empregos e desenvolvimento tecnológico para quem souber aproveitar essa janela. Nesse sentido, o Redata (Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento de Infraestrutura de Data Centers) é uma oportunidade fundamental para garantir que não fiquemos para trás nessa corrida. No entanto, o debate atual sobre a regulamentação desses incentivos fiscais tem girado em torno das fontes de energia que irão abastecer as estruturas de processamento de dados, em especial na questão de incluir apenas fontes intermitentes para atender à grande demanda energética dos data centers. A consequência direta de preterir fontes seguras e de baixa emissão pode ter um impacto preocupante: o aumento da conta de luz do consumidor comum. Data centers são instalações que funcionam sem parar. Por isso exigem energia contínua, estável e segura, 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana. Embora o Brasil tenha uma matriz elétrica invejável e predominantemente renovável, sabemos que as fontes eólica e solar são intermitentes. Quando o sol se põe e os ventos cessam, coincidindo com o horário de ponta de consumo, eles não são capazes de sustentar o fornecimento constante que esses centros de processamento exigem. Se o modelo não for bem estruturado, a expansão acelerada sobrecarregará o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) na ponta, exigindo uma contratação massiva de reserva de capacidade. Esse encargo de potência tem um alto custo, que acaba sendo rateado e repassado para a conta de luz de todos os brasileiros. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) já realizou uma segunda revisão do plano de carga para o horizonte 2026-2030, saltando a previsão da carga de data centers de 2.157 MW para alarmantes 5.653 MW. É uma diferença repentina de 3.496 MW. Para garantir que essa demanda seja atendida com segurança dia a dia no horário de pico, o sistema terá um custo de capacidade adicional de R$ 7 bilhões ao ano. Isso equivale a 13,35% de todo o orçamento previsto para a Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético (CDE) em 2026 (orçada em R$ 52,7 bilhões) e a 17,95% do LRCAP. Em outras palavras, seria um encargo severo imposto à tarifa de cidadãos e indústrias, que não têm relação nenhuma com a operação desses centros de dados. A saída para evitar essa penalização social não é frear o desenvolvimento, mas adotar uma política pragmática. O ideal é condicionar a instalação de novos data centers à autoprodução de energia. Esse é um modelo internacional já testado, que vem sendo aplicado de maneira eficiente nos Estados Unidos. Na definição do conteúdo do decreto do Redata, o poder público deve focar em estabelecer as regras de atendimento e deixar que o próprio empreendedor decida como supri-las da forma mais competitiva e eficiente. A melhor equação para esses complexos é a combinação inteligente de matrizes: aliar a energia limpa das renováveis ao atributo da confiabilidade e firmeza do gás natural. Dessa forma, os data centers não demandam do grid na hora da ponta, o que evita a criação de custos adicionais para o restante dos consumidores. O gás natural, como combustível da transição energética, viabiliza uma solução de baixíssima emissão para suprir essa intermitência, garantindo a resiliência operacional do investidor sem onerar os demais usuários da rede. A transição energética e a digitalização não podem ser desenhadas de costas para a realidade sistêmica do país. Restringir o Redata exclusivamente à energia renovável forçará o sistema a prover uma reserva artificial bilionária paga pela sociedade. Precisamos criar um marco legal que incentive a autoprodução e reconheça a importância da flexibilidade do gás natural, assegurando que o Brasil avance rumo à liderança digital sem transferir o custo dessa modernização para o bolso do cidadão. * Lino Cançado é CEO da Eneva

artigo.texto: Talbot County considers zoning rules for battery storage facilities Planning commission holds first public hearing on proposed regulations TALBOT COUNTY, Ga. (WTVM) - Talbot County leaders are looking at new rules to prepare for large battery storage facilities, the kind often used to power heavy developments like data centers. The planning commission held its first public hearing Monday on how to zone for them. County says current rules don’t cover private systems County leaders say their rules currently don’t cover private battery systems, which store extra electricity and pump it back out when the grid is strained. No developer has applied to build one yet, but neighbors and local planners are already weighing in. Clarence Napier said he believes more work needs to be done on the plan. “I think more work needs to be done with developing the plan,” Napier said. “Like I asked the question this plan came from a template and maybe the plan needs to be designed or scaled down or maybe even elevated for just this town.” Allison Slocum, assistant planning director for the River Valley Regional Commission, said the facilities could benefit the grid. “This is really going to help make our energy grid more resilient by taking power off the grid when it’s not being used, storing it and then releasing it when it’s most needed,” Slocum said. Existing facility not subject to local zoning Talbot County already has one battery storage facility, built by Georgia Power in North Talbot. Because Georgia Power operates as a utility, it was not required to follow local zoning rules. A private developer would be. The Board of Commissioners will hold a second public hearing next Monday at 6 p.m. Copyright 2026 WTVM. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Nebraska data center growth raises questions for host counties NORTH PLATTE, Neb. (KNOP) - Nebraska’s push to attract data centers is facing questions from the counties that would host them. Lincoln County commissioners met last Tuesday in Grand Island with power companies, water districts and Gov. Pillen for the first meeting of Nebraska’s Data Center Task Force. Task force reviews power, water strain The group is looking at how the state should handle the rapid growth of data centers and the strain they could put on power and water supplies. Lincoln County Commissioner Kent Weems said the county is not against the idea but wants any deal to come with benefits for taxpayers. “If we’re going to be the ones taking the heat for these, whatever they evolve into, if they evolve at all, which apparently there’s something and it works locally. It’s my hope and prayer that this community can, in fact, have substantial beneficial results and be mandated in the agreement so that the county can see property tax relief,” Weems said. Not all data centers are the same, commissioner says Lincoln County Commissioner Micaela Wuehler said data centers vary in scale and impact. “It’s important for people to remember: not all data centers are created equal. They’re not all hyperscale... they may not all be appropriate for Lincoln County. That’s where our good planning and zoning regulations come in,” Wuehler said. artigo.texto: Trending PARKERSBURG, W.Va. -- The Democratic challenger for one of West Virginia's congressional seats pitched legislation Friday to place a two-year moratorium on new, large data centers and to give local communities a say in whether they're built. Ace Parsi, a Morgantown community organizer running for U.S. House of Representatives 2nd District seat occupied by Rep. Riley Moore, said the proposed "Neighbors, Not Servers Act" would be "the very first piece of legislation that I would introduce as a member of Congress." Moore said Friday, "West Virginians need a voice in this important debate," and he has co-sponsored legislation to that effect. Parsi said the impact of data centers on the environment, communities and utility costs is an issue he's heard about from Democratic, Republican and independent voters alike. "Our communities do not have a say in whether these things go in our backyards," he said, referencing transmission lines as well. The legislation would pause new construction of data centers using 20 megawatts or more of power, according to a news release from Parsi. During that time, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine would conduct studies into the effects of such facilities on public health, water, jobs, utility bills, property values and the power grid. It proposes a fine of up to $1 million a day for developers who break the pause. The bill also would ban nondisclosure agreements between developers and public officials, including those already in place. NDAs signed by Washington County, Ohio, officials for a proposed data center in the Waterford area have ignited debate. Commissioners have said such agreements are standard for preliminary conversations about potential development and signing allowed them to enter into conversations with the developers. Parsi's proposed bill also would establish a referendum process so community members could seek a vote on approving construction of a data center. Before a vote, developers would be required to disclose information such as who is behind the project, who will use it, how much power and water it will use, noise levels, tax breaks sought and number of jobs it will create, the release states. Parsi said during an online news conference Friday that a public vote would not be mandatory, as local bodies like county commissions could make the call as representatives of residents. "We would direct those (federal) agencies to not give those permits (for data center construction) until they made sure the community" had a voice in the process through one of those mechanisms, he said. "The local people need to be able to determine this," Parsi said. "This bill is not about big government." Moore said "it is critical that America wins the AI race against countries like China, but we must do so responsibly. "I'm for local control. Local communities need to have a say about whether to build data centers in their backyard, and we need to ensure that Americans are not being forced to foot the bill for increased energy demands and water usage," he said. "That's why I proudly cosponsored and voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act in the House to ensure that local communities have a voice in these important decisions and ensure that West Virginians are not being forced to foot the bill for data center development." Moore announced in an Aug. 31 news release he was co-sponsoring that bill, which would "require state public utility commissions to consider standards ensuring that large data centers pay the full incremental costs associated with generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve their electricity demand." It adds that the bill would protect ratepayers while preserving the authority of state regulators to determine how its standards were implemented. OHIO ELECTION TOPIC Data centers are also a topic of interest in Ohio's gubernatorial election. Democratic nominee Dr. Amy Acton this week called for the state Legislature to enact a conditional moratorium on data centers, including prohibiting data centers and investors from passing along costs to ratepayers, banning their use of NDAs and requiring them to be built with union labor, maintain zero environmental impact and prioritize the use of brownfield sites. In the release, she also criticized Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's investments in data centers. "I am calling on lawmakers from across the aisle to come together and fight against the unchecked development of data centers driving up costs in our communities," Acton said. "I will always put the needs of working families over the wants of billionaires, corporations and special interests." Ramaswamy's campaign website lists three "non-negotiable" requirements for companies wanting to build data centers in Ohio: Ensure nearby families receive free electricity by providing power or compensation, pay their full property taxes so revenue can be used to provide relief for homeowners, and comply with strict air and water quality standards while minimizing water use and prioritizing brownfield and industrial sites over farmland.

artigo.texto: Saturday at Stable View Oktoberfest began with dressage for the Training and Modified riders, show jumping for the CCI2*-S competitors, and cross country for the Intermediate division. Christina Henriksen and her own Cisco’s Calor Z held their lead from start to finish in the Intermediate Division, finishing their weekend on a 38.1. Waylon Roberts and FVF Top Gun LLC’s FVF Top Gun moved up to second place after a quick trip around the cross country. The combination finished on a 54.7. Rebecca Brown and Team Junior Syndicate’s Fernhill Quite Frankly weren’t far behind, finishing in third on a 56.3. The CCI3*-S followed the Intermediate, and the division saw quite a few changes in the leaderboard, with the time proving difficult to make and several combinations having stops along the way. Karl Slezak was one of only two to produce a double-clear round, moving up to win the division by 6.8 points on a 30.7 aboard Elizabeth Leete’s HSH Marshall. Slezak also finished in second place on Elizabeth Leete’s Herald De La Rose. The combination finished on a 37.5. Allison Springer and Nancy Winter’s Herald De La Rose also finished on a 37.5, with Slezak finishing just ahead of her on the tie-break. As the time approached for the CCI4*-S, the Pavilion porches became lined with spectators. VIP attendees enjoyed cider, Stable View travel cups, and their own to-go charcuterie boards. Stable View sponsors, GGT Footing and The Sharer Dale Team, enjoyed their course-side gazebos with their clients and friends. The four-star saw plenty of shifting in the leaderboard as well. Overnight leaders Kim Severson and Ros and Bill Johnson’s Cooley Corraghy Diamond had a beautiful trip around the countryside. The combination ultimately added time penalties, dropping them down in the final standings. Severson shared yesterday, “I am really proud of Cory thus far; it has been a work in progress.” Alyssa Phillips and her own Rockett 19 added a handful of time penalties themselves. The pair ended their weekend in fifth place on a 43.4. Lucienne Bellissimo and Horse Scout Eventing LLC’s Dyri also ended their weekend on a 43.4, finishing just ahead of Phillips on the tie-break to take home fourth place. Only two CCI4*-S competitors managed to make the time on Helen West’s course. Waylon Roberts and Andrea McAllister’s Fernhill Salt Lake went double clear to move up to seventh place. Mary Bess Davis and her own Imperio Magic also went double clear. The combination brought home the win and was the only pair to finish sub-40, on a 39.9. Davis shared, “Mccoll was absolutely perfection today. I was so proud of him. He was all about business from the first to the last fence. It was such an honor to be his jockey today.” When asked what this win means for her, she said, “Well, it has taken me until the age of 48 to win a four-star, so today is a dream come true for me. I could not be more happy and proud.” Davis’s fall plans include a trip to Morven Park for the CCI4*-L. Davis said, “I think this track was a super prep run, and I am so excited for Morven!” Caroline Pamukcu and Mollie Hoff’s HSH Limited Edition moved up to second place, adding just nine seconds of time to their score to finish on a 40.4. Aiken-based Emily Hamel and Black Flag Option’s Corvett moved up to third place, finishing on a 41.2. Hamel spoke very highly of Corvette, saying, “He’s so good. He’s just like a packer out there. He’s fantastic. We have such a great partnership. It’s fun to just take him out.” Fans were happy to see the Aiken-based combination back out again at the upper levels. artigo.texto: Ontario EV shopper weighs Bolt or BYD Dolphin, then gets warning: 'A tin can with a battery' Buying an affordable EV is supposed to be a practical decision with objective pros and cons. But for one shopper in Canada, the calculation got complicated as they decided whether to buy a Chevrolet Bolt or wait for BYD's widely discussed Dolphin. Here's what to know The question came from an Ontario buyer turning to the r/BoltEV subreddit to decide whether to purchase a Bolt LT or hold off for BYD's compact EV. In a Reddit thread, the original poster wrote: "Currently deciding between a Bolt LT at 41k all in (incl taxes) and waiting for the BYD Dolphin." They asked owners what tipped them toward the Chevy and what to consider before deciding. Many of the replies favored the Bolt for a simple reason. It already has a foothold, as demonstrated by a vibrant Reddit community. Commenters repeatedly returned to the comfort of existing dealers, easier access to parts, and a service network buyers can count on instead of one that may take time to develop. The discussion also touched on materials and day-to-day livability. "The Bolt interior is nicer and will age better than the Dolphin," one commenter wrote. Another pointed out that some Dolphin versions sold abroad have smaller battery packs than the Bolt. One commenter was particularly harsh on the model. "Chinese cars sound nice on paper but in my experience with the BYD Dolphin it's a tin can with a battery, the Bolt feels more solid all around and way more reliable," they wrote. More background Affordable EVs remain one of the biggest sticking points for shoppers hoping to cut gas costs without paying luxury-car prices. The Bolt has long drawn attention as a relatively accessible all-electric hatchback, while the BYD Dolphin has built a reputation in other markets as a budget-friendly compact EV. EVs can lower ownership costs in meaningful ways. Home charging is often much cheaper per mile than paying for gasoline, and drivers also avoid oil changes. Still, those savings matter only if the vehicle is reliable and easy to service. In the thread, concern about after-sale support kept resurfacing. Buyers worried that a thinner Canadian presence could mean harder warranty claims, slower parts sourcing, or long drives for repairs, particularly outside the largest cities. What can be done? Comparing total ownership costs rather than focusing only on sticker price means looking at taxes, insurance, charging costs, expected winter range, battery warranty, and the distance to the nearest qualified service center. Ontario weather changes the calculation too. One commenter urged buyers to "be VERY aware of the Bolt LT trim." The commenter added, "Imagine not having heated seats and steering wheel in Ontario, Canada. Hard pass." How a driver expects to charge the car can matter just as much. Someone who plugs in at home every night may not care as much about weaker fast-charging performance, while a buyer who depends on public chargers or plans frequent longer trips may put far more emphasis on charging speed and network support. Some commenters were jealous of the original poster's predicament. "I wish I even had the opportunity to add BYD Dolphin to something I was considering," an envious commenter shared. Where can I learn more? The affordable EV market is one that is still evolving and facing perceived hurdles from some consumers. • In the U.K., BYD pushed cheap compact EVs closer to mainstream-car territory. • Persistent doubts about price and carbon still cloud EV decisions for first-time buyers. • A Nissan Leaf owner described the unexpected reality of owning an EV amid lingering myths. artigo.texto: “A fraction of proposed data centers will get built. Utilities are wising up.” That was the headline on a May 2025 Utility Dive article that explored the conundrum speculative data center requests pose for U.S. electric utilities. More than a year later, it’s unclear how much has changed. Community opposition has emerged as a major barrier to data center development, with other challenges including construction labor shortages, long lead times for critical electrical equipment, limited power availability in key markets and uncertainty around consumer demand for artificial intelligence tools. More than $170 billion in AI data center capacity has been “blocked, withdrawn, or stalled” by community opposition since January 2024, the energy advisory company Relae, formerly Carbon Direct, said in June. That’s a sizable chunk of the roughly $581 billion Goldman Sachs expects the big tech companies known as hyperscalers to spend in the U.S. on AI infrastructure, including data center construction, this year. Yet market analysts see no sign that the AI-driven construction boom will disappear anytime soon, despite challenges. Goldman Sachs said in May it sees U.S. data center power demand more than doubling from its 2025 levels to reach 66 GW in 2027. Only about half of data center capacity scheduled for the next one to two years is expected to come online on time amid delays and cancellations, it said. The Electric Power Research Institute, a research nonprofit, said in February that data centers will represent 9% to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and up to 20% by 2035. Questions persist around the scale, timing and location of new data center load. If anything, the uncertainty is growing amid public backlash to data centers that is fueling state-led efforts to impose stricter rules on data center development, up to and including moratoriums on new facilities in some places. Firmer answers would benefit not only the utility planners and regulators ensuring that the electric grid is neither over- nor under-built, but also the millions of other customers who could bear the consequences of a disorderly buildout, industry experts say. Texas hits the brakes on large loads as states assert control Many utilities and their regulators have turned to large-load tariffs to try and weed out speculative load by requiring minimum contract durations, minimum billing demand and collateral requirements, upfront payments for impact studies, exit fees and specific ramp schedules. Some states have also introduced incentives for developers that bring their own capacity, agree to be flexible in their energy use or commit to state clean energy or economic development goals. The question of just how much data center capacity is going to come online, and when, is particularly urgent in Texas, which has paused new data center interconnections pending an audit of its 474-GW queue. That’s more than five times the Texas grid’s recent all-time peak demand record of a little over 90 GW set this summer. Few experts expect all that load to materialize. Pablo Vegas, president and CEO of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, is among the skeptics. “We believe this forecast to be higher than expected future load growth,” Vegas said in an April statement, citing uncertainty around protocols for identifying, verifying and incorporating large load demand into long-range planning. Vegas said ERCOT would work with the Public Utilities Commission of Texas to adjust its forecasting methodology. Thomas Gleeson, the PUCT’s chairman, was more blunt in an appearance on the Energy Capital podcast in June. “The projections are extremely high, and what we know is that a lot of that load will not actually come here. A lot of it is speculative,” Gleeson said in comments made before the interconnection pause. The sheer number of large-load interconnection requests compounds the state’s challenge. Texas’s load growth — not only from large computing and industrial loads, but also garden-variety residential and commercial demand — is leading to congestion in load pockets that previously had capacity to spare, Gleeson said. That creates unwelcome uncertainty for large-load customers eager to put steel in the ground. “That has been the problem we have been trying to solve for the past eight or so months — that when [a customer has] an interconnection agreement and they are ready to move forward, they know that the capacity will be there to serve them so they can make proper business decisions,” Gleeson said. Texas has developed “gating” conditions to discourage speculative interconnection requests, balance load and capacity and “make sure that no one is harmed by these large loads,” Gleeson said. Last summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, signed Senate Bill 6, a sweeping measure requiring prospective large-load customers to demonstrate site control, substantially cover necessary grid upgrades, disclose duplicative interconnection requests elsewhere in Texas and accept curtailment during firm load shed events, among other provisions. On June 18, the PUCT adopted a cluster study framework for prospective loads larger than 75 MW that officials said would streamline a “lengthy and repetitive” sequential study process as ERCOT stakeholders work to develop a comprehensive transmission planning framework later this year. ERCOT said at the time that it expected to publish a final transmission plan for the first study cluster, known as “Batch Zero,” in late 2027. Gleeson said on the podcast that the cluster study and transmission planning frameworks will mitigate uncertainty for large loads, grid operators and generation owners across Texas. Together, they assure loads that “once they interconnect, they will get the electricity they need to fully energize,” and they assure other stakeholders that “all the loads coming here are real and will stay,” he said. artigo.texto: CATL, the world’s largest EV battery and energy storage manufacturer, began trial production at its newly built cell manufacturing gigafactory in Debrecen, Hungary, towards the end of September, 2026. This means the Chinese manufacturing giant has met all necessary preconditions and regulatory requirements for what is essentially a trial period, where equipment is optimised and validated ahead of full-scale series production. The €7.3 billion facility’s first two production lines are now operational for testing and are operating at a capacity of 34 GWh. As of autumn 2024, CATL’s Debrecen site has built over 537,000 battery modules. Since the firm’s foundation in 2011, CATL batteries have been fitted to more than 17 million vehicles globally. CATL-using manufacturers include Tesla, Volkswagen, Porsche, Audi, Kia, Changan, and Stellantis. With a 100 gigawatt-hour (GWh) capacity, the Debrecen plant will be CATL’s largest outside China. For context, a 1 GWh capacity factory can make enough batteries for some 17,000 vehicles. Earlier this year, local authorities from Debrecen’s surrounding Hajdu-Bihar county ordered a temporary shutdown of certain zones of the factory due to safety concerns when nine employees were exposed to nickel. CATL then implemented several health and safety changes, which the authorities confirmed met the correct regulatory frameworks. CATL is the latest EV player to join what appears to be a gold rush for manufacturing and production space in the Central and Eastern European (CEE) region. Also in Debrecen, Chinese battery specialists, EVE, have confirmed it will build a 30GWh factory next to the BMW plant where the new BMW iX3 is built. By the end of this year, BYD has promised to open a production site in the Hungarian town of Szeged to circumnavigate European Union tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles. Meanwhile, Toyota promises to build its next EV at its Kolín factory in the Czech Republic. In 2008, Ford built a factory in Craiova, Romania. At present, the facility manufactures the all-electric Puma Gen-E, E-Tourneo Courier, and E-Transit Courier. The Mercedes-Benz GLC’s electric drive system is also Romanian-made.

artigo.texto: Six major financiers signed on to fund Nvidia's AI build-out. Buried in the deal: Nvidia's promise to cover up to 25% of losses if the hardware loses value, a guarantee that could hit $125 billion, with much of that risk headed for insurers' balance sheets. On August 10, Nvidia announced memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to build financing platforms meant to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure, according to Axios. The pitch to these firms was straightforward: raise money from pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, use it to buy Nvidia chips and build data centers, then lease the capacity to AI companies for years of steady payments. To make that pitch land with investors who don't normally gamble on chip depreciation, Nvidia added a sweetener. It said it "may provide a residual-value support mechanism for up to 25% of an opportunity, assessed carefully on a project-by-project basis." That covers part of the gap if hardware turns out to be worth less than expected when a lease ends. Do the math across every deal Nvidia is courting, and that backstop could total $125 billion in exposure, per Axios's reporting on the plan. That's Nvidia, the company selling the shovels in this gold rush, agreeing to personally guarantee that the shovels won't rust. Here's the part that should catch your attention: none of that $500 billion sits on Nvidia's own balance sheet, and neither does most of the credit risk behind it. The GPUs get bought by special purpose vehicles. The vehicles issue debt. And increasingly, according to CNBC's reporting from April 2026, that debt gets placed with insurance and retirement capital managed by firms like Apollo and KKR. Data centers are expensive, decades-spanning projects, and they happen to match the long-dated liabilities insurers already carry - things like annuities and pension obligations. The risk doesn't disappear. It just changes owners, and it arrives on an insurer's books relabeled as investment-grade fixed income. CNBC's April reporting quotes the phrase "GPU debt treadmill," coined by AI commentator Dave Friedman, to describe the core mismatch driving this whole structure. GPUs have a useful life of roughly seven years. The data centers housing them are built to last 20 to 30. Lenders and insurers underwriting a 20-year facility are implicitly betting that today's Nvidia chips, or their replacements, will still be worth something in year fifteen, even though the hardware itself will have been swapped out two or three times by then. Nvidia's $108 billion fiscal third-quarter forecast assumes it sells zero AI data center chips to China, even though analysts peg potential Chinese demand at $30 billion. Trump hosts Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24, with Jensen Huang expected at the state dinner and chip access on the agenda. - Nvidia China AI chip sales forecast outlook - state dinner Xi Jinping impact on Nvidia revenue Capacity is also a live problem. One insurance executive told CNBC that insuring a single $20 billion data center campus was nearly impossible to price in 2023. By 2026, it's become, in that executive's words, a weekly conversation. Insurers have responded with new products built for this exposure: cover for credit losses, cover for declines in chip resale value, and cover for contract breaches tied to power outages or cooling failures at the facilities themselves, according to the same CNBC report. The scale of the debt underneath all of this has grown fast. Incremental borrowing funded about 9% of hyperscaler capital spending in fiscal 2024. By mid-2026 that figure had climbed to roughly 32% on a trailing basis, and U.S. data-center debt issuance roughly doubled to about $182 billion in 2025, per the reporting Axios cited in its financing coverage. Frankly, that's the kind of growth curve that makes credit analysts nervous even when the underlying business is healthy. Why the timing matters Nvidia isn't doing this in a vacuum. Bain & Company said this week that the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion a year in new revenue by 2031 just to justify the data center spending already committed. Existing AI services might cover $1.8 trillion of that, leaving a $4.2 trillion gap to fill from businesses that barely exist yet, like autonomous robotics and AI-driven drug discovery. Bain separately projects $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion in data center spending through 2030. Those are the numbers Wall Street is holding up against Nvidia's financing push. They explain why insurers are being asked to carry so much of the weight: the traditional lenders and Nvidia's own balance sheet can't absorb spending at that scale alone. Nvidia's arrangement doesn't eliminate risk. It reroutes it, from Nvidia's income statement and from the banks that might otherwise hold this debt, into the reserves of companies whose entire business model depends on correctly pricing tail risk decades in advance. If AI demand keeps compounding the way Nvidia's revenue guidance assumes, the residual-value guarantee mostly sits unused, a marketing device that made institutional capital comfortable enough to write the check. But if a major AI lab pulls back capacity, or a cheaper chip generation arrives faster than expected and strands the current fleet, the 25% backstop gets tested for real. Insurers holding the debt behind it find out how much of that "investment-grade fixed income" was actually GPU depreciation risk wearing a different label. None of the six firms named in the MOUs have disclosed how much capital they've actually committed, or whether the residual-value terms are even finalized. Nvidia's own release says the partnerships remain subject to final agreements. Open Free Demat Account Open Free Demat Account Mumbai, September 28: Advait Energy Transitions has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with HiTHIUM for the purchase of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells, covering cell supply of up to 1 GWh over the next year. Advait Energy Signs 1 GWh Battery Cell Supply Agreement According to the company’s exchange filing, the agreement was executed on September 18, 2026, with HiTHIUM, a global energy storage manufacturer and BloombergNEF Tier 1 supplier. Under the arrangement, HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic battery cells to Advait Battery Ecosystems Private Limited. The agreement is structured to support cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. The supply will be used for Advait’s upcoming cell-to-container Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility. The arrangement is linked to Advait’s planned 2.5 GWh annual-capacity BESS assembly facility, which is being developed for utility-scale, commercial and industrial energy storage as well as renewable energy integration applications. Stock Market Snapshot The Advait Energy share price stood at ₹1,871.80 as of 2:28:37 PM IST on September 28, 2026, down ₹34.20 or 1.79% from the previous close. The stock traded lower during the session, while the company disclosed its battery cell supply arrangement with HiTHIUM. The announcement comes as Advait continues to build out its domestic BESS manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities. HiTHIUM Deal Supports Advait’s BESS Manufacturing Plans The company said the cell supply arrangement is intended to support the planned scale-up of its domestic BESS assembly operations. Advait’s facility is being developed with capabilities spanning cell sourcing, module and pack assembly, container integration and system commissioning. The company said the HiTHIUM agreement will provide a structured supply framework as the facility moves towards commercial production. The upcoming assembly capacity is aimed at applications across utility-scale energy storage, commercial and industrial users, and renewable energy integration. HiTHIUM will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells under the agreement. The company is described in the release as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 global energy storage manufacturer supplying battery cells and energy storage systems across international markets. Advait Energy Expands Domestic Energy Storage Business Advait Energy Transitions is developing an integrated energy storage platform around its planned BESS manufacturing capabilities. The company is also building capabilities across battery module and pack assembly, container integration and related system commissioning. Its broader energy transition portfolio includes power transmission infrastructure, renewable energy, green hydrogen, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cell manufacturing and clean energy EPC activities. About Advait Energy Transitions Advait Energy Transitions Limited, formerly known as Advait Infratech Limited, is an energy transition and infrastructure company based in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The company operates across power transmission, renewable energy, BESS and other clean energy technologies. Its business portfolio includes battery energy storage manufacturing, green hydrogen projects, electrolyser manufacturing, fuel cells and clean energy infrastructure solutions. Conclusion The 1 GWh supply agreement with HiTHIUM gives Advait a defined cell supply framework for the next stage of its BESS manufacturing plans. The arrangement supports the company’s broader objective of developing domestic energy storage capabilities around its planned 2.5 GWh annual-capacity facility. artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

artigo.texto: S.C. Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews calls for moratorium on data centers WALTERBORO, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT) - South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews is calling for a two-year moratorium on new data center projects in the state. Andrews said large data centers are receiving billions of dollars in tax breaks while local families deal with high gas, diesel and living costs. She said local officials are outmatched by the corporations building the projects. “We have incredibly wealthy, powerful companies coming into these rural communities in South Carolina, dangling a few carrots, and then the communities are getting steamrolled,” Andrews said. “I’ve been really heartened to see people from both sides of the political spectrum joined together to fight back against these large corporation.” Andrews said the proposed moratorium would give communities more protection from the projects. She said the race is tightening and said she will continue to make data centers and family budgets central issues on the campaign trail. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Minister Lecce, IESO and more recognized at 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards Awards presented Sept. 22-23 at ESC Conference in Toronto. Talking Points Energy Storage Canada (ESC) honoured leaders in the energy storage sector at its 2026 Awards, held September 22-23 in Toronto. The awards recognized achievements across seven categories, including the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which went to Lesley Gallinger for his role in advancing utility-scale storage in Ontario. - Gallinger emphasized the importance of energy storage for Ontario’s electricity future. - The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was awarded to Jim Fonger, a former ESC chair. - Stephen Lecce, Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award for his support of energy storage initiatives. This recognition highlights the critical role of energy storage in enhancing grid reliability and supporting Canada’s transition to sustainable energy solutions. Energy Storage Canada (ESC) recognized outstanding examples of leadership, innovation, and research at its 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards, taking place September 22 and 23 at the Energy Storage Canada Conference in Toronto. The awards program is a technology-agnostic showcase of accomplishments from across the sector, recognizing generators, developers, utilities, regulators, researchers, manufacturers, and service providers across seven categories. Categories include the Grid Management Storage Award, the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award, the Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, the Energy Storage Milestone Award, the Friend of Energy Storage Award, and the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which is presented both as a standard award to an active member of the industry and as an “In Memoriam” tribute to a recently deceased industry leader. The Energy Storage Trailblazer Award is presented to individuals selected by the ESC’s board of directors who has demonstrated exceptional leadership and contributed to the development of energy storage that serves the overall needs of the industry at large. Lesley Gallinger, past president and CEO of the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO), received the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award for his contributions toward the procurement of more than three gigawatts of utility-scale storage projects in the province during his tenure with the IESO. “I am honoured to receive the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award. Energy storage has moved from the technology of tomorrow to an essential part of Ontario’s grid and Canada’s electricity future. I am grateful to have contributed to this remarkable journey,” Gallinger said. The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was presented to Jim Fonger, who once served as chair of ESC and held roles with Rodan Energy Solutions and Ameresco. Fonger passed away in July 2026. “Jim Fonger was a true trailblazer whose vision and leadership helped lay the foundation for Energy Storage Canada and the growth of the sector nationwide,” said Justin Rangooni, president and CEO of ESC. “His legacy lives on in the momentum he helped create and in all of us who continue advancing the storage advantage.” Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, Stephen Lecce, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes individuals from outside of the energy storage sector selected by ESC’s board of directors as a supporter of the industry. Minster Lecce was recognized for his continued commitment to the role of energy storage through the launch of initiatives such as Long Lead-Time Procurement and the modernization of the province’s electricity system. “From nuclear and hydro to battery storage, we are harnessing every resource to keep the lights on and our economy moving. This work has seen over 1,200 MW of battery storage capacity come online to help offset peak demand times, and I am proud to champion the technologies that continue to deliver reliable, affordable electricity to Ontario,” said Minister Lecce. BluWave-ai became the ESC Awards’ first consecutive winner after being recognized with the Grid Management Storage Award for the second year in a row. The award recognized a project that leveraged BluWave-ai’s artificial intelligence-driven platforms to coordinate stationary energy storage and electric vehicles as a single, grid-aware flexible resource. IESO’s Mohamad Shamelstein was presented with the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award for his demonstration of how energy storage assets supporting large data centres can provide services to the broader electricity system without compromising essential IT infrastructure. The Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes new energy storage technologies or innovations in existing technology, was presented to AlumaPower Corporation. AlumaPower was recognized for its off-grid microgrid demonstration that showed solutions beyond the traditional single-use model of aluminum-air energy storage through its usage of solid recycled aluminum. The Energy Milestone Award was presented to NextStar Energy in honour of the grand opening of its battery manufacturing facility in Windsor, Ont., and the benefits this development is set to bring to Canada’s domestic battery supply chain and the North American energy ecosystem at large.

artigo.texto: NANTICOKE — Newport Twp. residents gathered Sunday at West Side Park in Nanticoke to begin rallying against a developer who seeks to build 15 data centers in the township. The meeting, organized through a Facebook event, served as a preliminary step to gather interested residents and supporters and voice their opposition to the project. The packed field house was standing room only that spilled out into the park. Brenda Grabowski, who helped organize the meeting and started the Facebook event, said she did so after going to the previous commissioners’ meeting looking for answers and receiving none. “I don’t know a lot about data centers; I’m learning myself now. But I want to know what’s going to happen in my backyard,” said Grabowski. Fern Leard, who is running to capture a seat in the state House 120th District, spoke at the meeting, telling residents, “This is where it starts.” Leard, who is not running to represent Newport Twp., said she showed up and spoke to show support. “The fact that you guys organized this so quickly is amazing,” said Leard. “It just showcases how when communities come together and work together we can get it done.” Newport commissioners were asked about a rumored data center coming to the township at a meeting earlier this month. In response, Township Manager Joe Hillian issued a prepared statement that left residents with more questions than answers. Hillian said a developer seeks to build three gas generation facilities and 15 closed-loop data centers — seven in the mixed-use zone and eight in the industrial zone. The township’s zoning ordinance, drafted earlier this year, allows data centers by right in mixed-use zoning districts and permits them in industrial districts. Derek Sutcliffe, who has been fighting data center development in Lackawanna County, urged residents to think about how these facilities will be powered and what that will do to their community. “You are not defeated,” Sutcliffe told residents. “Where you are in your process is the beginning. If you think you’re going to lose, you’re going to lose. Don’t think that. You can beat this.” The next Newport Twp. commissioners meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. on Oct. 5.

artigo.texto: Tecnologia: novo plano divulgado na China prevê baterias de estado sólido em larga escala até 2030 e modelos com vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos (Imagem gerada por IA) Agência Publicado em 28 de setembro de 2026 às 15h45. A China quer levar as baterias totalmente de estado sólido a uma fase inicial de aplicação em larga escala até 2030. O país também estabeleceu como meta que baterias de lítio de longa duração cheguem a uma vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos. As metas fazem parte de um novo plano para a indústria de baterias divulgado nesta segunda-feira (28) pelo Ministério da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação e outros seis órgãos do governo chinês. O documento prevê avanços em diferentes tecnologias, incluindo baterias de lítio, sódio e fluxo. A estratégia também envolve o desenvolvimento de novos materiais para eletrodos, eletrólitos e outros componentes usados na fabricação. Uma das prioridades será ampliar o uso dessas baterias para além dos veículos elétricos e produtos eletrônicos. O plano prevê aplicações em embarcações, aviação, robôs inteligentes, máquinas de engenharia e equipamentos agrícolas. A expansão também deve alcançar sistemas de armazenamento de energia. As novas baterias poderão ser utilizadas junto à geração de energia, em redes elétricas, parques industriais e data centers. Outros formatos também aparecem no planejamento. Baterias flexíveis e de formatos especiais deverão ter aplicações ampliadas em dispositivos vestíveis, casas inteligentes e equipamentos médicos móveis. O plano inclui ainda medidas para aumentar a coleta, reciclagem e reutilização de baterias usadas. As empresas deverão participar da estruturação desses sistemas, diretamente ou por meio de terceiros, de acordo com o volume de produtos colocados no mercado. Fonte: China news

artigo.texto: A proposed battery storage project in Hadley, Massachusetts, is nearing approval after a consultant concluded it should remain within state noise limits. Here's what to know According to the Daily Hampshire Gazette, board members were told at a Sept. 15 continued hearing that the proposed 5-megawatt battery energy storage system would meet the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection's noise policy. With the proposed mitigation in place, sound from the facility would stay below 34 A-weighted decibels at the property boundary, Marc C. Wallace, a vice president at Tech Environmental Inc. in Chelmsford, said. Wallace noted that the noise reduction kit would cut sound by 20 decibels and keep that level from extending beyond the lot lines, even during the quietest overnight conditions. Planned for a nearly 5-acre former gravel pit, the stand-alone system would use five energy storage containers and related equipment. Peter Forte, vice president of ZP Battery Devco, said the project would also include inverters, converters, and a gravel access road, and would connect to three-phase lines along Breckenridge Road, the Daily Hampshire Gazette reported. Grid-scale batteries can store electricity when it is plentiful and discharge it later when demand rises. In New England, that can help shift less-needed midday power into the more in-demand evening peak, potentially easing pressure on the grid during periods of heavy use and extreme weather. More background The project has already taken a long road to reach this stage. The Gazette reported that Hadley's Planning Board rejected the plans in 2024, halting the development and setting up a legal dispute over whether the town could block it. That denial led the developers to sue in Hampshire Superior Court, after which the board resumed reviewing a proposal nearly identical to the one it had rejected. A central issue in the dispute was the Dover Amendment, a Massachusetts law that can limit local zoning restrictions on certain land uses tied to public health, safety, and environmental goals. Local officials were weighing whether nearby residents would face an unreasonable burden from the battery system. Although insect sounds created substantial background noise during the study, the consultant said the project would still meet the state standard under the quietest overnight conditions. What's being done? The developer is relying on a noise reduction kit to address the Planning Board's biggest concern. If the board accepts that analysis, the project could move much closer to final approval. Forte said the project must comply with the state's noise policy at all times and that residents can bring complaints to the building commissioner. The system will be monitored remotely 24 hours a day. Board members closed the public hearing, so no further comment will be accepted, and indicated a review by the town attorney and a vote on conditions would take place Oct. 6 or 20. Where can I learn more? Battery storage proposals across the country face similar local scrutiny, even as some continue to win approvals. They cover neighborhood concerns, permitting fights, and major approvals and financing. • In Massachusetts, regulators approved a battery site near seniors' homes after neighbors won 100 conditions. • In Pike County, Indiana, regulators approved a massive energy storage system near a power plant. • In Arizona, developers financed the state's largest battery storage project as the state's market surged. artigo.texto: On September 10, 2026, Reuters reported that Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) plans to expand its global data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032, more than tripling its current roughly 12-gigawatt footprint, according to Bloomberg News reporting that cited people familiar with the plans. Only about 2 gigawatts of Microsoft's current capacity is dedicated to AI-specific chips, a share the company expects to grow to roughly one-third of the much larger 38-gigawatt total by 2032, though Microsoft has not confirmed the target in any public filing or statement. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) already has strong cloud demand to support a major expansion of its data center footprint. Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43% year over year in fiscal Q4. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion for the quarter and $214.4 billion for fiscal 2026. Microsoft also said capacity constraints have limited its ability to satisfy some demand, so expanding from roughly 12 gigawatts toward the reported 38-gigawatt target could allow the company to capture cloud and AI business that its existing infrastructure cannot currently support. Microsoft's massive contracted backlog gives management substantial revenue visibility as it adds new computing capacity. Commercial remaining performance obligations increased 84% year over year to $678 billion, while Microsoft expects to recognize roughly 30% of that amount as revenue during the next 12 months. The large backlog gives Microsoft a significant pool of committed business that can help support the economics of its aggressive infrastructure expansion as new capacity comes online. Microsoft has already shown that it can add capacity quickly while securing long-term power for its expanding data center network. The company added another gigawatt of capacity in fiscal Q4 and remains on track to roughly double its overall capacity within two years. Microsoft has also signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy linked to the restart of the 835-megawatt Three Mile Island Unit 1. It gives the firm another long-term electricity source as AI workloads drive sharply higher power requirements. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)'s data center expansion requires enormous capital commitments that could continue weighing on free cash flow. Microsoft expects more than $50 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal Q1 2027 and about $175 billion during calendar 2026 under its broader capex definition, which includes finance leases. Microsoft reported roughly $145 billion of capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, while cash additions to property and equipment totaled about $116 billion. Power availability and growing political resistance could make a 38-gigawatt network harder to build on schedule. Texas temporarily halted approvals for new data center grid connections as officials reviewed the industry's electricity and water demands. New York imposed a moratorium on large new data centers amid concerns about electricity costs. Microsoft needs to secure enormous amounts of power, land and regulatory approval across multiple jurisdictions as it more than triples its reported footprint. The 38-gigawatt figure remains a reported internal roadmap rather than formal Microsoft guidance. It adds uncertainty to the long-term investment case. Bloomberg reported the target through people familiar with Microsoft's plans. Reuters said Microsoft did not immediately comment on the figure. Multi-year construction timelines, changing customer demand and improvements in computing efficiency could alter how much physical capacity Microsoft ultimately needs. So investors should treat the 2032 target as a planning framework rather than a guaranteed outcome. Azure's 43% growth, Microsoft's $678 billion commercial backlog and management's progress toward doubling capacity within two years give the company strong commercial support for further infrastructure investment. However, Microsoft must commit enormous amounts of capital, secure enough electricity, and navigate growing regulatory resistance to execute the roadmap. Investors should watch whether new capacity drives enough cloud revenue and cash flow to make attractive returns on the hundreds of billions of dollars Microsoft is committed to AI infrastructure. artigo.texto: Samsung SDI's (006400.KS) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) have passed a global fire safety test. The company said on Sept. 28 that its integrated ESS product, the SBB 2.0, met all evaluation criteria in a large-scale fire test conducted by UL Solutions, a global safety certification body. The SBB 2.0 is the first Samsung SDI energy storage solution to use LFP batteries. It will be produced at StarPlus Energy (SPE), the company's joint venture with Stellantis in Indiana. The test involved deliberately igniting a fire inside an SBB 2.0 container and checking whether the flames spread to adjacent containers. No fire spread occurred, and there was no gas venting, explosion or overheating. Samsung SDI attributed the result to the structural advantages of its prismatic batteries and to technology built up over many years. In July, the company also passed a large-scale fire test and won certification for an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) unit equipped with nickel-cobalt-manganese batteries. "Prismatic cells use a rigid aluminum can structure that withstands heat, impact and pressure, and they allow various safety devices to be added, which makes them superior to batteries in other form factors," a Samsung SDI official said.

artigo.texto: Nova Gales do Sul aprova projeto de armazenamento por bateria Deniliquin East de 100MW/200MWh O governo de Nova Gales do Sul deu sinal verde para o sistema de armazenamento de energia por bateria de Deniliquin East, um empreendimento de 100MW/200MWh na região australiana de Riverina apresentado pela BESS Arctic Pty Ltd. A BESS Arctic está levando o projeto adiante por meio da Gransolar Development Australia, subsidiária local do grupo espanhol Gransolar Group. A instalação está prevista para a Riverina Highway, na área do governo local de Edward River, situada a cerca de 7km a sudeste de Deniliquin. Depois de construída, a instalação será conectada ao Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade e ocupará um terreno de 3,53 hectares que historicamente serviu para pastoreio de ovelhas. O consentimento foi emitido pelo Diretor Executivo Interino de Avaliações de Energia, Recursos e Indústria, no exercício de autoridade delegada pelo Ministro de Planejamento e Espaços Públicos. Durante a avaliação, foram apresentadas 71 objeções públicas, além de uma única manifestação de apoio. Pela aprovação, o sistema de baterias fica limitado a uma potência máxima de 100MW e a uma capacidade máxima de armazenamento de energia de 240MWh no local. As condicionantes exigem um Estudo de Segurança contra Incêndio antes da construção, um Plano de Emergência antes do comissionamento e uma faixa corta-fogo trafegável de pelo menos 10 metros ao redor da área de armazenamento de baterias. O Departamento de Planejamento, Habitação e Infraestrutura concluiu que as vantagens do projeto superavam seus efeitos adversos, destacando sua capacidade de armazenar energia renovável para despacho nos picos de demanda e sua consonância com o Marco de Política de Mudança Climática de Nova Gales do Sul, a Estratégia de Eletricidade de Nova Gales do Sul e o Roteiro de Infraestrutura Elétrica de Nova Gales do Sul. Segundo o departamento, o risco de contaminação no local era baixo, conforme estabelecido por uma Investigação Preliminar e Detalhada do Local, e a perda de área agrícola seria insignificante, afetando menos de 0,0004% das terras agrícolas da área do governo local de Edward River. Risco de incêndio e perigos, os méritos da energia renovável e a compatibilidade do uso do solo formaram o núcleo das 71 objeções, enquanto várias manifestações também apontaram preocupações com o abastecimento de água para combate a incêndios, a garantia de descomissionamento e a contaminação por PFAS. O departamento determinou que essas questões poderiam ser adequadamente tratadas pelas condicionantes do consentimento, observando que nem o órgão do governo de Nova Gales do Sul nem o Conselho de Edward River apresentaram objeções ao projeto. O aviso de decisão avalia o investimento de capital do projeto em cerca de AU$ 118 milhões, ou US$ 82,6 milhões, e projeta até 52 empregos na construção e dois cargos operacionais. A BESS Arctic também se comprometeu com um Acordo Voluntário de Planejamento com o Conselho de Edward River que prevê AU$ 600.000 em contribuições de benefício comunitário. Essa aprovação insere um projeto regional em um pipeline estadual que vem se expandindo muito além da escala de qualquer empreendimento isolado. A AEMO registrou que 9,1GW de nova capacidade de geração e armazenamento atingiram plena produção no NEM durante o ano fiscal de 2026, um número recorde que mais que dobrou o volume do ano anterior, enquanto o pipeline mais amplo de conexões cresceu 42%, para 75,4GW. Outros projetos em estágio comparável ao de Deniliquin East estão avançando pelo processo de registro da AEMO. Vena Energy, o Tailem Bend BESS 3, na Austrália do Sul, e o Wooreen BESS, em Victoria, desenvolvido pela EnergyAustralia e pela Banpu Energy Australia, ambos entraram no Sistema de Gestão de Mercado da AEMO no início deste mês, contribuindo com 554MW de capacidade combinada enquanto avançam rumo à operação comercial. O próprio histórico de contratações de Nova Gales do Sul ilustra como um projeto como o de Deniliquin East poderia, em última análise, obter certeza de receita. Todos os projetos de armazenamento por bateria e resposta à demanda selecionados no leilão de firming de 2023 do estado já estão operacionais, proporcionando cerca de 1GW/3GWh de capacidade despachável e mais de AU$ 1,8 bilhão em investimento por meio de Acordos de Serviço de Energia de Longo Prazo concedidos à AGL Energy, à Akaysha Energy, à Iberdrola Australia e à Enel X. O órgão responsável pelos leilões do estado indicou que pretende continuar usando essa abordagem de contratação para ajudar projetos de alto valor a alcançar o fechamento financeiro mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: Saginaw approves new rules for future data centers as moratorium nears end The ordinance sets rules for water and energy use, noise, residential buffers and neighborhood meetings before any data center can set up shop in the city. SAGINAW, Mich. (WNEM) - Saginaw now has a rule book in place for data centers before any come to town. The Saginaw City Council approved a new ordinance Monday night setting regulations for any future data center development in the city. The ordinance comes ahead of Saginaw’s data center moratorium ending at the close of 2026. There are currently no data centers in development in the city. Under the new rules, data centers would only be allowed as special land uses in light industrial and general industrial districts. Developers would have to provide information on expected water and energy use, wastewater and noise. Data centers and most related equipment would generally have to stay at least 500 feet from homes and residential districts, with noise near residential areas capped at 55 decibels. Developers would also have to hold at least two neighborhood meetings before moving forward with a project. The moratorium remains in place through the end of the year. The new ordinance is expected to be added to Saginaw’s code of ordinances Oct. 9. Subscribe to the WNEM TV5 newsletter and receive the latest local news and weather straight to your email every day. artigo.texto: OCP, Envision power up first phase of BESS at Morocco mining site OCP Green Energy, a subsidiary of Morocco’s OCP Group, signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. OCP Green Energy, the OCP Group subsidiary dedicated to generating and storing electricity from renewable sources, has installed its first BESS (Phase I) at the Benguerir mining site in Morocco. This comes just a few months after Phase I of OCP Green Energy’s solar PV program entered service, with a total capacity of 202 MWp across the solar plants at Benguerir (67 MWp), Foum Tizi (30 MWp) and Oulad Farès in Khouribga (105 MWp), OCP said in a press release. OCP Green Energy signed a contract in 2025 with Chinese technology supplier Envision Energy to supply and commission a storage system based on LFP (lithium iron phosphate) technology. With a capacity of 25 MW / 125 MWh, equivalent to five hours of storage, the system is coupled with the existing solar plant at the Benguerir mining site. This investment of close to 170 million dirhams (approximately USD 17.5 million) covered the acquisition of BESS equipment and batteries, together with the full scope of integration works, including civil and electrical engineering, as well as studies and project management, OCP said. The project also benefits from USD 20 million in financing from the Clean Technology Fund (CTF), a program led by the African Development Bank. “As we announced last year when our first solar PV projects were commissioned, storage is the natural extension of our energy strategy,” Omar Kadir, General Manager of OCP Green Energy, said. “It allows us to reconcile the variable output of renewable energy with the continuous needs of our industrial platforms, while strengthening the reliability of our energy supply.” Envision Energy said that it provided the full storage system and led the commissioning work, integrating the BESS with the site's solar generation, grid conditions and industrial load profile. “The successful energisation of Morocco’s first large-scale battery storage project demonstrates the reliability, flexibility and cost-effectiveness of integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions in industrial applications,” said John Lee, General Manager of Envision Energy for the Middle East and Africa, according to a press release issued by Envision.
