artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment. International experience suggests that as the data center industry scales up, tensions emerge. In Ireland, data centers accounted for 21% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023 and could reach 32% this year. In the U.S., their share of demand is expected to triple from 4% in 2023 to a projected 12% by 2028. No surprise, then, that this is a source of growing political and public concern. A Gallup poll found that 71% of Americans oppose data center construction in their local community. Researchers at Cambridge University have identified what they call a “data heat island effect,” whereby large facilities can raise temperatures in surrounding areas. And a recent study by researchers from Yale and the University of Chicago found that the development of a new data center is associated with an increase in nearby housing prices. The question isn’t whether data centers are needed — they are — but how they are developed. What type of data centers do we need? And who will govern their expansion? Economic experience teaches a simple lesson: that proactive regulation is more effective than reactive intervention. And it’s certainly much better than no intervention at all. Having clear rules from the start makes it possible to separate responsible projects from unsustainable ones, align private incentives with public interests and ensure that investment and growth go hand in hand with protecting critical resources and communities. International experience is, again, instructive. Ireland tightened its rules only after data centers became a major source of pressure on the electricity grid. In the US, the state of New York has adopted a temporary moratorium, and a growing number of projects have faced delays or cancellation as local resistance intensified. The lesson could not be plainer: Failing to plan and regulate up front ends up being costlier and less effective. Spain is still a long way from facing that kind of pressure. And yet, our healthy economy and renewable capacity has sparked huge investor interest in building data centers. Current estimates of electricity demand for computing power run as high as 4 gigawatts by 2030, but requests and permits granted for this type of facility exceed that target several times over. We are approaching a tipping point, and we must act to stay ahead. In August, my government launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework designed to do exactly that. The proposal starts from a straightforward principle: Access to the electricity grid is a scarce strategic asset and should not be held up by projects that lack credibility, viability or a meaningful contribution to the economy and society. Our proposal introduces energy- and water-efficiency standards. Data centers will have to disclose key performance indicators, letting us assess and compare their resource use and discourage waste. Any increase in electricity demand must also be accompanied by additional renewable capacity. The framework includes requirements to make sure that a significant portion of data center consumption is supported by newly built clean-energy projects. The regulation recognizes, too, that data centers are a strategic asset. In a world where Europe still relies heavily on non-European digital capabilities, the framework combines safeguards on how data is controlled — and how the infrastructure is managed — with incentives designed to expand Europe’s technology sector and strengthen the continent’s sovereignty. Our objective must be to trade in bytes, not in watts. The challenge is making sure the infrastructure expands in line with the capacity of the power system, that valuable energy resources are directed toward useful projects and that this all makes Europe less dependent technologically. The goal is not to slow down growth or constrain innovation. Quite the opposite: It is to ensure that they remain economically sustainable, and environmentally and socially fair. Countries that understand this will be the ones best positioned to lead the next phase of the digital economy. Pedro Sanchez is the prime minister of Spain. He wrote this for Bloomberg Opinion.

artigo.texto: Vaisala Indigo Supervisor Vaisala Indigo Supervisor helps data centers scale environmental monitoring by enabling up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system. As monitoring requirements grow, the challenge is shifting from measurement coverage to operational scalability. Environmental monitoring must scale with AI infrastructure As data centers scale to support growing AI workloads, environmental monitoring infrastructure must keep pace. Higher computing densities and accelerated construction schedules are increasing the need for environmental measurements throughout data centers, including data halls, technical spaces, support areas, and other critical locations, while leaving less time for installation, commissioning, and maintenance. As monitoring requirements grow and measurement networks expand, operators need ways to deploy, standardize, and maintain environmental monitoring across facilities without adding complexity or slowing project timelines. From sensors to systems: a new approach to environmental monitoring To address this need, Vaisala today introduced the Vaisala Indigo Supervisor, a solution designed to simplify environmental monitoring in data centers by shifting from managing individual sensors to managing measurement networks as a unified system. The solution enables up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system through a local touchscreen interface and integrated into a building management system (BMS) through a single standardized connection. The Indigo Supervisor reflects a broader industry shift toward modularity and system-level environmental monitoring. As data center infrastructure expands, operators increasingly need solutions that can be deployed consistently across sites, scaled over time, integrated into building management systems, and managed efficiently throughout their lifecycle. Designing infrastructure for the next generation of data centers "AI is accelerating data center growth at a pace that is changing how supporting infrastructure is deployed, managed, and scaled," said Anu Kätkä, Product Line Manager for HVAC and Critical Buildings at Vaisala. "When a facility contains dozens or hundreds of measurement points, environmental monitoring can no longer be managed one sensor at a time. Operators need a system-level approach to environmental monitoring that can be commissioned efficiently, maintained without disrupting operations, and scaled consistently as capacity expands." artigo.texto: Loudoun County hosts open house as debate over data center growth continues ASHBURN, Va. - Loudoun County held the first in a series of community open houses in Ashburn Monday to give residents a chance to weigh in on the future of data center development in the community. What we know: The event, held at Broad Run High School, allowed community members to speak directly with county staff, take surveys and view noise-monitoring demonstrations. Similar open houses for tech infrastructure have taken place in Loudoun County and across the region, including in Prince William County. The feedback gathered from the sessions will help shape recommendations that are expected to go before the planning commission in 2027. The open house comes amid public debates and community pushback over rapid infrastructure expansion. Neighbors have expressed concerns over noise levels, power consumption, power substations and the proximity of data centers to surrounding neighborhoods. "I think they need some guidelines, especially for controlling some emissions and the noise. And too close to where people live... yeah, they need some standards," said Loudoun County residents Kathy and Paul Wagner, who noted they live just 500 feet away from existing infrastructure. In response to growing community concerns, Loudoun County supervisors recently approved a one-year pause on certain new AI data centers and substation applications, giving officials time to review standards for future projects. However, supporters of data center infrastructure emphasize the economic benefits, pointing to substantial local revenue and employment opportunities for workers like contractors and electricians. Don Slaiman, political coordinator for the IBW Local 26 electricians union, highlighted the financial and labor impact of the industry in the region. "That is a lot of revenue coming to this state, that is a lot of great jobs," Slaiman said. "I have 1,018 members who live in the richest county in the country right here in Loudoun... we have 17,500 members... we have doubled our membership in the last 9 years." artigo.texto: Can Supercapacitors Smooth AI’s Power Swings? Supercapacitors promise millisecond response for AI-induced power transients, but most experts see them complementing, not replacing, UPS systems and batteries. AI workloads can create load swings far sharper than steady-state compute, producing hard power spikes that conventional architectures struggle to absorb. Supercapacitors, also called ultracapacitors, sit between conventional capacitors and batteries. They store energy as a surface charge rather than through a battery’s chemical reaction, which gives them higher power density than batteries but lower energy density. That trade-off suits short, frequent bursts rather than sustained runtime. Operators are testing supercapacitors alongside batteries and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems rather than replacing them. Batteries and UPS systems still support the sustained load and provide a longer backup window. A September 2026 report from IDTechEx identifies three roles for supercapacitors in data centers: voltage stabilization, peak shaving, and short-term backup power. Supercapacitors charge and discharge in milliseconds to seconds – fast enough to track AI training cycles and recharge before the next spike. Market Outlook: Small Today, Growing Fast IDTechEx projects the data center supercapacitor market will reach $950 million by 2037, a 40.9% compound annual growth rate from 2026. That growth rate stands out against the wider category. A separate IDTechEx report from August 2025 puts total global supercapacitor revenue across automotive, grid, and industrial uses at $4.86 billion by 2036, growing 15.3% annually. Three Designs Vying for the Rack Slot IDTechEx groups data center supercapacitors into three categories, based on how they store charge and where they fit: - EDLCs (electric double-layer capacitors). The most commercially mature of the three, EDLCs store charge electrostatically at the electrode surface, much like a conventional capacitor. - Hybrid capacitors. These are usually lithium-ion (Li-ion) hybrids, combining an EDLC’s surface charge storage with the “rocking chair” lithium-ion chemistry in which ions shuttle back and forth between electrodes during charge and discharge. - Pseudocapacitors. These store charge through fast, reversible chemical reactions at the electrode surface rather than purely by electrostatic storage, delivering higher energy density than an EDLC but lower power density. Backup power is the narrowest application across all three. Typical EDLC deployments sustain output for approximately 2 minutes, while some hybrids can last up to 10 minutes – enough to prevent data corruption during brief outages but not enough to replace a UPS system. IDTechEx frames supercapacitors as a complement to backup infrastructure, not a substitute. From Pilots to Deployment: Pace and Roadblocks The market for supercapacitors in data centers is still in its early stages, but growing. “The market is transitioning from early evaluation to meaningful deployment, although adoption rates vary by technology type and supply chain maturity,” said Chris Butler, president of embedded and critical power at Flex, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “Instantaneous load transients can reach more than 150% of a power shelf’s rated capacity during certain AI compute events.” Rack designers are building in flexibility rather than committing to one architecture. “Rack designs typically include dedicated slots that can accommodate BBUs (battery backup units), CBUs (capacitor backup units), or mixed configurations, providing deployment flexibility,” Butler said. “Supply chain concerns remain a major hurdle, particularly for newer hybrid supercapacitor technologies with limited qualified suppliers.” Parag Nathaney, principal quantitative engineer for energy policy and power markets at Exelon, tied the pace of adoption to the reliability bar data centers operate under. He told Data Center Knowledge that the technology must meet 99.999% reliability for the power supply, which is why he sees the market as in its early stages. “Supercapacitors are advancing toward greater deployment, but the current state is characterized by pilot and early commercialization,” Nathaney said. Ian Wright, chief technology officer at DIMAAG, which builds battery systems designed to avoid supercapacitors, argued that the DC-to-DC conversion stage determines the response time, not the device alone. “The response speed to load changes is then determined by the DC/DC, which will be slower than either caps or batteries,” Wright told Data Center Knowledge. “If supercaps have been tried and not observed to get hot, that’s probably because they are not actually absorbing the cyclic loads.” What’s Next and How Operators Decide Whether IDTechEx’s forecast for supercapacitors plays out remains to be seen. Wright expects directly connected batteries, not supercapacitors, to become the primary tool for smoothing AI power swings. Nathaney reached a different conclusion, tied to reliability rather than economics. “I think the application of supercapacitors for data centers is novel, but the long track record of the technology in other applications could lower the barrier for adoption by data centers,” he said. Butler is somewhat more optimistic. As rack power levels scale from hundreds of kilowatts toward multi-megawatt designs, he expects CBUs to see growing use in managing transient peak demands. Over time, he anticipates workload-driven optimization will determine the mix of batteries and capacitors, with supercapacitors playing an increasingly important role in handling high-cycle, peak-power events. “I expect capacitor-based energy storage to become a mainstream element of next-generation AI power architectures,” Butler said.

artigo.texto: B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution Partner to Repurpose Batteries B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution announce a strategic partnership giving B2U priority access to the South Korean firm's batteries to develop large-scale stationary storage solutions in the United States. B2U Storage Solutions and LG Energy Solution have announced a strategic partnership aimed at developing battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions across the United States. The agreement gives B2U Storage Solutions priority access to LG Energy Solution's battery capacity and allows both companies to jointly explore business opportunities in this market. The partners plan to use B2U Storage Solutions' patented repurposing technologies to give LG Energy Solution batteries a second life in grid-scale storage applications. Extending battery life before recycling The joint initiative aims to extend batteries' service life through repurposing, keeping them in operation longer while deferring the costs and environmental impacts associated with recycling. Once integrated into BESS systems, these batteries could continue generating value for several years, according to both companies. "This partnership advances our strategy to extend the value of our batteries beyond their original applications," said Seung Tak Joo, leader of the Energy as a Service (EaaS) business department at LG Energy Solution. "By repurposing batteries for grid-scale energy storage, we can lengthen their useful life and create new growth opportunities that deliver long-term economic returns." Company LG Energy Solution: company profile Targeting data centers and grid operators The partnership intends to make BESS more accessible by offering cost-competitive storage solutions to utilities, energy storage developers, and large commercial energy users, including data centers. Both companies are working to expand energy storage infrastructure and strengthen the stability of the U.S. electrical grid by leveraging repurposed batteries, with the ambition of delivering storage capacity measured in gigawatt-hours. "We are committed to driving down the cost of energy storage by unlocking the inherent value of repurposed batteries. The alliance unites proven technology with a reliable supply of batteries, making energy storage more cost-effective and bankable," said Freeman Hall, founder and chief executive officer of B2U Storage Solutions. A response to mounting pressure on the U.S. grid The announcement comes as rising electricity demand and the growing integration of intermittent renewable energy sources place increasing pressure on the U.S. electrical grid. By storing electricity for use when needed, BESS systems help balance supply and demand, ease strain on the grid, and improve energy resilience for communities across the country. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %

artigo.texto: Pune, 28th September 2026: COEP Technological University is set to establish India's first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre at its Research Park in Chikhali, with an investment of over ₹800 crore. The university has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with JSW Projects, part of the JSW Group, to develop the facility in two phases. The proposed centre will focus on developing indigenous lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. It will support battery cell design, simulation, prototyping and testing, providing a platform for research and innovation in India. The project is expected to strengthen the country's battery manufacturing ecosystem and reduce dependence on imported technologies. The project will be developed in two phases, with a combined investment of more than ₹800 crore. The first phase will focus on establishing a cell research and development centre to design, simulate and prototype lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced chemistry-based battery cells. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of developing battery cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 ampere-hours (Ah). The facility will support testing and validation, helping develop battery technologies suited to Indian conditions. The partnership is expected to create more than 1,000 employment opportunities across the battery technology ecosystem. The centre will also provide students with access to advanced battery research and practical training, strengthening industry-academia collaboration. The project is expected to support the development of electric vehicles, grid-scale energy storage and clean energy solutions. It will also contribute to India's long-term goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2070. JSW Group Chairman Sajjan Jindal said, "Battery cells will become the new fuel of this century, and the time has come to manufacture them in India. Our partnership with COEP, which has a 172-year legacy in engineering, will bring a new dimension to industry-academia collaboration. It will also help design, test and validate battery cells suited to Indian climatic conditions." COEP Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud said, "This project has the potential to develop indigenous alternatives for battery manufacturing. It will give students an opportunity to learn advanced battery technologies while providing a platform for research, innovation and technological development." The MoU was signed by COEP Registrar Dr D. N. Sonawane and JSW Group Executive Vice-President Naresh Lalwani. Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud, RIIL Director Dr S. P. Mahajan, Dean Dr P. A. Sadgir, Dr Ranjit Date, Dr Sarika Kelkar, Mandar Bhatwadekar and Officer on Special Duty Dr Avinash Joshi were among those present.

artigo.texto: Trinity Airways (091810) will work with NH Investment & Securities to prepare for the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Trinity Airways said on the 28th that it signed a memorandum of understanding on CORSIA and emissions trading with NH Investment & Securities on the 21st at Sono Trinity Commons in Seoul's Gangseo District. It is the first such agreement between a Korean airline and a financial firm in the areas of CORSIA and emissions trading. The two companies plan to cooperate on exchanging information and building a joint response system for CORSIA and the domestic greenhouse gas emissions market and related policies, jointly pursuing emissions credit projects, and carrying out activities to develop the carbon market. As a first step toward meeting its CORSIA offset obligations, Trinity Airways purchased 20,000 tons of CORSIA-eligible carbon credits and signed a contract to retire them, becoming the first Korean airline to do so. The company plans to buy additional eligible credits by the end of this year, gradually securing more than 10% of the volume it must offset by January 2028. "Through this partnership with NH Investment & Securities, we have laid the groundwork to secure emissions credits at home and abroad on a stable basis and to respond systematically to carbon regulations," said Seo Dong-bin, head of management support at Trinity Airways. artigo.texto: Hobart residents opposing the Amazon Web Services data center project are pursuing a legal strategy to hopefully hit the reset button on the city’s site plan approval process. The plaintiff’s petition, filed in Lake Superior Court, seeks injunctive relief over procedural matters involving the city’s plat and zoning approval process. However, the lawsuit experienced another delay when one of the plaintiff’s attorneys was unable to make a September 22 court appearance due to personal reasons, according to Hobart resident Barbara Koteles. Koteles is one of the plaintiffs in the case and a resident of the Eagle Creek subdivision, which is located directly across the street for the data center along 61st Avenue. An attorney conference is scheduled for Sept. 30. Koteles is joined in the complaint by fellow Hobart residents Joe Conn, Angelita Soriano and Albina Venegas-Roman. The complaint, filed against the Hobart Plan Commission and the Hobart Common Council, seeks a preliminary injunction to nullify a fill permit allowing mass grading on the property, according to court documents. Earlier this year, Hobart Plan Commission voted to treat the project’s site plan application as an application for a fill permit, the court filing states. Furthermore, “the Plan Commission voted (without findings of fact) to approve the morphed fill permit for mass construction grading activities in preparation for the project …”. The plaintiffs are challenging the fill permit solely on legal grounds, contending that the Plan Commission had no power to authorize it because it failed to provide all of the information required for a such an application nor did it produce the required findings of fact required for issuance of the permit. In series of court filings over the past several months, including motions by the city to dismiss the case, the matter reached a possible ruling on September 22. But as the case has dragged out in court, the city of Hobart has allowed grading and fill work on the 723-acre site to proceed. The Plan Commission granted the data center preliminary plat approval at a highly-charged five-hour meeting in May, but tabled final plat approval at its September 4 meeting. Final plat approval concerns two separate parcels of land. One area is 555-acre parcel, located south of 61st, east of Colorado Street and north of 69th Avenue, known as Hobart Tech Park and is owned by Amazon Web Services. The other parcel, described as the Ewen Farm property, encompasses 168 acres and is located southeast of 61st and Arizona Street. That parcel will be leased by Amazon Web Services from the current owner Meanwhile, the plaintiffs are hopeful that their legal strategy can turn back the clock and re-start the plat approval process, as well as reexamine the site plan altogether. By seeking to invalidate the fill permit, which concerns only grading of the land, the plaintiffs hope they can win new concessions, such as air and truck traffic monitoring, if not permanently halt the project. Koteles said that a judge’s order to re-start the planning process could trigger a review of the community benefits agreement signed between Amazon and the city of Hobart. She also hoped the city would develop a comprehensive ordinance governing data center development and operations. “The ordinances the city has passed, such as the one involving noise, have been done rather piecemeal,” Koteles said. She added that there has not been so much work done on the site yet, primarily grading of the land, over which the project could not be reasonably halted without a detrimental financial impact to either Amazon or the city. The plaintiffs also contend in the court filing that the data center development is negatively impacting their property values (within Eagle Creek), and will do so in the future. The city argues in court documents that the plaintiffs have failed to meet the requirements for a preliminary injunction. “I wish it (the data center) was just half the size and farther away from residents,” Koteles said. “I’ve been saying that from day one, and if that were the case it wouldn’t even be an issue.” Soriano said she is concerned about air quality in the neighborhood from the ongoing site work. “We have asked the city to measure particulate matter and monitor the air quality to make sure that all the dust blowing around is not harmful to residents,” she said, adding that she received a portable air purifier and gift cards for car washes from Amazon. The city is already spending direct payments from Amazon, having granted tax abatement on the development. Hobart Mayor Josh Huddelston explained that the city negotiated a plan for direct payments, thus granting Amazon a 35-year tax abatement on personal property (equipment on site) and a 10-year abatement on real property (buildings). The city has already received $47 million, with another $10 million arriving in September, according to Huddleston. He expects a $45 million payment in-hand by the end of 2026, with a $43 million coming in 2027. The city will receive approximately $40 million in both 2028 and 2029 and approximately $52 million in 2030 when the project is expected to be completed. Then, Hobart will receive approximately $52 million per year over the next 35 years. The data center will have 26 buildings spread out across the two sites, with six buildings at the 61st Avenue location and 20 at the Colorado Street location. Amazon is planning 170 emergency backup diesel generators at the location on 61st, and 612 emergency backup generators along Colorado, enabling a combined power capacity of 2,119 megawatts. Attempts to reach Hobart City Attorney Heather McCarthy by phone at the city’s Law Department on Thursday and Friday for comment were unsuccessful. Jim Masters is a freelance reporter for the Post-Tribune.

artigo.texto: Brasil amplia infraestrutura de inteligência artificial enquanto gigantes da tecnologia aceleram construção de data centers pelo mundo Por Sandro Felix Publicado em 27/09/26 às 07:24 A corrida pela inteligência artificial está transformando a infraestrutura digital global, com investimentos bilionários em data centers, chips especializados e energia elétrica. No Brasil, novos projetos buscam ampliar a capacidade de processamento e reduzir a dependência de estruturas instaladas no exterior, enquanto Estados Unidos, China e países europeus disputam espaço na expansão dessa tecnologia. A mudança vai muito além dos chatbots. Para treinar e operar modelos avançados de IA, empresas precisam de instalações capazes de abrigar milhares de processadores, sistemas de refrigeração e redes de alta velocidade. Quanto maior a demanda por serviços como ChatGPT, Gemini e Copilot, maior a necessidade de infraestrutura para sustentar essas operações. O Brasil participa desse movimento com projetos concentrados principalmente nas regiões Sudeste, Sul e Nordeste. A disponibilidade de energia renovável, a conectividade internacional e a possibilidade de atender empresas locais estão entre os fatores que atraem investimentos. Brasil já ultrapassa 1 GW de infraestrutura de data centers O mercado brasileiro atingiu 1 gigawatt (GW) de capacidade de TI comissionada no primeiro trimestre de 2026, segundo dados da datacenterHawk divulgados pela Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). O indicador considera a capacidade de equipamentos de tecnologia já comissionada e não deve ser confundido com a potência total anunciada para empreendimentos ainda em construção. Outro levantamento, realizado pela consultoria JLL e divulgado pela Exame em 16 de setembro, apontou 706 megawatts (MW) de capacidade instalada no primeiro semestre, com previsão de entrega de mais 134 MW até dezembro. As diferenças entre os números refletem metodologias e recortes distintos de acompanhamento do setor. O crescimento ocorre em um mercado que já concentra aproximadamente 48% da capacidade instalada de data centers da América Latina, conforme relatório publicado pelo GRI Institute em julho. Entretanto, nem toda essa infraestrutura é dedicada à inteligência artificial. Parte dos equipamentos atende serviços tradicionais de nuvem, armazenamento, aplicações corporativas e plataformas digitais. Ceará receberá data center do TikTok com investimento superior a R$ 200 bilhões Um dos maiores empreendimentos anunciados no país está no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, no Ceará. O TikTok confirmou um investimento estimado em mais de R$ 200 bilhões para instalar seu primeiro data center na América Latina, com início da operação previsto para 2027. O projeto envolve a Omnia, operadora de data centers do grupo Pátria Investimentos, e a Casa dos Ventos, responsável pela parceria energética. Do investimento anunciado, R$ 108 bilhões estão previstos para equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035, enquanto o restante contempla expansões e atualizações ao longo dos anos seguintes. A primeira etapa prevê aproximadamente 200 MW de capacidade de TI e demanda energética próxima de 300 MW. A expansão poderá levar o complexo a uma potência de até 900 MW, conforme informações divulgadas sobre o empreendimento. A empresa afirma que a instalação utilizará energia renovável proveniente de novos parques eólicos dedicados ao projeto. O sistema de refrigeração terá circuito fechado, com recirculação de água e resfriamento por ar. Embora a instalação represente uma expansão expressiva da infraestrutura digital brasileira, não se trata de uma confirmação de que toda sua capacidade será destinada ao treinamento de modelos de IA. O complexo foi anunciado para atender operações do TikTok. Rio Grande do Sul e Rio de Janeiro apostam em grandes complexos de IA No Rio Grande do Sul, a Scala Data Centers desenvolve o projeto Scala AI City, em Eldorado do Sul, na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre. A primeira fase prevê investimento de R$ 3 bilhões e capacidade de 54 MW, com infraestrutura voltada ao processamento de inteligência artificial. O empreendimento foi concebido para permitir ampliações conforme a demanda e a viabilidade das próximas etapas. Em maio de 2026, o projeto avançava na elaboração do plano de negócios e na preparação para o licenciamento, segundo informações divulgadas pela GaúchaZH. A proposta de longo prazo contempla a formação de uma cidade de data centers, mas as dimensões futuras dependem da concretização das expansões planejadas. O Rio de Janeiro também participa dessa disputa com o Rio AI City, da Elea Data Centers, que combina infraestrutura existente com planos de ampliação voltados à computação de alto desempenho. Em São Paulo, a concentração de clientes corporativos e de infraestrutura de conectividade continua atraindo operadores. A Scala mantém operações e projetos em Barueri, Campinas e Jundiaí, enquanto a Tecto, do grupo V.tal, anunciou um empreendimento de 200 MW em Santana de Parnaíba. Estados Unidos concentram megaprojetos de IA Fora do Brasil, os Estados Unidos continuam no centro da expansão das instalações destinadas aos modelos mais avançados de inteligência artificial. O projeto Stargate, liderado pela OpenAI em parceria com outras empresas, tem como objetivo desenvolver uma ampla rede de infraestrutura computacional no país. Em abril de 2026, a OpenAI informou que havia superado o marco de 10 GW de capacidade de infraestrutura assegurada, inicialmente estabelecido para 2029. Segundo a companhia, mais de 3 GW foram adicionados nos 90 dias anteriores ao anúncio. O número representa compromissos de capacidade e não significa que toda essa potência já esteja em funcionamento. Entre os locais associados à expansão estão Abilene, no Texas, e outros campi norte-americanos desenvolvidos por diferentes operadores. artigo.texto: O comunicado declarava: Para acelerar o processo de transformação digital na garantia da ordem e segurança do trânsito, em 20 de março de 2026, o Primeiro-Ministro emitiu a Decisão nº 456/QD-TTg aprovando o Projeto de construção de um Centro de Dados para gerenciar, monitorar, lidar com infrações e operar o trânsito no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050 (o Projeto). Finalizar o Plano de Implementação do Projeto do Centro de Dados de Tráfego antes de 28 de setembro. (Inspeção) - O Gabinete do Governo emitiu o documento nº 498/TB-VPCP, datado de 25 de setembro de 2026, anunciando as conclusões do Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc na reunião de revisão do Projeto de Resolução do Governo que promulga o Plano de implementação da Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, datada de 12 de junho de 2026, do Comitê do Partido do Governo, sobre a aplicação de mecanismos e políticas para implementar o Projeto de construção de um centro de dados para gerenciamento, monitoramento, tratamento de violações e operação de tráfego no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050. Estas são tarefas importantes e urgentes que precisam ser implementadas rapidamente para contribuir com a modernização antecipada do monitoramento e gerenciamento de tráfego. Portanto, em 12 de junho de 2026, o Comitê do Partido do Governo emitiu a Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, que determina a implementação de diversas soluções para a execução do Projeto. Ao longo do último período, o Ministério da Segurança Pública assumiu a liderança proativa e coordenou com ministérios, setores, localidades e unidades o desenvolvimento do plano do Governo para implementar a Resolução 05-NQ/DU; e coordenou com o Gabinete do Governo a implementação dos procedimentos de reporte ao Governo, em conformidade com o regulamento interno do Governo. Implementação das tarefas do Projeto de Garantia da Qualidade e Interconexão Síncrona Para agilizar a publicação do Plano de Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc solicitou ao Ministério da Segurança Pública que coordenasse com o Gabinete do Governo a revisão e finalização da minuta da Resolução Governamental, e que a apresentasse ao Primeiro-Ministro para publicação antes de 28 de setembro de 2026. Durante a implementação do Projeto, o Ministério da Segurança Pública é o órgão permanente responsável, coordenando-se com ministérios, agências e localidades para definir cada item de trabalho, cada unidade responsável pela implementação e atribuir claramente cada tarefa a uma unidade específica, com a coordenação das agências relevantes; cada agência deve implementar proativamente as tarefas de acordo com a urgência do Projeto. Ministérios, setores e localidades devem implementar as tarefas do Projeto, garantindo o pleno cumprimento dos procedimentos e regulamentos legais para cada projeto de investimento, assegurando a qualidade, a sincronização e interconexão dos sistemas, a segurança, a eficiência e evitando a duplicação de tarefas; e prevenindo o desperdício e a corrupção. artigo.texto: Volkswagen and Gotion expand partnership in LFP batteries — InsideEVs Volkswagen is expanding its partnership with Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion through three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. As InsideEVs reports, the agreements are intended to develop a manufacturing base for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for the mass-market electric vehicle segment. Investment in Valencia Gotion will pay $1.25 billion for a 49% stake in PowerCo's plant in Valencia, Spain. The facility will be jointly managed by PowerCo and Gotion. Volkswagen said the plant is to become a European production hub for unified LFP cells. According to financial documents, its production capacity will amount to 29.1 GWh. The unified prismatic battery cell is being developed by Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo. The group plans to use this platform for different battery chemistries, including potentially solid-state batteries, in models of various brands, from Volkswagen to Porsche. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Projects in Slovakia and Morocco Volkswagen also plans to spend about $535 million by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake in a Gotion plant in Slovakia and establish a facility in Morocco. The Slovak plant, with a capacity of 8.4 GWh, is expected to produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. The Moroccan facility will manufacture cathode materials for such batteries. Volkswagen called LFP batteries a key technology for affordable electric mobility in the mass-market segment. The company expects their share of the European market to increase from the current 10% to 40–60% by 2030. At the same time, the automaker noted that Europe currently lacks significant LFP battery production capacity.

artigo.texto: Many gather to discuss proposed Newport Township data centers NANTICOKE — A standing-room crowd filled the hall at West Side Park Sunday as Newport Township residents gathered to learn more about proposed data center development and hear from activists, residents, and others who have been following similar projects across Northeast Pennsylvania. The roughly hourlong community meeting came less than two weeks after residents learned that zoning permits had been issued for 15 data centers and three natural gas generation facilities proposed in Newport Township. For Jennifer Lobb, a Newport Township resident and one of the meeting’s organizers, the goal Sunday was less about providing residents with all the answers and more about making sure they knew questions remained to be asked. “We’re just here to let people know about what’s going on, to encourage them to get involved with our local government, to attend the commissioners meetings, to let them know how they feel, and to bring the power back to the people who have to live with these decisions,” Lobb said in an interview before the meeting. Lobb said residents began organizing after learning about the scope of the proposed development earlier this month. “A lot of us woke up in the morning to a newspaper article about 15 data centers and three new gas power plants that were permitted for our township,” she said. Sunday’s turnout suggested the issue has gotten residents’ attention. Chairs filled the hall, while others stood along the perimeter as speakers discussed potential effects of large-scale data center development, including water and electricity use, noise, pollution, emergency response, and changes to surrounding communities. Much of the meeting also focused on encouraging residents to attend the Newport Township commissioners meeting Oct. 5 and press township officials for additional information. Luzerne County resident Nate Eachus, who said he has spent about a year attending municipal meetings throughout the region and researching environmental issues associated with data center development, urged residents to ask detailed questions about water, wastewater, diesel fuel, and power generation. “Everybody needs to show up at this October 5 meeting,” Eachus told the crowd. “Ask good, hard questions.” Eachus pointed to data center development elsewhere in Luzerne County as examples residents could study as they consider what may come to Newport Township. Jeremy Benscoter, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 117th District who described himself as having a background in information technology, told residents the scale and demands of newer hyperscale data centers distinguish them from traditional facilities used to host websites and other internet services. Benscoter focused much of his remarks on the complexity of regulating the facilities, particularly when it comes to water use, electricity demand, and municipal zoning. “We have to basically decide, as a community, what you think is the best option for you,” Benscoter said. He also encouraged residents to consider effects beyond Newport Township, arguing that the rapid development of data centers throughout the region could have implications for the electrical grid and other infrastructure shared across municipal boundaries. Fern Leard, a candidate for the state House’s 120th District, focused on community organization and emergency preparedness, telling residents that first responders could require additional equipment and training to respond to emergencies at large data center facilities. “What I see in this room is people taking the time to listen to one another,” Leard said. She encouraged residents to continue attending municipal meetings and participating in the public process. Paul Shiptuski, who said he has lived in Newport Township’s Lee section for 42 years, spoke about changes his neighborhood has already experienced from nearby industrial activity. Shiptuski said residents contend with truck traffic, dust, noise, and blasting associated with a quarry near his home. He questioned what additional development could mean for residents who rely on wells and value the area’s rural surroundings. “How does that benefit us in the long run?” Shiptuski asked. Other speakers brought perspectives from neighboring communities. Derek Sutcliffe, a Moosic resident involved in opposition to a proposed data center development in Archbald, discussed the substantial electrical infrastructure required by hyperscale facilities and encouraged Newport Township residents to scrutinize how proposed facilities would be powered. Dr. Gere Reisinger, who spoke as a representative of the Seneca Nation and local Native American historian, emphasized the cultural and environmental importance of the Susquehanna River and Wyoming Valley. Lauren McCurdy, a candidate for the Pennsylvania House’s 119th District who attended Sunday’s meeting, said she sees the issue as one that extends beyond individual municipal boundaries. McCurdy, who did not address the crowd, said in an interview that she is concerned about the potential long-term environmental effects of rapid data center development throughout Northeast Pennsylvania. “We have an obligation to protect our communities from interests that are not coming here to improve the quality of life for people in Northeastern Pennsylvania,” McCurdy said. For Lobb, Sunday’s meeting was a starting point. She said residents have not yet formed a formal organization but came together quickly after learning about the permits and are encouraging neighbors to educate themselves and become involved. “They just really need to stay informed,” Lobb said. Residents were repeatedly encouraged Sunday to attend the next Newport Township commissioners meeting, scheduled for 6 p.m. Oct. 5 in the Nanticoke Area High School auditorium. artigo.texto: Lowndes County residents continue to oppose proposed data center project LOWNDES COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA) -Lowndes County residents continue their fight against the so-called red clay project as they packed out another county commission meeting. “The truth does not fear light or hard questions,” said Lowndes County resident Dennis Blair. Opponents of a proposed data center in Lowndes County say a majority of residents have been against the project for months. What’s unclear to some, like Marie Barnes, is the current status of the project, known as “red clay.” “We live here. This is our world, this is our property, this is our land, and we don’t want a data center here because we don’t want to look like a Silicon Valley,” said Barnes. So far, residents say they only know the name of the developer, Cloverleaf Infrastructure, and the proposed site, a piece of farmland along Highway 80 near Highway 21. This is about 6 miles southwest of Montgomery. “I think anyone with common sense would say this is not a part of the county that’s economically distressed, so why here? It looks like they gerrymandered pretty good to get enough undeserved people in it to qualify for an opportunity zone,” said Blair. “It’s not in the right place. Within 2 and a half miles of this data center, there are 276-something families right around it,” said Elder Tom Gardner III of Beulah Primitive Baptist Church. “It shouldn’t be that these residents have to show up week after week after week after week and not get answers, said Alabama state Rep. Phillip Ensler. This is the third commission meeting Ensler attended. He says he’s not against data centers as a rule, but says transparency is key. “We have to do it in a way that is smart and responsible. We have to do it in a way that if the community really doesn’t want it or it’s going to hurt the community, we shouldn’t have it. And this here in Lowndes County, it feels like and seems like to a lot of residents that it’s being forced on them. And we first need answers before it goes to those.” “No matter what they do, how they do it, when they do it. We’re still going to be here until this is done,” said Barnes. artigo.texto: Data centers powering AI have rapidly become a new layer of critical infrastructure worldwide that are central to technology innovation, economic growth, and national sovereignty. US capital investment in data centers as a share of GDP now rivals what it spent building its railroads, telecom networks, and electrical grid: generational projects. The data center boom is moving faster. Five years ago, a 50-megawatt (MW) facility was considered large. Now, hyperscalers are planning to build data center campuses 100 times bigger: 5 gigawatts (GW) or more, costing $150 billion to $200 billion each. AI compute demand is already outrunning supply, and the shortage is intensifying. To overcome it, the tech industry is planning investments at unprecedented scale and speed. In a base case, Bain’s Data Center Model projects approximately $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of spending to build nearly 150 GW of new compute capacity by 2030 (see Figure 1), almost tripling global capacity in just five years. Most of the growth will come from the US, but compute capacity will grow by double digits across regions. What many business leaders are missing is that the AI compute shortage is unlikely to resolve on its own. The usual assumption that supply chains respond to demand and that they’ll eventually balance doesn’t hold here. Power, hardware, and skilled labor are simultaneously constrained (see Figure 2), and public approvals are increasingly difficult to secure. Lead times are long enough that decisions made today determine capacity several years from now. - Power: Grid connection is delaying and freezing projects. Adding grid capacity takes four-plus years, and critical equipment inventory (e.g., transformers, etc.) is scarce. Onsite, behind-the-meter power relieves some of the bottleneck, but it adds regulatory exposure, longer equipment lead times, and more project complexity. - Semiconductors: GPUs, memory, optical networking, and other components are being locked in years ahead. Operators without long-term supply agreements are effectively out of the queue. - Labor: Skilled trades are the human version of the same problem, with too few electrical workers, mechanical tradespeople, and cooling specialists. Meeting demand means recruiting, training, and retaining talent far above historical rates. - Regulations and public opinion: Complex permitting rules across local, state, and national levels add time and uncertainty, even when primary inputs are secured. Citizens and politicians are increasingly pushing back regarding water use, energy prices, and noise. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 projects worth $130 billion in the first quarter of this year alone, nearly matching the $156 billion worth of projects disrupted in all of 2025. In July, New York became the first US state to pause construction of the largest data centers; 14 others have introduced similar legislation. Countries including Ireland, the Netherlands, and Denmark have restricted or paused new grid connections, at least temporarily. Structural solutions are required Individual projects are finding workarounds, but they can’t be replicated at scale, and some are controversial. Colossus (from xAI, now part of SpaceXAI) was built in under a year by repurposing a factory and leasing dozens of gas turbines without federal clean air permits, drawing a lawsuit. Constructing a 1 GW data center typically takes one to four years, even on sites with existing power (see Figure 3), and it can take longer when new generation and transmission infrastructure is needed. Meeting the global ambition instead will require system-level fixes outside the usual free-market playbook. A grand challenge on this scale demands grand solutions, and executives planning on business as usual will get blindsided. The forces below are deliberately provocative and mostly long term, and some will create new challenges, even as they mitigate others. But overcoming the shortage will take at least one of the following forces: consolidation, new power at scale, orbital data centers, government investment, and social license. Consolidation: Consolidation could occur as capital requirements grow so large that only a handful of companies survive. Hyperscalers’ data center capex could top $1 trillion by 2028. Semiconductors provide a useful corollary. Staying at the leading edge grew so costly (tens of billions of dollars per generation) that missing one generation made catching up effectively impossible. Companies exited, were acquired, or retreated to older nodes (see Figure 4). Facing unsustainable costs, data center providers may also turn to once-unthinkable solutions: shared power procurement, colocated servers, and jointly funded grid upgrades. New power at scale: Power is one of the most challenging, multidimensional bottlenecks, and no single source solves it. The realistic path combines near-term options that could come online this decade with long-term ones that are scheduled to pay off in the 2030s. Near term, behind-the-meter generation (mostly natural gas today) is one of the few ways to add large blocks of power on data center timelines. Pairing it with carbon capture, utilization, and storage could make it cleaner, but that’s unproven at scale. Tech companies are also turning to renewables, storage, and virtual power plants (VPPs) that use software to aggregate and redirect power in real time from distributed sources such as batteries and smart thermostats. Google, for instance, is funding 1.6 GW of renewables (mostly wind) and 300 MW of storage alongside a new Minnesota data center. North America’s VPP market grew by 13.7% last year, to 37.5 GW, per Wood Mackenzie. Novel VPP agreements are emerging, such as the Google-Voltus deal that would aggregate up to 100 MW annually over three years in the PJM grid. Nuclear is another clean source that could eventually help, but new, large-scale capacity realistically won’t arrive until the mid-2030s. Recommissi

artigo.texto: Kuehne+Nagel and battery manufacturer CATL have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to cooperate on battery logistics, transport electrification and emissions reduction. The partnership will initially focus on practical projects in Europe and Asia. These include the electrification of CATL’s transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China, which is expected to launch in 2026. Partnership targets battery and road logistics Under the agreement, Kuehne+Nagel and CATL will also explore cooperation in battery recycling and aftersales support, as well as energy storage and charging solutions for logistics facilities. The companies said these initiatives will support efforts to reduce Scope 3 emissions across their logistics and transportation value chains. “Battery-electric vehicles are essential to decarbonising road freight,” said Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel. “Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both high-performing and operationally viable.” Schmidt added that combining CATL’s battery expertise with Kuehne+Nagel’s logistics capabilities could support projects aimed at reducing emissions from both the company’s operations and those of its customers. Heavy-duty battery swapping pilot planned in China One of the first projects will involve a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China using technology provided by Qiji. The two companies will also work on electrifying CATL transport flows in Europe, although no details have been provided on the number of vehicles or routes involved. The partnership comes as demand for batteries used in electric trucks continues to increase. According to the companies, demand for electric truck batteries rose by more than 75% in 2024, while global battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand. “As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share a commitment to accelerating the energy transition and achieving a net-zero emissions future,” said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. The companies did not disclose any investment value or timeframe for expanding the cooperation beyond the initial projects.

artigo.texto: PJM to Data Centers: Stop Bailing on the Grid Every Time It Blips Remember that July morning when 4,000 megawatts (MW) of Northern Virginia data centers yanked themselves off the PJM grid because of a routine, properly cleared fault on a single transmission line (see PJM: Data Centers Panicked, Nearly Crashed the Grid on Purpose)? PJM hasn't forgotten either. On Sept. 8, PJM's Planning Committee got its first look at proposed "ride-through" standards that would require big data centers and crypto mines to stay connected and keep drawing power when the grid wobbles — instead of hitting the eject button and running for their diesel generators. And PJM isn't easing into it: new facilities entering the study process would have to demonstrate compliance starting Nov. 1, 2026 — about five weeks from now. artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, its battery subsidiary PowerCo SE and Gotion High-tech have expanded their battery production partnership, with an agreement to establish joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. The agreement will see facilities covering lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery-cell production developed in Valencia, Spain and Šurany, Slovakia, while Kenitra, Morocco will house a cathode-material operation. It also includes joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The moves form part of a wider strategy by the groups to ‘jointly accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe’. ‘Major breakthrough’ “I am delighted that we are expanding our long-standing partnership with Gotion into the joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry,” commented Thomas Schmall, member of the board of management of Volkswagen Group for technology and chairman of the supervisory board of PowerCo SE. “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.” As the groups noted, the market share of LFP batteries is expected to rise from around 10% today to between 40% and 60% by 2030, with Europe currently lacking LFP battery production capacity. Project structure The largest project under the partnership, in Valencia, is being positioned as a future ‘European production hub for unified LFP battery cells’, and will be 51% owned by PowerCo and 49% by Gotion. The companies also plan a joint venture around Gotion’s battery project in Šurany, Slovakia, with Gotion holding a 51% majority stake, to PowerCo’s 49%, while a similar structure will be maintained at Kentira. The Morocco project will supply cathode material to the two European battery operations. Li Zhen, chairman of Gotion Hith-tech said that the latest announcement follows “six years of close collaboration” between Volkswagen and Gotion. “Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry,” he commented. artigo.texto: O workshop contou com a presença de especialistas, palestrantes, parceiros nas áreas de energia solar e armazenamento de energia, bem como empresas e investidores atuantes no setor. Soluções integradas de energia solar e armazenamento para uso comercial e industrial. No dia 29 de setembro, em Dak Lak, a Unitek, a Uhome e a Usolution organizaram em conjunto o seminário ALL-IN-ONE ENERGY TOUR 2026 com o tema "Soluções Integradas de Energia Solar + Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias - Liderando o Mercado". Segundo avaliações, o mercado de energia do Vietnã está entrando em um período de transformação significativa, o que impõe novas exigências em termos de gestão e otimização dos custos de eletricidade. Juntamente com as regulamentações do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio sobre horários de pico, o Decreto nº 243/2026/ND-CP, de 26 de junho de 2026, do Governo, ampliou o mecanismo de venda do excedente de energia elétrica proveniente de sistemas solares fotovoltaicos instalados em telhados. Essas mudanças criaram novas exigências, que incluem não apenas a geração de energia, mas também a otimização do fornecimento no momento adequado. Segundo os organizadores, a energia solar gera a maior parte da eletricidade durante o dia, enquanto a demanda e os custos de energia elétrica podem aumentar à noite. Portanto, a combinação de energia solar com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é considerada uma solução para armazenar o excedente de eletricidade, utilizando-o em momentos oportunos, otimizando custos e melhorando a eficiência do investimento. O mercado atual oferece diversas tendências, tecnologias de armazenamento e soluções Solar + BESS para atender a diferentes necessidades. Para que um sistema seja eficaz, a questão reside não apenas na seleção de dispositivos individuais, mas também na capacidade de conectar, sincronizar e otimizar os componentes em uma solução completa que atenda às reais necessidades do negócio. No workshop, o Comitê Organizador atualizou os participantes sobre as mudanças do mercado e apresentou soluções práticas, tais como: sincronização e otimização da eficiência do investimento; modelos e soluções adaptados às necessidades de negócios; operação, manutenção, teste e melhoria do desempenho e estabilidade do sistema… fornecidas pela Pylontech, Fox Ess, Fluke e Goneo. Durante o programa, palestrantes e parceiros também discutiram diretamente e responderam a perguntas de empresas e investidores sobre a implementação de sistemas de energia solar combinados com armazenamento de energia. O conteúdo focou na seleção da capacidade adequada, na capacidade de suprir a demanda, nas opções de armazenamento e na utilização eficiente da eletricidade em diferentes momentos. Portanto, o workshop contribuiu para fornecer mais informações e soluções tecnológicas para empresas em processo de transição para modelos de uso de energia mais eficientes, tornando-se mais proativas no fornecimento de eletricidade e reduzindo gradualmente os custos operacionais. artigo.texto: O relatório Flexera State of the Cloud 2026 indica que 73% das organizações operam com um modelo de Nuvem Híbrida (essa taxa sobe para 78% em empresas com mais de 5.000 funcionários). Notavelmente, a taxa de migração de cargas de trabalho e dados da Nuvem Pública para outros ambientes também aumentou 2% em comparação com o ano anterior. Essa mudança reflete uma tendência real: as empresas estão cada vez mais posicionando suas cargas de trabalho de forma proativa onde alcançam a máxima eficiência operacional. Isso não significa que as empresas estejam "abandonando a nuvem". Pelo contrário, os gastos com a nuvem continuam a crescer. A realidade é que, quanto mais disseminada for a adoção da nuvem, mais clara ficará para as empresas a compreensão de quais cargas de trabalho podem aproveitar o ambiente da nuvem e quais exigem uma arquitetura especializada. Essa necessidade de diferenciação clara redefiniu o papel do Data Center na arquitetura híbrida. Quando uma arquitetura simplesmente não consegue "se adequar" a todas as cargas de trabalho. Uma aplicação digital que exige escalabilidade rápida para atender às demandas de tráfego certamente terá requisitos de infraestrutura diferentes de um sistema central que necessita de estabilidade 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Da mesma forma, uma carga de trabalho de análise de dados pode exigir poder computacional flexível, enquanto um sistema de segurança demanda hardware dedicado, arquitetura de armazenamento ou uma arquitetura independente de rede. Este é o grande diferencial da Nuvem Híbrida: liberar as empresas da pressão de ter que "amontoar" todas as cargas de trabalho em um único ambiente. Embora as nuvens públicas ofereçam um vasto ecossistema de serviços com recursos de alocação instantânea, para componentes que exigem um nível mais profundo de personalização, as empresas ainda precisam de "espaço" para projetar proativamente sua infraestrutura de acordo com suas necessidades. É essa lacuna que os data centers preenchem na arquitetura híbrida. Em vez de ser apenas um "local de hospedagem" para servidores, um data center (DC) é uma plataforma de lançamento para que as empresas implementem sua própria infraestrutura: desde computação e armazenamento até redes e segurança. As empresas podem ajustar a configuração para cada carga de trabalho principal, aproveitando ao máximo o poder da nuvem para os demais componentes. Em outras palavras, as soluções híbridas ampliam as opções, enquanto os data centers ajudam as empresas a manter o controle sobre essa personalização. Quanto mais nos aprofundamos na computação em nuvem, mais importante se torna o papel dos centros de dados. No entanto, uma infraestrutura perfeitamente "sob medida" não tem significado algum se se transformar em um oásis isolado. As aplicações em nuvem ainda precisam extrair dados de bancos de dados localizados em infraestrutura privada. O sistema central deve sincronizar-se continuamente com as plataformas digitais na nuvem. E, à medida que o negócio se expande, a arquitetura atual precisa ser flexível o suficiente para se conectar com outras nuvens, plataformas ou parceiros. É aqui que entra em jogo o segundo papel do Data Center: a infraestrutura dedicada não só precisa estar operacional, como também precisa estabelecer uma "via expressa" perfeita que a conecte à parte da Nuvem da arquitetura híbrida. O estudo de caso da Equinix e do Credit Saison no Japão é um exemplo claro. Essa instituição financeira migrou aproximadamente 80% de seus sistemas para a nuvem. Com o aumento do uso da nuvem, o Credit Saison precisava resolver o problema de conectar seus sistemas internos aos serviços em nuvem. Por meio da infraestrutura de data center da Equinix e da solução de interconexão direta, a largura de banda do Credit Saison para a AWS saltou de 10 Mbps para 10 Gbps. Ainda mais impressionante, o tempo para ativar uma nova conexão foi reduzido de vários meses para apenas 3 dias úteis. Esta história oferece uma nova perspectiva: o fato de 80% dos sistemas serem baseados em nuvem não significa que os data centers estejam se tornando infraestrutura "obsoleta". Pelo contrário, o uso em larga escala da nuvem gerou uma nova tarefa para os data centers: garantir que a infraestrutura privada e a nuvem se comuniquem na velocidade desejada pelos negócios. Portanto, à medida que a presença da nuvem se expande, a questão central não é mais "Qual é o volume de trabalho da empresa em seu data center?". Uma pergunta mais prática deveria ser: "A partir desse data center, qual o alcance da arquitetura híbrida da empresa em termos de conectividade e escalabilidade?". De "Estação de Armazenamento" a "Camada de Suporte" para a Nuvem Essa mudança não diminui o valor de padrões tradicionais como fornecimento de energia, capacidade, segurança ou disponibilidade do data center. No entanto, a arquitetura híbrida impõe uma camada adicional de requisitos. As empresas precisam conhecer o grau máximo de personalização de sua própria infraestrutura; como conectar essa parte à nuvem; e a adaptabilidade do sistema atual quando uma nova carga de trabalho ou plataforma é adicionada. Isso é especialmente crucial à medida que a arquitetura de TI se torna cada vez mais complexa. O relatório da Flexera para 2026 aponta para um crescimento contínuo do modelo de Nuvem Híbrida, com um crescimento de 2% em Multicloud; simultaneamente, fluxos de migração e repatriação para a Nuvem ocorrem de forma concomitante. A infraestrutura corporativa agora é um ecossistema multiambiente adaptado a necessidades específicas, em vez de uma jornada com um único destino: a Nuvem. Dentro desse ecossistema, o Data Center surge como uma poderosa camada de infraestrutura de suporte. Ele fornece espaço para a personalização de ativos que exigem controle profundo, além de servir como um hub central que conecta sistemas internos com o poder ilimitado da Nuvem. artigo.texto: A single photo of the BYD Great Seagull at a Flash Charging station has changed the outlook for affordable electric cars. The image points to a big jump in charging speed and tech for city drivers. One photo has changed the story for budget electric cars in China. The BYD Great Seagull, once thought too basic for the brand’s top Blade 2 battery, has now been seen parked at a Flash Charging station—BYD’s own megacharger. No camouflage. No staged press event. Just a real car, out in the open. This is the first hard sign that BYD might bring ultra-fast charging to the city car class. The image, posted by Liang Xiao Ping on Weibo and reported by CarNewsChina, shows the new Seagull set up for what looks like an official photo shoot. Carmakers don’t do this unless the car can actually use the charger behind it. The message is simple: BYD is getting ready to show off the Great Seagull’s ability to use Flash Charging. This could change what buyers expect from entry-level EVs. Reuters has reported that BYD already has megawatt-class Flash Charging systems and Blade batteries that can charge from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. This tech is real, not just a rumor. But BYD is keeping the details close. There’s no official word on the system voltage or the top charging power. The MIIT homologation lists two LFP batteries—30 kWh and 39.2 kWh—both made by FinDreams. They offer CLTC ranges of 320 and 420 kilometers. The LFP label doesn’t say if these are first or second generation Blade batteries. Chinese sources, as cited by CarNewsChina, say Flash Charging will likely be for higher trims, probably the bigger battery. That fits BYD’s pattern with other models. The numbers matter. If the Great Seagull gets the Blade 2 battery, the specs are eye-catching. BYD says it can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, and 10% to 97% in nine minutes—even at minus 30 degrees Celsius. For the 39.2 kWh battery, that’s about 23.5 kWh in five minutes. The average power is 282 kW, with peaks over 300 kW. For comparison, the Dolphin Surf charges at under 90 kW. The Geely E2 averages 60 kW between 10% and 80%, taking about 30 minutes for a similar charge. The Great Seagull could do it in five. That’s a sixth of the time. It could add 200 kilometers of range in five minutes. Still, the 1,500 kW figure often linked to Flash Charging is about the charger, not the car. The real test is whether the Seagull’s system runs at 400 or 800 volts. Higher voltage means less current for the same power, but it costs more. It needs better electronics and cooling. Most CCS2 chargers in Europe max out at about 500 amps. So, the Seagull’s real charging speed will depend on both its voltage and the chargers it plugs into. Price is still unknown. The current Seagull sells in China for 69,900 to 85,900 yuan (about 9,200 to 11,300 euros before taxes and homologation). The new model is bigger and better equipped, so it will cost more. If BYD can offer Flash Charging below 100,000 yuan (around 13,100 euros), it would be a first for the brand at this price. Until now, the cheapest BYDs—Seagull, Dolphin, Yuan UP—haven’t had Blade 2, even though half the lineup already uses it. Earlier reports said the Seagull and Dolphin wouldn’t get Blade 2 until 2027. This new photo hints at a much earlier launch. Market pressure is building. In August, BYD sold 10,103 Seagulls in China. The rival Geely Xingyuan (sold in Spain as the Geely E2) sold 39,651 units. Geely is ahead in size, seats, and sales. BYD’s best move is to jump ahead in charging speed, not fight on price. The Great Seagull’s place in the lineup is still unclear. It was first announced as a model between the Seagull and Dolphin. Later, BYD’s Zhang Zhuo called it the “second generation Seagull.” The company hasn’t said if it will replace the current Seagull or sit above it. The new car is 4,205 mm long—42.5 cm longer than the old Seagull and just 6.5 cm shorter than the Dolphin. It has a single 95 kW front motor and a top speed of 150 km/h. The design brings trident-shaped headlights, a lower window line, and a simple interior with all info on a central floating screen. For buyers in Europe, things get tricky. The 3.78-meter Seagull is sold as the Dolphin Surf, stretched to 3.99 meters with bigger bumpers. BYD just launched five-seat versions of the current body in Spain, starting at 24,490 euros for the Boost trim. The fifth seat came through rehomologation, not a new model. This shows BYD plans to keep the current Dolphin Surf in Europe for now, especially after sales dropped due to the missing fifth seat. But in China, the Seagull was refreshed in May and replaced just four months later. Europe could see the new model sooner than expected, but there are no confirmed dates yet. BYD’s charging plans are just as bold. The company has promised 300 Flash Charging stations in Spain, open to any car with a CCS2 plug and priced under 0.50 euros per kWh. The first station is already running in Leganés. There, a Denza Z9 GT charged from 10% to 97% in under nine minutes. But only the Denza, which starts at 115,000 euros, can use this speed in Spain. No BYD sold in Spain has the Blade 2 battery yet. The brand says it will take about 24 months before these models arrive. For now, the stations mostly serve cars limited to 150 kW. A small city car that can add 200 kilometers in five minutes would change everything for urban drivers without home charging. As Chinese brands put pressure on Spain’s electric car market, with recent analysis showing the shift, BYD’s push to bring ultra-fast charging to the masses could force the whole segment to adapt. If the Great Seagull launches with Flash Charging before the end of 2026, BYD will have moved faster than anyone expected. It would set a new standard for what city drivers can get from an affordable EV. The next few months will show if this photo is the start of something big or just a clever tease. The stakes for city EVs have never been higher.

artigo.texto: Crusoe Developing Data Center Campus in Armstrong County, Texas Data center to be built at the source of West Texas clean energy CLAUDE, TX – September 28, 2026 – Crusoe, the AI factory company, today announced it is the developer of Google’s data center campus under construction in Armstrong County outside of Amarillo. The campus is engineered to provide capacity to power advanced AI. “Building the future of AI requires a new kind of infrastructure, starting with energy. Crusoe’s strategy is to build AI factories directly at the source of abundant, low-cost energy – to both improve utilization of existing assets as well as catalyze new energy generation,” said Chase Lochmiller, CEO and Co-founder of Crusoe. “The Armstrong County campus is a prime example of this energy-first strategy. We're bringing new, affordable clean energy online. We broke ground in June 2025 and are building at the same swift pace we set in Abilene.” The campus has a direct connection to Serena's adjacent Goodnight 1 (265.5 MW) wind farm, which is operational, and Goodnight 2 (265.5 MW) wind farm, which is currently under construction and was catalyzed by Crusoe’s development at the site. When wind generation exceeds campus demand, surplus power is supplied back to the grid – benefiting local ratepayers and reducing curtailment of West Texas wind energy. By co-locating directly at the source of West Texas wind energy, Crusoe’s approach actively supports the region's buildout of clean, affordable energy. In addition to its innovative energy sources, the campus is designed for water efficiency. The project will utilize a closed-loop, non-evaporative liquid cooling system, which is designed to significantly limit the facility's water footprint to primarily domestic uses such as kitchens. Construction broke ground in June 2025 and is underway, with more than 5,500 skilled laborers on-site daily, bringing significant investment and employment to the local community. Local investment in the community also includes Google’s Energy Impact Fund, which recently announced support for efficiency upgrades in public buildings and homes in Armstrong County. The campus is part of Crusoe's growing West Texas portfolio, which includes two campuses under development in Abilene, further establishing West Texas as a critical region for the future of American digital infrastructure. Read more about Crusoe's energy approach here: www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/co-located-power-for-ai-data-centers. About Crusoe As the AI factory company, Crusoe is on a mission to accelerate the abundance of energy and intelligence. The company provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure. By harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform, Crusoe empowers its customers and partners to build the future faster. For more information, visit crusoe.ai. Media Contact: media@crusoe.ai

artigo.texto: Tesla, Inc. Leading EV and battery manufacturer with Gigafactories NineDot Energy has commissioned a battery energy storage system in the New York City metro area, according to a report from Solar Power World. The 20-MW Hunts Point BESS in the Bronx is expected to supply enough power for nearly 20,000 homes during peak grid hours, the report said. Adam Cohen, NineDot's chief technology officer and co-founder, described the project as an honor for the company and said the site represents a turning point for the local environment and grid reliability, according to the report. Cohen noted that Hunts Point has historically carried a heavy burden from high-emitting fossil fuels. NineDot states that residents of Hunts Point have endured decades of environmental injustice. The company points to more than 10,000 diesel trucks passing through the area each day and two high-emissions peaker power plants in nearby Port Morris. In 2023, the combined Hunts Point and Mott Haven area recorded asthma-related emergency room visits at two to three times the citywide average, a figure the company attributes to fine particle air pollution. artigo.texto: NineDot Energy opened a large battery storage site in the Bronx, New York. Company leaders joined elected officials and community groups to cut the ribbon on a project replacing a former fuel oil trucking facility. By the time next summer’s heat waves arrive, this setup will be fully ready. It will deliver almost 20 megawatts of power to the community, enough energy to power about 20,000 homes during the busiest times for the grid. Addressing the Environmental Issues For decades, Hunts Point residents have dealt with serious environmental issues. For example, local leaders say that more than 10,000 diesel trucks pass through the area daily. Additionally, two high-emissions “peaker” power plants operate nearby. These plants only run when the grid needs extra power, but they produce heavy pollution. Advertisement This new site stores energy and releases it during peak hours. This means older gas-fired plants won’t have to run as much, and eventually, they can be retired. It also provides reliable energy as the local produce market, fish market, and truck fleets switch to electric power. “We’re honored to bring this battery storage site to the Hunts Point community,” said Adam Cohen, NineDot’s Chief Technology Officer and Co-founder. “Hunts Point has historically been overburdened by high-emitting fossil fuels, and this battery storage facility marks an inflection point in improving the local environment and grid reliability.” Storing Energy for Years to Come During the extreme heat wave from July 1 to 4, 2026, NineDot’s community batteries helped ease the strain on the electric grid. Across nine projects, they sent nearly 34 megawatts of power to Con Edison’s system when it was needed most. That is like taking 50,000 window air conditioners off the grid, or powering 34,000 homes for four hours a day. NineDot currently has 11 operating projects across Staten Island and the Bronx, making it the largest battery fleet in Con Edison’s city territory. The company plans to hit 400 megawatts of battery storage by the end of 2026, with over 60 more projects already in the works.
