artigo.texto: Securing the energy storage surge This article is authored by Arun Goyal, former CERC member and senior advisor, MSL, and Jaisal Sarma, public policy professional, MSL. India’s ambitious commitment to establish 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030 marks one of the most dramatic clean energy expansions. Achieving this goal, however, hinges on an operational reality: solar and wind power are inherently variable, requiring massive utility-scale energy storage capacity to keep the electric grid balanced, stable, resilient, and reliable. The Central Electricity Authority’s National Generation Adequacy Plan estimates that India will need the energy storage installed capacity of 174 GW/888 GWh including Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) of 80 GW/321 GWh by the year 2035-36 to effectively manage this clean power transition. Yet, as the nation accelerates its energy transition, it faces a new and complex strategic vulnerability. Clean energy technology is no longer simply an environmental and economic transaction; it is fundamentally a global contest for critical raw materials. Without secure, cost-effective access to key battery inputs, such as lithium, graphite, cobalt, and nickel, India’s energy storage deployment remains deeply exposed to global price volatility, unilateral export restrictions, and geopolitical disruption across international supply corridors. To build energy sovereignty in an increasingly fractured global order, India cannot rely on conventional market imports alone. It must instead execute a thoughtful, dual-track strategy that pairs strategic international technology alliances with a robust domestic circular economy. Across the globe, clean energy supply chains are re-aligning along geopolitical lines as major economies seek to de-risk their manufacturing hubs and secure raw material inputs. Multilateral frameworks like the US-led Pax Silica initiative, designed to build resilient supply chains across semiconductors, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, alongside the Minerals Security Partnership, reflect a historic shift towards friend-shoring. For India, active participation in these technological coalitions offers vital strategic advantages. It provides access to international co-investment mechanisms for overseas mineral processing, technology sharing for next-generation battery chemistries like sodium-ion and helps diversify raw material inputs away from single-country concentrations. However, foreign alliances, no matter how well-negotiated, are an incomplete shield against supply chain volatility. Diplomatic access to minerals extracted or refined abroad does not fully eliminate risks of long maritime shipping routes, foreign exchange volatility, or international refining bottlenecks during global crises. To turn global partnerships into lasting national resilience, India requires a strong domestic anchor. Through the National Critical Mineral Mission, supported by a ₹16,300 crore central outlay up to 2030-31, the Indian government has formally elevated secondary mineral recovery to a cornerstone of national economic policy. The mission’s dedicated ₹1,500 crore incentive scheme for critical mineral recycling explicitly targets the extraction of battery-grade minerals from e-waste, manufacturing scrap, and end-of-life electric vehicles. This strategy complements domestic exploration by focusing on urban mining that converts domestic waste into high-value strategic mineral reserves. From an economic perspective, establishing a closed-loop domestic recycling ecosystem fundamentally improves the financial viability of clean energy infrastructure over its entire operational lifecycle. Processing secondary battery scrap inside India creates an immediate buffer against wild fluctuations in global critical mineral spot prices, thereby stabilizing long-term power purchase agreements and lowering the overall lifetime cost of storage systems. At the same time, implementing clear Extended Producer Responsibility guidelines ensures that valuable battery materials remain within the domestic industrial ecosystem rather than moving overseas as unprocessed scrap. A predictable stream of recycled secondary feedstocks lowers raw material costs for domestic cell manufacturers, creating a self-sustaining feedback loop that supports long-term industrial competitiveness. By recovering these critical inputs locally, India can expand its energy storage capacity while significantly reducing the net capital outlay required for fresh critical mineral imports. Translating this strategic blueprint into an operational reality requires pragmatic policy execution, cluster-based industrial infrastructure, and aligned fiscal structures. Foremost among these is updating tax policy to support new clean technologies. Lowering the GST on standalone energy storage systems and specialised recycling machinery to a uniform 5% can immediately lower upfront capital barriers and attract private investment. Simultaneously, regulatory bodies can establish clear, standardised quality and safety benchmarks for battery state-of-health diagnostics, enabling second-life electric vehicle batteries to be safely repurposed for stationary grid storage applications. Furthermore, public procurement agencies and energy developers should modernize their evaluation frameworks to assess storage projects based on full lifecycle economic value, factoring in secondary material recovery and recycling buybacks, rather than relying strictly on initial capital expenditure. Ultimately, India’s clean energy sovereign future cannot be built on import dependencies or uncoordinated execution. International technology blocs like Pax Silica open vital doors to global capital and advanced research, but internal administrative execution will decide whether India achieves true energy independence. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage: 6 security questions operators should be asking Tue, 29th Sep 2026 (Today) Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) play a critical role in grid stability and renewable energy utilisation. But as these infrastructures become more sophisticated, the risk of cyberattacks grows, potentially compromising operations, safety and energy reliability. In Centrii's recently published GRIDLOCK report, using risk modelling to analyse what an attack on BESS would cost the grid, it put the chance of a major coordinated attack on the UK's battery storage fleet at 92% within the next five years. The estimated financial cost is between £2 billion and £10 billion. But what's interesting from our analysis is that the probability of an attack falls as the security investment and enhancements increase. For example, under voluntary improvements adopted gradually and unevenly across the sector, the probability falls to 78%. With mandatory IEC 62443 certification and attack-readiness drills, it fall to just 61%. BESS are not passive assets. They are software-controlled, grid-interactive systems that directly influence frequency, load balancing and stability. The integration of IT and OT in energy storage systems increases their vulnerability. As more countries shift toward long-duration energy storage, these systems could face more frequent attacks. The issue is whether operators and asset owners are prioritising security. These are the questions every operator should be asking: 1. Do I have visibility into my distributed assets? When operators lose visibility into distributed assets, whether that's down to communication failures, misconfigurations, or malicious interference, the response becomes reactive rather than coordinated. Unlike centralised generation, battery assets are often remote and dispersed, and heavily dependent on real-time telemetry. Last year's attacks on Poland's power grid show just how threat actors understand how to manipulate remote locations simultaneously to destabilise critical power networks. Without continuous, validated visibility into operational states, operators are managing blind. 2. What happens if dispatch signals are manipulated? Battery systems do not just store energy; they respond to it. Charging and discharging decisions are driven by automated signals tied to grid frequency, market conditions, and control system inputs. If signals are altered, delayed, or spoofed, the behaviour of the battery changes accordingly. A coordinated manipulation of dispatch signals could cause batteries to discharge during peak stress or charge when supply is already constrained. At scale, this could become a major grid stability event. 3. How secure is my remote access infrastructure? Remote access is critical to today's energy operations. But it's also one of the most consistently exploited pathways into operational environments. The challenge is not just whether remote access exists, but whether it is continuously monitored, authenticated and segmented. One example of a UK battery facility revealed remote connectivity and VPN management as key vulnerabilities before security improvements were made. Without robust controls these pathways could directly access systems responsible for charging discharging and grid interaction. Remote access must be treated as a critical control point, or it becomes an attacker's shortcut. 4. Are my OT systems designed for today's threat environment? Many battery installations rely on industrial control systems (ICS) originally designed for isolated environments. But in today's environment, SCADA platforms, battery management systems and programmable logic controllers are connected to external networks. While this enables efficiency and scalability, it also exposes them. Advisories by CISA in the US have highlighted vulnerabilities in widely used ICS components, including unauthorised command execution, denial-of-service conditions, or system manipulation. In the UK BESS example, outdated firewalls, irregular patching and poor segmentation led to exploitable conditions within the operational environment. 5. Is cybersecurity being managed at the speed of deployment? The simple fact is that battery storage is being deployed faster than many operators can secure it. According to the IEA, global energy storage capacity is expected to grow more than six-fold by 2030. As growth accelerates, it creates a gap between what is operationally critical and what is operationally secured. In practice, this gap shows up in incomplete asset inventories, delayed patch cycles and limited monitoring of newly deployed systems. When basic vulnerabilities exist, attackers will always sense an opportunity. 6. Do I understand how cyber risk translates into financial impact? Cybersecurity in energy is often framed as a data protection issue. In BESS environments, it is an operational and financial issue. The GRIDLOCK report backs this up. It estimates that bringing the UK's battery storage infrastructure up to IEC 62443 Security Level 2 – the standard the modelling shows meaningfully reduces attack probability – would cost between £400m and £1bn across the national fleet. This is a return on proactive security investment of roughly 5x to 25x. The earliest likely attack window also changes, from 2027–28 under a baseline posture to 2029–31 under the most rigorous one. What's clear is that security investment reduces risk, but also buys time The grid is becoming far more distributed, connected and automated – and BESS is at the heart of this energy transformation. Distributed control without distributed visibility creates fragility rather than resilience. For operators the question is not whether cybersecurity matters, but why it matters.

artigo.texto: How Data Center Growth Is Reshaping Facility Design Rapid demand, AI workloads and power constraints are pushing developers into new markets while changing how data centers are designed and operated. September 28, 2026 By Jeff Wardon, Jr., Assistant Editor Key Takeaways: - Data center demand is pushing developers beyond traditional markets as they seek available power, land, connectivity and workforce capacity in emerging locations. - AI workloads are increasing power density and driving greater adoption of liquid cooling, adaptive reuse and other approaches to meet growing capacity needs. - Rapid growth is accelerating changes in data center mechanical and electrical design as operators seek new ways to overcome power and capacity constraints. North American data center demand reached 25 gigawatts (GW) of absorption in the first half of 2026, while vacancy has fallen to 1 percent or below, according to JLL’s North America Data Center Report Midyear 2026. However, this rapid growth isn’t due to AI alone. Society continues to create and consume more data, with data creation growing at roughly 23 to 25 percent annually, says Sean Farney, vice president of data center strategy at JLL. The bigger picture is that data center development is basically responding to the increasing demand for and dependence on digital services. “This is similar to what happened 100 years ago or so with the introduction of electricity,” Farney says. “Once people saw the benefits of electricity, they wanted to have electrical devices and they consumed more electricity. So, we’re dealing with a very similar kind of societal force. The industry is positioned well to take advantage of this new paradigm and the way we operate as humans.” Changes in site selection The ongoing shortage of land and power in traditional data center markets is changing how developers select sites. Historically, development was clustered around major metropolitan or telecommunications hubs such as Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta, Washington, New York and Los Angeles. Farney describes this as a shift towards what he calls a “de-marketization” of data center site selection. “So, it’s forced this new, what I call this new de-marketization of data center site selection,” Farney says. “It used to be there were things like markets, a real estate topic. Now the data center developers are simply going to where they can get to revenue fastest.” Factors influencing site selection now include power availability, fiber and network connectivity, land, taxes and regulations and workforce availability. New areas for data centers are being considered as well, including West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and Wisconsin. Moreover, developers are becoming more willing to solve individual site constraints rather than limiting development to established markets. However, this geographic shift poses a second issue: What happens when major infrastructure projects enter communities that haven’t traditionally hosted them? “When a data center comes into town, a whole bunch of jobs are created,” Farney says. “I built a data center in suburban Chicago years ago, and I kept 600 union electricians busy for more than nine months working triple shifts. That supported a lot of families, putting a lot of meals on tables.” Similarly, he points to large multi-gigawatt developments in West Texas as examples where entire towns are being employed for development projects. “JLL hired more than a couple of 100 people to staff a large project in Abilene over the last few years,” Farney says. “We work with local trades, local colleges and so on, to find, train and hire folks.” AI and changing data center requirements While AI is the fastest-growing segment, Farney cautions against treating it as the only source of growth. Traditional cloud-service-provider data centers continue to be built as well. AI facilities can operate at 50+ kilowatts (kW) per cabinet, he says. They also require much higher power density, and liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important for those environments. Farney adds that liquid cooling can be about 40 percent more efficient than moving air around in a closed-loop system. The bigger idea is that the basis of design for data centers is changing rapidly, as mechanical and electrical technologies have evolved significantly in just the past few years. Additionally, enterprises are reconsidering older on-premises data centers that had previously been emptied in favor of cloud computing. Some of these facilities may be retrofitted to support higher-density AI workloads. “It generally saves money over the long term for the enterprises,” Farney says. “It’s an adaptive reuse project. It’s not going out and trying to build a new data center. You don’t have to compete with the big guys. So that’s a great solution to some of this low vacancy that we’re seeing across the US.” Another consistent constraint is utility power availability. Developers are increasingly exploring their own power generation, including natural-gas generation, rather than waiting on traditional utility connections. This further illustrates how the industry is adapting its infrastructure strategy to keep pace with demand. Overall, the industry has historically been relatively conservative about mechanical and electrical systems because reliability is paramount, says Farney. However, pressure to bring capacity online is accelerating the adoption of cutting-edge technologies. “I really like to emphasize the massive change in data center basis of design,” Farney says. “We’ve experienced more change in the last three years from a tech perspective, the mechanical and electrical tech that runs data centers than we saw in the prior 20 years. I see all kinds of fascinating new technologies as part of this creative destruction as we move faster.” Jeff Wardon, Jr., is the assistant editor for the facilities market. artigo.texto: Projeto de níquel na Indonésia avança com plano híbrido de solar e armazenamento A Indonésia avançou com um projeto híbrido de energia solar fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia em baterias desenvolvido pela PT. Kolaka Nickel Indonesia, segundo comunicado da fonte. A instalação fica em Oko Oko, Pomalaa, na Regência de Kolaka, no Sudeste de Sulawesi, e combina um parque solar de 20 MWp com um sistema de armazenamento de energia de 20 MW / 30 MWh. O projeto representa um investimento corporativo em energia limpa autogerada, destinado a apoiar operações industriais. O financiamento foi obtido em janeiro de 2026 por meio de financiamento sem recurso de três bancos: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (Indonesia) Limited, também conhecido como ICBC Indonesia; Standard Chartered Bank Indonesia; e China CITIC Bank International Limited, ou CNCBI. A contratante de engenharia, aquisição e construção é a The 11th Design & Research Institute of Electronics Industry Co., Ltd., referida como EDRI. Essa empresa supervisionará o projeto, a aquisição e a construção da instalação de solar com armazenamento. Os módulos fotovoltaicos de alta eficiência da usina estão sendo fornecidos pela fabricante ZNSHINE SOLAR. Os módulos foram selecionados por sua durabilidade e desempenho e são projetados para resistir às condições tropicais da Indonésia, ao mesmo tempo que sustentam a confiabilidade de longo prazo do sistema. A entrada em operação está prevista para março de 2027. Uma vez em operação, espera-se que a instalação proporcione benefícios de descarbonização para as operações locais do setor de níquel. O projeto é apresentado como evidência de que a colaboração entre o desenvolvedor, a contratante de EPC e os credores internacionais pode apoiar tanto a gestão ambiental quanto a competitividade industrial. Seu desenvolvimento é descrito como um marco no caminho da Indonésia rumo a maior sustentabilidade e autossuficiência energética, à medida que o país continua a expandir a infraestrutura de energia renovável para a descarbonização industrial. artigo.texto: Kandi Technologies’ China Battery Exchange Secures Follow-On Order for CATL Heavy-Truck Battery Swap Stations Second Batch Order in Two Months Underscores Growing Value of CATL Partnership Jinhua, China, Sept. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kandi Technologies Group, Inc. ("Kandi" or the "Company") (NASDAQ GS: KNDI), a global innovator in intelligent equipment and a technology-driven platform company, today announced that its wholly-owned subsidiary, China Battery Exchange (Zhejiang) Technology Co., Ltd. ("China Battery Exchange"), has secured a second batch procurement order for heavy-truck battery swap station equipment from QIJI Energy, a subsidiary of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited ("CATL"). The order follows just two months after the initial batch order placed in July 2026, highlighting the continued commercial development of the Company's relationship with CATL. China Battery Exchange's cooperation with CATL began in August 2025, when the two companies signed a Framework Procurement Contract under which China Battery Exchange became part of CATL's global supplier network and began coordinating CATL's first order for a heavy-truck battery swap station, which was secured later that month. In January 2026, China Battery Exchange entered into a three-year strategic cooperation agreement to serve as a designated equipment supplier for QIJI Energy's heavy-truck battery-swapping program. In July 2026, QIJI Energy placed its first batch procurement order under the strategic cooperation agreement, marking China Battery Exchange's transition from product validation to commercial deployment. With its supplier relationship with CATL and approved-supplier status with QIJI Energy, China Battery Exchange is positioned to pursue additional equipment orders in connection with CATL's heavy-truck battery-swapping program . China Battery Exchange's Lin'an intelligent manufacturing facility commenced production in July 2026. With an expected annual production capacity of up to 200 battery swap stations, the facility is intended to support China Battery Exchange's ability to fulfill existing and potential future orders from CATL and serve additional battery swap equipment customers. Feng Chen, CEO of Kandi, commented, "We have received two batch orders within eight months of signing the QIJI Energy agreement, reflecting CATL's continued confidence in our products and delivery capabilities as well as the commercial potential of this partnership. We will continue to advance product development, expand production capacity and improve delivery efficiency to capture opportunities in the emerging heavy-truck battery swap market and establish battery swap equipment as a new growth engine for Kandi."

artigo.texto: Democrats See Opening In Long-Red Seat Over Data Center Tax Breaks Rally in River Falls spotlights anger over a $1.6 billion exemption and its GOP author, Shannon Zimmerman. Democrats trying to flip a Wisconsin Assembly seat long held by Republicans are hoping anti-data center sentiment will help them oust a GOP incumbent they call the “architect” of tax breaks helping drive a data center building boom in Wisconsin. Republican Assemblyman Shannon Zimmerman has held the 30th District for a decade. He says Democrats are trying to mislead voters, but Democratic challenger Kevin Knoke says Zimmerman is an AI executive with a conflict of interest. The sounds of speeches and the occasional chants of opposition to AI data center development and the state tax break for the industry echoed from the small Veterans Park in Downtown River Falls on a warm, sunny Wednesday evening. The 50 or so people were members of the western Wisconsin grassroots activism group called GROWW and they held signs that read “No Blank Checks For Big Tech” and “No Deals Behind Closed Doors.” The rally was aimed squarely at Zimmerman, R-River Falls, who authored legislation resulting in a tax exemption for the data center equipment and software. The Wisconsin Department of Revenue has estimated the tax exemption would cut an estimated $1.6 billion from the state’s coffers. “AI data centers are not only extracting water, but they’re also extracting wealth from our communities that could be invested into the things that real people need in their lives,” GROWW co-executive Director Bill Hogseth told the crowd before encouraging them to support Zimmerman’s Democratic challenger, Knoke, who was standing in the audience. Zimmerman’s 2023 bill had backing from Microsoft, business groups and several utilities that would be selling massive amounts of electricity to data centers. It even garnered some Democratic votes, but it never cleared the Legislature. Instead, the bill’s language was included in that year’s state budget, which was signed by Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Wisconsin has seen a data center building boom since the tax breaks were enacted, which has given rise to a surge of opposition from communities around the state. In an interview with WPR, Knoke said the high cost of gas, groceries and housing are top of mind for voters he’s talked to, but they’re also concerned about data centers looking to build in the 30th District. “One thing I can tell you right away is, I am not interested in tax giveaways to corporations,” said Knoke. “They need to pay their fair share.” Knoke has been accusing Zimmerman of having a data center conflict of interest because the lawmaker’s job history shows he’s held two executive positions with AI companies that could benefit from the tax breaks. Knoke said he’s not proposing an outright data center ban, but the state has to be careful. “We’ve got to move incredibly slow,” said Knoke. “I want to see that there’s ratepayer protections. I want to see that there are environmental protections. I want to see that there’s transparency, and most importantly, I want to see that there’s accountability. I want to know that these places are going to be held accountable for everything that they do.” In an emailed statement sent to WPR, Zimmerman said the criticisms from Knoke and fellow Democrats are “political fodder in a desperate act to mislead voters on a topic that is hyper political.” He said he started a tech business in River Falls 20 years ago and Knoke can’t prove a conflict of interest “because it simply is not true.” “My opponent is losing so he must now invent a narrative to scare voters,” Zimmerman wrote. “The original sales and use tax exemption is a long-standing economic practice used to drive major investment into WI. Gov Evers signed it. It was bipartisan. Evolving from that, for those who expressed concerns, I responded as the author of AB840. It specifically addresses energy, water, land and taxpayer concerns.” Zimmerman’s bill sought to require the Wisconsin Public Service Commission to ensure costs of upgrading electrical grids were not passed on to residential customers and require data centers to report how much water they use and set money aside for reclaiming land after the facilities close. The bill passed the Assembly with the help of just three Democrats, but died in the Senate. This year, the Public Service Commission took matters into its own hands by modifying a proposal from We Energies setting electric rates for data center-scale customers. At the time, the commission said the changes were meant to protect residential ratepayers and ensure data centers pay their own way. As public opposition to data centers has grown, Republican and Democratic candidates have been accusing each other of cozying up to big tech. Whether that line of attack on Zimmerman will help Knoke flip the Assembly seat is an open question, as Democrats have been unable to win the 30th District since 1977. artigo.texto: A expansão da inteligência artificial no mundo inteiro tem levado à corrida pela construção de data centers para suprir as necessidades de processamento desta tecnologia, e o Brasil é um palco importante para este desenvolvimento. Ao mesmo tempo que as empresas querem expandir os seus negócios, crescem as notícias sobre o impacto da construção de data centers nas cidades. Um exemplo é a cidade de Paracatu, em Minas Gerais, onde vereadores da Câmara Municipal descobriram que em breve a obra de um data center começará na região. O site O Eco fez uma reportagem sobre a referida obra, mostrando que não se trata de um data center qualquer: o equipamento terá a potência de 1 gigawatt, “maior que a soma total de todos os data centers atualmente instalados no país, que consomem cerca de 800 megawatts”. Só que a construção de data centers pode provocar danos ambientais, alto consumo de água e aumento do custo de energia para o consumidor, sem trazer benefícios reais para a população e para o país. Este assunto foi discutido em audiência pública no Senado em 4 de agosto na Comissão de Ciência e Tecnologia (CCT). O diretor-executivo do Instituto de Defesa do Consumidor (Idec), Igor Britto, ressalta que os data centers de inteligência artificial representam um alto consumo de energia elétrica sem capacidade de adaptação horária das atividades. “Temos empreendimentos de vários setores produtivos que já são organizados e se controlam para, por exemplo, evitar operar e consumir energia nos horários de maior pico. Isso não acontece com os data centers, que vão acabar sobrecarregando o sistema nesses horários. Todos nós pagamos. É necessário ter infraestrutura para mais geração, para mais distribuição, e o pior é que todos esses custos também são bancados pela tarifa. Cidades onde existem data centers tiveram aumento considerável na conta de energia e, quanto ao consumo de água, algumas residências chegam a ficar sem o abastecimento. As cooperativas nas diversas regiões do país precisam ficar atentas aos projetos vindouros, principalmente após a sanção da Lei 15.504, que cria incentivos fiscais para estimular a instalação de data centers, os centros de processamento de dados, e favorecer investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA) no Brasil. Apesar das preocupações com geração de energia e consumo de água, os data centers podem também ser uma forma de expansão tecnológica das cooperativas. Oportunidades No Paraná, um grupo de investidores apresentou em julho, ao Governo do Estado e a instituições paranaenses, a proposta de implantação de um super data center no município de Pinhais, na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba. Na oportunidade, os investidores informaram que têm interesse em realizar negócios com produtos do agronegócio das cooperativas paranaenses, contemplando especialmente soja, milho e proteínas animais. Segundo eles, o grupo projeta movimentar grandes volumes de exportação e conta com estrutura logística própria, incluindo frota e terminais portuários. Foi ainda mencionada a possibilidade de facilitar a aquisição de matérias-primas para a produção de fertilizantes e o fomento na região. Apesar de acreditarem ser um projeto promissor, seguir compromissos de sustentabilidade é necessário para o avanço do projeto.

artigo.texto: Setor de gás natural teme exclusão do Redata e se mobiliza por decreto Regime especial para datacenters prevê incentivos ao uso de fonte de "baixa emissão" para abastecer projetos, mas Fazenda quer limitar incentivos O setor de gás natural iniciou uma ofensiva junto ao governo para evitar que o insumo seja excluído do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center) como fonte de suprimento energético. Conforme relatos feitos à CNN, o decreto de regulamentação da nova lei está perto de sair. Hoje, segundo fontes, a tendência é que prevaleça um entendimento do Ministério da Fazenda de que o gás natural não se enquadra nos critérios para receber os incentivos do Redata. Na reta final de tramitação do projeto, aprovado neste mês pelo Senado, uma emenda de redação substituiu a exigência de uso de energias renováveis e limpas por fontes de "baixa emissão". Entre os combustíveis fósseis, o gás natural é o que menos emite gases-estufa e visto como uma fonte complementar à matriz elétrica, assegurando energia firme de menor geração das renováveis (como solar e eólica). O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) já se posicionou favoravelmente à inclusão do gás na regulamentação do Redata, mas a Fazenda é contra. Diante da indefinição, o setor foi na sexta-feira (25) ao MDIC (Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços), encarado como um possível aliado no impasse entre Fazenda e MME. Representantes do IBP (Instituto Brasileiro do Petróleo), da Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado) e da Abraget (Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas) estiveram com o secretário-adjunto de Desenvolvimento Industrial do MDIC, Luis Felipe Giesteira. Quatro possibilidades estão sendo aventadas: - Liberação do gás natural como fonte de suprimento energético - Liberação do gás natural com compensação das emissões geradas - Incentivos somente para fontes renováveis (energia nova ou existente) - Incentivos somente para investimentos novos em fontes renováveis (critério de adicionalidade) Para o diretor-executivo da Abegás, Marcelo Mendonça, a característica de renováveis como solar e eólica é a intermitência, o que comprometeria a estabilidade necessária para o investimento em data centers. O uso de térmicas a gás natural, segundo ele, possibilitaria oferecer uma energia "competitiva e firme" para atrair projetos no setor tecnológico. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), no entanto, tem dado sinais na direção contrária. "Não vamos deixar que a energia produzida vá somente para o data center. Quem quiser vir para cá terá que investir na construção em energia renovável", disse o petista, no dia 19, em campanha em Santa Catarina. A fala foi interpretada como uma tendência de que o governo optará pelo critério de adicionalidade em fontes limpas como habilitação para o Redata. A iniciativa privada e setores na Esplanada dos Ministérios que discordam disso tentam, nos bastidores, ganhar tempo para discutir melhor a regulamentação antes do decreto presidencial.

artigo.texto: Gotion High-Tech has secured 6 GWh of battery energy storage capacity under Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) procurement program, representing around 75% of the total capacity awarded in the first phase. The award was made by Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) as part of the Kingdom’s efforts to expand energy storage alongside renewable energy deployment. The G1 project has a total capacity of 2 GW/8 GWh and an estimated value of $1.16 billion. Gotion has been selected for three sites: Al Muwayah, Haden, and Al Kahafa. Each site will have a capacity of 500 MW/2 GWh. The award makes Gotion the largest single technology supplier in the first phase of Saudi Arabia’s utility-scale storage program. The projects will deploy Gotion Grid, marking the first international large-scale deployment of the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. According to Gotion, the system is designed for harsh desert conditions and can operate between -30°C and 55°C. The company said its thermal management system is optimized for high-temperature and dusty environments, allowing the batteries to maintain output during sandstorms and reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The system has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. Gotion Grid also incorporates an artificial intelligence-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, safety monitoring, and lifecycle diagnostics. The three projects will be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380 kV transmission network. The award strengthens Gotion’s presence in the Middle East and North Africa energy storage market. The company said its regional pipeline and projects total around 9 GWh, including a 1.5 GWh BESS project in Egypt and a 1.2 GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. In Egypt, Gotion is also planning a 3 GWh local manufacturing facility. Globally, the company said its cumulative system-level energy storage projects have exceeded 10 GWh. Its international portfolio includes a 281 MW/843 MWh solar-plus-storage project in Australia, which is under construction and expected to achieve commercial operation in the first half of 2027. Saudi Arabia has already started the next stage of its storage procurement program, with G2 underway. The G1 award is therefore expected to provide an important reference for future utility-scale BESS tenders as the Kingdom increases renewable energy capacity and strengthens grid flexibility. artigo.texto: ORANGEBURG- Congressman Mike Lawler (R, NY-17) is demanding that Governor Kathy Hochul and the New York Power Authority disclose the value of discounted electricity being provided to data centers in Orangeburg. Lawler’s action follows reporting that three of the four data centers in the Orangeburg section of Orangetown receive discounted hydropower through NYPA’s ReCharge NY program. NYPA has declined to disclose the rates individual facilities pay or the value of their discounts, saying the information is proprietary and protected by contracts. Lawler is calling on the state to at least disclose the total annual cost of the discounts and the average subsidy provided to participating businesses. ReCharge NY is a statewide economic-development program that provides qualifying businesses and nonprofits access to lower-cost hydropower through long-term contracts. NYPA says the program is intended to support business growth and job retention across the state. The issue comes as data centers face increased scrutiny in New York because of their electricity demands. Hochul announced a one-year moratorium on certain new large-scale data center projects in July and said the state would pursue additional protections for ratepayers. Lawler said greater transparency is needed as New York weighs the economic benefits and infrastructure demands associated with data center development. “Transparency has to apply to government too,” Lawler said. “If New York is going to use public power to attract data centers, it should be able to tell the public what the deal is and what taxpayers get in return.”

artigo.texto: Suntech has showcased its latest N-type PV and energy storage solutions at the 2026 edition of Solar & Storage Live UK in Birmingham, highlighting advances in quarter-cut cell technology, high-efficiency modules and integrated solar-storage applications. The UK solar market continues to expand, driven by strong growth in rooftop installations and the growing integration of solar and battery storage. With solar becoming increasingly important across residential, commercial and utility-scale applications, the market is placing greater emphasis on technologies that can make effective use of available space while delivering reliable energy generation. As solar-storage integration gains momentum, demand for high-efficiency and reliable PV technologies continues to grow across utility-scale projects, industrial and commercial rooftops and residential applications, making module efficiency, energy yield and long-term performance increasingly important considerations for projects in the UK. Against this backdrop, the exhibition featured Suntech’s products across key stages of PV manufacturing, from silicon wafers and solar cells to modules. It also highlighted the continued refinement of N-type quarter-cut cell technology, with a focus on optimizing cell architecture and current distribution to reduce energy losses and improve power generation. By carrying these cell-level advances into module design, the company is further developing high-efficiency module solutions for a range of applications. This approach is particularly relevant to projects where making the most of available installation space and maximizing energy yield are important considerations, including residential and commercial rooftops. This technology is further demonstrated in its Ultra T 3.0 quarter-cut modules, a key highlight of the exhibition. Built on Suntech’s proprietary TOPCon 3.0 cell technology, Ultra T 3.0 combines an optimized quarter-cut cell architecture with advanced high-density encapsulation. The module achieves a cell conversion efficiency of up to 27.5% and a module efficiency of more than 25.2%, enabling higher power output while supporting long-term reliability, its high-efficiency design helping make effective use of available rooftop and project space. Also featured at the exhibition was the Ultra T 2.0, a 520W half-cell N-type TOPCon module, further extending Suntech’s module offering for commercial and residential applications. In addition to its PV portfolio, the company also showcased its self-developed SunStorage energy storage systems for commercial and residential applications. Featuring a modular design, high-voltage architecture and flexible expansion capability, the systems can be combined with Suntech PV modules to provide integrated solutions for households and small businesses, enabling daytime solar generation, energy storage, night time power supply and backup electricity during outages. SunStorage offers both AC-coupled and DC-coupled solutions, providing flexibility for different system configurations and application needs. The combination of PV modules and energy storage enables a more coordinated approach to solar generation, storage and power consumption, supporting the growing demand for integrated solar-storage solutions across the UK market.

artigo.texto: BYD says it will have an electric vehicle with a solid-state battery in 2027 — InsideEVs Chinese company BYD plans to have its first electric vehicle model with a solid-state battery in 2027. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said this in an interview with Carwow.es, InsideEVs reports. First model with the new technology According to Li, the company will “have one model” with this technology next year. She also said that BYD holds a leading position in the development of solid-state batteries. At the same time, the top manager did not specify which model would be equipped with the new battery or when it would appear. It is also unclear whether this refers to a full market launch of the vehicle or a demonstration prototype. The publication notes that Chinese automakers, including BYD, are rapidly introducing new technologies into production models. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Possible Yangwang flagship CarNewsChina sources claim that the solid-state battery may be used in the recently teased flagship sedan of the Yangwang brand. BYD has not confirmed this information. The InsideEVs author suggests that the expensive technology at an early stage could first be used in a premium model, such as the Denza Z9 or BYD Great Tang. Solid-state batteries are considered a promising technology for electric vehicles: they may be lighter and safer, have higher energy density, and support faster charging. At the same time, automakers are still working to resolve technological issues and establish mass production of such batteries. Toyota plans to launch an electric vehicle with this technology in 2027 or 2028, while Honda and Mercedes are targeting a period closer to 2030.

artigo.texto: Redata aproxima o Brasil da soberania na infraestrutura digital A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, criou condições para acelerar projetos represados e ampliar a capacidade brasileira de processamento. Essa medida gerou uma oportunidade industrial de alcance. Chegou no momento em que a inteligência artificial exige mais servidores, memória, energia e capacidade de rede. O novo modelo tributário destrava bilhões em aportes paralisados diante da corrida pela computação de alto desempenho. Mais de 106 megawatts foram entregues no primeiro semestre de 2026 e outros 134 megawatts estão previstos até dezembro. Cerca de 56% do estoque de data centers em construção no país já apresentava contratos de pré-locação consolidados antes mesmo da aprovação parlamentar e da sanção presidencial. Havia uma demanda latente. O Redata catalisou um mercado preexistente ao eliminar a trava tributária que adiava decisões urgentes. O marco regulatório canaliza e multiplica essa força. A norma alcança dois atores fundamentais. Um deles é a empresa habilitada, responsável por operar o data center. O outro é a coabilitada, que fabrica os equipamentos para essa infraestrutura de TI. Em troca das isenções federais, o operador reserva ao menos 10% da capacidade instalada ao mercado interno e aplica 2% do valor dos equipamentos adquiridos em inovação. O formato operacional dessas contrapartidas, os critérios de sustentabilidade e os trâmites de coabilitação ainda dependem de regulamentação complementar do Executivo. A direção estratégica, contudo, já está dada. Esse percentual ganha corpo ao lado dos 5% injetados compulsoriamente pelas fabricantes de servidores por meio da Lei de Informática. Essa união de cifras constrói a maior transferência de recursos já destinada à pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país. O ponto central do marco legal, previsto no artigo 11-C da Lei 11.196/2005, com redação dada pela Lei nº 15.504/2026 e que instituiu o Redata, revela uma engenharia regulatória inteligentíssima. A desoneração da contribuição ao PIS-Pasep e da Cofins alcança de forma horizontal toda cadeia produtiva. A manutenção da cobrança do Imposto de Importação para equipamentos com produção nacional equivalente e do IPI para os equipamentos produzidos na Zona Franca de Manaus, cria as travas de proteção essenciais. Incentivo fiscal para tecnologias inexistentes no país constitui política industrial coerente e responsável. Desonerar importações predatórias de máquinas já fabricadas internamente causa desindustrialização subsidiada. A regra atual protege quem produz no Brasil, seja qual for a origem do capital investido. Empresas globais de hardware mantêm fábricas aqui ao lado de companhias brasileiras, sob o mesmo rigoroso critério. O mercado nacional de servidores ganha uma expansão sem precedentes com essa barreira inteligente. Permitir a importação isenta de um equipamento pronto anularia a competitividade das operações industriais instaladas no país e destruiria cadeias inteiras de fornecedores. O Redata evitou essa armadilha. A legislação assegura a previsibilidade necessária para as fábricas investirem pesado em novas linhas de produção e contratarem mais talentos para a engenharia local. O parque fabril no nosso país superou, definitivamente, a fase de mera linha de montagem. A realidade das fábricas expõe uma maturidade densa e o domínio prático de uma etapa decisiva. Engenharia de ponta, arquitetura térmica, integração complexa, testes exaustivos e suporte contínuo ocorrem no território nacional. Fabricar a infraestrutura da inteligência artificial exige calibração milimétrica de energia e certificações rigorosas que consomem meses de dedicação exclusiva de times altamente especializados. Nos últimos anos, a título de exemplo, entregamos sucessivos sistemas de supercomputação para o setor de óleo e gás, com integração nacional completa. Construímos sólida tradição tecnológica nesse segmento, e essas máquinas operam hoje entre as maiores do mundo em capacidade de processamento de dados. As placas aceleradoras vêm de fora, mas toda a inteligência da integração ganha forma, escala e excelência aqui. A repatriação veloz de cargas de trabalho tem impulsionado a demanda por hardware local. Em paralelo, os custos financeiros para treinar modelos computacionais aumentaram exponencialmente. Faturas forçam as organizações a transferir operações complexas das nuvens públicas para ambientes locais blindados. Diretores de tecnologia encontram na escolha de um servidor nacional a convergência exata entre eficiência de custos e segurança de dados. Esses líderes corporativos valorizam a vantagem estratégica de ter o fabricante do hardware fisicamente próximo. Essa proximidade garante a customização ágil da arquitetura, viabiliza manutenções críticas em tempo recorde e assegura a continuidade das operações sem o risco atrelado à dependência de um suporte técnico estrangeiro distante. A soberania digital do Brasil ganha uma dimensão muito concreta com o Redata. O país dispensa a fantasia da autossuficiência em semicondutores para desenvolver uma indústria real de inteligência artificial. Nós podemos importar GPUs e processadores e, ainda assim, dominar a engenharia que transforma esses componentes isolados em sistemas capazes de processar dados, sustentar aplicações críticas e receber suporte local. Os próximos cinco anos serão decisivos para essa estratégia. O Brasil reúne mercado vigoroso, matriz elétrica favorável, conectividade internacional e uma indústria de servidores totalmente preparada para acompanhar o aumento expressivo da demanda. O avanço dependerá, essencialmente, da coordenação entre política tributária, energia, infraestrutura, ciência e regulamentação tecnicamente precisa. O Redata cria oportunidade rara de converter novos investimentos estrangeiros em produção fabril, engenharia aplicada e capacidade computacional instalada no país. artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial não mora na nuvem. Ela ocupa terrenos, usa equipamentos, consome eletricidade, rejeita calor e exige redes de transmissão e fibra ótica. É legítimo perguntar quem pagará por essa infraestrutura e o que receberão as comunidades que a abrigarem. Uma pesquisa divulgada em 22 de setembro pelo Fórum Econômico Mundial registra a expectativa de seus economistas-chefes de que os data centers contribuam para o crescimento, mas também tragam pressão sobre serviços públicos, poucos empregos diretos e resistência local. É um alerta importante. Não é, porém, uma lei da física nem uma sentença para todos os países e projetos. A demanda por energia já cresce por razões muito mais amplas. Queremos casas mais confortáveis, ar-condicionado, mobilidade elétrica, serviços digitais, equipamentos de saúde e processos produtivos mais sofisticados. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers responderão por cerca de um décimo do crescimento mundial do consumo elétrico até 2030: uma parcela relevante, mas inferior à de motores industriais, climatização de edifícios e veículos elétricos. Culpar exclusivamente a IA por toda alta da conta de luz seria tão impreciso quanto afirmar que ela não terá impacto algum. Também precisamos distinguir duas coisas que frequentemente aparecem misturadas. Uma família pode pagar mais porque passou a consumir mais eletricidade e, portanto, a usufruir mais serviços e conforto. Pode pagar mais, também, porque subiu o preço de cada quilowatt-hora. Nesse segundo caso, importam os custos da geração, das redes, dos encargos e dos tributos, assim como as decisões sobre quem financia novos investimentos. Chamar tudo isso de “efeito dos data centers” encobre escolhas de política energética e distribuição de custos que devem ser transparentes. Uma grande instalação mal localizada pode, sim, disputar capacidade elétrica e água com a população. Se a rede precisar ser ampliada para atendê-la, não é aceitável simplesmente espalhar a conta entre consumidores residenciais sem demonstrar os benefícios correspondentes. Mas o resultado pode ser diferente quando o empreendedor paga pelas instalações que provoca, contrata geração renovável adicional, ajuda a viabilizar armazenamento e flexibilidade e se instala onde há capacidade ou geração hoje restringida. No Nordeste, essa possibilidade merece estudo projeto a projeto: energia renovável sujeita a curtailment não equivale automaticamente a suprimento firme, disponível 24 horas por dia. O mesmo rigor vale para a água. Um circuito fechado dentro do data center não assegura consumo hídrico próximo de zero: é preciso saber como o calor será finalmente rejeitado. Em regiões de escassez, a localização e a tecnologia de refrigeração devem ser escolhidas antes da licença, com divulgação de captação, consumo efetivo, origem da água e desempenho verificado. Reúso, refrigeração seca e sistemas híbridos são alternativas a comparar, não promessas genéricas. Quanto aos empregos, não devemos vender um data center como uma fábrica que manterá milhares de trabalhadores em seu interior. Seu valor potencial está também na construção, nos serviços especializados e, sobretudo, no que uma região consegue desenvolver ao redor da infraestrutura: pesquisa, formação, computação, aplicações de IA e empresas locais. Esse efeito não nasce sozinho. Requer contratos, investimento em pessoas e instituições capazes de ligar a capacidade computacional à economia regional. A resistência das comunidades tampouco pode ser descartada como medo do futuro. Uma pesquisa da Universidade da Pensilvânia encontrou oposição à instalação de data centers próximos entre 61% dos adultos consultados nos Estados Unidos. Esse dado não descreve automaticamente o Brasil, mas ensina algo: as pessoas percebem quando os custos são locais e os benefícios, distantes. Reprimir ou execrar data centers não resolve a demanda por processamento. Afastá-los sem critério pode apenas transferir consumo de energia, impactos e oportunidades para outros lugares. A resposta é estabelecer condições para recebê-los: conexão planejada; custos de expansão atribuídos com justiça; energia progressivamente menos emissora; metas auditáveis de eficiência elétrica e hídrica; participação das comunidades desde o início; e contrapartidas proporcionais, verificáveis e duradouras. Feito assim, um data center pode deixar de parecer um grande consumidor que chegou para disputar recursos e tornar-se parceiro na expansão da infraestrutura local. As comunidades não têm obrigação de acolher qualquer projeto. Têm o direito de exigir que ele melhore, em vez de encarecer, suas condições de vida. Portanto, a questão é menos sobre quem pagará essa conta, e mais sobre quem colherá os benefícios e quem fará regras impedirão que o futuro dos data centers seja construído às custas dos seus vizinhos. ❗ Se você tem algum posicionamento a acrescentar nesta matéria ou alguma correção a fazer, entre em contato com [email protected]. ✅ Receba as notícias do Brasil 247 e da TV 247 no Telegram do 247 e no canal do 247 no WhatsApp. Marque o Brasil 247 como fonte preferida no Google: Apoie o jornalismo independente do 247:

artigo.texto: A Rússia atingiu neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, e um data center da Vodafone Ukraine, a segunda maior. Zelensky disse que um data center em Kiev foi atingido duas vezes, ferindo duas crianças e um adulto. Os ataques a data centers não são um caso isolado. Na semana anterior, a Rússia já havia atingido centros de dados de provedores de internet, deixando cerca de 100 mil residências de Kiev e região sem conexão ou com internet degradada. A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais — eles salvam vidas. Por que a Rússia mudou de alvo agora? Segundo o instituto de pesquisa ISW, o Kremlin amplia o conjunto de alvos em busca de "mecanismos alternativos de derrota", porque as ofensivas russas em 2026 não avançaram no campo de batalha, enquanto a Ucrânia registrou ganhos que o próprio instituto chama de estrategicamente significativos. Entre 23 e 25 de setembro, ataques russos danificaram pelo menos quatro data centers em Kiev: os operados pela UTELS e pela Pavutyna, e depois os da Cosmonova e da Datagroup. Um representante do ponto de troca de tráfego de internet 1-IX resumiu a mudança de padrão: os ataques a data centers passaram a ser sistemáticos desde setembro, e não mais esporádicos. O Ministério da Defesa russo afirma que o alvo são sistemas de comunicação militares. O governo ucraniano diz não ter encontrado dano a redes militares ou institucionais. A diferença separa dois tipos de guerra: uma contra alvos militares, outra contra a vida civil. Especialistas ouvidos pela imprensa ucraniana avaliam que um apagão nacional completo de internet é improvável, graças a sistemas de backup e à distribuição da infraestrutura entre fronteiras. O ataque a data centers é parte de um padrão mais amplo: dias antes, a Rússia já havia mirado a maior siderúrgica da Ucrânia, forçando a parada da produção. O contexto de fundo é um front que praticamente não se move: Zelensky recorreu recentemente a uma métrica pouco usual para mostrar o custo do imobilismo russo, contando baixas do Exército russo por quilômetro quadrado conquistado. A resposta ucraniana também mira infraestrutura: em setembro, drones atingiram uma refinaria em Moscou no dia da eleição russa. O episódio mostra que ataques a infraestrutura estratégica correm nos dois sentidos da guerra. O ponto em aberto Se a mudança de alvo é resposta a um impasse militar, a pergunta é até quando a Rússia sustenta essa estratégia sem conseguir travar de fato o funcionamento da internet ucraniana, dada a infraestrutura de backup já existente no país. O que acontece agora Zelensky anunciou a decisão de reforçar a proteção física de data centers e instalações de comunicação no país. Não há, porém, prazo definido para a conclusão dessas medidas.

artigo.texto: The expert speaker slated to address the City of Sheboygan on data center issues cancelled out on Monday, but tomorrow’s meeting will still be held. From 6-7 PM Wednesday at Uptown Social there will be a review of the previous three speakers and a question-and-answer session. In previous sessions the meetings included the President of Alliant Energy, Becky Valcq, who told attendees that while there are tangible benefits to data centers, challenges to the grid are inevitable. Dr. Ben Green, co-author of “What Happens When Data Centers Come to Town” gave an overview during the second session of local impacts on economies of energy and resources, and how local governments need to craft careful zoning laws to manage those impacts. The Senior Policy Coordinator for the Great Plains Institute, Bridget Williams, was the speaker at last Wednesday’s session and warned that while some data centers use only as much electricity as a hotel, the largest can use almost 3 times the capacity of the entire Point Beach Nuclear Plant. Those and other discoveries will be used to eventually craft zoning laws to regulate data centers should one ever want to locate in Sheboygan.

artigo.texto: A Rússia atacou neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, localizada na capital Kiev. Segundo a empresa, que confirmou o episódio à agência de notícias Interfax Ucrânia, o prédio foi danificado, mas nenhum funcionário ficou ferido. A estrutura já havia sido atingida em outros ataques realizados ao longo deste mês. O bombardeio faz parte de uma ofensiva russa mais ampla contra data centers e a infraestrutura de comunicações do país, intensificada nas últimas semanas. De acordo com o ministro das Relações Exteriores ucraniano, Andrii Sybiha, o objetivo de Moscou é interromper o fluxo de informações, o que afeta também os alertas sobre mísseis e drones enviados à população. Leia mais: - TIM segue na bolsa após Correios da Itália não atingir 90% das ações - Vero amplia portfólio B2B com nuvem, móvel e câmeras com IA - Empresas tentam comprar a Oi Soluções ‘fiado’ mas Justiça do Rio rejeita VODAFONE UCRÂNIA TAMBÉM FOI ALVO O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia afirmou, também no domingo, que atingiu um data center da Vodafone Ucrânia, segunda maior operadora de telefonia celular do país. A companhia não respondeu aos pedidos de comentário e não havia confirmado o ataque à agência Reuters. Até o momento, não há informações sobre possíveis impactos no serviço prestado aos clientes da operadora. No mesmo dia, o presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, relatou que a Rússia atingiu duas vezes um data center em Kiev durante a manhã. Segundo ele, duas crianças e um adulto ficaram feridos na ação. Não foi divulgado qual empresa é responsável pela instalação atacada, nem se houve interrupção nos serviços de conectividade oferecidos a partir do local. PROVEDORES DE INTERNET NA MIRA A ofensiva de domingo não foi um caso isolado. Na semana anterior, Moscou já havia atingido data centers de provedores de internet ucranianos, provocando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e nos arredores, segundo o Ministério da Transformação Digital da Ucrânia. Algumas operadoras precisaram recorrer a instalações de backup para manter os clientes conectados. Empresas de telecomunicações atingidas recentemente: - Kyivstar: sede em Kiev atingida no domingo (27), sem feridos - Vodafone Ucrânia: data center atingido, segundo o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia - UTELS, Pavutyna e Datagroup: provedores com data centers danificados na última semana Quer acompanhar tudo em primeira mão sobre o mundo das telecomunicações? Siga o Minha Operadora no Canal no WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, X e YouTube e não perca nenhuma atualização, alerta, promoção ou polêmica do setor! O PAPEL ESTRATÉGICO DAS TELECOMUNICAÇÕES Para o chanceler ucraniano, a estratégia russa tem um alvo claro e coloca vidas em risco. Em publicação feita na rede social X na quarta-feira (23), Sybiha escreveu: “A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais. Eles salvam vidas”. Os ataques evidenciam a vulnerabilidade da infraestrutura de comunicações da Ucrânia, que tem se mantido em funcionamento durante a guerra graças a redes redundantes, instalações de backup e trabalhos rápidos de restauração. Em um país sob bombardeios frequentes, manter a telefonia móvel e a internet ativas é essencial para a circulação de informações e para os alertas de segurança.

artigo.texto: Building Resilience Into Digital Infrastructure As infrastructure expands beyond traditional regions, organizations will be better positioned by using a lifecycle approach to network resiliency. September 28, 2026 Sponsored by SES AI Growth Is Changing Infrastructure Assumptions Major hyperscale cloud providers have launched over 50 cloud regions in the past five years, and the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure is forcing data center operators to rethink long-standing assumptions about site selection and deployment. Growth in cloud services and AI workloads is pushing infrastructure into a wider range of geographies, exposing operators to new risks as facilities move beyond traditional connectivity hubs. While considerations of power, land acquisition, cooling, and permitting all remain important, connectivity readiness in some geographies can be just as consequential as power readiness. Connectivity Risk Is Changing Beyond well-documented financial impacts of outages, operators must also consider the potential cost to customer trust. If a fiber or power cable is cut, can you answer questions about the security systems in the data center? Can you tell a customer if their cage door was recently opened? Operators must also account for disruptions that occur well beyond the data center itself. As AI infrastructure footprints expand into new regions, connectivity can be affected by subsea cable failures, natural disasters, regional infrastructure disruptions, geopolitical events, civil instability, and other factors out of a facility operator’s control. For example, in 2024, a rockslide off the coast of West Africa caused multiple subsea cable breaks, disrupting service in West Africa. The Red Sea has experienced two incidents of simultaneous fiber cuts. As operators expand into new geographies and new risk environments, connectivity resilience is becoming a core design consideration. From the operator perspective, the question isn't whether connectivity outages occur but how critical management systems will remain reachable when those outages occur. Resilience Beyond Redundancy Traditional planning suggests that multiple fiber providers deliver resilience. But subsea routes and regional infrastructure concentration can create hidden dependencies. Resilient designs will look at carrier, path, and infrastructure diversity. Operators should consider if their resiliency plans provide: - Guaranteed capacity to help avoid consumer-grade congestion concerns. - Private routing options to avoid public internet exposure. - Flexible traffic routing that can support in-country routing, specific cloud destinations, and recovery sites outside a potential disruption zone. - Meaningful upload throughput for continuous support and visibility of operational systems, infrastructure management, and security platforms. Sovereign Infrastructure Is Raising the Stakes As both governments and enterprises place more emphasis on compliance, data control, and transparency, connectivity decisions now extend beyond uptime and resilience. During outages or failover events, organizations may also need visibility into where traffic is routed and how network paths align with jurisdictional requirements. This is driving interest in network designs that combine resilience with greater visibility into routing decisions. One Planned Connectivity Lifecycle Joining Construction, Commissioning, and Operational Resilience Resilience is most effective and cost-efficient in the long term when it is designed into a facility from the outset. By viewing connectivity as a lifecycle consideration rather than a series of point solutions, operators can take a more consistent approach to ensuring critical management, monitoring, and security systems remain accessible throughout the life of the facility. For example, a facility’s connectivity requirements may evolve like this as it moves from construction to operations: - During construction, delivering communications, site monitoring, security support, and temporary operational access before permanent infrastructure is in place. - As the facility approaches launch, enabling initial network access, testing, commissioning, and operational readiness. - Once the facility enters production, a shift from enablement to resilience with satellite serving as an independent management path, operational backup, and recovery communications channel. Conclusion Old connectivity assumptions are becoming harder to sustain as operators expand into new geographies and face new sources of infrastructure risk. In the AI era, the impact of lost connectivity grows, and connectivity resilience is a design decision that should be made well before a facility's first workload goes live. Successful infrastructure projects will evaluate connectivity with the same rigor applied to power, land, and cooling infrastructure. About the Author: Robert Hegblom is Sr. Principal Product Manager for Land and Sovereign Enterprise at SES, where he builds multi-orbit satellite connectivity offerings for global businesses and telco partners. He also has a decade of experience expanding data centers to underserved locations for hyperscale cloud providers, content delivery networks.

A infraestrutura será integrada na plataforma da empresa, permitindo reforçar a oferta dirigida a empresas e administrações públicas. O investimento anunciado poderá atingir os 100 milhões de euros e será direcionado para novas infraestruturas digitais, seguindo os padrões de sustentabilidade e eficiência definidos pela empresa. A NxN Data Centers afirma pretender construir uma presença de longo prazo em Portugal e continuar a identificar novas oportunidades de crescimento no mercado nacional.

artigo.texto: Lexington residents rally against proposed data center near Green Acres Park Neighbors cite water, utility bills, and traffic concerns as city leaders urge public turnout ahead of an Oct. 6 meeting LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) — Residents gathered Sunday near Green Acres Park to voice sharp opposition to a proposed Lexington data center, just weeks before the city’s development moratorium is set to expire. The pushback centers on Texas-based developer DartPoints, which recently purchased a portion of the former Lexmark campus off New Circle Road. The company plans to use 20 to 30 megawatts of power initially, with capacity to expand up to 70 megawatts. For neighbors living less than two miles from the site, the proposal sparked serious concerns over water usage, rising utility bills, and increased traffic. “I am here today to say no to the data center,” one young resident said from the podium during Sunday’s community meeting. Officials urge public turnout ahead of key meeting Lexington Mayor Linda Gorton joined residents at Sunday’s meeting, reiterating that city officials were never given advance notice of the private real estate transaction. “What happened downtown that day, when we read it, we all said, ‘Did you know about this? Did you know about this?’” Gorton told the crowd. “No one knew about this.” Gorton said the Urban County Council should not rush to a decision and urged the public to attend an upcoming special hearing to voice their concerns. The council’s Committee of the Whole will hold a public input session at 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 6 at City Hall (200 E. Main St.) — weeks before the city’s current moratorium expires on Oct. 31. Vice Mayor Dan Wu, Councilmember Tyler Morton, and Fayette County Public Schools Board Chair Tyler Murphy also attended Sunday’s meeting and addressed the crowd. Mayoral candidate Raquel Carter spoke to WKYT following the event, arguing that concern over the project reaches well beyond the immediate neighborhood. “I think it’s clear no one wants them. There is no place for them here,” Carter said. “Large-scale data centers are just concerning to everyone.” Neighbors lean on ‘people power’ Community organizers say public turnout at City Hall is their strongest leverage against the developer heading into October. “It’s people power. That is the power that we have,” organizer Katie Dapkus said. “We don’t have the financial resources to advocate for our position, but what we do have is community. And I think now more than ever we need reminded of how powerful that can be.” WKYT reached out to DartPoints for comment regarding Sunday’s meeting and is waiting to hear back. Copyright 2026 WKYT. artigo.texto: Granbury residents stage walkout during city council meeting amid data center controversy GRANBURY, Texas - Dozens of Granbury residents walked out of Monday night's city council meeting as city leaders pushed back on petitions for their removal over alleged plans to build a data center in the city. Granbury data center concept Granbury data center concept What we know: Earlier in 2026, Granbury City Council voted to annex 2,200 acres of land near Meadow Wood Road. Now, there are plans for a data center to be built on the land. The city says it has received concept plans for the center, which is called Project Patriot. Project Patriot's website says the data center is being planned as a "self-sufficient campus with on-site power generation and privately funded infrastructure designed to minimize impacts on local utilities, public services, and taxpayers." Recall petition Local perspective: Some Granbury residents believe their city's leaders didn't disclose enough information about the potential data center before the land was annexed. Those concerns led to 15% of the city's population signing a petition to recall Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt and four city council members, with over 1,300 signatures on the petition. "They tend to do this. We speak, they don’t hear what we’re saying," Rachael Jacobson, a resident, tells FOX 4's David Sentendrey. "Maybe they hear it, but they don’t hear what we’re saying — and then the rest of this show goes on and they just do whatever they want." "The city council, whatever their intentions may be, neglected to listen to the citizens and the citizens have decided they’re not going to tolerate than anymore — to the tune of over 1,300 signatures on multiple recall petitions," said Alex Wolf, a Granbury resident and Granbury City Council-elect. Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt "A circus" The other side: "I will not resign." At Monday's Granbury City Council meeting, Jarratt and city council members defended themselves. Jarratt said he believes there are procedural issues with the recall petition. "The petition against me does not explain any substance whatsoever, which makes it impossible for me to defend my public record against a generic accusation that could potentially span over the past five-and-a-half years. That’s how long I’ve been your mayor." When Granbury City Councilman Skip Overdier began speaking against the recall petition, dozens of Granbury residents walked out of the meeting. Rachael Jacobson described the meeting as "a circus." "You could tell they weren’t listening when we spoke during public comment." What's next: Petitioners are hoping to get the recall on the November ballot. A court battle over the proposed data center is also looming. City officials say any official development plans for the data center would go through the city's normal review process, and would need to meet zoning and development standards before approval. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Granbury City Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Reporter's Notebook: Why data center fights cut across party lines NPR's Scott Neuman went to Virginia and Maryland to report on data centers. In this reporter's notebook, he shares why opposition to new ones is bringing together people who rarely agree on politics. DEBBIE ELLIOTT, HOST: A little more than a month out from the midterm elections, one issue is uniting voters. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT) SCOTT NEUMAN, BYLINE: Across the country, local leaders are being held to account over allowing data centers that deliver more tax revenue but also bring a host of concerns over electricity demand and water consumption. ELLIOTT: That's NPR's Scott Neuman, reporting earlier this week on the growing movement against data centers. In his reporting, Scott came across Maryland farmer Steve Black. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT) NEUMAN: About a mile from his farm, a new 2,000-acre data center is under construction. In November, he plans to support a diverse slate of local candidates with just one requirement - they must oppose data centers. STEVE BLACK: Some people are Democrats that I'm supporting, and some are Republicans, and it no longer matters to me. ELLIOTT: So for this week's Reporter's Notebook, we wanted to speak with Scott about what he learned covering this movement. I started by asking him what made him realize this opposition to data centers was becoming such an important story he wanted to dig into. NEUMAN: Any part of the country, you could find these grassroots groups that were popping up on social media, and you could find local news stories that said, you know, the city council members who had signed nondisclosure agreements in some cases with AI developers or governments. ELLIOTT: Yeah, I've run across that in my region, covering... NEUMAN: Yeah. ELLIOTT: ...Other stories. NEUMAN: Exactly. ELLIOTT: And you run into the activists, right? NEUMAN: Right. So this is all over the country, this is going on. And the interesting thing is that you think of - you know, I think - and especially in the last, say, decade, people's minds have been kind of - like, at the national level, the - all the oxygen, you know, the political oxygen, has... ELLIOTT: Right. NEUMAN: ...Been at that level. And all of a sudden, you know, this is an issue that crosses party lines. It really challenges, like, traditional alliances on the local level. And you're seeing, like, people get engaged on the local level. Like, I haven't seen anything like that or that's taken off that quickly. ELLIOTT: Kind of taking us back to that old adage, all politics is local, which... NEUMAN: Exactly. ELLIOTT: ...We haven't been able to say for - what? NEUMAN: Right. ELLIOTT: ...A decade now. NEUMAN: Exactly. ELLIOTT: So how did you pick where to tell this story from? Was there a particular community that seemed to be the perfect spot where all of the elements were there? NEUMAN: Yeah, well, Loudoun County, Virginia, is kind of the epicenter of the whole data center thing. It's the highest concentration of data centers in the world, really... ELLIOTT: Oh, OK. NEUMAN: ...About 250 that are already built. There are, you know, dozens actually that are still in the pipeline, and it's starting to be seen by the rest of the country as this, you know, canary in the coal mine kind of poster child for AI rampant - unchecked AI data center development. And so that was an obvious place to go. And I went to visit a data center there and talked to residents who lived near it, and it was like, well, OK, so what's the counter-example? I wanted to find a couple of different places that were sort of at different stages in the AI buildout. ELLIOTT: One of the people you spoke with was Darrell West, and he described what I think is a sentiment that we've been hearing more and more about with the rapid development. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT) DARRELL WEST: People just feel like they no longer have control over the technology. That worries them. They worry about the impact on their children. They see technology as an existential threat. ELLIOTT: You know, that powerless feeling and that fear is something that we have heard so much about in the last couple of weeks, especially with all these new warnings about where the technology is heading. How did that sentiment shape your approach to telling this story? NEUMAN: Yeah, I mean, I think it was more like a - it's a reflection of the way that people are thinking about this issue. So you've got, like, the, you know, ground-level - the NiMBY issue, the not in my backyard. It's very local and actually very powerful because people really care about their own communities and what's going on in their own communities. So there's that. I mean, people are concerned about, obviously, the things that we've heard about - the huge power consumption, power draw that these data centers have, the water that they are using for cooling - and actually, in some cases, the noise, which was an issue in Sterling. But you've got that kind of level, and then you've got this other level, which is - I think the two are kind of dovetailing. They're kind of coming together, which is, you know, this - again, this, like, existential dread about AI. Is it going to take our jobs? Is it going to kill us? You know, either of those things is true or not, they're definitely starting to contribute to the way people are thinking about this issue. So it's not only, I don't want a data center in my backyard, but is AI... ELLIOTT: Good for me, right? NEUMAN: Is AI good for me? Right. But, you know, one interesting thing - I made a point of asking everybody I talked to - like, the most ardent - people who are the most ardent about opposition to data centers, do you personally use AI? I mean, of course, we all do when we're Googling or whatever. That comes up automatically. But make a point of, like, using a chatbot, like ChatGPT, for example. ELLIOTT: And?
