artigo.texto: Sterling does not have a code or ordinance allowing or forbidding data centers or battery energy storage systems from locating within the city limits. “We can’t simply say no,” Tim Zollinger, Sterling city attorney, told the Sterling Plan Commission at its Thursday meeting. That meeting was the first one following the City Council’s unanimous vote at its Sept. 7 meeting to impose a 180-day application moratorium on processing and approving applications for data centers and battery energy storage systems. “We don’t have any code that says you can have either of those entities in the city,” said Dustin Wolff, city planner. Wolff said the city has been receiving requests from battery energy storage system companies but has not received any requests from data center developers wanting to locate within city limits. Why the city needs codes and ordinances to set out rules and regulations for data centers and BESS, and why the City Council cannot issue an overall ban on those specific facilities, was one of the main topics of discussion for the commission. “We need to have those rules because, as a non-home-rule municipality, the City of Sterling does not have the authority to completely ban what is a lawful business. Within the state of Illinois right now, a data center is a lawful business. We can’t simply ban something permanently. We can have a moratorium but we cannot permanently ban something,” Zollinger said. “I just don’t understand why, if you don’t want it in your community, why you can’t deny, say, ‘You can’t come here,’” one of the audience members said during a public comment period in the meeting. The state of Illinois, based on court decisions from the 1970s and 1980s, does not allow communities to ban specific businesses or industries. Those court cases stemmed from the adult entertainment industry. “Years ago, communities wanted to get rid of all types of adult entertainment. Those businesses went to court and said you can’t completely zone us out of the town. We are a lawful business permitted by state law, you can’t say we can’t be anywhere in your community,” Zollinger said. When courts ruled in favor of those businesses, communities turned to zoning and regulation to control what businesses and industries could locate within their city limits. “Those cases developed and the courts said, ‘Correct, if you are a lawful business permitted to operate, the city can zone it, the city can adopt rules to regulate it but you can’t completely ban it,’” Zollinger said. At a ribbon cutting in Monee on Thursday, Gov. J.B. Pritzker said he does not have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on data centers on his own. Pritzker said he hopes that the state legislature will take up the POWER (Protecting Our Water, Energy and Ratepayers) Act during the legislative veto session after the November elections. The POWER Act was introduced in the spring session as Senate Bill 4016 and House Bill 5513. The bill requires data centers to pay for their own infrastructure connection costs, source clean energy for their electric service, and imposes water use guidelines. The bill stalled before the May 31 legislative deadline. On June 1, Pritzker ordered the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to halt tax incentives for data centers, effective July 1, 2026. Unless the state takes further action to limit or ban data centers and BESS facilities, communities like Sterling will have to address data centers and BESS facilities through their own ordinances and zoning codes specifically addressing those businesses. “The goal here is to say where is the balance that the community is comfortable with, we know we can’t say no. So where do you balance that with if you want to come here, if you want to be in Sterling, these are the rules you have to play with. You have to play by these rules to locate here. It’s going to be this setback, it’s going to be this fire rating, suppression system, it’s going to be this zoning district, it’s going to be this noise level or lower. You adopt the rules that you are comfortable with and balancing that with still permitting a form of that business operating if they want to play by those rules,” Zollinger said. If the city cannot develop an ordinance and rules within the 180-day moratorium, that moratorium can be extended, but it cannot be extended indefinitely. In answer to a question from the audience, Zollinger said a company could sue the city for delaying its decision via repeated or indefinite moratoriums on an application to locate a BESS facility or data center. “I would rather that the council and the city be proactive in saying we want to make sure we can address this. Better to be proactive and address it than be reactive,” Zollinger said. The Plan Commission will next meet at 6:30 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 22.

artigo.texto: NH Investment & Securities will team up with Trinity Airline to cooperate on carbon finance spanning the supply of credits under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and brokerage trading of domestic greenhouse gas emissions permits. NH Investment & Securities said on Sept. 28 it signed a memorandum of understanding with Trinity Airline on Sept. 21 for mutual cooperation on CORSIA and the greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme. CORSIA is an international carbon offset scheme designed to manage carbon emissions from international flights. Airlines must secure eligible carbon credits to offset emissions that exceed a certain standard. Under the agreement, Trinity Airline will use NH Investment & Securities' expertise in carbon markets and financial capabilities to procure the credits needed to meet CORSIA requirements. NH Investment & Securities will support efforts such as managing procurement timing and costs by providing market analysis and trading services. The company said this is the first time a domestic securities firm and an airline have built a cooperative relationship covering both CORSIA credit supply and brokerage trading of domestic greenhouse gas emissions permits. The two companies will first procure 20,000 tons of CORSIA credits through NH Investment & Securities. Trinity Airline plans to secure in stages by the end of this year more than 10 percent of the volume of credits it must offset ahead of the first-phase settlement deadline in January 2028. The companies will also expand cooperation under the domestic greenhouse gas emissions trading scheme (K-ETS). NH Investment & Securities plans to support Trinity Airline's domestic carbon credit trading through its own brokerage trading system and provide related information such as market analysis and policy trends. The airline industry faces a situation where, as international carbon emissions regulations tighten, it must secure the necessary credits in a stable manner while managing procurement costs stemming from fluctuations in market prices. Park Geon-hoo (박건후), head of Client Solutions Division at NH Investment & Securities, said, "This agreement is meaningful in that it is a strategic cooperation model that connects a securities firm's expertise in carbon finance with an airline's demand for emissions permits." He added, "Based on the supply of CORSIA credits and brokerage trading of domestic emissions permits, we will expand tailored carbon finance services."

artigo.texto: Russia hit the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile service provider, on Sunday, the company told local media, as Moscow continued a bombardment of Ukrainian data centers and communications infrastructure. Kyivstar told Interfax Ukraine news agency that its head office in Kyiv had been hit, but there were no casualties. Russia's Defense Ministry also said on Sunday it hit a data center belonging to Vodafone Ukraine, the country's second-largest cell network provider. Vodafone Ukraine did not respond to a request for comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia struck a data center in Kyiv twice on Sunday morning, wounding two children and an adult. Moscow has also hit data centers belonging to Ukrainian internet providers over the past week, causing service outages to about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraine's Digital Ministry. "Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential — they save lives," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on Wednesday. artigo.texto: The Science Newswise — Battery materials called electrolytes allow ions (charged particles) to move from one end of a battery to the other. This process is necessary for charging and discharging. Superionic conductors (SICs) are materials that are solids, but some of their ions move like liquids. As a result, they conduct electricity very well. One SIC, lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride, is a promising type of solid-state battery material. Using neutron scattering and computer simulations, researchers gained a better understanding of this material’s atomic dynamics. By raising the material to more than 400 K (260 F), they put it in the superionic state where ions act like a liquid. In that state, the scientists found that lithium ions can hop quickly through the material’s crystal structure. The team also documented how specific types of vibrations in the crystal enable ions to jump through vibrating crystal bottlenecks. The scientists discovered that these vibrations enable long-range flow and significant improvements in conductivity. The Impact These findings show researchers how to improve ion flow inside a solid-state battery material, which would increase its performance. This information could enable a solid-state battery material that offers very high quantities of mobile ions as well as good chemical and thermal stability. This structure would enable a battery to use solid electrolytes that could perform as well as liquid ones. (Ions move more freely through liquid electrolytes than solid ones.) As such, this change could enable faster and safer battery charging. The ability to tailor SIC materials could also guide researchers in developing and improving other devices, such as fuel cells and computers. Summary One class of materials, superionic conductors (SICs), has the properties of both a crystalline and liquid electrolyte. When warmed above a specific temperature, the material remains partly crystalline, but also develops ion flow properties like those of liquids. This study combined machine-learning simulations with inelastic and quasielastic neutron scattering at the Spallation Neutron Source, a DOE Office of Science User Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The researchers investigated lithium-ion dynamics in the SIC lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride. The team found the crystalline framework facilitated fast, liquid-like hopping of lithium ions between stable crystalline lattice sites. Additionally, they documented significant enhancements in lithium-ion diffusion across a range of temperatures through the dynamic breathing (unified relaxation) of vibrating diffusion bottlenecks. They also observed how the vibrational spectra of mobile lithium ions in Li₆PS₅Cl evolve from a crystal-like to liquid-like phase. The research bridges conventional diffusive and lattice vibrational models. These findings offer important insights into the rapid ionic motion in SICs for potential use in solid electrolyte batteries, fuel cells, and computing systems. Funding The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation (DMREF project); the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Basic Energy Sciences, Division of Materials Sciences and Engineering; and the German Research Foundation. This work used resources at the Spallation Neutron Source and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, both DOE Office of Science User Facilities.

artigo.texto: O que a guerra na Ucrânia e a guerra no Irã têm em comum? Ataque de Kiev a um navio iraniano no mar Cáspio expõe uma rede densa de inteligência militar circulando entre os dois conflitos. Maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, a Kyivstar foi alvo de um ataque da Rússia no domingo (27), em meio a bombardeios lançados por Moscou contra a infraestrutura de telecomunicações do país vizinho. A ofensiva não resultou em vítimas, como informou a empresa à agência de notícias Interfax. Além do ataque à sede da prestadora em Kiev, um data center da Vodafone também teria sido atingido, como divulgado pelo Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. No entanto, a empresa que possui a segunda maior rede celular da região optou por não comentar o assunto. Ucranianos sem acesso à internet Os ataques do domingo, que também incluíram outro data center na capital ucraniana, ferindo um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky, não são casos isolados. Na última semana, os sistemas de comunicação do país sofreram diversos bombardeios. - Como relata a Reuters, centros de dados utilizados por operadoras locais estavam entre os principais alvos; - Em um dos casos, as explosões teriam interrompido a conectividade para cerca de 100 mil residências ao longo da semana; - Os clientes que ficaram sem acesso à internet residem principalmente em Kiev e cidades próximas, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia; - Autoridades do país disseram que os bombardeios afetaram sistemas críticos para a segurança, aumentando os riscos de mortes durante os ataques. “A Rússia tem como alvo importantes centros de dados ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais, eles salvam vidas”, afirmou Andrii Sybha, Ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, em mensagem compartilhada no X. Na rede social, ele também disse que alguns dos ataques russos incluem drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, uma nova variante da aeronave não tripulada. Essas versões se destacam pela capacidade de alcançar mais de 600 km/h de velocidade e operar em altitudes mais elevadas, dificultando as ações dos sistemas de defesa aérea. Um drone guiado por IA lançado pela Rússia matou três civis na Ucrânia no mês passado, em um dos primeiros ataques realizados por aeronaves autônomas. Relembre o caso. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE — The Janesville City Council on Monday voted unanimously to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers within the city. The southern Wisconsin city is just the latest community to put the brakes on the rush of data center developments across the country. The ordinance comes as residents are preparing for a November referendum that if approved, would allow voters a say in any future major developments in the city, including data centers. According to a staff memo accompanying the ordinance, the moratorium would pause the acceptance, processing, review and approval of any application related to the development of a data center, including rezoning of property, permits, action taken on annexation requests, or other development approvals. During the moratorium, city staff would not solicit or actively encourage data center development, nor enter nondisclosure agreements related to such development projects. The purpose of the moratorium is to allow sufficient time to research environmental, economic, health, safety and land-use compatibility impacts; continue preparation of zoning code review, processes, and specific development standards for data center projects. It also would allow time for city staff to complete and the council to consider the Data Center Companion Ordinance.

artigo.texto: Archbald will hold back-to-back public hearings this week to gather testimony as council weighs developers’ applications for a power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road and seven data centers at a quarry. Council will convene at 5 p.m. Tuesday to continue to hear testimony on the 400-megawatt Essential Energy LLC natural gas power plant proposed near Staback Park and across from the same developer’s Project Boson data center. Then, the borough will hold a hearing Wednesday at 5 p.m. on Project Green Mountain’s proposal to build a data center campus across nearly 271 acres at the Stavola Quarry off the Casey Highway. Essential Energy Power plant representatives faced criticism and pushback during five preceding hearings over the conceptual nature of their plans as council considers Essential Energy’s March 12 application for a natural gas power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road. The debate over how much information is enough to satisfy Archbald’s zoning requirements has prevailed across data center and power plant hearings in the borough this year. Residents advocate for specific information during the hearings, while developers argue they can’t refine their plans until after they have approval. Developers’ representatives contend that permitting and regulations from agencies such as the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will protect the community. Archbald has held hearings on Essential Energy’s plans April 27, May 21, June 22, July 21 and Aug. 18. The most recent hearing concluded with testimony from Andrew Markle, the technical lead of power generation for KCI Technologies of Mechanicsburg, which is the engineering firm representing Essential Energy. Markle spoke broadly about the operations and safety features designed into power plants, touting his experience overseeing power plant development both domestically and abroad. The hearing concluded before cross-examination, so Tuesday’s hearing will likely open with questions posed to Markle. Cross-examiners include attorney Justin Richards of Elliott Greenleaf PC in Wilkes-Barre, who represents Archbald residents opposing data centers; Stop Archbald Data Centers co-founder Tamara Misewicz-Healey; Highlands Archbald residents Karen Timmons and Meg Nudelman; Valley View School District Solicitor Kyle Callejas; and Archbald’s special counsel, attorney Brett C. Flower of Eckert Seamans in Harrisburg. Project Green Mountain Representatives for Project Green Mountain will return to Archbald on Wednesday after a three-month hiatus. Green Mountain 6 LLC, using a Pittsburgh law firm as its address, filed a conditional-use application Jan. 26, making Project Green Mountain Archbald’s sixth proposed data center project, with plans for seven two-story data centers, each 65 feet tall with 138,000-square-foot footprints. Project Green Mountain’s data centers would span an L-shaped campus at the Stavola Quarry. It is the only application so far in Archbald that sites data centers opposite the Casey Highway away from residential development. The data centers would use a projected 525 megawatts of electricity, divided into 75 megawatts per building, while using up to 14,000 gallons of water daily from Pennsylvania American Water for domestic uses like sinks and toilets. During an outage, Green Mountain would use 196 backup diesel generators, each storing up to 10,000 gallons of diesel fuel, totaling 1.96 million gallons stored on site. Project Green Mountain’s initial hearing March 19 largely discussed the campus’s utility demands and potential economic incentives. On May 11, it focused on air emissions from backup generators, as well as traffic from the data centers. The June 18 hearing focused on the noise of data centers and their generators. Though Project Green Mountain’s sound study found that the campus would remain below Archbald’s 55-decibel residential daytime limit, even with all 196 backup generators running, it was heavily scrutinized in cross-examination During the latest hearing, Project Green Mountain attorney Jeffrey Wilhelm of Reed Smith LLP in Pittsburgh responded to a question from Councilwoman Lisa Osborne asking if the developer had finished any other data center campuses with a post-construction sound study to give the borough additional insight. Wilhelm told Osborne they would come back with an answer to her question at another hearing. Both hearings will be at the Valley View High School auditorium, 1 Columbus Drive, Archbald. Borough Solicitor Jay O’Connor announced the Essential Energy hearing at the conclusion of the last hearing on the power plant in August, and the borough announced the Project Green Mountain hearing via a public notice published Sept. 15 in The Times-Tribune. Both Essential Energy, which is tied to Archbald-based Kriger Construction Inc. and its executive leadership, and Project Green Mountain seek conditional-use approval from Archbald council, which requires the developers to testify at public hearings to explain how their projects abide by the borough’s zoning regulations for data centers and power plants. Other companies tied to Kriger and its leadership also proposed four data centers and three power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City. Affected residents who received party status and their attorney, borough officials and the Valley View School District’s solicitor all have the opportunity to cross-examine each witness presented by the developers. Once they conclude their testimony, any of the opposing parties can then present their own evidence. Council will accept public comment prior to voting, though it is unclear exactly when any decisions will occur. There are currently 51 data centers formally proposed in the borough across half a dozen projects, although two other data center developers look to expand in Archbald around the Valley View Business Park. artigo.texto: HSBC maintains bearish stance on Ola Electric despite battery manufacturing gains While acknowledging the electric vehicle maker's progress in cell localisation and gigafactory capacity, the brokerage cited weak financial performance and balance sheet concerns in maintaining a reduce rating. Global brokerage HSBC has maintained a bearish Reduce rating on Ola Electric Mobility Ltd., setting a target price that implies a nearly 38 per cent downside, despite acknowledging significant operational progress in the company's battery manufacturing and localisation efforts. The divergence between Ola Electric's technological advancements and its financial realities was laid bare in a recent brokerage note following visits to the company's manufacturing facilities. While HSBC praised the electric two-wheeler maker's vertical integration and proprietary cell technology, it cited weaker-than-expected recent financial performance and low confidence in management's near-term estimates as primary drivers of its cautious stance. Gigafactory milestones and technological optimism HSBC analysts recently conducted site visits to Ola Electric's Gigafactory and its future electric vehicle assembly plant. The brokerage noted that the Gigafactory's capacity has successfully reached 6 gigawatt-hours (GWh), a critical milestone in the company's strategy to reduce reliance on imported battery cells. The firm expects the facility's manufacturing yields to improve to approximately 90 per cent from the current 70 per cent over the next six to nine months. The brokerage specifically highlighted Ola's development of the 4680 cell utilizing proprietary dry-cathode technology. Management asserts that this innovation can reduce operating costs by 20 to 30 per cent compared to traditional wet-cathode processing. Furthermore, HSBC observed that the future factory reflects a high degree of automation and vertical integration, which supports management's claims of achieving better operating margins in the long term. On the retail front, the company is aggressively expanding its footprint. Ola Electric's dealer network is projected to jump from 30 to approximately 150 outlets by the Navratri festival, a crucial sales period for the Indian automotive sector. Notably, HSBC does not currently view the company's unsold inventory levels as a red flag, attributing them to the transitional phase of new product rollouts. Balance sheet realities and market reaction Despite the operational positives, HSBC's financial modeling remains deeply conservative. The brokerage set a target price of Rs 24 per share, implying a steep 37.6 per cent downside from recent closing levels. This bearish valuation reflects the firm's pricing of weaker-than-expected performance metrics and a fundamental lack of confidence in the company's aggressive forward estimates. The market reacted swiftly to the brokerage's assessment. Ola Electric's stock took a significant hit in Monday trade, falling as much as 3.5 per cent to Rs 36.53. This decline notably outperformed the broader market downturn, with the benchmark Nifty index falling 0.86 per cent and the overall auto sector slipping 0.7 per cent. The company's first-quarter results for the current fiscal year reflect the ongoing transition following a major operational reset undertaken previously. While the consolidated net loss narrowed to Rs 336 crore, revenue from operations fell sharply by 45 per cent year-on-year to Rs 455 crore. Management described the quarter as the first full period reflecting its restructuring efforts, emphasizing a sequential recovery in the automotive business. The road to operational restructuring For Ola Electric, the immediate challenge lies in reconciling its heavy capital expenditure on localisation with the need for near-term revenue growth. The company's diversification attempts beyond China for equipment sourcing and its focus on higher energy density cells are viewed positively as long-term strategic moats. However, rebuilding brand image and ensuring consistent delivery commitments remain key monitorables for investors. The broader electric two-wheeler sector in India is also navigating a period of moderated growth. Slower penetration rates and intense competition from legacy automakers and emerging startups have forced companies to prioritize unit economics over sheer volume accumulation. Until Ola Electric can demonstrate that its battery manufacturing prowess translates into sustained market share and improved cash flows, brokerages like HSBC remain cautious, advising investors to weigh the promise of vertical integration against the immediate realities of the balance sheet. artigo.texto: ANEEL vai votar regra que beneficia acesso à energia pelos data centers O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, propôs uma regra de transição na Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) para atender cargas como data centers. O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, propôs uma regra de transição na Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) para atender cargas como data centers. A proposta teria alcance até 2029 e beneficiaria os centros de processamento de dados que têm implementação por etapas, o que levaria ao aumento do consumo de energia nos próximos anos. Conforme voto-vista apresentado nesta quinta-feira (24), o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) deverá priorizar, no acesso ao sistema de transmissão de energia, os empreendimentos que já tinham parecer positivo de viabilidade técnica emitido antes das novas regras, que começaram a valer em dezembro de 2025. Sandoval argumenta que o decreto que criou a Pnast, ao ter vigência imediata, impediu a “adoção de providências prévias” por consumidores como data centers, que têm previsão de acesso escalonada à carga. Ou seja, aqueles que já tinham acesso ao sistema e estavam aumentando o seu montante de uso de energia ano a ano teriam sido prejudicados pela criação da política, que substituiu a análise dos pedidos de forma cronológica pelas Temporadas de Acesso. O processo era relatado pelo ex-diretor Fernando Mosna, que apresentou voto em julho deste ano, quando Sandoval pediu vista. O assunto está na pauta do circuito deliberativo da ANEEL, marcado para terça-feira (29). Se aprovado, será iniciada consulta pública de 45 dias. *Com informações da Agência Infra

artigo.texto: AURORA | Monday’s Aurora City Council meeting featured three hours of public comment opposing what would be Colorado’s largest data center. Around 100 residents of The Reserve, a local senior housing community, and the surrounding Windler and Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods attended the meeting to voice their concerns and disagreement with the planned Trident data center, located at 23001 East 48th Ave in northeast Aurora. Before public comment started, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked the audience to stand if they opposed the data center and nearly every attendee stood. No one stood in support of the data center. Speakers, who ranged in age from 16 to 86, were emphatic in their requests for council to impose regulations on data centers, including residential buffers, and require the Trident data center to have more safeguards for health and the environment. Dan Bergander, a resident of The Reserve, highlighted the potential health and quality of life impacts the data center will have on older and disabled neighbors. As he spoke, 50 or more people in the audience stood to support him while he spoke and then burst into applause when he finished. “I’m here speaking for the other at-risk neighbors in the audience and at home, and surprisingly enough, I’m also speaking for your future,” Bergander said. “You on city council will one day settle into retirement and I certainly hope you’re not betrayed by developers and government officials.” When the comments reached the typical hour limit, council voted 9-1 to hear all of the speakers who signed up, with Council member Curtis Gardner opposed. Other than some council members thanking the public for attending, the council did not respond to the wave of comments or address the Trident project at Monday’s meeting. Council did unanimously approve a ban on evaporative cooling, which is a more water intensive cooling system used by some data centers. Planning documents show the Trident data center will be around 860,000 square feet and located in Airport District zoning, which allows data centers as a use by right, which means the project can be approved administratively by the city without a public hearing, unless the project is requesting a variance. While Trident is not requesting a variance, city spokesperson Jennifer Soules said the city is working with the developer, Vantage Data Centers, to schedule a community meeting, but a date has not yet been set. A development application and site plan for the data center were first submitted in August 2025 and the project is on its third round of reviews, according to the city. Neighborhood opposition has grown swiftly, with a local town hall on Sept. 22 drawing about 150 people, while a Change.org petition against the project has more than 2,500 signatures. Ray Czaplewski, a resident of The Reserve whose home will be about a quarter-mile from the data center, said he found out about the project just two weeks ago from his neighbors. Czaplewski described feeling appalled and betrayed when he found out about the data center. “We were blindsided by it,” he said. “Never in our wildest dreams would we expect our city government to be complacent with putting in a hyperscale data center literally right next to residential areas.” Czaplewski said he has a lot of unanswered questions and he raised concerns about noise, air pollution and the toll of the facility on water and energy resources. He also disapproves of the city’s development process allowing data centers without public hearings or notification. “The use by right categorization in the airport district is designed to be opaque,” Czaplewski said. “If we had known a year ago and knew the magnitude of this, we could have started working with Vantage.” Czaplewski and other residents want the city to require a fourth review period to ensure all of the concerns are mitigated. Should they not be addressed, the group is considering legal action for possible damages to health and property values, Czaplewski said. Vantage’s Misty Allen, vice president of public policy for North America, said the company is planning more community outreach as the project moves into construction, including neighborhood meetings and a public website where construction updates will be shared. “It’s perfectly reasonable when people have questions of new developments coming into their community and it’s our commitment that we will be having open community conversations as the design for the project moves forward,” Allen said. “All of that engagement will start to kick off as the project moves forward, so we’re just at the beginning of this.” Allen said the meetings will include subject matter experts to answer questions and connect residents to company representatives. “We’re going to be here for the long-term, so it’s important for folks to get to know the new neighbor in town and to make sure that we have that relationship,” Allen said. In response to concerns from the community, Allen said the facility will have setbacks which will provide at least a 350-foot buffer from homes, as well as a brick wall and water-wise landscaping surrounding the property. Aurora also restricts the noise level at data centers to the same level as other businesses, with different allowances based on zoning and time. The data center is expected to use 334 megawatts of energy for computing capacity, which would be more than twice the state’s current largest data center — the 160 megawatt QTS facility, also in Aurora. artigo.texto: ERS Energy Sdn Bhd has surpassed 1.5 GWh of cumulative utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity across Southeast Asia, with the company securing the majority of its portfolio over the past 12 months. The milestone includes a 520 MWh BESS project for ACEN in Zambales, Philippines, which ERS Energy described as a landmark project. The company has also secured two utility-scale projects under Malaysia’s inaugural Battery Energy Storage Programme (MyBeST), with the projects having a combined capacity of 800 MWh. ERS Energy said the latest project wins build on its expansion across strategic markets in Southeast Asia. The company combines project structuring, financing frameworks and energy storage system integration capabilities as part of its utility-scale BESS business. The company has expanded from its earlier focus as a solar engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) specialist into utility-scale energy storage development and system integration. Its growing BESS portfolio is aimed at supporting grid stability and addressing the intermittency associated with renewable energy generation. Jonathan Kan, Managing Director of ERS Energy, said the company’s 1.5 GWh milestone reflects its execution capabilities and the confidence of its partners, lenders and regional grid operators. ERS Energy said renewable energy expansion across Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Australia is increasing the need for grid flexibility and energy storage. The company’s BESS portfolio is intended to provide grid services and support the deployment of renewable energy across the region. The company said it works with technology partners and financial institutions to support utility-scale storage projects from design and project financing through to grid synchronisation. artigo.texto: Vena Energy has announced that its NRE Nakagawa 2 Battery Storage Project, with an awarded capacity of 46.828 MW, has been selected under Japan’s FY2025 Long-Term Decarbonised Power Source Auction (LTDA) conducted by the Organisation for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO). The battery storage project is currently under development in Japan and is designed as a grid-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) near Matsumoto City in Nagano Prefecture. The LTDA scheme was introduced in fiscal year 2023 to support Japan’s target of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The programme provides long-term revenue certainty for selected decarbonised power projects, supporting investment and helping developers recover development and capital costs. The selection of the NRE Nakagawa 2 project expands Vena Energy’s battery storage portfolio in Japan. It follows the commencement of commercial operations at the company’s Hikone Battery Storage Project in 2025. According to Vena Energy, battery storage deployment is expected to play a role in managing the intermittency of renewable generation and improving the efficient utilisation of electricity as Japan increases its reliance on decarbonised power sources. Raul Rienda, Head of Japan at Vena Energy, said the selection of the project under the FY2025 LTDA would support efforts to strengthen the reliability and resilience of Japan’s power system. Vena Energy said it will continue to engage with local communities and consider environmental factors as it advances the NRE Nakagawa 2 project. The company is developing the project as part of its broader focus on battery storage and renewable energy infrastructure in Japan, supporting the country’s long-term decarbonisation objectives. artigo.texto: BYD says a long-awaited upgrade to electric vehicle batteries is finally getting close to real-world use. The world's largest EV maker is preparing to take solid-state technology out of the lab and put it into vehicles people can actually drive. BYD's Solid-State Battery For EV Is Nearly Ready BYD's executive vice president Stella Li said the company sits in the leading position in the solid-state battery race, with plans to introduce its first EV powered by the new technology in 2027. The company has been researching solid-state batteries since 2013, and by 2023 it had shown that mass production was feasible. Testing of prototype cells rated at 20 and 60 ampere-hours followed throughout 2024, laying the groundwork for the move from lab proof to commercial manufacturing. The batteries rely on sulfide-based electrolytes, which offer higher conductivity and better safety than the liquid setups found in most EVs today. BYD's battery business, FinDreams, aims to begin producing them in limited batches in 2027 before ramping up toward mass production by 2030 (via CarNewsChina). BYD Solid-State EV Battery For Open Roads The first vehicles to get the technology will likely come from BYD's premium brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fangchengbao, before it trickles down to higher volume models. According to Engadget, the first two years are expected to serve as a demonstration phase with limited production. Early estimates suggest cars using these batteries could reach roughly 800 kilometers, or nearly 500 miles, on a single charge, with some observers speculating the range could eventually pass 1,000 kilometers. Reports point to energy density targets of up to 400 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with roughly 160 to 180 for BYD's current lithium iron phosphate batteries and around 300 for the best nickel manganese cobalt cells. Charging times as short as 12 minutes have also been mentioned in early projections. Other Brands Have Been Working on the Tech BYD is not alone in chasing the technology. Chery has said its prototypes reach 400 watt-hours per kilogram and aims to push that to 500, while Toyota, Honda, and Mercedes Benz are also developing their own solid-state solutions. Even so, BYD executives describe the company as out in front, and its CTO has said scaled production could eventually bring solid-state costs down to parity with conventional liquid electrolyte batteries. BYD expects the technology to reach more affordable models between 2030 and 2032 as production costs come down. The company also does not see its Blade batteries, built on lithium iron phosphate, disappearing anytime soon, with its chief scientist projecting they will stay important for budget-friendly EVs for the next 15 to 20 years. Why Are Solid-State Batteries a Big Deal? Most EVs today run on lithium-ion batteries, where charged particles called ions move through a liquid medium. Solid-state batteries swap that liquid for a solid layer, which improves safety because EV batteries are known for catching fire, and the flammable liquid inside conventional cells is often part of the problem. A solid electrolyte offers better thermal stability, lowering the risk of fires and leaks. Solid-state cells also pack more energy into the same space, which means longer range and more compact battery packs. Sulfide electrolytes in particular are described as longer-lasting and more stable than liquid options, giving the batteries a more durable life and faster charging. The technology is difficult to build, since ions move through liquids more easily than solids and gaps between solid layers can raise electrical resistance.

artigo.texto: Handwritten on pieces of cut-up poster paper, Amy Wright made her case that members of her city council have allegedly voted on issues they had a financial stake in and violated open meetings laws along the way. Tensions are ratcheting up in Carroll County, where two different data center developers are planning hyperscale projects in the rural community of 11,000 people. One project in particular, pitched by Louisville-based Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, has drawn the ire of local residents after the project went public a year after Carrollton city officials signed land deals with the company. Now, community members, including Wright, are filing ethics complaints saying several members of the city council who voted to move forward with that secret land deal should have abstained from the vote because they or an immediate family member works for Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, which stands to profit from the energy-intensive data center. KPR obtained financial disclosures filed by each city council member via open records request — they are sparse, but at least two members noted LG&E-KU as a source of income for themselves or their spouse. Multiple Kentucky communities have been divided over hyperscale data center concerns, with opponents accusing officials of not keeping the community’s best interests in mind. Poe and PowerHouse are building a center in Louisville, where anti-data center activists have filed numerous complaints, including with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Office of Civil Rights. In Mercer County, activists uncovered emails showing an LG&E-KU employee in public office pushing other officials to support a controversial data center project. Proponents of data centers argue they would pay huge dividends to local governments through taxes to fund better schools, roads and more. The Carroll County Ethics Commission heard one set of complaints on Sept. 17 — several anti-data center activists and representatives of council members accused of violating the ethics code attended the hearing. After coming out of a lengthy closed discussion, Ethics Commission member Zach Spencer addressed the room of waiting community members. The commission voted to table the complaint over the financial conflicts, but moved forward with another complaint, and Spencer said they would open a formal investigation into “the alleged misconduct [and] required disclosure of withheld records.” “I want to air this out. I don’t want to keep coming back in for more and more complaints,” Spencer said. “I want everything. I want it out in the open.” Community concerns to be aired out Two days before the county ethics commissions met, the Carrollton City Council was scheduled to start the process of opting-out of those very ethics rules and “create its own ethics commission.” According to multiple people present at that public meeting, Mayor Robb Adams decided not to move forward with the reading and did not explain why it was on the agenda. Anastasia Coots, who lives in Carrollton and has previously clashed with Adams during her stint on the city’s Planning and Zoning Board, said she believes the council has violated multiple state and local ethics laws. “This is so much bigger than just a data center,” Coots said. “All of those people that voted and the mayor and the Carrollton Utilities Commission are beholden to the actual city to do anything in the best financial interest of the city, so when they went into executive session and signed an [agreement] with Poe, it actually only benefited Poe.” She has submitted complaints to various law enforcement agencies, including the commonwealth attorney’s office. She and Wright allege that multiple members of the Carrollton City Council have conflicts with LG&E-KU — they say one is a current employee, one is retired with a KU pension, and another has a son working with KU. Another council member’s husband got a job with the company after voting in favor of the land deal. Kentucky Public Radio asked for comment from the council’s lawyer, each council member allegedly tied to KU, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a statement to KPR, LG&E-KU spokesperson Drew Gardner said the company has not reviewed the complaint. He said the company “has an obligation” to serve businesses seeking to locate in the area and have established procedures for doing so. “This project is no exception, and a connection to LG&E and KU gives no one special standing in that process,” Gardner said. “Because the review is ongoing, we won’t speculate about the allegations.” The Carroll County code of ethics specifically calls on officers with a prohibited financial interest to submit the “precise nature and value of the interest, in writing.” The code says that officers are prohibited from participating in public duties that present a “substantial conflict” to the business interests of themselves or “any immediate family member.” “The officer or employee shall refrain from taking any action with respect to the matter that is the subject of the disclosure,” the ethics code reads. As Wright showed me her handwritten complaints in the Carrollton Public Library, she explained that she isn’t trying to wage war against the city council, but she also doesn’t want this data center coming to her community. She said she’s glad the ethics commission is taking her complaints seriously and is interested in a “fair and impartial review.” “I'm glad that they're willing to just take a step back, look at all of the facts together, and make a determination on it,” Wright said. The ethics commission’s chair recused himself from the committee hearing — he too is a retired employee of KU. Spencer, who took his place to lead the meeting, read a lengthy open records request he was making to the city. It’s the start of the group's investigation into how the council came to enter a contract with Poe to sell hundreds of acres of land, near residential proper

artigo.texto: The next generation of data centers is changing more than how much electricity utilities must supply. It is also changing the speed, concentration and uncertainty of load growth. This demand is arriving amid transmission constraints, lengthy interconnection timelines and competition for grid capacity. Artificial intelligence is creating large, power-dense loads while also giving utilities tools to automate studies, analyze data and plan faster. That dual role was central to Siemens Grid Software’s webinar, Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness, featuring experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy. Utilities need more infrastructure, but also smarter, faster and more collaborative planning. AI factories are changing the scale of demand Traditional data centers hosted enterprise applications and delivered computing and storage services. AI factories create value through model training and inference. As AI advances toward reasoning models and physical AI systems, its computing and electricity requirements are rising dramatically According to NVIDIA’s webinar remarks, traditional data center racks typically consume 15 to 25 kilowatts. Current AI infrastructure can require approximately 230 kilowatts per rack, while future systems could approach one megawatt per rack. For utilities, this is not incremental growth. Large loads may cluster geographically and seek service much faster than generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure can be planned, permitted and built. The grid is part of the AI technology stack As NVIDIA observed during the webinar, energy has become part of the AI technology stack. AI cannot operate without reliable electricity, making power availability a strategic factor in where AI infrastructure is developed. Utilities, regulators, system operators, developers, technology providers and customers must coordinate earlier on project certainty, ramp schedules, location, reliability and potential load flexibility. Dominion Energy’s Northern Virginia experience reinforced that integrating large loads is not solely a utility challenge. Stakeholders must align timelines and assumptions early. Planning must account for uncertainty Deterministic forecasts alone become less effective when planners face many possible futures. An AI facility may be delayed, resized, relocated, or phased. Its load profile may change as technology evolves, while renewable output, electrification, distributed resources and transmission constraints add variables. Utilities should complement deterministic studies with scenario-based and probabilistic planning. Key considerations include project probability and timing, load ramp rates, hourly and seasonal demand, generation and transmission availability, storage performance, flexible-load participation, behind-the-meter resources and permitting timelines. The goal is not to predict one future perfectly, but to identify decisions that remain sound across many futures. Flexibility could change the equation Some AI workloads may be more flexible than commonly assumed. Certain training processes could be shifted, throttled, or scheduled for different times or locations, although inference and other time-sensitive applications may have strict availability requirements. Even partial flexibility could reduce stress during constrained periods, improve use of existing assets and potentially defer selected investments. Options include workload scheduling, demand response, battery storage and phased energization. Utilities cannot assume flexibility. They need dependable information about which workloads can move, response speed, duration and operational limits. Behind-the-meter generation may accelerate projects, but it raises fuel, permitting, reliability, market and economic questions. AI can help utilities plan for AI Planning teams are evaluating more interconnection requests, operating conditions and investment scenarios, often without equivalent growth in engineering resources. Automation and AI-enabled workflows can expand analytical capacity by handling repeatable tasks, supporting data analysis and helping planners focus on higher-value engineering decisions. Faster simulation, improved data integration and interoperable platforms can shorten study cycles and create a consistent view of assumptions and results. Combined with probabilistic methods, AI can expand scenario analysis without compromising engineering rigor. The objective is not to replace engineers, but to give them the speed, scale and information to plan across more possible futures. Preparing for the AI factory era Utilities must preserve reliability, safety and affordability while becoming more agile and growth-oriented. Physical reinforcement will remain necessary, but building alone is not enough. Utilities must also use existing capacity more effectively, improve data quality, automate repeatable work and evaluate uncertainty systematically. AI factories make the urgency visible, but the implications extend beyond data centers. Electrification, renewable integration and distributed resources are increasing grid complexity. AI is creating part of the challenge, but it can also be part of the solution. Utilities that recognize both sides will be better positioned to support economic growth while maintaining reliable, resilient and affordable service. Watch Planning the grid at the speed of AI: From interconnection queues to grid readiness on demand to hear experts from Siemens, NVIDIA and Dominion Energy discuss how utilities can prepare for AI-driven load growth.

artigo.texto: Sungrow has announced the successful grid connection and completion of full acceptance testing for the Cambodia EDC Kandal Stueng station (GS79), a 108.4 MW/215.6 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Takmao, Kandal Province. The project deploys grid-forming technology at utility scale and is designed to support grid stability, black-start capability, and coordination with hydroelectric and thermal generation. The facility is located at a key point in Cambodia’s central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. During system-restoration testing, 516 grid-forming power conversion system (PCS) units successfully energized the entire BESS plant from zero voltage while establishing stable voltage and frequency. The system also supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations as the network was progressively restored. As part of the testing, the BESS supported the startup and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant. The restored network was subsequently operated with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, the energy storage system, and connected loads. The project remained stable during five transformer energization events, including one involving a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stable operation while synchronizing different power sources with a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees. The BESS demonstrated extended islanded operation for 3.5 hours, allowing it to continue supporting the local network while separated from the main grid. The project also completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded modes, with voltage deviation maintained below 2% and transient frequency fluctuations within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. Sungrow said the project was delivered under strict testing requirements, a compressed construction schedule, and rainy-season conditions with ambient temperatures reaching 40°C. The commissioning and testing activities were completed within 20 days. The project team carried out hot commissioning and three rounds of performance testing during the commissioning period to support timely grid connection. Sungrow provided services covering storage and monitoring system design, equipment design, commissioning, EPC-related support, and operations and maintenance. The company said the integrated approach was intended to address the project’s grid-level requirements across design, delivery, and operation. The project adds a large-scale grid-forming BESS installation to Cambodia’s power system and demonstrates the use of energy storage for grid restoration, islanded operation, and coordination with multiple generation sources. artigo.texto: [DigitalToday Seung-ah Yoo, intern reporter] Hyundai Motor Group reaffirmed its position that it will continue pushing ahead with the development of all-solid-state batteries. From startups to major automakers, companies are continuing to invest in all-solid-state batteries, touted as a “dream technology” to deliver ultra-fast charging and longer driving range for electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, the performance of conventional lithium-ion batteries is improving quickly. Geely’s latest battery technology takes less than 9 minutes to charge from 10 percent to 97 percent. Even so, is there still a need to keep developing all-solid-state batteries? On Sept. 27 (local time), EV-focused outlet InsideEVs reported that Hyundai Motor Group R&D chief Manfred Harrer (만프레드 하러) gave a firm “yes” to that question. Harrer told reporters last week, “We cannot give up now. That is clear,” adding, “We must be part of this competition.” Current EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to move lithium ions between the cell’s anode and cathode. All-solid-state batteries, by contrast, mainly replace that liquid electrolyte with a solid material such as ceramics or polymers. This could raise both safety and performance. But no company has yet succeeded in producing solid-state cells at a scale suitable for automobiles. Harrer cited smaller batteries, improved fast-charging performance and longer driving range as potential advantages of all-solid-state batteries. He forecast that a symbolic vehicle produced in small volumes with an all-solid-state battery would appear within the next 5 years. QuantumScape is also aiming to apply all-solid-state batteries to high-performance vehicles by the late 2020s. Raw material costs are expected to remain very high for years as the technology scales up. Harrer said this would make it difficult for all-solid-state batteries to enter the mass market. “In the end, you can solve everything, but it costs money. It comes at an enormous cost,” he said. Hyundai is developing all-solid-state batteries in-house while also working with partners such as Solid Power. Harrer described all-solid-state batteries as “the industry’s big bet right now.” Toyota has been developing all-solid-state batteries for at least 20 years and is targeting mass production within the next few years. Volkswagen is making large-scale investments in QuantumScape, while BMW is working with Solid Power. General Motors, Ford, Honda and Nissan are also moving into all-solid-state battery development. Some companies have already unveiled demonstration prototypes. Examples include a Ducati equipped with QuantumScape cells and a Mercedes vehicle using Factorial’s technology. But there are still no cases of all-solid-state batteries being fitted in mass-produced vehicles that consumers can actually buy. Harrer’s goal is for Hyundai to enter the market with its own supply chain and manufacturing capabilities once the technology matures. “We want to be the owner of this key technology,” he said. “That is why we are also investing in our own battery manufacturing.” Harrer explained that it is important to deeply understand battery manufacturing methods and the associated costs. Batteries are the most expensive component in EVs and are also used in other electrified vehicles. Hyundai plans to apply its in-house nickel·manganese·cobalt (NCM) cells to the extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) version of the Tafe, which is scheduled to launch early next year. In a recent announcement, Hyundai said it plans to launch the Tafe EREV in the first half of 2027. All-solid-state batteries are expected to take considerable time before reaching the mass market. “I do not think we can solve the raw material cost issue within 5 years from now,” Harrer said.

artigo.texto: The Chinese company Gotion buys 49% of Volkswagen's battery plant in Sagunto The Chinese manufacturer will invest €1,100M and will have 49% of the gigafactory - CAT - CAST BarcelonaThe Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and the Chinese company Gotion High-Tech have agreed to "deepen their strategic alliance" through a joint venture for the development and operation of the battery cell gigafactory currently under construction in the town of Sagunto (Valencian Community). In this way, the Chinese manufacturer is investing some 1.1 billion euros to obtain 49% of the gigafactory. The battery plant in Sagunto, which should start operating this year, had planned an investment of about 3 billion euros, with aid from the Spanish government within the PERTE for the electric and connected car. This plant should supply batteries to the Seat plant in Martorell and the Volkswagen plant in Landaben (Navarre). The German consortium is already manufacturing electric cars at both plants: the Cupra Raval and the ID Polo in Martorell, and the ID Cross and the Skoda Epiq in Navarre. The planned collaboration between the Volkswagen Group and the Chinese company Gotion "enhances the plant's technological capabilities, which represents a new milestone in the industrial development of the project and strengthens its role within the growing European battery value chain," company sources told Europa Press. The agreement signed this Monday maintains PowerCo (Volkswagen Group) with a majority stake of 51% in the Sagunto gigafactory, which guarantees "continuity in the governance, strategic direction and operational oversight of the project." In addition, the investment commitments and employment targets –3,000 jobs– previously announced "remain unchanged". The same sources point out that as the European automotive industry moves towards electrification, the demand for LFP battery technology (lithium iron phosphate batteries) is expected to grow significantly. According to market forecasts, LFP batteries will be dominant and could represent between 40% and 65% of total demand in Europe by 2030, driven by their competitiveness, safety, durability and suitability for high-volume electric vehicle segments. Currently, practically all LFP cells used in Europe are manufactured in China. With the joint venture, Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion are turning the Sagunto project into a key piece to establish a competitive European production base for this strategically important technology with cells destined for the European market. Its long-term competitiveness is reinforced thanks to a larger scale, manufacturing experience and supply chain resilience. First phase commitments The joint venture has been designed to "strengthen the long-term viability and competitiveness of the Sagunto project, while preserving the strategic commitments already made". The investment of more than 2.3 billion euros already in execution and the creation of more than 1,500 direct jobs in the initial phase –which includes the first two production blocks– remain unchanged, thus consolidating the gigafactory's position as one of the most relevant industrial projects currently under development in Europe. Sagunto will begin operations with two production blocks and a combined annual capacity of up to 30 GWh in a first phase.

artigo.texto: Note: Welcome To RCBJ’s “Your Voices” Column, an occasional column prompted by readers’ commentary. If you have something to say, in a well-reasoned essay of 500 to 700 words, email the editor at ttraster@rcbizjournal.com Battery Storage Projects Are Good For The Economy, Good For Reducing Energy Bills, And Safe By Justin Wilcox New York’s energy policy must be measured by more than the ambitions it sets. It must also deliver electricity that households and businesses can afford, a grid that remains reliable and an economy capable of supporting future growth. That requires practical investments in the infrastructure needed to meet the state’s energy needs. Battery energy storage is one of those investments. For years, batteries have held the promise of storing electricity when it is abundant and returning it to the grid when it is needed. Without substantial energy storage, the renewable mandates established by the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act become more difficult and more expensive to integrate reliably. They can also supplement dispatchable resources and displace generation from some of the least efficient and highest-emitting plants during certain hours. That is a legitimate grid function, and one that should not be overlooked simply because battery storage cannot solve every challenge facing the electric system. Upstate United has consistently argued that New York needs a diversified energy resource mix. Existing natural gas generation will remain necessary for years to maintain reliability, and the state should support strategic investments in generation and fuel supply that can reduce costs and emissions. Battery storage should be understood as part of that same practical approach. Yet as battery projects move from planning documents to individual communities, their promise is increasingly colliding with the public’s safety concerns. There are valid safety considerations associated with virtually every form of energy infrastructure. Natural gas pipelines, nuclear power plants and fuel storage facilities must all be engineered and operated with safety as a fundamental guiding principle. Battery storage should be held to the same standard. That principle was behind the creation of New York’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group in 2023. Following several battery fires, the state brought together fire safety experts and agencies to examine incidents, inspect operating facilities and identify improvements to safety standards and emergency response. The working group inspected 57 large, operating battery storage projects. Those inspections produced important lessons about fire code requirements, inspection procedures and coordination with local emergency responders. Many of the group’s recommendations were subsequently incorporated into New York’s updated Fire Code, which took effect in January 2026. The updated requirements address matters including emergency response planning, inspections, fire department coordination and independent review of project safety. These are not substitutes for careful local oversight. They are tools that can help communities evaluate proposed facilities with greater confidence and ensure that safety remains central to the process. New York’s Public Service Commission has approved a target of 6 gigawatts of energy storage by 2030. Meeting that target will require more than setting a number in Albany. It will require the state to provide communities with the technical resources, clear standards and support necessary to make informed decisions about proposed projects. Local governments should retain their authority to review land use and evaluate the impacts of development. At the same time, legitimate concerns should be addressed through rigorous standards, transparent information and meaningful engagement, rather than allowing uncertainty to become an indefinite barrier to investment. New York cannot afford an energy policy that encourages new resources in principle, while making it increasingly difficult to build the infrastructure necessary to support them. Battery storage is not a silver bullet. But it can help diversify our resource mix, improve grid efficiency and support a more orderly transition to lower emissions. Policymakers must acknowledge that new technologies can raise legitimate safety concerns, just as existing energy technologies carry risks of their own. But the answer should be to manage those risks, not to turn away from the benefits. New York needs to evaluate these investments on their merits, insist on strong safety standards and build the infrastructure that can deliver measurable benefits. If we are serious about an affordable, reliable and lower-emissions energy future, battery storage must be part of the solution. Justin Wilcox is executive director of Upstate United, a coalition of businesses, organizations and community leaders working to strengthen Upstate New York’s economy, improve affordability and create opportunities for growth.

artigo.texto: NLC India, the Indian PSU which was earlier primarily involved into thermal energy generation company is steadily moving towards green energy. After boosting its solar and wind portfolio, the listed company is now working towards making renewable energy firmer by steadily increased its energy storage portfolio. However, unlike the private companies engaged in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), this company is working towards building an integrated storage portfoli-comprising both BESS as well as Pumped Hydro Storage (PSP) projects. As per the company’s FY2025-26 Integrated Annual Report, NLC India and its wholly owned subsidiary NLC India Renewables Ltd. (NIRL) have secured multiple energy-storage projects, with the company reporting a contracted storage pipeline of 3,300 MWh across three arrangements. The portfolio includes a 250 MW/500 MWh BESS project in Tamil Nadu, which has progressed to a signed power purchase agreement. NLC has also secured a Letter of Award for a 600 MW solar project coupled with a 300 MW/1,800 MWh BESS from the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), while another 500 MWh BESS project has been awarded by Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL). The company has subsequently won bids for a 50 MW/200 MWh BESS project from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. and a 275 MW BESS project from Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd, hintings towards its hunger for bet for more storage projects. First large-scale BESS project The 250 MW/500 MWh Tamil Nadu project represents NLC's first large-scale BESS deployment. NIRL secured the project from Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Ltd. (TNGECL) through tariff-based competitive bidding under the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. The Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA) was signed with Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Ltd., while the land lease agreement with TANTRANSCO was subsequently executed. The project is proposed to be financed by KfW Germany, and NLC has placed an order with Pace Digitek for the battery and other EPC activities. NLC says the project will enable renewable electricity to be stored and released when required by the grid, helping improve grid stability and increase the utilisation of clean power. Storage being integrated with new renewable capacity The company is increasingly combining storage with new renewable-generation projects rather than treating BESS as a standalone business. Its renewable project pipeline includes large-scale solar, wind-solar hybrid and battery-storage projects. NLC specifically identifies the 250 MW/500 MWh BESS project and the 600 MW solar project with 300 MW/1,800 MWh of battery storage as important steps towards firm renewable energy. This marks a shift in the company's renewable strategy from adding generation capacity alone towards combining generation with storage to improve the availability and flexibility of renewable electricity. NLC currently has 1,785 MW of operational renewable capacity and generated a record 2.26 billion units of renewable electricity in FY2025-26. It is targeting 10,110 MW of renewable capacity by 2030, with 5,810 MW of projects under implementation or active development. BESS alongside pumped storage NLC's storage strategy is not limited to batteries. The company is also pursuing pumped-storage projects, including two 50 MW projects in Neyveli mine voids, as well as larger projects at Palar-Porathalar in Tamil Nadu and Salandi in Odisha. The company says feasibility work has been prepared for the two 50 MW Neyveli projects, while the larger projects include a proposed 1,100 MW pumped-storage development at Palar-Porathalar and a 500 MW project at Salandi. This gives NLC two parallel storage pathways: battery systems for grid-scale short-duration storage and pumped hydro for larger, longer-duration applications. Renewable portfolio broadens NLC's expansion into storage comes alongside a significant increase in its solar and wind portfolio. During FY2025-26, the company commissioned its 300 MW Barsingsar Solar Project in Rajasthan and a 50 MW solar project at Neyveli. Its renewable pipeline also includes wind and wind-solar hybrid projects. NLC has secured a 450 MW ISTS-connected wind-solar hybrid project from NTPC and has been pursuing additional solar and wind projects through SECI, GUVNL, SJVN and other agencies. The company has therefore begun positioning storage as a component of a broader renewable portfolio rather than as a standalone diversification activity. Beyond generation The expansion into BESS is part of a wider diversification strategy at NLC. Alongside renewables and storage, the company is developing a 4 MW PEM electrolyser-based green hydrogen plant at Neyveli and has entered critical minerals, including blocks containing vanadium, titanium and aluminous laterite. For NLC, the emerging model is increasingly built around solar and wind generation, backed by BESS and pumped storage, with green hydrogen and critical minerals forming additional clean-energy businesses. The company has set aside ₹10,669 crore for diversification through 2030 and has received government approval for an additional ₹7,000 crore investment in NLC India Renewables Ltd. to accelerate its renewable ambitions.

artigo.texto: Aprovar uma resolução para implementar o Projeto de Centro de Dados e Gestão de Tráfego antes de 28 de setembro de 2026. O Gabinete do Governo emitiu o documento nº 498/TB-VPCP, datado de 25 de setembro de 2026, anunciando as conclusões do Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc na reunião de revisão do projeto de Resolução Governamental que promulga o Plano de implementação da Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, datada de 12 de junho de 2026, do Comitê do Partido Governamental, sobre a aplicação de mecanismos e políticas para implementar o Projeto de construção de um centro de dados para gerenciamento, monitoramento, tratamento de violações e operação de tráfego no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050. O comunicado declarava: Para acelerar o processo de transformação digital na garantia da ordem e segurança do trânsito, em 20 de março de 2026, o Primeiro-Ministro emitiu a Decisão nº 456/QD-TTg aprovando o Projeto de construção de um Centro de Dados para gerenciar, monitorar, lidar com infrações e operar o trânsito no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050 (o Projeto). Estas são tarefas importantes e urgentes que precisam ser implementadas rapidamente para contribuir com a modernização antecipada do monitoramento e gerenciamento de tráfego. Portanto, em 12 de junho de 2026, o Comitê do Partido do Governo emitiu a Resolução nº 05-NQ/DU, que determina a implementação de diversas soluções para a execução do Projeto. Ao longo do último período, o Ministério da Segurança Pública assumiu a liderança proativa e coordenou com ministérios, setores, localidades e unidades o desenvolvimento do plano do Governo para implementar a Resolução 05-NQ/DU; e coordenou com o Gabinete do Governo a implementação dos procedimentos de reporte ao Governo, em conformidade com o regulamento interno do Governo. Implementação das tarefas do Projeto de Garantia da Qualidade e Interconexão Síncrona Para agilizar a publicação do Plano de Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Pham Gia Tuc solicitou ao Ministério da Segurança Pública que coordenasse com o Gabinete do Governo a revisão e finalização da minuta da Resolução Governamental, e que a apresentasse ao Primeiro-Ministro para publicação antes de 28 de setembro de 2026. Durante a implementação do Projeto, o Ministério da Segurança Pública é o órgão permanente responsável, coordenando-se com ministérios, agências e localidades para definir cada item de trabalho, cada unidade responsável pela implementação e atribuir claramente cada tarefa a uma unidade específica, com a coordenação das agências relevantes; cada agência deve implementar proativamente as tarefas de acordo com a urgência do Projeto. Ministérios, setores e localidades devem implementar as tarefas do Projeto, garantindo o pleno cumprimento dos procedimentos e regulamentos legais para cada projeto de investimento, assegurando a qualidade, a sincronização e interconexão dos sistemas, a segurança, a eficiência e evitando a duplicação de tarefas; e prevenindo o desperdício e a corrupção. artigo.texto: Standalone battery storage now sits alongside community solar and agrivoltaics in the Illinois portfolio of Lightstar Renewables, a United States-based community solar and agrivoltaic developer. Storage widens the land the company can use, because a battery site needs far less room than solar and fits on smaller or less accessible parcels. On each site the owner keeps the land and collects a fixed lease payment for 20 years or longer. Lightstar handles the permits, the building and the running of it. Illinois gives that model room to grow. A 2026 state law sets new storage targets, and the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act lets projects up to 10 MW share a parcel. The company already has a footing there in the 2.75 MW AC US Highway 136 Solar Project in Fulton County. The same lease model sits behind its pipeline of more than 1,000 MW across 15 states. Lightstar expands Illinois pipeline across BESS and community solar Standalone BESS joins community solar and agrivoltaics in the Illinois program Lightstar Renewables runs on leased private land, anchored by a 2.75 MW project.
